title: Lease Provisions That Are Void Under Kansas Law
bodyText: Kansas law voids four categories of lease provision outright (K.S.A. 58-2547): a clause where either party waives rights or remedies under the Kansas Residential Landlord and Tenant Act; a confession-of-judgment clause; any provision requiring either party to pay the other's attorney's fees — unlike Colorado, which only requires attorney-fee clauses to be mutual, Kansas does not allow one at all, in either direction; and broad exculpation, liability-limitation, or indemnification language, except that a tenant may agree to limit the landlord's liability for fire, theft, or breakage specifically in common areas. If a landlord knowingly uses a lease containing a prohibited provision, the tenant can recover actual damages. Standing rule: check every clause in this library against this list before tagging it for a Kansas lease — this specifically rules out ever adding a mutual attorney-fee clause, or general liability/indemnification language, to a KS lease.

title: Security Deposit Amount Limits
bodyText: Kansas caps the security deposit at one month's rent for an unfurnished unit, up to 1.5 months' rent if you're renting it furnished with your own furniture, plus up to an additional half-month's rent if you allow pets (K.S.A. 58-2550(a)) — these stack, so a furnished, pet-friendly unit could allow up to 2 months' rent total. Since 2026 no Kansas city or county may set a lower limit: a 2026 act bars any local ordinance limiting the amount of a security deposit a landlord may require, and voids any adopted before July 1, 2026 (L. 2026, ch. 152, § 1(a)(3), (b)). This is a ceiling, not something the lease needs to recite to the tenant; enter your actual amount in the Security Deposit clause. A separate schedule applies to certain subsidized municipal-housing-authority tenancies — not relevant to a typical Steinoak lease.

title: Penalty for Mishandling a Security Deposit
bodyText: If you don't comply with Kansas's return and itemization requirements (K.S.A. 58-2550(b)), the tenant can recover the wrongfully withheld amount plus damages equal to 1.5 times that amount (K.S.A. 58-2550(c)).

title: A New Owner Inherits Your Deposit Obligations
bodyText: If you sell or transfer the property, whoever holds your interest in it at the time the tenancy ends is bound by Kansas's security deposit rules (K.S.A. 58-2550(f)) — the obligation follows the property, not just the original landlord.

title: What Happens If You Don't Keep Your Disclosure Current
bodyText: If you don't disclose (or don't keep current) the manager and owner information Kansas law requires, whoever signed the lease on your behalf becomes your tenant's implied agent for service of legal process and for receiving notices and demands (K.S.A. 58-2551(c)) — not a result most landlords want. Update the Landlord and Manager Disclosure clause promptly whenever this information changes.

title: When You Can Shift Maintenance Duties to a Tenant
bodyText:
Kansas allows a landlord and tenant to agree in writing that the tenant will perform some of the landlord's duties — trash removal and water/heat systems, plus specified repairs, maintenance, or remodeling — but only in a property with 4 or fewer households sharing common areas, and only if the arrangement is genuinely good-faith rather than a way to dodge your obligations (K.S.A. 58-2553(b)).

For any other multi-unit property (not a single-family home), tenant-performed repairs are allowed under narrower conditions: a separate written agreement with real consideration, work that isn't needed to fix a building-code violation, and no effect on your duties to other tenants (K.S.A. 58-2553(c)). Either way, you can't make the tenant's cooperation with this separate agreement a condition of the main lease itself (K.S.A. 58-2553(d)).

title: Kansas's Entry Standard Has No Fixed Notice Period
bodyText: Kansas law only requires 'reasonable notice' and 'reasonable hours' for landlord entry (K.S.A. 58-2557(a)) — there's no codified number of hours, despite what some landlord-advice sites claim. Entry without the tenant's consent is allowed only for an extreme hazard involving potential loss of life or severe property damage (58-2557(b)) — narrower than a general emergency exception. You may not abuse the right of access or use it to harass the tenant (58-2557(c)). The lease's 24-hour standard satisfies 'reasonable' under common practice, but there's no statutory floor forcing that specific number.

title: Consequences of Violating the DV/SA Housing Protection
bodyText: If you violate the domestic-violence/sexual-assault housing protections (K.S.A. 58-25,137), a court can award the tenant $1,000 in statutory damages plus reasonable attorney fees and costs — this is a court-awarded remedy for violating the statute, not a lease provision, so it doesn't conflict with Kansas's general ban on attorney-fee clauses. Submission of false information by an applicant or tenant claiming this protection can itself be grounds for denying tenancy or pursuing eviction.

title: Notice Periods for Tenant Noncompliance
bodyText: For a material lease violation or a health/safety-related violation (K.S.A. 58-2555), give written notice describing the breach and stating the lease will terminate at least 30 days after receipt if not remedied within 14 days. If the tenant cures in good faith within that 14-day window, the lease continues — but if the same or a similar breach recurs after that window, you can terminate on 30 days' notice without offering another chance to cure (K.S.A. 58-2564(a)). For nonpayment of rent, give written notice of the unpaid rent and your intent to terminate if not paid within 3 days; that 3-day period is counted as three consecutive 24-hour periods starting at personal delivery, delivery to a resident over 12, or conspicuous posting — add 2 extra days if you mail the notice instead (K.S.A. 58-2564(b)).

title: Kansas Holdover Damages: One Case Has a Figure, One Does Not
bodyText:
Kansas sets a holdover damages figure for one case only. If Tenant's holdover is willful and not in good faith, you may recover an amount not more than 1.5 times periodic Rent or not more than 1.5 times the actual damages you sustained, whichever is greater (K.S.A. 58-2570(c)). For an ordinary good-faith holdover — the commoner case, where the tenant simply has not got out yet — Kansas sets no figure at all, so you recover what you can prove as your actual loss. In both cases you may bring an action for possession, and the statute runs from expiration of the term or from an earlier termination, not from a notice date.

The shared Holdover clause defers to 'the maximum amount permitted by applicable law', which states the willful ceiling correctly but leaves the good-faith case with no stated figure; "Holdover Charge" clause is the optional clause that fills it, set at the daily equivalent of Rent plus documented further loss rather than a multiple.

One trap worth knowing: if you consent to the tenant staying on, or accept Rent for a continued tenancy, you are no longer dealing with a holdover at all — K.S.A. 58-2545(d) governs instead and the tenancy becomes month-to-month, or week-to-week for a roomer paying weekly rent.

title: Additional-Terms Warning on a Notice-to-Vacate Document
bodyText: If you give a tenant a document to sign as their written notice of intent to vacate, and it includes any terms not already in the lease, Kansas law requires this exact statement in at least 10-point boldface type: 'YOUR SIGNATURE ON THIS DOCUMENT MAY BIND YOU TO ADDITIONAL TERMS NOT IN YOUR ORIGINAL LEASE AGREEMENT. IF YOUR LEASE REQUIRES YOU TO GIVE WRITTEN NOTICE OF YOUR INTENT TO VACATE, YOU HAVE THE RIGHT TO DECLINE TO SIGN THIS DOCUMENT AND TO PROVIDE WRITTEN NOTICE IN ANOTHER FORM.' (K.S.A. 58-2570(e)). Without that statement, the added terms don't bind the tenant even if they sign.

title: Retaliation Against a Tenant Is Prohibited
bodyText: Kansas law bars you from raising rent or cutting services because a tenant complained to a government agency about a health/safety code violation, complained to you about a habitability issue, or organized or joined a tenants' union (K.S.A. 58-2572(a)). This doesn't stop a genuine, good-faith rent increase to cover rising costs like utilities, property taxes, or other operating expenses, as long as it doesn't conflict with the current lease (58-2572(c)) — and it doesn't stop you from pursuing possession if the code violation was actually caused by the tenant's own lack of care, the tenant is behind on rent, or fixing the violation would require work that effectively ends the tenant's ability to use the unit (58-2572(d)).

title: When Landlord Rules Are Enforceable
bodyText: A rule or regulation you adopt about a tenant's use of the property is only enforceable if it serves a legitimate purpose (tenant convenience/safety/welfare, protecting your property, or fair distribution of shared services), is reasonably related to that purpose, applies equally to all tenants, and is specific enough to fairly tell a tenant what is and isn't allowed (K.S.A. 58-2556). If the tenant had notice of the rule at signing, it's part of the rental agreement. A new rule adopted afterward that substantially modifies the deal the tenant signed up for is only enforceable if the tenant consents in writing — Kansas sets no specific advance-notice period for this in the standard Act (unlike the Mobile Home Park Act's parallel section, which requires 30 days' notice of rule changes).

title: No Landlord Lien on Tenant Property
bodyText: Kansas abolished a landlord's ability to claim a lien or security interest in a tenant's household goods, furnishings, or other personal property (unless perfected before the 1975 Act took effect), and abolished distraint for rent entirely, except as allowed under the abandoned-property procedure at K.S.A. 58-2565 (K.S.A. 58-2567). Don't include a clause purporting to give you a lien on tenant property for unpaid rent or damages — it wouldn't be enforceable.

title: Accepting Late Rent Can Waive Your Right to Act on It
bodyText: Kansas law says accepting late rent, rent with knowledge of a default, or any performance that varies from the lease terms, without reservation, waives your right to terminate the lease for that specific breach — unless you and the tenant agree otherwise after the breach has already occurred (K.S.A. 58-2566). See "Drafting Fix for the Late-Rent Waiver Issue" for a drafting approach addressing this.

title: Drafting Fix for the Late-Rent Waiver Issue
bodyText:
K.S.A. 58-2566's actual text says accepting late rent 'without reservation' waives your right to act on that breach — not that acceptance always waives it. Framing the lease's non-waiver language as an express, standing reservation of rights (rather than a flat 'acceptance doesn't waive anything' statement) tracks the statute's own wording and gives you a real textual argument that late-rent acceptance is never 'without reservation' under this lease.

Suggested replacement language: 'Any acceptance by Landlord of a late or partial payment, or of performance that varies from this Lease, is accepted with reservation of Landlord's rights and remedies under this Lease and applicable law, and does not waive Landlord's right to require timely and full performance in the future or to pursue any remedy for the breach.'

This is a textually grounded fix, not a certainty — a court could still read 'reservation' as requiring something more contemporaneous than standing boilerplate, so this is a reasonable drafting choice rather than a guarantee.

Also worth noting: Schutt v. Foster (Kan. Sup. Ct.) involved a $20/day late fee found unconscionable by the Court of Appeals after compounding to $21,240 — the Supreme Court reversed on a procedural technicality without reaching the merits, so uncapped/compounding daily late fees carry real unconscionability risk in Kansas.

title: No Interest Required on Security Deposits
bodyText: Unlike Connecticut, Maryland, Massachusetts, New Jersey, or Ohio, Kansas doesn't require you to hold a tenant's security deposit in an interest-bearing account or pay the tenant any interest on it — you can keep whatever interest the funds happen to earn.

title: No Radon Disclosure Requirement
bodyText: Unlike Colorado, Kansas has no statewide requirement to disclose radon information to tenants before signing a lease. Kansas does have a radon disclosure statute, K.S.A. 58-3078a, but it applies to SELLERS of residential real property, not to landlords. If you're aware of an elevated radon reading at the property, general habitability principles could still create exposure if you say nothing and a tenant is harmed — but there's no specific statutory disclosure form or notice period to follow here. If a licensed real estate broker or salesperson leases the property for you, though, the licensee must disclose to a prospective tenant any adverse material facts the licensee actually knows, including the property's physical condition and any material defects (K.S.A. 58-30,106(d)(1); 58-30,113(b)(2)(F)).

title: No Residential Bed Bug Disclosure Statute
bodyText: Unlike Colorado, California, or Maine, Kansas has no bed bug disclosure or fixed inspection/treatment-timeline statute for residential rentals. If a licensed real estate broker or salesperson leases the property for you, though, the licensee must disclose to a prospective tenant any adverse material facts the licensee actually knows, including the property's physical condition and any material defects (K.S.A. 58-30,106(d)(1); 58-30,113(b)(2)(F)). Kansas's bed bug regulations (K.A.R. 4-27 series - bed bugs are an 'imminent health hazard' under 4-27-2(f); 4-27-5 requires ceasing operations and notifying within 12 hours; 4-27-9 bars renting an infested guest room) apply to hotels and lodging establishments, not standard leases — a residential bed bug infestation is handled under the general habitability duty (K.S.A. 58-2553) instead. Note: online sources describing a specific inspection/treatment timeline for 'Kansas' landlords are often actually describing Kansas City, Missouri's separate municipal ordinance, not Kansas state law — worth double-checking which side of the state line any cited rule applies to.

title: Fair Housing Protected Classes in Kansas
bodyText: The Kansas Act Against Discrimination makes it unlawful to discriminate in renting because of race, religion, color, sex, disability, familial status, national origin or ancestry (K.S.A. 44-1016), subject to the Act's own exemptions (K.S.A. 44-1018). Ancestry is a Kansas class in addition to national origin, so Kansas does not simply copy the federal list. Kansas hasn't added source of income, sexual orientation or gender identity as a state-level protected class, and since 2026 no Kansas city or county may add a source-of-income mandate by ordinance (L. 2026, ch. 152, § 1(a)(1)). If your property is in the Kansas City metro, source-of-income protections you may have heard about are Kansas City, Missouri ordinances and don't apply on the Kansas side.

title: Service Animal Misrepresentation Penalty Does Not Reach Housing
bodyText: Kansas's service-animal misrepresentation crime is real but does not reach rental housing. K.S.A. 39-1112 makes misrepresentation a class A nonperson misdemeanor, but by its own terms it applies only to misrepresenting a right to be accompanied by an assistance dog "in or upon any place listed in K.S.A. 39-1101" - common carriers, hotels and lodging places, places of public accommodation, and other places to which the general public is invited - or, for a professional therapy dog, places listed in K.S.A. 39-1110. Residential rental housing appears on neither list. The housing rights are granted separately by K.S.A. 39-1102 (guide dog), 39-1107 (hearing assistance dog) and 39-1108 (service dog), each of which adds "the acquisition and use of rental, residential housing" on top of the 39-1101 places rather than being part of that list. A tenant who misrepresents a service animal to a landlord therefore does not commit this offense. The same limit applies to the statutory verification procedure at K.S.A. 39-1111, which is also scoped to the 39-1101 and 39-1110 place lists: Kansas extended the substantive rights into housing but extended neither the verification procedure nor the misrepresentation penalty. Kansas also has no emotional-support-animal misrepresentation crime in housing - a bill creating one was introduced four times and never passed.

title: No Mold Disclosure Requirement
bodyText: Kansas has no statutory mold disclosure requirement or required disclosure form. If a licensed real estate broker or salesperson leases the property for you, though, the licensee must disclose to a prospective tenant any adverse material facts the licensee actually knows, including the property's physical condition and any material defects (K.S.A. 58-30,106(d)(1); 58-30,113(b)(2)(F)). A mold problem caused by a landlord-controlled moisture source (a roof or plumbing leak, for example) falls under the general habitability duty (K.S.A. 58-2553) instead — no separate disclosure obligation, but still a real repair obligation once you're on notice.

title: No EV Right-to-Charge Statute
bodyText: Unlike Colorado and a growing list of other states, Kansas has no right-to-charge statute giving tenants a legal right to install an EV charging station at their rental. Whether to allow one, and on what terms, is entirely up to you.

title: No Housing-Voucher Acceptance Mandate
bodyText: Kansas doesn't require landlords to accept Housing Choice Vouchers (Section 8) or any other subsidy source, and since 2026 no Kansas city or county may require it either. A 2026 act bars any local ordinance or resolution that prohibits a landlord from refusing to lease because the applicant's source of income is, in whole or in part, a housing choice voucher or any other housing assistance program in which landlord participation is voluntary, and it makes any such ordinance adopted before July 1, 2026 null and void (L. 2026, ch. 152, § 1). You can decline an applicant because of how they intend to pay, the same way you can screen on any other lawful criterion. Federal fair housing law still applies, so apply your criteria the same way to everyone. If your property is in the Kansas City metro, voucher rules you may have heard about were a Kansas City, Missouri ordinance and never applied on the Kansas side.

title: No Deposit Installment-Payment Right
bodyText: Kansas doesn't give tenants a statutory right to pay the security deposit in installments — you can require it up front. One source claimed a general 2-month installment right, but that claim wasn't supported by the actual statute text (K.S.A. 58-2550) or by any other source, and its own wording suggests it was describing a subsidized municipal-housing-authority-specific provision, not a rule for ordinary Kansas tenancies.

title: Court Can Void an Unconscionable Lease Provision
bodyText: Kansas courts can refuse to enforce an entire rental agreement, a single unconscionable provision, or limit a provision's effect, if they find it was unconscionable when made (K.S.A. 58-2544). This is a real, live doctrine in Kansas landlord-tenant practice — in Schutt v. Foster, a Kansas Court of Appeals panel found a $20/day late fee that compounded to $21,240 over 1,062 days unconscionable and cut it to $1,700; the Kansas Supreme Court later reversed only on a procedural technicality (a briefing-preservation rule), not on the merits, so the underlying unconscionability finding was never actually overturned. Keep late fees, and any other open-ended dollar-amount clause, at a level that could survive this kind of scrutiny.

title: Kansas Consumer Protection Act as a Backstop
bodyText: Beyond the KRLTA's own unconscionability rule (K.S.A. 58-2544), Kansas has a broader Consumer Protection Act (K.S.A. 50-623 et seq.; the unconscionable-acts provision is K.S.A. 50-627 and the deceptive-acts provision is K.S.A. 50-626) covering 'deceptive and unconscionable' trade practices generally, which can independently apply to landlord-tenant disputes when the KRLTA doesn't already address the issue (it reaches a landlord as a 'supplier', meaning a lessor who leases to consumers in the ordinary course of business) — Kansas courts have held the more specific KRLTA controls where the two overlap, but the KCPA can still fill gaps. Unlike Colorado's Honest Pricing Act, Kansas has no rental-fee-specific transparency law (no all-in-pricing mandate, no free-payment-method requirement, no unprovided-service-fee ban) — the KCPA's protection here is the general unconscionability standard, not a fee-disclosure regime.

title: No Tenant-Death Lease-Termination Statute
bodyText: Kansas has no statute letting a deceased tenant's estate terminate the lease early without liability (unlike some states' 'Letty's Act'-style protections). A tenant's death doesn't end the lease — the estate remains liable for rent through the end of the term under ordinary contract principles, subject to your duty to mitigate damages by making reasonable efforts to re-rent.

title: No Alternate-Housing Requirement During Repairs
bodyText: Nothing in the KRLTA requires you to house a tenant or pay relocation costs while repairs are underway. A tenant's real options during a habitability failure are the notice-and-cure process (K.S.A. 58-2559) and, if the property is damaged or destroyed by fire or casualty specifically, the immediate-vacate or partial-vacate rights in K.S.A. 58-2562 (see "Fire or Casualty: The Tenant's Options") — not a right to alternate housing at your expense.

title: No Tenure-Based For-Cause Eviction Protection
bodyText: Unlike Colorado, where a tenant who has lived in a property for 12 months or more generally can't be removed without a specific legal cause or defined no-fault reason, Kansas has no tenure-based just-cause requirement at all. A month-to-month tenancy can be ended with plain 30-day written notice regardless of how long the tenant has lived there, no reason required (K.S.A. 58-2570(b)) — subject only to the retaliation prohibition (K.S.A. 58-2572) and fair housing law. Ending a tenancy mid-lease still requires cause, the same as any state, since that's ordinary contract law, not a tenure-based protection.

title: No Immigrant Tenant Protection Act
bodyText: Unlike Colorado's Immigrant Tenant Protection Act, Kansas has no state law specifically barring a landlord from asking about, collecting, or threatening to disclose a tenant's immigration or citizenship status. General federal Fair Housing protections against national-origin discrimination still apply (see "Fair Housing Protected Classes in Kansas"), but that's a different, narrower protection than Colorado's dedicated statute.

title: No State-Level Right-to-Call-Police Statute
bodyText: Unlike Colorado's non-waivable right to call police or emergency services, and unlike states such as Minnesota with a dedicated statute (Minn. Stat. § 504B.205), Kansas has no state-level law specifically barring a landlord from penalizing a tenant for calling police or emergency assistance, or requiring that right to be non-waivable. Kansas's domestic-violence housing protection (K.S.A. 58-25,137, see "Domestic Violence, Sexual Assault, Trafficking and Stalking: Housing Protections" and "Early Termination Fee — Protected Person" clause) covers denial of tenancy and eviction based on victim status, but doesn't itself address calling the police as a protected act the way Minnesota's statute does. Local nuisance/crime-free-housing ordinances, which can effectively penalize tenants for police calls, are a municipal-level issue in Kansas — the same category of city-by-city complexity that's keeping Ohio deliberately deferred in this project, and not audited here. Kansas's state common-nuisance law (K.S.A. 22-3901 to 22-3905) does reach rental property used for drug activity and certain other crimes, but it targets the crime, not a call for help: an owner's written report to local law enforcement that the property is suspected of such use counts as evidence of a good-faith attempt to abate the nuisance (K.S.A. 22-3904(5)).

title: Criminal Penalty for Denying a Service Animal in Rental Housing
bodyText:
In Kansas the criminal exposure around assistance animals runs toward the landlord, not the tenant. K.S.A. 39-1103 makes it a misdemeanor for any person, or the agent of any person, to deny or interfere with the rights recognized in K.S.A. 39-1101, 39-1102, 39-1107, 39-1108 and 39-1109 - and 39-1102 (guide dog), 39-1107 (hearing assistance dog) and 39-1108 (service dog) each expressly extend their right to "the acquisition and use of rental, residential housing and... the purchase and use of residential housing without being required to pay an extra charge" for the dog.

Refusing one of these dogs in a rental, or charging a pet fee, deposit or pet rent for one, is therefore a crime in Kansas, not merely a fair housing violation. K.S.A. 39-1103 does not state a class, so it is an unclassified misdemeanor sentenced as a class C misdemeanor under K.S.A. 21-6602(a)(4): up to 1 month in county jail and a fine of up to $500. The tenant remains liable for any damage the dog does to the premises, which each of the three sections preserves expressly.

This applies only to individually trained dogs - K.S.A. 39-1113(a) defines "assistance dog" as only a guide dog, hearing assistance dog or service dog, each "specially selected, trained and tested," and 39-1113(f) excludes an animal kept for comfort, protection or personal defense. The act also covers dogs only, so a non-canine assistance animal falls outside it entirely and is governed by the Kansas Act Against Discrimination and federal fair housing law instead.

title: Kansas's Own Reasonable Accommodation and Modification Duties
bodyText:
Separate from federal fair housing law, the Kansas Act Against Discrimination imposes its own housing duties. K.S.A. 44-1016(h)(3)(B) makes it discrimination to refuse to make reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices or services when necessary to afford a person with a disability equal opportunity to use and enjoy residential real property - this is the provision a request to waive a no-pets policy for an assistance animal falls under, and it does not mention animals or reference federal law.

K.S.A. 44-1016(h)(3)(A) is a separate and narrower duty: permitting reasonable modifications of the existing premises, at the tenant's own expense, where necessary for full enjoyment. K.S.A. 44-1016(h)(7) preserves the ability to decline where the tenancy would constitute a direct threat to the health or safety of others or would result in substantial physical damage to the property of others. K.A.R. 21-60-16 bars requiring an increased security deposit from a person with a disability.

Complaints are handled by the Kansas Human Rights Commission.

Two limits worth knowing: the KAAD's disability definition excludes current illegal use of a controlled substance in housing discrimination (K.S.A. 44-1002(j)), and K.S.A. 44-1018(d) permits acting against a person convicted two or more times of the illegal manufacture or distribution of a controlled substance. These duties do not apply to a landlord who falls inside the small-landlord exemptions - see the Small-Landlord Exemptions item.

title: Small-Landlord Exemptions from Kansas Fair Housing Duties
bodyText: Kansas's housing discrimination provisions open with "Subject to the provisions of K.S.A. 44-1018," so the exemptions are built into the operative section itself rather than sitting elsewhere as a separate limit. K.S.A. 44-1018(b) exempts two situations: the sale or rental of a single-family house by an owner who owns or has an interest in no more than three single-family houses at any one time and rents it without a real estate broker, agent or salesperson (limited to one such sale in any 24-month period if the owner was not the resident or most recent resident); and rooms or units in a building containing living quarters for no more than four families living independently, where the owner actually maintains and occupies one of those units as a residence. A landlord inside either exemption is outside K.S.A. 44-1016 in its entirety, including its disability accommodation and modification duties. One provision survives the exemption: the ban on discriminatory advertising, notices, statements and applications at K.S.A. 44-1016(c) applies regardless. The federal Fair Housing Act carries broadly parallel owner-occupied and single-family exemptions, so a landlord may fall outside both - but the two sets are not identical, and each must be checked on its own terms rather than assumed to match.

title: Kansas Smoke Detector Rules and the Two Shields They Carry
bodyText:
Placement (K.S.A. 31-162(a)-(b)): every single-family residence needs at least one smoke detector on every story of the dwelling unit. A structure with multiple dwelling units, or a mixed-use structure containing at least one dwelling unit, needs at least one detector at the uppermost ceiling of each interior stairwell plus one on every story in each dwelling unit.

Power source (31-162(d)): detectors in units that existed on January 1, 1999 may be battery-powered or wired and need not be interconnected, but detectors in units CONSTRUCTED AFTER January 1, 1999 must be wired permanently into the structure's electrical system - a hard threshold worth checking against your build year before assuming battery units are compliant.

Two provisions work in your favor. First, K.S.A. 31-162(g): evidence that an owner failed to provide an operational smoke detector, and evidence that an occupant failed to properly maintain one, are both inadmissible in any action for the purpose of determining any aspect of civil liability. Second, K.S.A. 31-162(h): the Smoke Detector Act cannot be used as grounds to offset, reduce, or deny payment under any insurance contract or policy.

Enforcement officials also may not enter a dwelling solely to check compliance, except during a pre-occupancy or building-permit inspection, when responding to a real fire, or during an owner- or occupant-requested home safety inspection (31-162(f)). Manufactured homes follow federal construction and safety standards instead, but their owners and occupants remain subject to the Act's testing and maintenance rules (31-162(e)).

title: No Carbon Monoxide Alarm Requirement
bodyText:
Kansas has no state law requiring carbon monoxide alarms in residential rental property. Unlike the smoke detector duty, which is statutory, no Kansas statute makes CO alarms compulsory in a rental.

One caution: a 2026 act smooths the way for the state fire marshal to update the Kansas fire prevention code to the International Fire Code, 2024 edition, which has carbon monoxide provisions, and rewrites the fire marshal's rule-making power over fire detection equipment in buildings where people live (L. 2026, ch. 74). The fire marshal's regulations still adopt the 2006 edition, so check whether an update has been adopted, and whether it reaches existing rentals, before relying on state-law silence.

Kansas does regulate CO detection in lodging establishments - hotels and motels - under K.A.R. 4-27-8, but that does not reach residential leases.

Two cautions. A widely circulated claim that Kansas landlords must install CO alarms 'at the request of the renter' appears on at least one alarm manufacturer's website and is not supported by any Kansas statute. And if your property is in the Kansas City metro, check which side of the state line it sits on: Kansas City, Missouri municipal requirements do not apply in Kansas. Installing CO alarms anyway remains a reasonable safety decision, and a local ordinance may require them even though state law does not.

title: Eviction Expungement and Mediation — and Your Right to Object
bodyText: Kansas changed its eviction law in 2026 (L. 2026, ch. 132, Substitute for HB 2357, approved April 9, 2026, in force on publication in the statute book; July 1, 2026, the 2026 Session Laws' publication date, is the working date), for eviction actions under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. Expungement is NOT automatic. A tenant must file for it electronically with the clerk of the district court, at no cost, under the docket number of the original eviction action, and must serve process on you by return receipt delivery. You then have 30 days after delivery to file an objection. If you do not object, the court decides without a hearing and PRESUMES any money judgment you were owed has been satisfied - so missing the 30-day window can cost you. If you do object, the court must hold a hearing. The court must grant expungement only if all three are met: three years have passed since judgment was entered; the tenant shows any money judgments owed to you are satisfied; and the tenant has no additional judgment in a covered eviction action within that three-year period. Two provisions work strongly in your favor. An unsatisfied money judgment blocks expungement entirely unless you agree to it. And if the tenant picks up another eviction judgment during the three years, the earlier judgment cannot be expunged until the later one becomes eligible. Expungement also does not wipe out the debt: it does not satisfy, extinguish, or otherwise affect any monetary obligation from the tenancy, and you keep the right to bring a separate action for rent or damages. On mediation, the court must consider mediation unless it finds that mediation would not aid the parties materially, or is impracticable. Trial in an RLTA eviction must still occur within 14 days of the appearance date, but where the parties are participating in court-ordered mediation the court must order a continuance of up to 14 days from the date of the mediation order, and the tenant does not have to post the bond that otherwise conditions any continuance. The Judicial Council is to develop the expungement form.

title: Returned-Check Service Charge Capped at $30
bodyText:
Kansas caps the service charge on a dishonored check at $30 (K.S.A. 60-2610(g)).

Separately, K.S.A. 60-2610(a) creates civil liability for a worthless check: you may recover the amount of the check, court costs, the service charge, interest at the statutory rate, collection costs including reasonable attorney fees, plus the greater of (i) treble damages capped at the check amount plus $500 or (ii) $100 - but only after making a written demand and allowing 14 days for payment (60-2610(b)). Note that the attorney-fee recovery here comes from this statute, not from a lease provision, so it does not conflict with Kansas's flat ban on attorney-fee clauses in leases.

One more thing worth knowing, because it cuts the other way from the Kansas rule that a lease may never shift attorney's fees: K.S.A. 60-2610(a) itself awards 'the costs of collection including but not limited to reasonable attorney fees' on a worthless-check claim. That is a statutory award, not a lease term, so it is unaffected by the K.S.A. 58-2547(a)(3) ban — a Kansas landlord can recover fees on a bounced rent check while still being unable to put a fee-shifting clause in the lease. The court may waive all or part of those fees if it finds the other amounts awarded already compensate you, and must make written findings if it does.

title: Rent Control Is Preempted Statewide
bodyText: No Kansas county, city, or township may enact or enforce rent control, or control the purchase price of real estate (K.S.A. 12-16,120). This is a statewide preemption, so no Kansas municipality can impose a rent cap or rent-stabilization ordinance on your property, and under subsection (d) a city or county may not require you to agree to one as a condition of considering or approving a building permit or plat, or a zoning or conditional-use request, change or variance. Two carve-outs matter. Subsection (b) leaves a political subdivision free to manage and control property it has an ownership interest in. Subsection (c) lets you VOLUNTARILY agree to rent limits in return for grants or incentives a political subdivision provides — so if you take a city incentive, rent restrictions you accept in that deal are enforceable against you, and the preemption does not rescue you from them. Kansas also has no state rent-increase notice statute: a rent increase on a month-to-month tenancy is effected through the same 30-day written notice used to terminate that tenancy (K.S.A. 58-2570(b)), and rent under a fixed-term lease cannot be raised mid-term unless the lease itself provides for it.

title: One-Year Cap on Leases Formed by Conduct
bodyText: If a rental agreement takes effect through conduct rather than full signature - because you accepted rent without reservation, or because the tenant took possession under an agreement you signed and delivered but they did not - Kansas caps its term at one year. K.S.A. 58-2546(c): if such an agreement provides for a term longer than one year, it is effective only for one year. This does NOT cap a fully signed and delivered written lease; the KRLTA imposes no maximum term on those. The practical point is narrow but real: a long-term arrangement that was never properly executed by both parties will not hold for its stated term.

title: Tenant Habitability Notice Must Be in Writing
bodyText: A Kansas tenant's right to terminate for a habitability breach requires WRITTEN notice as a strict element. K.S.A. 58-2559(a) provides that the tenant may deliver a written notice specifying the acts and omissions constituting the breach and stating that the rental agreement will terminate on a periodic rent-paying date not less than 30 days after receipt - and your 14-day period to cure runs from that written notice. An oral complaint does not start the clock. Kansas imposes no operational duties beyond the repair itself: no deadline to contact the tenant with your intentions or an estimate, no duty to inform the tenant of any relocation right, no record-retention requirement, no mold containment protocol, and no licensed-professional requirement for specific hazards. Kansas also imposes no obligation to house a tenant or pay relocation costs during repairs.

title: No Rental Application or Tenant Screening Regulation
bodyText: Kansas does not regulate the rental application or tenant screening process at all. There is no cap on application fees and no prohibition on charging them, no portable-screening-report rule, no limit on how far back criminal or rental history may be considered, and no state adverse-action or denial-notice requirement. Kansas also has no statute restricting consideration of an applicant's criminal history. The constraints that do apply come from elsewhere: the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act governs adverse-action notices where a consumer report is used, and federal fair housing law together with the Kansas Act Against Discrimination limits screening practices that discriminate against a protected class or produce a discriminatory effect. Two 2026 changes sit alongside this. No Kansas city or county may restrict your ability to use or consider income-qualifying methods, credit scores, credit reports, eviction history, property damage history or criminal history, or to request that information, when you apply your customary criteria (L. 2026, ch. 152, § 1(a)(2)). And eviction records are no longer permanent: a tenant may apply to expunge a Residential Landlord and Tenant Act eviction judgment three years after it was entered, so an older eviction may not appear at all (see the note on eviction expungement and mediation).

title: Renter's Insurance Is Unregulated in Kansas
bodyText: Kansas neither requires renter's insurance nor restricts your ability to require it. You may make renter's insurance a lease condition and may require that you be named as an additional insured. Kansas also has no equivalent to Colorado's rule barring a landlord from requiring a tenant to claim on the tenant's own policy for landlord-responsible repair costs, or from filing against that policy without the tenant's express written permission. This is an unregulated area in Kansas, so the lease governs.

title: No Environmental-Event Termination Right
bodyText: Kansas gives a landlord no statutory right to terminate a lease because of a sudden environmental public health event, a government order rendering occupancy impossible or unlawful, or condemnation. The only Kansas casualty-termination provision is K.S.A. 58-2562, which covers fire or casualty damage and grants the right to the TENANT, not the landlord. Unlike Colorado - where the landlord's environmental-event termination right exists only if the lease provides for it, so a silent lease forfeits it - there is no Kansas statutory right here to opt into. If you want any termination right in these circumstances, it has to be built as a contract term and will stand or fall on ordinary contract principles.

title: No Expedited Eviction Track for Criminal Activity
bodyText: Kansas has no expedited or shortened eviction procedure for drug activity, violent crime, or other criminal conduct on the premises. An eviction based on criminal activity proceeds on the ordinary track: the notice requirements of K.S.A. 58-2564 and the limited-actions procedure in Chapter 61. You have no faster hearing window and no immediate-eviction trigger of your own. The one exception runs through a prosecutor: after someone is arrested for drug activity or another crime listed in K.S.A. 22-3901, the attorney general or a city, county or district attorney may ask the court for a hearing (normally within 30 days), and if the court finds the crime occurred, the lease is void and possession reverts to you to evict; if you don't start an eviction within 30 days, the prosecutor may move against the property itself (K.S.A. 22-3902(2)(A)). A 1998 bill that would have created a 'Kansas expedited eviction of drug traffickers act' with a 7-day hearing window died in the legislature and was never enacted.

title: Termination Notice Periods for Periodic Tenancies
bodyText: Kansas sets three different notice periods for ending a periodic tenancy, all under K.S.A. 58-2570. A week-to-week tenancy: either party may terminate on at least 7 days' written notice before the termination date stated in the notice (58-2570(a)). A month-to-month tenancy: either party may terminate by written notice stating the tenancy ends on a periodic rent-paying date not less than 30 days after receipt (58-2570(b)). Military exception: not more than 15 days' written notice is needed to end a periodic tenancy where the tenant is in the military service of the United States AND termination is necessitated by military orders. Two limits on that exception are worth noting. It runs to the TENANT only - it does not shorten the notice a landlord must give a military tenant. And it requires both conditions, military service and orders necessitating the termination, not merely military status. This sits alongside, and is separate from, the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act termination rights referenced in the Early Termination clause. Finally, a rental agreement for a definite term of more than 30 days is not a month-to-month tenancy even if rent is payable at 30-day intervals (58-2570(b)).

title: No Double-Letting Rent Relief
bodyText: Kansas has no statute addressing double-letting - renting the same room to more than one tenant. Unlike North Dakota, where the first tenant is entitled to the whole room and every other tenant in the building under that landlord is relieved of all rent obligations for as long as the double-letting continues, Kansas imposes no statutory penalty of that kind. A double-letting dispute in Kansas would be resolved under ordinary contract and possession principles.

title: No Statutory Fraud-Inducement Termination Right
bodyText: Kansas has no statute letting a party who was induced into a lease by fraudulent misrepresentation terminate it and recover the deposit plus accrued interest. North Dakota has such a provision; Kansas does not. A Kansas party claiming fraudulent inducement relies on general contract and common-law fraud principles - rescission and damages - and potentially the Kansas Consumer Protection Act, which treats residential leasing as a consumer transaction and prohibits deceptive and unconscionable acts.

title: No Restriction on Payment-Method Fees
bodyText: Kansas does not restrict what a landlord may charge in connection with a particular rent payment method. North Dakota bars charging a fee merely for accepting cash, a check, or a money order; Kansas has no equivalent, so a convenience or processing fee tied to a payment method is a matter for the lease. This is separate from a returned-payment charge, where Kansas does impose a limit - see the Returned-Check Service Charge item.

title: Termination Mechanisms Outside the Eviction Process
bodyText: For a residential tenancy governed by the Kansas Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, termination runs through the Act's own notice-and-cure structure - K.S.A. 58-2564 for tenant noncompliance and K.S.A. 58-2559 for landlord noncompliance - followed, if necessary, by the limited-actions eviction procedure in Chapter 61. Kansas does not provide a separate direct-termination mechanism for KRLTA tenancies of the kind North Dakota gives its landlords and tenants. Kansas does retain an older body of termination provisions at K.S.A. 58-2501 through 58-2533, covering tenancies at will, year-to-year tenancies, and farm and pastureland tenancies, with their own notice rules. Those govern arrangements that fall outside the KRLTA rather than standard residential leases, and where the two overlap the KRLTA controls.

title: Kansas Penalizes Lockouts and Utility Shutoffs Directly
bodyText: Kansas bars a landlord from taking possession into their own hands and gives the tenant a direct money remedy when one does. The prohibition is in K.S.A. 58-2569: "A landlord may not recover or take possession of the dwelling unit by action or otherwise, including willful diminution of services to the tenant by interrupting or causing the interruption of electric, gas, water or other essential service to the tenant, except in case of abandonment, surrender or as otherwise permitted in this act." Read that literally — it reaches recovering possession "by action or otherwise," so the lawful routes are the ones the Act itself permits, and everything else is barred whether or not you ever touch a lock. The remedy is in K.S.A. 58-2563: if the landlord unlawfully removes or excludes the tenant from the premises, or willfully diminishes services by interrupting electric, gas, water, or another essential service, the tenant may recover possession OR terminate the rental agreement — and in either case recover the greater of one and one-half months' periodic rent or their actual damages. If the tenant terminates, you must also return the recoverable portion of the security deposit. Kansas courts have allowed punitive damages on top where the landlord's conduct was wanton and malicious. Two things worth knowing: this remedy does not require the tenant to give you the 30-day notice that the habitability statute requires, so a lockout or deliberate shutoff is actionable immediately; and the same remedy is what attaches to a retaliatory rent increase or service cut under the retaliation statute.

title: Removing a Squatter Without an Eviction Action (2026 Act)
bodyText: Kansas enacted a removal of squatters act in 2026 (L. 2026, ch. 56; H.B. 2378). It lets the owner of a dwelling unit, or the owner's agent, have a squatter removed by law enforcement instead of filing an eviction case. A squatter is a person occupying a dwelling who is not entitled to occupy it under a lease or rental agreement and is not authorized to occupy it by a tenant. The owner submits a notarized affidavit to local law enforcement stating six things: that the affiant is the owner or the owner's agent; that the person entered and remains unlawfully; that the person was not authorized to enter; that the person is not a tenant or a holdover tenant; that the affiant asked the person to leave and the person refused; and that the person is not an immediate family member. Law enforcement verifies the affiant's ownership and apparent entitlement to relief, and no sooner than 24 hours after receiving the affidavit an officer serves a notice to vacate immediately, either by hand or by posting it on the front door or entrance. Occupancy by a squatter is excluded from the Kansas Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, and removing a squatter does not require an eviction action under that Act. Three limits make this a poor tool to reach for casually. A current or former tenant is not a squatter, and a holdover tenant is expressly excluded, so a tenant who overstays still goes through the Chapter 61 eviction process. An immediate family member cannot be removed this way; the act's list runs to spouse, child, grandchild of any degree, parent, mother-in-law, father-in-law and grandparent, among others. And the downside is severe: a false affidavit is a class A nonperson misdemeanor, and a person wrongly removed may recover possession, actual costs and damages, treble the fair market rent as punitive damages, court costs and attorney fees. Use this only where you are certain there is no tenancy and no family relationship. Anything short of that belongs in an eviction action.

title: Abandonment Ends the Lease Unless You Try to Re-Rent
bodyText:
If a Kansas tenant abandons the dwelling unit, you must make reasonable efforts to rent it at a fair rental (K.S.A. 58-2565(c)). This is not only a duty to mitigate damages — the statute attaches a consequence that ends the lease. If you re-rent for a term beginning before the original rental agreement would have expired, the agreement is deemed terminated as of the date the new tenancy begins. And if you fail to use reasonable efforts to re-rent at a fair rental, or you accept the abandonment as a surrender, the rental agreement is deemed terminated by you as of the date you had notice of the abandonment. Either way rent stops accruing from that date, so a landlord who leaves an abandoned unit sitting and later sues for the balance of the term will find the claim cut off at the notice date rather than running to the end of the lease.

Two practical consequences. Document the re-letting effort — when it was listed, at what rent, showings, applications, why any applicant was turned down — because that record is what preserves a rent claim past the abandonment date. And note that the statute deems the termination to be by the landlord, which matters anywhere your rights or a tenant's turn on which party ended the tenancy.

title: What You Can Sue For When the Lease Ends
bodyText: On termination of the rental agreement, K.S.A. 58-2568 gives you a claim and lets you file an action for possession, for rent, or for both. It also gives you a separate claim for actual damages for breach of the rental agreement, and that damages action may be filed before the rental agreement's termination date — you do not have to wait for the term to run out to sue on a breach. Two things follow. Possession and money are not alternatives in Kansas: suing for possession does not make you give up the rent claim, and you can combine them. And because the damages claim is for actual damages, it is bounded by the other Kansas limits already in this library — the re-letting duty on abandonment, which cuts rent off at the notice date (K.S.A. 58-2565(c)), and the holdover cap of one and one-half times periodic rent or actual damages (K.S.A. 58-2570(c)). Kansas gives you no statutory right to accelerate the remaining rent, and no right to recover attorney fees, because K.S.A. 58-2547(a)(3) voids a lease fee-shifting provision outright.

title: Tenant Counterclaims and Rent Paid Into Court
bodyText: In a Kansas action for possession based on nonpayment of rent, or an action for rent where the tenant still occupies the premises, the tenant must raise any counterclaim for amounts recoverable under the rental agreement or the Kansas Residential Landlord and Tenant Act in that action or forfeit the right to bring it (K.S.A. 58-2561(a)). The court may order the tenant to pay accrued and future rent into court and then determine each party's net obligation; the party owed money is paid first out of the funds on deposit, with any remainder paid by the other party. Where no rent remains due after that netting, the tenant may prevail in the possession action. If the tenant has already vacated and you are suing only for rent, the tenant may still counterclaim but is not required to deposit rent into court (58-2561(b)). What this means in practice is that a habitability counterclaim normally lands inside your own eviction case rather than arriving as a separate suit later. A security-deposit claim is different: the Kansas Court of Appeals held that a claim for the deposit plus damages is not a compulsory counterclaim under this section (Asbury v. Mauk, 9 Kan. App. 2d 699 (1984)), so a tenant can bring it separately. Either way, the rent on deposit is the fund your judgment gets paid from — so expect the case to turn on the net number, not on possession alone.

title: Remedies When Entry Is Refused — and When You Enter Wrongly
bodyText:
Kansas attaches remedies to entry in both directions (K.S.A. 58-2571). If the tenant refuses to allow lawful access to the dwelling unit, you may obtain injunctive relief to compel access or terminate the rental agreement, and in either case recover actual damages. If you make an unlawful entry, or a lawful entry in an unreasonable manner, or make repeated demands for entry that are otherwise lawful but have the effect of unreasonably harassing the tenant, the tenant may obtain injunctive relief or terminate the rental agreement, and recover actual damages.

Read this with the entry standard itself: Kansas requires only reasonable notice at reasonable hours, with no fixed number of hours, so what counts as a lawful entry is judged against that standard rather than against a statutory clock.

The practical point for a landlord is that refusal of access is a remedy you have to go get — Kansas gives you an injunction or termination, not a right to let yourself in — and that a pattern of entry demands can itself be the violation even when each individual entry would have been lawful.

title: The Kansas Eviction Process, Step by Step
bodyText: A Kansas eviction runs as a limited-actions case under Chapter 61, Article 38, and it is separate from the notice the lease and the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act require. Before filing, you must give a notice to leave the premises at least three days before starting the lawsuit (K.S.A. 61-3803). That three-day period is counted as three consecutive 24-hour periods, intermediate weekends, legal holidays and days the clerk's office is closed are included in the count, and if you mail the notice you add two days. It may be delivered to the other party, left with a person over 12 years of age at the premises, posted in a conspicuous place, or mailed to the premises. The statute allows this notice to be combined with a notice under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, so one properly drafted notice can serve both purposes rather than requiring two. You then file a petition, and the court sets the appearance date in the summons: not less than three nor more than 14 days after the summons issues (K.S.A. 61-3805). After a judgment for possession the court issues a writ of restitution at your request, and the writ must be executed within 14 days after the person named in it receives it (K.S.A. 61-3808). If an appeal stay is entered, execution stops immediately, and if possession has already been restored to you it goes back to the tenant. Nothing in this process lets you shortcut the Act's own notice-and-cure periods, which run first. Two things sit outside Chapter 61 and still bite. Kansas has no court rule making a federal notice a condition of filing, but the federal CARES Act's 30-day notice to vacate may apply on its own terms to a 'covered dwelling' — one with a federally backed mortgage, or in a covered federal housing program or the rural housing voucher program (see the federal note on it) — so check whether the property is covered before relying on the three-day notice alone. And for an eviction under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act the court must consider mediation unless it finds mediation would not aid both parties or is impracticable; see the eviction-record row for that and for the expungement rules that follow a judgment.

title: When a Tenant's Unpaid City Utility Bill Can Become a Lien on Your Property
bodyText: In Kansas, unpaid fees for utility service supplied by a municipally owned utility can become a lien on the property served, certified to the county clerk and collected on the tax roll with the usual tax penalties (K.S.A. 12-808c). One subsection decides who carries that risk in a rental: "A lien shall not attach to property for unpaid utility fees or charges, when the utility service has been contracted for by a tenant and not by the landlord or owner of the property to which such service is provided." So whose name is on the utility account is not an administrative detail — it determines whether the city can put the tenant's unpaid water, sewer, trash, gas or electric bill on your tax bill. If the tenant contracts for the service, no lien attaches to your property. If you keep the account in your own name for convenience, for a master-metered building, or because the tenant could not get service, the exception does not apply and the lien can attach. The practical rule is to require tenant-name accounts wherever the service is separately metered, and to treat any account you hold yourself as your own credit exposure rather than the tenant's. Note the limit: this concerns municipally owned utilities. Investor-owned utilities and rural water districts are outside it, and a rural water district's own collection remedies are a separate question.

title: A Deposit Refund the Tenant Never Cashes Is Not Yours
bodyText: When you mail a security deposit refund and the tenant never cashes it, the money does not revert to you. Under the Kansas Disposition of Unclaimed Property Act it becomes presumed abandoned and has to be reported and delivered to the state. A refund owed to a former tenant falls in the Act's catch-all category, "all other property, five years after the owner's right to demand the property or after the obligation to pay or distribute the property arises, whichever first occurs" (K.S.A. 58-3935(a)(16)). A holder of property presumed abandoned reports it to the state administrator before November 1 each year, covering the 12 months ending the preceding July 1 (K.S.A. 58-3950). There is a small-holder exemption: no report is required if you have no individual item over $100 and your aggregated total is under $250, unless the administrator requires otherwise — which will not cover most deposit refunds, since a typical Kansas deposit is capped at a month's rent and exceeds $100. Two practical points. Keep the unclaimed refund in a form you can still deliver five years later rather than writing it back into income. And this is separate from the deposit return rules themselves: complying with K.S.A. 58-2550's 14-day and 30-day deadlines is what avoids the 1.5-times penalty, while this Act governs what happens to the money afterwards.

title: Holding Deposits Sit Outside the Deposit Cap — Until the Lease Names Them
bodyText: Kansas defines a security deposit as "any sum of money specified in a rental agreement, however denominated, to be deposited with a landlord by a tenant as a condition precedent to the occupancy of a dwelling unit" (K.S.A. 58-2543(m)). Two limits in that sentence matter. It is denomination-blind, so calling money a fee, a reservation charge or a last-month payment does not keep it out — if the lease specifies it and occupancy depends on it, it is a security deposit and the K.S.A. 58-2550 cap, retention rules and return deadlines apply. But it is also agreement-scoped: money taken at application, before any rental agreement exists, is not specified in a rental agreement. A true pre-lease holding deposit therefore sits outside the deposit statute — which also means the tenant does not get 58-2550's remedies for it, and Kansas does not otherwise regulate the rental application process. The trap is the handoff. The moment the signed lease recites the holding money, or credits it toward the deposit or first month's rent, it becomes money specified in a rental agreement, counts against the cap, and starts the return clock. Decide up front which of the two you are taking, say so in writing to the applicant, and if you intend it to become part of the deposit, count it against the cap from the start.

title: Nobody Can Collect the Rent Free of the Habitability Duties
bodyText: Kansas law provides that "A rental agreement, assignment, conveyance, trust deed or security instrument may not permit the receipt of rent free of the obligation to comply with subsection (a) of K.S.A. 58-2553" (K.S.A. 58-2549). Subsection (a) of 58-2553 is the landlord's habitability duty — codes materially affecting health and safety, common areas, the electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning systems, trash removal, running water and reasonable hot water and heat. What the section does is close the gap between who takes the rent and who owes the duties. An assignment of rents to a lender, a deed, a trust deed or a security instrument cannot be drafted so that the party receiving rent escapes the habitability obligation, and neither can the lease itself. This matters in three ordinary situations: financing that assigns rents as collateral, a receiver or lender collecting rents during a default, and a sale where rent is directed to a new party. In each case the duty travels with the rent. Check any rent-assignment language in your loan documents against this section rather than assuming the lease is the only place the problem could arise.

title: No Kansas Foreclosure Notice or Lease-Survival Statute for Tenants
bodyText: Kansas has no state statute requiring a landlord to disclose a pending foreclosure to a tenant or applicant, and no state statute governing whether a lease survives a foreclosure sale. Several states in this library do have one; Kansas does not. What governs instead is Kansas's judicial foreclosure process, including the redemption period in K.S.A. 60-2414, and the federal Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act, which requires a successor in interest to honor an existing bona fide lease and to give a bona fide tenant at least 90 days' notice to vacate. Two practical consequences. If you are selling or losing a tenanted property, Kansas law gives you no disclosure obligation to the tenant, but the tenancy is not yours to terminate merely because the property is in foreclosure. If a licensed real estate broker or salesperson leases the property for you, though, the licensee must disclose to a prospective tenant any adverse material facts the licensee actually knows, including a material limitation on your ability to perform the lease (K.S.A. 58-30,106(d)(1)(E); 58-30,113(b)(2)(F)(v)). And if you are buying at a Kansas foreclosure sale, expect to inherit the tenancy rather than an empty unit, and expect the federal 90-day floor to apply before you can require the tenant to leave.

title: No Foreign-Adversary Property Ownership Restriction in Kansas
bodyText: Kansas has no statute restricting the ownership of real property by foreign adversaries or by entities tied to designated countries. The legislature passed one in 2024 — House Substitute for Senate Bill 172 — and the Governor vetoed it on May 10, 2024. The veto was not overridden: the bill appears in the 2024 session laws only as a governor's veto message, with no session-law chapter number, and no Kansas enactment on the subject followed in 2025 or 2026. So a Kansas landlord selling to, buying from, or leasing to an entity with foreign ownership faces no state-law ownership restriction or registration duty of this kind. Federal rules still apply on their own terms, including CFIUS review of certain real estate transactions near sensitive sites and the federal agricultural foreign-investment reporting requirement, neither of which this Kansas absence affects.

title: No State Towing Rules for Your Parking Lot
bodyText:
Kansas does not regulate towing from private rental property the way some states do. There is no state statute requiring signs at the entrances to your lot, no requirement that you sign a written authorization for each tow, and no state cap on what a towing carrier may charge the vehicle's owner.

What Kansas does have is an abandoned-vehicle route and a tower's lien. Under K.S.A. 8-1102, where a vehicle is abandoned on private property the public agency for that jurisdiction may remove and dispose of it "upon request of the owner or occupant of such real property" — a request, not a written authorization — and whoever removes the vehicle at that agency's request has a possessory lien on it for the costs of removing, towing and storing it. K.S.A. 8-1103 carries the related lien provisions.

The practical upshot is that the lease clause and your own arrangement with the towing company are doing most of the work here, because no state signage or authorization statute backs them up. Two cautions: Kansas cities have home-rule authority and many do regulate towing by ordinance, and the Kansas Corporation Commission regulates motor carriers — neither was researched, so check the ordinance for each property's city before relying on this.

title: No State Pool Barrier Requirement for Rental Property
bodyText: Kansas has no state statute imposing a pool fence, barrier, gate or safety-notice requirement on a residential landlord. The Kansas pool rules that do exist sit in the Department of Health and Environment's child care regulations — K.A.R. 28-4-129 for child care centers and K.A.R. 28-4-594 for family child care homes — and they apply because of the licensed child care activity, not because the property is rented. Pool barrier requirements in Kansas therefore come from whichever building or pool code the city or county has adopted, which varies from place to place. Two things follow for a landlord. Check the local adopted code for each property with a pool rather than assuming a statewide rule exists, since the absence of a state statute is not the absence of a requirement. And note the overlap with the residential-use clause: if a tenant runs a licensed child care operation out of the home, the K.A.R. 28-4 pool and fencing rules start applying to your property through the tenant's license, which is one more reason the residential-use-only restriction is worth enforcing.

title: Deposit Return Deadline and Itemization
bodyText: If you keep any part of the deposit for damages or other allowable charges besides rent, return the balance within 14 days after determining the amount kept, and no later than 30 days after the lease ends, possession is delivered and the tenant demands the deposit. If the tenant doesn't demand it within 30 days after the lease ends, mail the balance to the tenant's last known address. Itemize anything you keep in a written notice to the tenant (K.S.A. 58-2550(b)). See the penalty note for what happens if you don't.

title: Your Basic Habitability Duties
bodyText: Except when prevented by an act of God, a failure of public utility services or other conditions beyond your control, Kansas requires you to: comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety; take reasonable care of common areas; keep the electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning systems you supply in good and safe working order; provide trash receptacles and arrange removal, unless a government entity does; and supply running water and reasonable hot water and heat, unless the building isn't required by law to have them or the unit's heat or hot water comes from a tenant-controlled installation on a direct utility connection. You also can't interfere with or refuse a tenant access to a municipally franchised cable or communication service (K.S.A. 58-2553(a)). See the note on when you can shift some of these duties to the tenant.

title: Domestic Violence, Sexual Assault, Trafficking and Stalking: Housing Protections
bodyText: Kansas protects a tenant or applicant who has been, is, or is in imminent danger of becoming a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, human trafficking or stalking within the preceding 12 months (K.S.A. 58-25,137). You can't deny tenancy to, evict, or find a lease violation against that person based on that status if they otherwise qualify. A tenant who asks to end the lease early under this protection owes no rent after moving out, though you may charge a reasonable early-termination fee of up to one month's rent, and you may ask for supporting documentation as the law allows. The lease continues for any remaining co-tenants. Neither side can waive these rights. See the note on the consequences of violating this protection.

title: If You Can't Deliver Possession on Time
bodyText: If you fail to deliver possession as the lease requires, rent abates until you do, and the tenant may either end the lease on at least 5 days' written notice, in which case you return the full deposit, or demand that you perform, sue for possession against you or anyone wrongfully in possession, and recover damages. If your failure is willful and not in good faith, the tenant can recover up to 1.5 times the periodic rent or 1.5 times actual damages, whichever is greater (K.S.A. 58-2560).

title: Fire or Casualty: The Tenant's Options
bodyText:
If fire or casualty damages the property enough to substantially impair its use and habitability, the tenant may move out immediately and notify you in writing within 5 days that they are ending the lease, which then ends on the date they moved out; or, if continued occupancy is lawful, vacate only the unusable part and pay rent reduced in proportion to the drop in the property's fair rental value (K.S.A. 58-2562). If the lease ends this way, return the part of the deposit the tenant is entitled to and account for rent as of the date they moved out.

One asymmetry is worth your attention: this casualty right has no tenant-fault exception. Kansas puts one in the habitability track — a tenant may not terminate under K.S.A. 58-2559 for a condition caused by or attributable to the tenant, or to anyone or any pet on the premises with the tenant's permission — but K.S.A. 58-2562 contains nothing like it. So a tenant whose own negligence caused the fire can still vacate and terminate, and can still have rent reduced for the part of the home rendered unusable. You cannot take that away by lease: a term removing it would be a waiver of a right under the Act. What you can do is hold the tenant liable for the damage they caused, which is a separate claim.

title: No Rule on Algorithmic Rent-Setting
bodyText: Kansas has no statute on setting rents with algorithmic pricing software, and none on sharing rent or occupancy data with other landlords or with a pricing service. Federal and state antitrust law and the Kansas Consumer Protection Act still apply to the conduct itself, and Kansas cannot be overridden locally on the rent amount: K.S.A. 12-16,120 bars any county, city or township from controlling what rent you charge, so a city cannot answer this question either.

title: No Statute Treating Fees as Rent
bodyText: Kansas's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act defines rent as all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement, other than the security deposit (K.S.A. 58-2543), so on the statute's own words a fee the lease makes payable to you can count as rent. No Kansas statute speaks more specifically to a late fee or a utility charge, so how the lease describes a fee still matters. That matters because Kansas's three-day pay-or-quit notice runs on unpaid rent (K.S.A. 58-2564(b)): calling fees 'additional rent' is how some leases try to reach them, and an eviction resting on unpaid fees rather than unpaid rent is untested in Kansas. This library's clauses do not label fees as rent, and the Tenant Default clause says plainly that failing to pay an assessed late fee, apart from the rent itself, is not by itself a ground to terminate or evict.

title: No Statutory Covenant of Quiet Possession
bodyText: No Kansas statute gives a residential tenant a covenant of quiet possession or quiet enjoyment. Kansas's one statutory use of the phrase runs the other way: K.S.A. 58-2555 makes it the tenant's duty not to engage in, or allow any person or pet on the premises to engage in, conduct that will disturb the quiet and peaceful enjoyment of the premises by other tenants. So the statutory right belongs to the neighbours, not to the tenant complaining about you. A tenant's protection against your interference comes instead from the habitability duty (K.S.A. 58-2553), the lockout and utility-shutoff remedy (K.S.A. 58-2563), the entry limits (K.S.A. 58-2557) and Kansas common law, not from a statutory covenant.

title: No Statutory Right to Cure a Tenant's Breach and Bill It as Rent
bodyText: Kansas gives you no statute letting you fix a tenant's breach — damage, a maintenance failure, an unremoved hazard — and add the cost to the next month's rent as rent. Several URLTA states have that right; Kansas did not adopt it. What you have instead is the notice-and-cure route in K.S.A. 58-2564(a), your claim for actual damages under K.S.A. 58-2568, and the security deposit under K.S.A. 58-2550. The practical difference matters: a cost you bill as rent can support a three-day pay-or-quit notice, while the same cost as damages cannot, so doing the work yourself and charging it does not give you an eviction route for nonpayment.

title: No Statutory Rule on Blank Spaces in a Lease
bodyText: Kansas has no statute requiring every blank in a residential lease to be filled in before signing, and no statute making a blank a breach or a deceptive practice. Fill them in anyway. Two Kansas rules bite on an incomplete lease from different directions: a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable lease or term (K.S.A. 58-2544), and where a lease is never signed and delivered but the parties act on it, K.S.A. 58-2546 gives it effect for no longer than one year whatever term the document states. A blank left for later also invites the K.S.A. 58-2570(e) problem, where a document you hand the tenant to sign adds terms the lease does not contain.

title: The One Form of Words Kansas Puts in Your Hands
bodyText: Kansas prescribes one piece of verbatim text a landlord may have to use, and it is not in the lease. Under K.S.A. 58-2570(e), if you give a tenant a document which, signed, would be the tenant's written notice that they intend to vacate, and that document contains any additional terms not contained in the rental agreement, the document must include this statement in no less than ten-point boldface type: 'YOUR SIGNATURE ON THIS DOCUMENT MAY BIND YOU TO ADDITIONAL TERMS NOT IN YOUR ORIGINAL LEASE AGREEMENT. IF YOUR LEASE REQUIRES YOU TO GIVE WRITTEN NOTICE OF YOUR INTENT TO VACATE, YOU HAVE THE RIGHT TO DECLINE TO SIGN THIS DOCUMENT AND TO PROVIDE WRITTEN NOTICE IN ANOTHER FORM.' Leave it out and the tenant's signature does not bind them to any of those additional terms. The way to avoid the problem is to put your move-out terms in the lease itself, because then they are not additional terms and no statement is needed. Kansas supplies no statutory lease form, no notice-to-quit form and no deposit-accounting form; the three-day notice content comes from K.S.A. 61-3803 and 58-2564(b), not from a form.

title: No Rule on Tenant Security Cameras or Video Doorbells
bodyText: No Kansas statute says whether a tenant may install a security camera or a video doorbell, so the lease controls, including its alterations terms where mounting hardware is involved. Two Kansas points are worth knowing. A device that records sound is a different question from one that only records pictures, and Kansas's eavesdropping statute reaches recording a private conversation without the consent of a party to it, so a doorbell capturing audio in a shared hallway or a neighbour's doorway can raise an issue a video-only device does not. And nothing here limits your own entry rules: you still owe reasonable notice at reasonable hours under K.S.A. 58-2557, and a tenant's camera does not change that.

title: Waiver of Collection Exemptions
bodyText:
Kansas law lets a tenant waive, in writing, the benefit of this state's exemption laws for debts contracted for rent (K.S.A. 58-2530), and the lease can be that writing.

What the waiver reaches matters: K.S.A. 60-2304 exempts from seizure and sale a person's household furnishings, equipment and supplies including food, fuel and clothing reasonably necessary at the residence; ornaments of the person including jewelry up to $1,000; one vehicle up to $20,000, with no limit where the vehicle is designed or equipped for a person with a disability; a burial plot; and the tools and other means of production of a trade or business up to $7,500 in total.

The library offers an optional waiver clause ("Waiver of Personal Property Exemptions" clause), off by default, and it deliberately reaches only the jewelry, the vehicle and the business tools. It leaves the household basics alone, because that is the term a court is most likely to refuse, and refusing it could cost you the whole clause.

Three things a waiver cannot do, whatever the lease says. It cannot reach wages: Kansas caps wage garnishment at the lesser of 25% of disposable earnings or the amount above 30 times the federal minimum hourly wage (K.S.A. 60-2310), and federal law caps it as well (15 U.S.C. 1673). It cannot reach a homestead, which under K.S.A. 60-2301 and the Kansas Constitution cannot be given up without the joint consent of husband and wife where that relation exists — and a tenant who owns a manufactured or mobile home on a rented lot may hold one. And it cannot reach pensions, public assistance, workers compensation, unemployment benefits, crime-victims awards or insurance proceeds, each of which is exempt under its own statute (K.S.A. 60-2313).

A court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable lease provision or limit it (K.S.A. 58-2544), with the Consumer Protection Act's unconscionability standard in the background (K.S.A. 50-627).

This is a collection term aimed at the tenant that many residential leases leave out, so use it only as a deliberate choice.

title: Renting an Accessory Dwelling Unit: Kansas Speeds Up Approval, It Does Not Give You the Right
bodyText: Kansas legislated on accessory dwelling units in 2026, but read carefully what it did.
