The by-right housing development act says its purpose is to streamline approval for by-right housing development, including single-family homes, townhouses and accessory dwelling units, and it defines an accessory dwelling unit as a secondary housing unit subordinate to the primary dwelling unit on the same lot, which may include a separate kitchen, bathroom and entrance. If your project meets the act's definition of a by-right housing development and the criteria in the local zoning code and land use regulations, it must be approved as a matter of right, without discretionary review or approval by a planning commission, zoning board or other regulatory body, and your complete application is deemed approved unless it is denied within 30 days of receipt — 60 days if it needs a subdivision plat, 90 days if the plat covers more than 40 single-family homes. To qualify, the project must need no federal or state discharge permit or stormwater drainage study, must not increase impervious surface so as to affect drainage into a special flood hazard area, must not sit in a National Register district or otherwise be subject to historic preservation review, and any required public infrastructure extension must already be done, unnecessary, or a condition you have agreed to; a townhouse project is capped at 12 attached units. Here is what the act does not do. It does not entitle you to an accessory dwelling unit on a lot where the zoning code does not allow one — the by-right approval runs only to projects that comply with the established land use regulations. It does not bar an owner-occupancy requirement, does not set a minimum size or parking rule, and says nothing at all about renting the unit out or about short-term rental. And it expressly leaves private restrictions alone: nothing in it invalidates or limits the legality, enforceability or effect of restrictive covenants or condominium or homeowners association regulations, and courts are directed to recognize and enforce them. Two neighbouring changes help. All land inside a city's corporate limits that is zoned for any type of residential use is now also considered zoned for single-family residential use, subject to reasonable setback, development, utility, subdivision and platting rules. And for new single-family residences under 2,500 square feet of livable floor area on their own lot, every city and county must allow the 2018 International Residential Code, single-car garages, architectural finish on one side only, and a minimum lot size of 3,000 square feet subject to reasonable setbacks, with any conflicting local code provision null and void as applied. Practical course: confirm in writing with the city or county that the use is permitted and that no owner-occupancy or short-term-rental condition applies, keep the date you filed a complete application because the 30-day clock is your best protection, and check the recorded covenants and any association declaration before you build or advertise.

title: No Agreed Actual-Notice Method — and Why a Text Will Not Serve a Statutory Notice
bodyText: Kansas has no "actual notice" rule for residential tenancies and no provision letting you and the tenant agree on an extra method, such as a text message, that counts as statutory notice. The Kansas Residential Landlord and Tenant Act does not define notice at all, and nothing in it validates an agreed substitute. Two limits follow. First, where a statute names the method, that method controls: a notice terminating a lease or tenancy must be served on the tenant, or by leaving a copy at the tenant's usual place of residence, or by delivering a copy to a person over 12 years of age residing on the premises, or, if nobody is found on the premises, by posting a copy conspicuously there, or by registered mail or certified mail with return receipt requested addressed to the tenant's usual place of residence. Second, Kansas's electronic transactions act says in terms that where another law requires a record to be sent by a specified method, it must be sent by that method, and that this requirement cannot be varied by agreement — the one exception is a first-class-mail requirement, which is not what the termination statute says. So a lease clause making a text or an e-mail the agreed way to serve a statutory notice will not hold, and requiring the tenant to accept it instead of the statutory method risks being an unenforceable waiver of rights under the act. For ordinary lease notices that no statute governs, you may agree on a method, including electronic delivery, if both sides have in fact agreed to deal electronically and the record can be retained and printed by the person receiving it. The safe practice is to keep an agreed electronic channel for routine communication and serve every statutory notice the statutory way, keeping the affidavit or the return receipt as proof.

title: Claims Against the Property: Attornment Is Void, but No Statute Makes the Tenant Tell You
bodyText:
If someone other than you claims the property or the rent, Kansas protects your position in two ways. A tenant's attornment to a stranger — agreeing to hold the premises under that person or to pay rent to them — is void and does not affect your possession, unless you consented or it is pursuant to a judgment at law or the order or decree of a court. And when you convey the property, the conveyance is valid without the tenant attorning to the buyer, though rent the tenant pays you before the tenant is given notice of the sale is good against the buyer.

What Kansas does not do is require the tenant to tell you about a lawsuit, foreclosure, tax proceeding or other claim against the property. There is no Kansas counterpart to the states that impose that duty by statute, so the only way to get it is to put it in the lease.

Practical effect: if a stranger serves papers on your tenant or demands the rent, the tenant's cooperation with that stranger does not cost you possession, but you may not learn about the proceeding in time unless your lease requires the tenant to forward it.

title: No Alarm Tampering Fee — Charge Your Actual Cost Instead
bodyText: No Kansas statute authorizes or caps a fee for a tenant who removes, disables or tampers with a smoke detector, and Kansas requires no carbon monoxide alarm at all, so there is no fee to attach to one. Kansas also has no criminal tampering offense aimed at smoke alarms. What you can recover is your actual cost. A tenant is responsible by statute for any destruction, defacement, damage, impairment or removal of any part of the premises caused by the tenant or by anyone on the premises with the tenant's permission, so the cost of repairing or replacing a detector the tenant pulled down, painted over or disabled is ordinary damages for breach, and it can be deducted from the security deposit as an itemized charge. Keep three things in mind when you write the charge. Charge the cost, not a flat penalty: a residential lease is a consumer transaction in Kansas and an unconscionable practice in connection with one violates the Consumer Protection Act, with a lease term that is excessively one-sided in the supplier's favor named among the circumstances a court weighs. Do not dress the charge up as indemnity or as a limitation of your own liability, because the act forbids a rental agreement in which either party agrees to exculpate or limit liability or to indemnify the other for it. And do not frame the charge as a penalty for failing to maintain the alarm: inside a rental unit the statutory duty to test and maintain is the tenant's, but evidence of an occupant's failure to properly maintain a detector is inadmissible in any action for the purpose of determining any aspect of civil liability, so a maintenance-failure charge may be unprovable where a damage-or-removal charge is not. For scale, the state's own penalty for failing to place or maintain a detector is a misdemeanor with a fine capped at $25. Local fire codes can add requirements on top of the state act, so check the city or county.

title: Animals Left in a Rental — Kansas Gives You No Entry or Custody Right
bodyText:
Kansas gives you no special right to enter a unit to check on, feed or remove a tenant's animal, and no procedure for taking custody of an animal a tenant leaves behind. You are left with the ordinary entry rules: you may enter at reasonable hours after reasonable notice to inspect, make necessary or agreed repairs or improvements, supply necessary or agreed services, or show the unit; you may enter without the tenant's consent only in case of an extreme hazard involving the potential loss of life or severe property damage; and you may not abuse the right of access or use it to harass the tenant.

Do not assume an animal in distress is itself an extreme hazard involving potential loss of life — that phrase reads as aimed at human life and severe damage to the building, and no Kansas case or statute settles whether an animal's life counts. The cautious course is to get the tenant's advance written consent in the lease, naming the person you may let in, and otherwise to call law enforcement or the local animal control agency and let them act rather than entering on your own judgment.

Kansas gives those officers the power you do not have. A public health officer, a law enforcement officer, a licensed veterinarian or an officer or agent of an animal shelter or other appropriate facility may take into custody any animal, on private or public property, that clearly shows evidence of cruelty to animals, and may inspect, care for or treat it or place it with a shelter or a veterinarian; the owner must be notified in writing, and after 21 days ownership can be transferred by court order unless the owner posts and keeps renewing a bond covering the cost of care.

Cruelty to animals includes knowingly abandoning an animal anywhere without making provisions for its proper care, which is what a tenant who walks out and leaves an animal behind has done, and the offence is a class A nonperson misdemeanor for a first conviction. That is the route to use. It also carries a warning for you: the same offence covers having physical custody of an animal and knowingly failing to provide the food, water, protection from the elements, exercise and other care that kind of animal needs. So if you do take an animal in, you have assumed that duty, and handing it to a shelter or a veterinarian promptly is safer than keeping it yourself.

Two other limits matter. If the tenant is away more than 30 days you may enter at times reasonably necessary, which is far too late to help an animal. And the statute for property a tenant abandons — 30 days of storage at the tenant's expense, newspaper publication, then sale or disposal — is written for household goods and furnishings and is not a workable or humane route for a living animal.

Finally, none of this reaches an assistance dog: a person who is legally blind, deaf or hard of hearing, or who has a disability and uses a guide, hearing assistance or service dog, has the right to that dog in the acquisition and use of rental residential housing without being required to pay an extra charge, though the person is liable for damage the dog does to the premises.

title: Asbestos in Rentals: No Disclosure Duty, but the Work Is Licensed
bodyText: No Kansas statute requires you to tell a tenant or an applicant that a rental contains asbestos, to inspect a rental for it, or to give a tenant notice before asbestos work. Nothing in the residential landlord and tenant act mentions asbestos at all. What Kansas regulates is the work, and only a defined slice of it. Under the Kansas asbestos control act, no business entity may engage in an asbestos project unless it holds a license from the secretary of health and environment, and a city may not accept a bid to remove or encapsulate asbestos-containing material from anyone without that license or certificate. An asbestos project means an activity undertaken to remove or encapsulate friable asbestos containing materials, and friable asbestos containing material means material containing more than 1% asbestos by weight, applied to ceilings, walls, structural members, piping, ductwork or any other part of a building, which when dry may be crumbled, pulverized or reduced to powder by hand pressure. Two things follow for a landlord. Leaving intact, non-friable asbestos alone is not an asbestos project at all, so the licensing duty never arises — which is another reason not to disturb it. And the moment the material is friable and you remove or encapsulate it, the act is engaged unless the own-employee exemption below applies. A licensee must keep a record of each project for at least three years — who supervised it and who worked on it, the location and description and the amount of asbestos removed, the start and completion dates of each removal or encapsulation, how it complied with the standards, and the disposal site — and must notify the secretary of the date the project is to begin. There is one exemption that matters to landlords: the act does not apply to a business entity that uses its own employees to remove or encapsulate asbestos for the purpose of renovating, maintaining, repairing or demolishing the entity's own facilities. So if your own staff do the work on your own buildings, the state licensing act does not reach you. Treat that as a licensing exemption and nothing more. FEDERAL: the EPA asbestos work-practice and notification rules and the OSHA asbestos standard apply to the work and to your employees regardless of the state exemption, and the federal lead-paint disclosure rule, which Kansas rentals built before 1978 must follow, has no asbestos counterpart. Practical course: do not create a disclosure obligation you do not have by guessing about asbestos in writing; if you know of asbestos-containing material, say what you actually know, leave it undisturbed, warn the tenant not to drill, sand or remove it, and use a licensed contractor rather than relying on the own-employee exemption. What counts as asbestos-containing material is fixed by statute — friable, and more than one percent asbestos by weight — while the work practices that govern how it must be handled in an occupied building sit in state regulations, which require isolation of the work area, posted warning signs, exclusion of everyone without a job to do there, and a hold on re-entry, but which do not require you to notify the tenant.

title: No Association Disclosure Duty — but the Tenant Is Bound Anyway
bodyText:
Kansas requires no association disclosure in a lease. Nothing makes you give a tenant the declaration, the bylaws or the rules, nothing makes you name a maintenance contact for the unit or the common areas, and nothing makes a developer tell a tenant that the unit sits in a common interest community. Kansas has no operative public offering statement or resale certificate requirement either — the common interest owners bill of rights act mentions both in passing, but it contains no section that actually requires one, for a buyer or for a tenant.

What Kansas does have is the opposite problem. Under the apartment ownership act, every apartment owner, every tenant of such an owner, their employees and anyone who in any manner uses property submitted to that act is subject to the act and to the declaration and bylaws adopted under it, and every lawful decision of the association of apartment owners binds all apartment owners. So in a condominium created under that act the tenant is bound by documents the tenant may never have seen, and you are the one who holds them.

The newer Kansas common interest owners bill of rights act reaches further than it looks. It applies to every common interest community containing twelve or more units that may be used for residential purposes — not only those created after it took effect on 1 January 2011, but also those created before, prospectively. For an older community it does not invalidate the existing declaration, bylaws, plats or plans and does not reach decisions about events before that date, but a provision of the declaration or bylaws that is contrary to the act's mandatory provisions cannot be enforced as to anything happening after it, and the older documents may be amended to achieve any result the act permits. Its provisions are mandatory: except where the act itself says otherwise, they apply notwithstanding anything contrary in the declaration or bylaws and cannot be varied or waived by agreement, and where the act conflicts with other Kansas law the act prevails. Communities of fewer than twelve such units are outside it and run on their own recorded declaration, the apartment ownership act or the townhouse ownership act.

Two things in that act reach your tenant directly, and they cut the landlord's way. The association may suspend a unit owner's rights and privileges for unpaid assessments, but it may not deny the owner or any other occupant access to the unit, and it may not withhold a service it provides to the unit or the owner where withholding it would endanger anyone's health, safety or property. So an association cannot lock your tenant out or cut off a safety-related service because you are behind on assessments. And if the declaration requires votes on specified matters to be cast by lessees rather than by owners of leased units, then as to those matters the act treats the lessee as the unit owner: you may not vote on them, and your tenant is entitled to notice of meetings, access to records and the other rights that go with them. Check the declaration before you assume the vote is yours.

Practical course: even though no statute requires it, give the tenant a copy of the rules, the declaration and the recorded covenants that limit use and occupancy, get a signed acknowledgment, and tell the tenant in writing whenever the association changes them. That is what makes the restrictions you will be asked to enforce actually enforceable against a tenant in practice, and it is the only reliable way to avoid being fined for conduct your tenant never knew was prohibited.

Keep the association's own rules in view too. As a general matter its enforcement powers and its notice duties run to unit owners rather than to your tenant — notice of meetings, the records right and the rule-change notice are all owner-facing — which is exactly why the tenant learns the rules only from you. The two exceptions above are the occupant-access and health-and-safety-service protections, and the lessee-voting case where the declaration provides for it.

title: Kansas Bans Attorney-Fee Clauses Outright — Don't Draft One
bodyText: Do not put an attorney-fee clause in a Kansas residential lease. No rental agreement may provide that the tenant or landlord agrees to pay either party's attorneys' fees. The ban runs both ways and has no exceptions, so there is nothing to fix by making the clause mutual: a prevailing-party fee clause is just as void as a landlord-only one. Kansas does not need a reciprocity rule, because no fee clause of any kind survives. A prohibited provision is unenforceable, and if you deliberately use a rental agreement containing provisions you know are prohibited, the tenant can recover the actual damages the tenant suffers — so leaving a boilerplate fee clause in a form lease you reuse is a live risk, not a harmless one. With no clause available, fees follow the ordinary Kansas rule: each side pays its own unless a statute awards them. The costs a court can tax do not include attorney fees; the list is docket fees, service and process-server expenses, publication charges, witness fees and mileage, deposition and reporter charges, postage under the service statute, alternative-dispute-resolution fees, payment convenience and electronic-filing fees, and other charges a statute authorizes to be taxed as costs. Statutes that can award fees in matters a landlord may find itself in: if you lose a small claims case and the other side wins the appeal, the court must award the successful appellee reasonable attorney fees as part of the costs; in a Consumer Protection Act case, where a residential lease is a consumer transaction and you are the supplier, the court may award reasonable fees including on appeal to a consumer who proves a violation, or to you if the consumer brought or maintained an action the consumer knew to be groundless; a contempt proceeding against a judgment debtor can carry the judgment creditor's reasonable fees; and a party who wrongly denies a request for admission can be ordered to pay the reasonable expenses of proving the point, including fees. Under the 2026 Removal of Squatters Act, an owner or agent who wrongly uses the affidavit route faces actual costs and damages plus punitive damages of triple the fair market rent of the dwelling, court costs and reasonable attorney fees. None of these depends on the lease, and none can be created or enlarged by it.

title: Automatic Renewal Is Allowed in Kansas, With No Notice or Formatting Rule
bodyText:
Kansas has no automatic-renewal statute for residential leases. There is no requirement to remind the tenant of a renewal clause before the term ends, no boldface or type-size rule for the clause itself, no requirement that the tenant opt in affirmatively, and no consumer negative-option statute that reaches a lease. An automatic-renewal clause is therefore simply a lease term, permitted because the parties may include terms not prohibited by the residential landlord and tenant act or another rule of law, and nothing on the act's list of prohibited terms touches renewal.

Four drafting points follow. First, say what the renewal term is. If the lease does not fix a definite term, the tenancy is month-to-month by default — week-to-week for a roomer who pays weekly rent — and either side can end it on the statutory notice.

Second, a renewal for a definite term of more than 30 days is not a month-to-month tenancy, even though rent is payable at 30-day intervals, so a renewal clause that rolls the lease into a further fixed term locks both sides in for that term rather than leaving a 30-day exit. Decide deliberately which of those you want.

Third, if renewal is to run beyond one year from the agreement, keep it in the signed writing: a lease or interest in land exceeding one year must be in writing signed by the party granting it. Where a tenant simply holds over with your assent after a term of a year or more, the law makes the tenant a tenant from year to year rather than renewing the written lease.

Fourth, watch the one Kansas formatting rule in this area. It is not about the renewal clause: if you hand a tenant a document that would serve as the tenant's written notice of intent to vacate and it contains any terms not in the rental agreement, that document must carry a specific statutory warning in no less than ten-point boldface type, and without it the tenant's signature does not bind the tenant to the added terms. Never use a move-out or renewal-election form to slip in new terms.

title: No Balcony Inspection Mandate — but the Common-Area Duty Still Bites
bodyText: Kansas has no statute requiring periodic inspection of balconies, decks, porches, walkways or exterior stairs in rental buildings. There is no Kansas counterpart to the states that make an owner hire an architect, engineer or certified inspector on a fixed cycle, and no state registry, report or filing. The word balcony appears once in the whole of Kansas's statutes, and only to say that a balcony serving a single condominium unit is a limited common area belonging to that unit. What does apply is the ordinary landlord duty, and it is enough to carry real liability. You must comply with applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, and where that duty is greater than any other it governs; and you must exercise reasonable care in the maintenance of the common areas — which is where a shared balcony, deck, landing or exterior stair sits. On top of that, the state fire marshal's rules reach the construction and maintenance of exits and fire escapes in buildings where people live, though not in a building used wholly as a dwelling house containing no more than two families, and the Kansas fire prevention code has uniform force statewide: a city may not enact or enforce an ordinance inconsistent with it, except in exercising its zoning or fire-district powers. In 2026 the legislature directed the fire marshal to update that code to the International Fire Code, 2024 edition, so the detailed standards for elevated exterior elements are in the adopted code and the fire marshal's regulations rather than in any statute. Kansas's own design and construction standards apply only to a dwelling built with public financial assistance, and a 2026 act narrowed what counts as public financial assistance; none of it requires inspection of an existing balcony. Practical course: treat elevated wood structures as the highest-risk thing you own. Put them on a written inspection schedule of your own — at least annually, and after any heavy snow, ice or wind — looking for soft or rotted framing where the structure ties into the building, rust on fasteners and connectors, loose or low railings, and standing water. Document each inspection and each repair, keep the records, and have a licensed engineer look at any structure you are unsure about. Also check the city or county: a local building, housing or rental-licensing ordinance can impose an inspection duty the state does not, and that is a question for your locality, not one this answer settles. As of 2026-10-24 the fire marshal has not carried that direction out: K.A.R. 22-1-3 still adopts the International Fire Code 2006 edition and the International Building Code 2006 edition, and K.A.R. 22-1-2 accepts in the alternative the 1997 Uniform Building Code or the 2006 IBC with a certificate of occupancy. Those 2006 editions are the standard in force.

title: No Bed Bug Statute — Where the Pest Duty Actually Comes From in Kansas
bodyText:
Kansas has no bed bug statute. The words bed bug appear nowhere in Kansas law, and there is no duty to inspect, no duty to treat on a timetable, no tenant cooperation mandate, and no statutory cost allocation.

Note also what the residential landlord and tenant act does not contain: Kansas has no general warranty that a rental be fit for human habitation. The landlord's duties are a specific list — comply with applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, exercise reasonable care in maintaining the common areas, keep the electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning appliances you supply in good and safe working order, provide common waste receptacles and arrange removal, and supply running water, reasonable hot water and reasonable heat. Pest control is not named.

That makes the codes limb the one that matters, and it is defined broadly: a building and housing code means any law, ordinance or governmental regulation concerning fitness for habitation or the construction, maintenance, operation, occupancy, use or appearance of premises or a dwelling unit. So a local rule becomes your statutory duty.

Three places that happens in Kansas. A county served by a local health department may adopt a sanitary code, and the subjects it may reach expressly include insects and rodents and housing. A city may treat vermin infestation as a condition making a structure unsafe, unsanitary or detrimental to the neighborhood, which can trigger a repair, closing or demolition ordinance against the owner. And the same vermin-infestation language appears in the municipal housing-rehabilitation authority.

Two tenant-side rules shape the rest. A tenant who gives you written notice of a condition that is a noncompliance materially affecting health and safety can terminate on not less than 30 days' notice, but not if you adequately initiate a good faith effort to remedy it within 14 days of receiving the notice — and the tenant may not terminate at all for a condition caused by the tenant or by any person, animal or pet on the premises with the tenant's permission. The tenant must also keep the part of the premises the tenant occupies as clean and safe as its condition permits, remove waste, and bear responsibility for damage the tenant or the tenant's guests or pets cause.

Practical course: because nothing is statutory, put reporting, access for inspection and treatment, preparation instructions and cost allocation in the lease, respond to any written pest notice inside the 14-day window, use a licensed applicator, and check your county's sanitary code and your city's housing code, because that is where a Kansas pest obligation will actually come from.

title: Arbitration Clauses in Kansas Leases — Why the Library Does Not Offer One
bodyText: No Kansas statute deals with arbitration clauses in residential leases. Unlike some states, Kansas does not say that a landlord and tenant may agree to arbitrate disputes arising out of the rental agreement, does not say that an action for possession must stay in court anyway, and does not preserve the right to be represented by counsel. Kansas does have a general arbitration statute, the revised uniform arbitration act, which the legislature put in place of the older act in 2018. That act has now been read. It governs any agreement to arbitrate made on or after July 1, 2018, and an earlier one only if all parties agree in the record. An arbitration agreement contained in a record, covering any existing or later controversy between the parties, is valid, enforceable and irrevocable except on a ground that exists at law or in equity for revoking a contract — and the act carves out no category of claim, so Kansas does not exclude tort or personal-injury claims from arbitration the way some states do. Before a controversy arises, which is exactly when a lease is signed, the act makes certain things non-waivable: the parties may not vary the rules on applying to a court for relief, on the validity of the agreement itself, on provisional remedies, on witnesses and subpoenas, on the court's jurisdiction or on appeals; may not unreasonably restrict the right to notice that an arbitration has been started or the right to an arbitrator's disclosure of facts; and may not waive a party's right to be represented by a lawyer. A lease arbitration clause that purported to do any of those things would be ineffective to that extent. The act also lets an arbitrator award attorney fees and expenses where the law would allow them in a civil action on the same claim or where the parties' agreement allows it, and lets a court add fees and expenses of a later court fight over the award; a fee award made under that act by a court or arbitrator is not a lease term, so it does not collide with the separate Kansas ban on a rental agreement requiring either party to pay the other's attorney fees. Three Kansas-specific cautions matter more than the general act. First, no rental agreement may provide that the tenant or the landlord waives or foregoes rights or remedies under the residential landlord and tenant act. Such a provision is unenforceable, and a landlord who deliberately uses an agreement containing a provision known to be prohibited is liable for the tenant's actual damages. Whether a pre-dispute arbitration clause is such a waiver is genuinely unsettled in Kansas: the act defines an action to include any other proceeding in which rights are determined, which is an argument that an arbitration determining the act's rights is not a waiver at all — but no Kansas statute resolves it. Second, the act channels these disputes to court. The district court has jurisdiction over any landlord or tenant as to conduct governed by the act or any claim arising from a transaction subject to it, and such actions may be commenced under the code of civil procedure for limited actions, which governs unless the act specifically provides otherwise. Eviction runs on its own statutory track. Nothing gives a private arbitrator power to award possession or to issue the writ that removes anyone. Third, a court can refuse to enforce a rental agreement provision it finds unconscionable when made, and a residential lease is also a consumer transaction, where an excessively one-sided term is something a court weighs. Separately, and this is new, Kansas now builds dispute resolution into the eviction case itself rather than into the lease: in an eviction where the rental agreement is governed by the residential landlord and tenant act, the court must consider mediation unless it finds that mediation would not materially aid the parties or is impracticable, and must grant a continuance of not more than 14 days from the mediation order if the parties are participating. The cautious course, and the library's position: do not put a binding arbitration clause in a Kansas residential lease. If you use one anyway, never let it reach an action for possession, never let it purport to cut off a remedy the act gives the tenant, and never let it waive the right to counsel.

title: Cannabis Is Still Illegal in Kansas — What That Means for Your Lease
bodyText: Kansas has not legalized cannabis in any form — not recreationally, not medically. There is no Kansas medical cannabis programme, no patient or caregiver card, and therefore none of the landlord-facing rules other states have: nothing forbids you to refuse a tenancy or penalise a tenant over cardholder status, nothing requires you to allow non-smoked use inside a unit, nothing limits you to banning only smoking or only cultivation, and nothing makes a cultivation permission turn on the owner's written consent. Marijuana remains a controlled substance under Kansas law, and the legislature reaffirmed that in 2026 when it re-enacted the criminal-code definition: marijuana means all parts of all varieties of the plant Cannabis whether growing or not, the seeds, the resin extracted from any part of the plant, and every compound, manufacture, salt, derivative, mixture or preparation of the plant, its seeds or resin. The exclusions are narrow and worth knowing: mature stalks and products made from them, sterilized seed incapable of germination, substances in schedules II through V, drug products the federal Food and Drug Administration has approved, cannabidiol, and industrial hemp when cultivated, produced, possessed or used for activities the commercial industrial hemp act authorizes. So cannabidiol and authorized hemp are carved out of the definition; cannabis for use is not. Possession is still prosecutable, including in municipal court. A first marijuana-possession offence is a class B nonperson misdemeanour, a class A nonperson misdemeanour on one prior conviction, and a drug severity level 5 felony on two or more. The practical effect on your lease is the opposite of the problem landlords face in legal-cannabis states. You do not need a cannabis-specific clause to prohibit it, because a criminal-activity clause covering the illegal possession of a controlled substance already reaches it and a smoking policy already reaches the smoke. You also do not need to carve out medical use, because Kansas recognises no medical cannabis programme to carve out. There is one narrow Kansas exception, and it is not a programme: a person with a medically diagnosed chronic disease or condition causing serious impairment of strength or ability to function, or that person's parent or guardian, has an affirmative defence to a possession prosecution for a cannabidiol treatment preparation — an oil whose tetrahydrocannabinol concentration is no more than 5% of its cannabidiol concentration, verified by an accredited independent laboratory — provided the person carries a letter on the diagnosing Kansas physician's letterhead, signed and dated within the preceding fifteen months, and shows it to an officer on request. That is a defence in a criminal case, not a card, not a registry, and not a right against a landlord; and the statute says in terms that nothing in it allows the possession, sale, production, redistribution or use of any other form of cannabis. Two cautions. Do not treat cannabis as a ground for a faster eviction than Kansas allows: Kansas has no expedited criminal-eviction track, so the ordinary written notice and cure rules apply. And a tenant's possession of a lawful cannabidiol product or of authorized industrial hemp is not possession of marijuana under the Kansas definition, so do not write a rule or send a notice that treats it as a lease violation. FEDERAL: cannabis also remains a federally controlled substance, which matters independently if your property is federally assisted.

title: No Carpet Cleaning Rule — and No Wear-and-Tear Standard Either
bodyText:
Kansas has no statute on carpet cleaning at move-out. Nothing lets you require professional cleaning as a matter of law, nothing forbids a lease term requiring it, and no statute conditions such a term on having had the carpets professionally cleaned before the tenancy.

Something more surprising is also missing: Kansas has no statutory normal wear and tear standard. The phrase appears nowhere in the residential landlord and tenant act. What the act gives you instead is the tenant's duty to keep the part of the premises the tenant occupies and uses as clean and safe as the condition of the premises permits, and the tenant's responsibility for any destruction, defacement, damage, impairment or removal of any part of the premises caused by the tenant or by any person, animal or pet on the premises with the tenant's permission.

So a carpet charge in Kansas has to be grounded either in that statutory duty or in a lease term, and the practical answer is to do both: say it in the lease, and record the carpets' condition on the joint move-in inventory the act already requires you and the tenant to complete within five days of occupancy.

The deposit route is open, and wider than in some states. On termination the deposit may be applied to accrued rent and the amount of damages you have suffered by reason of the tenant's noncompliance with the tenant-duties section and the rental agreement, all itemized in a written notice delivered to the tenant. Because the statute names the rental agreement as well as the statutory duties, a cleaning obligation the lease creates can be deducted — but only as damages you actually suffered, itemized, and within the deadlines: return the balance within 14 days of determining the amount and in no event more than 30 days after termination, delivery of possession and the tenant's demand, and if the tenant makes no demand within 30 days, mail it to the last known address. Get this wrong and the tenant recovers the amount due plus damages equal to one and a half times the amount wrongfully withheld.

Charge your actual reasonable cost with a receipt, never a flat carpet fee and never the cost of replacing a carpet that merely wore out.

title: Casualty and Mitigation Cannot Be Waived in a Kansas Lease
bodyText:
Both of these rules sit inside the Kansas Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, and the act's anti-waiver provision is flat: no rental agreement may provide that the tenant or the landlord agrees to waive or forego rights or remedies under the act. There is no exception for a right the parties both want to trade away, and no provision anywhere in the act that lets a particular right be waived expressly. So you cannot contract around either of the following.

First, casualty. If the dwelling unit or premises are damaged or destroyed by fire or casualty to an extent that the use and habitability of the dwelling unit is substantially impaired, the tenant may vacate immediately and must notify you in writing within five days afterwards of the intention to terminate, in which case the agreement terminates as of the date of vacating; or, if continued occupancy is lawful, the tenant may vacate any part of the unit rendered unusable, and the tenant's liability for rent is reduced in proportion to the diminution in the fair rental value of the unit. On termination you must return the portion of the deposit the tenant is entitled to, and rent is accounted for or apportioned as of the date of vacating.

Second, mitigation. If the tenant abandons the unit, you must make reasonable efforts to rent it at a fair rental. If you do not, the agreement is treated as terminated by you as of the date you had notice of the abandonment — which cuts off the rent you can claim.

A lease term purporting to waive either of these is unenforceable, and if you deliberately use a lease containing a provision you know is prohibited, the tenant can recover actual damages.

One structural point tells you how seriously to take this. Where the legislature meant a default rule to be alterable, it said so in the section itself: several provisions of the act begin or end with the words unless otherwise agreed, and that phrase appears nowhere in the casualty section or in the abandonment and re-rental duty.

What you may legitimately do is draft around the edges rather than through the middle: record the condition of the unit, require the written notice the statute already requires, state how a proportional rent reduction will be calculated and documented, and keep your own termination rights after a casualty in a separate clause. Do not write anything that shortens the tenant's five-day notice window, removes the proportional reduction, or releases you from re-letting after an abandonment.

title: No Occupancy Certificate Disclosure — and No State Rental Licence At All
bodyText: Kansas has no statute requiring you to tell a tenant whether the unit has a certificate of occupancy, to give the tenant a copy, or to state in the lease that one is or is not currently valid. Kansas also has no rent-barring rule of the kind some states use, under which no rent may be recovered for a period during which a building is occupied without a required certificate. And Kansas has no state rental licence or landlord registration scheme of any kind — that phrase appears nowhere in Kansas's statutes. Certificates of occupancy in Kansas are a local matter, issued under a city or county building code, and Kansas has not told localities to disclose them to tenants. The legislature has, however, put real limits on what a locality may do with residential inspections, and those limits are worth knowing. A city or county may not adopt, enforce or maintain a residential property licensing ordinance that includes a requirement for periodic interior inspections of privately owned residential property for code violations, unless the lawful occupant has consented. That bar does not apply to mixed-use residential and commercial property, and it does not stop a locality from carrying out plan reviews, periodic construction inspections or final occupancy inspections required by building permits. Separately, a lawful occupant may ask the city, or the county for unincorporated property, to inspect for code violations at any time — so your tenant can summon an inspection even where the locality cannot schedule one itself. On the permit side, Kansas now imposes deadlines on localities. A local government must approve or deny a building permit application for a single-family residential improvement and give written notice within 60 days of receiving a complete application, must tell the applicant within 15 days if the application is incomplete, and if it misses the 60-day deadline the application is deemed approved. It may not deny an application on the basis of a rule or ordinance adopted after the complete application was submitted, nor attach conditions from one adopted later. A 2026 act adds a streamlined by-right approval route for qualifying housing developments, and in a locality that elects into it, third-party review or inspection becomes available when the locality misses its own 30-day deadlines. Practical course: Kansas gives you nothing to disclose and no form of words to use, so get the certificate and keep it, because occupying without a required local certificate is a code problem with your locality rather than a statutory defence for your tenant. Check the city or county, because that is where every one of these requirements actually lives.

title: Families With Children: Protected in Kansas, but Occupancy Limits Survive
bodyText: Familial status is a protected class in Kansas housing. It means having one or more individuals less than 18 years of age domiciled with a parent or another person having legal custody, or with that person's designee holding written permission. So you may not refuse to rent, make a unit unavailable, or set different terms, conditions, privileges, services or facilities because a household includes children, and you may not publish or use any notice, statement or advertisement indicating a preference or limitation based on familial status. What survives is the occupancy limit. The Kansas Act Against Discrimination says expressly that nothing in it limits the applicability of any reasonable local, state or federal restriction on the maximum number of occupants permitted to occupy a dwelling. So a reasonable occupancy cap is lawful — but note what Kansas does not give you: there is no Kansas persons-per-bedroom figure, no statewide occupancy standard, and no safe harbour number. The restriction you rely on has to be a reasonable one from a local, state or federal source, not a number you invented. Write your occupancy limit by reference to the applicable local code and apply it to every occupant regardless of age, never as a rule about children. Kansas also requires no particular lease language about children; there is no required-content list for a Kansas lease, so nothing has to be said at all. Two exemptions matter. The familial-status protection does not apply to dwellings provided under a state or federal programme specifically designed and operated to assist elderly persons, or to housing for older persons, which Kansas defines as a community intended for and at least 80% occupied by at least one person 55 or older per unit while providing significant facilities and services designed for such persons, or a community intended for and occupied solely by persons 62 or older. And the act's general small-owner exemptions can apply: the sale or rental of a single-family house by an owner with an interest in no more than three such houses at a time, rented without a broker, agent, salesperson or anyone in the business of renting dwellings; and rooms or units in a building of no more than four families living independently where the owner actually maintains and occupies one of them as a residence. Those two exemptions do not reach the advertising prohibition, which still applies. FEDERAL: the federal Fair Housing Act protects familial status independently, with its own exemptions and its own occupancy-standard guidance, and it applies whether or not a Kansas exemption fits.

title: No Cold-Weather Vacate Notice — Use the Extended-Absence Route Instead
bodyText:
Kansas has no rule requiring a tenant to tell you before leaving the unit empty in cold weather. There is no seasonal window, no notice period, and no statute tying a vacancy notice to freezing pipes.

What Kansas gives you instead is a notice right the lease has to create. The rental agreement may require the tenant to notify you of any anticipated extended absence from the premises in excess of seven days, no later than the first day of the absence — and this is the part worth having: if your rental agreement contains that requirement and the tenant willfully fails to give the notice, you may recover actual damages from the tenant. The remedy is tied to the lease term, so a landlord who never wrote the requirement into the lease has no claim.

Entry while the unit is empty is narrower than most landlords expect. You may enter at reasonable hours after reasonable notice for the ordinary purposes, including to make necessary or agreed repairs; you may enter without the tenant's consent only in case of an extreme hazard involving the potential loss of life or severe property damage; and during any absence of the tenant in excess of 30 days you may enter at times reasonably necessary. Thirty days is far too long to help a pipe in January, so the seven-day notice requirement and a burst-pipe response plan matter more than the entry right does.

Practical course: use the extended-absence notice clause, and if you want winter-specific protection, add to your lease that the tenant will keep the heat on at a stated minimum temperature while the unit is occupied or vacant during the term, and will tell you before leaving the unit unoccupied in freezing weather. Both are contract terms, not statutory duties, so draft them as obligations with ordinary damages for breach — do not attach a fixed penalty, and do not write anything that purports to make the tenant responsible for a freeze caused by a heating system you were obliged to keep in good and safe working order.

One point of confusion to avoid: Kansas's Cold Weather Rule is a utility regulation about when a regulated utility may disconnect service in winter. It is not a tenant notice rule and it gives you nothing to enforce against a tenant who leaves.

title: Collection Fees: No Kansas Authorization, and the Attorney-Fee Limb Is Void
bodyText:
No Kansas statute authorizes a landlord to charge a tenant a collection fee, and none conditions one. Kansas also has no collection-agency licensing statute to hang such a fee on: the old Kansas collection agency act was repealed when the Consumer Protection Act was enacted and has not been replaced. So unlike states where a licensing statute both permits a collection fee and caps it, Kansas supplies neither the permission nor the ceiling. Nor is there any Kansas rule barring a fee on a past-due rent debt unless the lease expressly authorizes it — but write the authorization into the lease anyway, because a third-party collector's own federal obligations turn on whether the agreement authorizes the amount.

What Kansas does give you is a damages claim. On termination you may claim and sue for possession, or for rent, or both, and you may have a separate claim for actual damages for breach of the rental agreement, which you may file even before the termination date. Actual damages is the measure: what the collection effort actually cost you, proved, not a round number.

Now the trap, and it is specific to Kansas. No rental agreement may provide that the tenant or the landlord agrees to pay either party's attorneys' fees. A provision that does is unenforceable, and if you deliberately use a lease containing a provision you know is prohibited, the tenant can recover actual damages. Collection-fee clauses in other states commonly route the debt to a registered agency or a licensed attorney and make the tenant pay either one's charge. In Kansas the attorney limb of that sentence is void. Keep any collection-fee term to the amount a collection agency actually charges you, exclude attorney fees expressly, and let a court award litigation costs if it will.

Two more limits. A residential lease is a consumer transaction in Kansas, so an unconscionable act or practice in connection with it violates the Consumer Protection Act, and a term excessively one-sided in your favour is one of the circumstances a court weighs; a consumer cannot waive those protections. And a court may refuse to enforce a lease provision it finds unconscionable when made.

FEDERAL: the federal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act governs a third-party collection agency you hire, and it bars collecting an amount that is neither expressly authorized by the agreement creating the debt nor permitted by law — which is the practical reason to put the authorization in the lease and to keep it honest.

title: No Common-Area Lighting Standard — Only a Reasonable-Care Duty
bodyText:
Kansas has no statute that tells you how a hallway, stairway, entry or parking area must be lit, and no statute saying whether common-area lights may be wired to a tenant's own electric meter. What Kansas does impose is general: you must exercise reasonable care in the maintenance of the common areas, you must keep all electrical appliances you supply in good and safe working order, and you must comply with any building or housing code that materially affects health and safety.

That last duty is where a lighting standard will actually come from, and in Kansas it is more likely to be a state standard than a local one. The state fire marshal adopts the Kansas fire prevention code by regulation, that code has uniform force and effect throughout the state, and no municipality may enact or enforce an ordinance inconsistent with it. In 2026 the legislature directed that the code be updated to the International Fire Code, 2024 edition, and streamlined the rulemaking to get there. An egress-illumination standard for a common corridor or stairway is the kind of requirement that lives in that code rather than in any statute, so check the current Kansas fire prevention code, and the local housing code as well.

Two limits are worth knowing: the fire marshal's exit and fire-control regulations do not apply to a building used wholly as a dwelling house containing no more than two families, and a municipality keeps its power to zone and to run fire-district regulations. The fire marshal's regulation adopts the International Fire Code and International Building Code by reference without reproducing their text, so treat the content of any lighting standard as something to confirm with the fire marshal or the local code official, not as settled.

In a building that houses no more than four households with common areas, you may agree in writing that the tenant performs the trash-removal and water-and-heat duties plus specified repairs, but only in good faith and not to evade your obligations; in any building other than a single-family residence you may shift specified repair and maintenance tasks only by a separate signed agreement, supported by consideration, that does not cover work needed to meet a building or housing code and does not reduce what you owe other tenants. You cannot shift the reasonable-care duty for common areas itself.

Nothing in Kansas law stops you from putting common-area electricity on a tenant's bill, because the statute says the tenant's obligation to pay for utility service is whatever the rental agreement provides — but if that is your arrangement, say so in the lease before signing, identify the areas involved, and keep the deal to paying for power rather than maintaining the fixtures.

As of 2026-10-24 the fire marshal has not carried that direction out: K.A.R. 22-1-3 still adopts the International Fire Code 2006 edition and the International Building Code 2006 edition, and K.A.R. 22-1-2 accepts in the alternative the 1997 Uniform Building Code or the 2006 IBC with a certificate of occupancy. Those 2006 editions are the standard in force.

title: No Communal-Land Approval Requirement — but Tribal Trust Land Is Federal Ground
bodyText: Kansas has no communal, tribal or native land tenure system of its own, and no Kansas statute makes a residential lease wait on a government officer's approval before it is valid. A private owner leasing private land in Kansas needs no state or county sign-off; the lease binds when the parties sign it, subject only to the writing requirement for terms over one year. The nearest thing Kansas has to a communal body with a say over your lease is a common interest community — a condominium, townhouse or similar development whose owners share costs of common elements — and the Kansas statute governing those does not give the association any approval power over a lease. That statute applies to every such community containing twelve or more units that may be used for residential purposes, whether created before or after it took effect in 2011, and its provisions are mandatory: they apply notwithstanding anything contrary in the declaration or bylaws and cannot be varied or waived by agreement. Nowhere in it is there a requirement that an association approve, consent to or be notified of a lease, and the words landlord, tenant and rent do not appear in it at all. What can still bite is the declaration. If the recorded declaration itself restricts leasing, that restriction runs with the land and binds you as owner — so read the declaration before you let, not after. But the association cannot create such a restriction by rule after the fact. Rules affecting the use of or behaviour in units that may be used for residential purposes may be adopted only to implement a provision of the declaration, or to regulate behaviour in or occupancy of a unit that violates the declaration or adversely affects other owners' use and enjoyment, and every rule must be reasonable. Two further points about that act. A leasehold is not ownership under it, so your tenant is not a unit owner and the association's owner-facing machinery does not reach them — with one exception: if the declaration requires votes on specified matters to be cast by lessees rather than by owners of leased units, the act treats your tenant as the owner on those matters and bars you from voting on them. And whatever your arrears, the association may not deny your tenant access to the unit or withhold a service where withholding it would endanger anyone's health, safety or property. One situation does sit outside state law entirely. Kansas is home to four federally recognized tribes with land in the northeast corner of the state, and land held in trust or restricted status for a tribe or an individual Indian owner is federal ground: a lease of it is governed by federal statute and federal regulation, needs approval from the Bureau of Indian Affairs before it takes effect, and may also need tribal approval under the tribe's own leasing law. A tribe operating under federally approved tribal leasing regulations can approve residential leases itself without going to the Bureau. If the property you are leasing is on or near a reservation, confirm the land's title status before you sign anything: for trust or restricted land, do not take rent or give possession on an unapproved lease, and get the approval in writing. For land held in ordinary fee title, including fee land inside reservation boundaries, this does not apply and the lease is a normal Kansas lease.

title: No Statutory Rent Bar After Condemnation — What Actually Stops the Rent
bodyText: Kansas has no statute like Minnesota's or Washington's that forbids you to collect rent or hold a deposit once a unit has been condemned or ordered vacated, and no statutory treble-damages penalty for doing it. Kansas also has no statute barring you from renting out or advertising a placarded unit. What Kansas gives cities instead is condemnation power. A city may hold a hearing and order an unsafe or dangerous structure repaired or demolished, and if the enforcing officer finds an immediate hazard the officer may barricade the property or cause it to be vacated with no prior notice or hearing at all. Separately, a city that has adopted the enabling ordinance may have a public officer order a structure unfit for human use or habitation either repaired or vacated and closed, may set minimum standards for occupancy, and may prevent the use or occupancy of any structure injurious to public health or safety. The cost of any of this becomes a lien or a special assessment against your property. Four things do limit you even without a rent-bar statute. You must comply with building and housing codes that materially affect health and safety, and no lease, conveyance, trust deed or security instrument can let anyone receive the rent free of that duty. If the condition is a material noncompliance affecting health and safety, the tenant can give you written notice and terminate, and can sue for damages and an injunction whether or not the tenant terminates. If fire or casualty substantially impairs habitability, the tenant may vacate immediately and terminate within five days, or — only where continued occupancy is lawful — vacate the unusable part and pay rent reduced in proportion to the lost rental value; a closing order makes continued occupancy unlawful, so that second option is off the table. And on termination you must return the recoverable part of the deposit. The practical course: once a vacate, closing or demolition order lands, stop billing rent, do not re-let until the order is lifted, return the deposit under the normal deadlines, and treat the order as the end of your right to the rent rather than waiting for a statute to say so.

title: Confession of Judgment Is Flatly Banned in a Kansas Lease
bodyText: Kansas bans the clause outright. No residential rental agreement may provide that the tenant or the landlord authorizes any person to confess judgment on a claim arising out of the rental agreement. The ban runs both ways, so a lease cannot do this to either party. Two consequences follow. First, the provision is simply unenforceable — a court will not give it effect. Second, if you deliberately use a rental agreement containing provisions you know are prohibited, the tenant may recover actual damages. That second penalty is not limited to the confession clause: it attaches to deliberate use of any prohibited term, so an old form lease carrying a cognovit or confession paragraph is a live exposure, not a dead letter. Delete the paragraph rather than relying on it being void. There is a reason Kansas treats this harshly. In the limited actions code, which is where an eviction or a small rent claim is filed, a party may appeal from a final judgment except a judgment rendered on confession — so a confessed judgment is the one kind you cannot appeal. Collect rent and possession through the ordinary eviction process instead. Three related bans do not do this work for you and should not be cited in their place: a door-to-door sales contract may not contain a confession of judgment, and a consumer lease-purchase agreement may not either, but that act reaches only personal property rented for personal, family or household use, not a dwelling. Note also that the lease ban sits inside the residential landlord and tenant act, so it does not reach an arrangement the act excludes, such as transient hotel occupancy, occupancy conditioned on employment, or premises used primarily for agricultural purposes; in those settings there is no statutory ban, and the clause would still be a poor idea.

title: Habitability Protections Kansas Does Not Have
bodyText: Kansas is a light-touch 1975 URLTA state that never received the habitability machinery many other states added later. Six things are confirmed absent, and knowing they are absent tells you what a tenant can and cannot do to you. (1) NO REPAIR-AND-DEDUCT: no Kansas statute lets a tenant hire a repair and subtract the cost from the rent. A tenant who does it is simply short on rent. (2) NO RENT WITHHOLDING OR RENT ESCROW: Kansas has no statute authorizing a tenant to stop paying rent, or to pay it to a court or escrow agent, because of a condition in the unit. The one place rent goes into court is in your own action for possession for nonpayment, where the tenant must counterclaim or lose the claim and the court may order rent paid in and then determine what each party owes. (3) NO MINIMUM INDOOR TEMPERATURE: the statute requires reasonable heat and sets no number of degrees. (4) NO STATUTORY LIST OF DANGEROUS OR UNINHABITABLE CONDITIONS: Kansas names no catalogue of imminent hazards and no official unfit-for-habitation designation in the landlord-tenant act; that work is done by city and county codes. (5) NO STATUTORY WARRANTY OF HABITABILITY BY THAT NAME: your duty is the short list in the act — comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, exercise reasonable care in the common areas, keep supplied electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning appliances including elevators in good and safe working order, provide waste receptacles and arrange removal, and supply running water, reasonable hot water and reasonable heat. (6) AIR CONDITIONING IS NOT ON THE SUPPLY LIST, AND KANSAS HAS NO COOLING DUTY AT ALL: nothing requires you to provide cooling, and no Kansas statute sets a maximum indoor temperature or requires a cooling device. Supplying cooling and maintaining cooling are two different questions, and the answers differ: you need not supply it, but if you do supply it, you must keep it in good and safe working order like any other appliance you supplied, and you may not simply switch it off. Treat it with care once supplied: the statute that penalizes willfully interrupting electric, gas, water or other essential service does not name air conditioning, and whether cooling counts as an 'other essential service' is not settled by the text, so do not shut off a tenant's air conditioning as leverage — assume it counts. What tenants do have instead of all six: written notice of a noncompliance materially affecting health and safety, then termination on a rent-paying date at least 30 days out unless you begin a good-faith cure within 14 days; damages and an injunction either way; and immediate termination after fire or casualty that substantially impairs habitability.

title: Other Rules Kansas Does Not Have
bodyText: Four more rules that exist in other states have no Kansas counterpart. (1) NO TENANT-BANKRUPTCY RULE: Kansas has no statute on what happens to a tenancy when the tenant files bankruptcy. Federal bankruptcy law governs — the automatic stay stops an eviction the moment the petition is filed, and the trustee or the tenant decides whether to assume or reject the lease — so if a tenant tells you they have filed, stop and get advice before taking any further step toward possession. (2) NO LEASE TYPE-SIZE OR CONSPICUOUS-TYPE RULE: nothing requires a Kansas residential lease, or any clause in it, to be set in a minimum point size, in boldface, or in capitals. The only type-size requirement anywhere in Kansas's landlord-tenant law is a different document: if you hand a tenant a form that would serve as the tenant's written notice of intent to vacate and it carries any term not already in the lease, the form must bear a ten-point boldface warning, or the tenant's signature does not bind them to the extra terms. (3) NO INITIALING REQUIREMENT: no Kansas statute makes a lease clause depend on the tenant initialing it separately. Initial lines are a drafting choice, useful as evidence that the tenant read a clause, not a legal condition. (4) NO TRANSLATION OR LANGUAGE DUTY: Kansas does not require you to give the lease in the tenant's own language or to provide a translation, even where the whole negotiation happened in another language. Note that Kansas did legislate a same-language rule for door-to-door sales — that contract must be in the same language as the oral sales presentation, Spanish for example — and chose not to extend it to leases, so this is a deliberate gap rather than an oversight. It is not a free pass: the Kansas Consumer Protection Act's unconscionability standard has long been read to reach selling in English to someone who cannot read it, and a court can refuse to enforce an unconscionable lease provision. If the dealing was in another language, give the tenant a translation anyway and keep a record that you did.

title: Three Things Kansas Has No Statute For
bodyText: (1) NO CASH-RENT RECEIPT DUTY: nothing requires you to give a tenant a written receipt for rent, including rent paid in cash or by money order. The contrast is pointed — Kansas does require a written receipt for every cash or money-order payment under a consumer rent-to-own agreement, but that act covers personal property rented for household use, not a dwelling, so the legislature wrote the duty for one kind of renting and not for yours. Give a receipt anyway. In a dispute over whether February's rent was paid, the receipt is your evidence as much as the tenant's, and you are the one who will be arguing about whether a three-day notice was properly grounded. (2) NO STATEWIDE RENTAL REGISTRATION OR LANDLORD LICENCE: Kansas has no state rental registry and no landlord licence, and nothing in Kansas law makes holding one a condition of filing an eviction or winning a judgment for possession. A different filing can: an out-of-state LLC or corporation doing business in Kansas must register with the Secretary of State, and until it does it may not maintain any action, including an eviction, though its leases stay valid and it may defend a suit (K.S.A. 17-7931, 17-76,126, 17-7307) (see "Out-of-State Owners: Companies Must Register Before Suing"). The eviction statutes require a three-day notice to leave the premises and nothing about your licensure status. A 2026 act did add two steps to a Kansas eviction — the court must consider mediation where the underlying rental agreement is governed by the residential landlord and tenant act, and must order a continuance of up to 14 days if the parties are mediating — but neither step has anything to do with registration or a licence. Some Kansas cities run their own rental registration or inspection programmes; those are local, and an unregistered unit can still expose you to municipal enforcement even though it will not sink your possession case. Kansas's 2026 housing legislation went the other way on local control: it streamlined development permitting and loosened single-family zoning rather than adding any registration duty on landlords. (3) NO TENANT RIGHT OF FIRST REFUSAL, AND CITIES MAY NOT CREATE ONE: if you sell the property, the tenant has no statutory right to be offered it first, no right to match a third party's offer, and no right to notice of the sale beyond the ordinary disclosure duties. This is not merely a gap. In 2026 the legislature forbade any city or county to adopt or enforce an ordinance or resolution requiring landlords to grant an automatic right of first refusal to tenants, and declared any such ordinance adopted before 1 July 2026 null and void. The same act bars a city or county from limiting the amount of a security deposit you may require, from restricting your ability to consider or request income-qualifying methods, credit scores, credit reports, eviction history, property damage history or criminal history under your customarily applied criteria, and from requiring you to rent to a person because their income comes from a housing choice voucher or another housing assistance programme in which a landlord's participation is voluntary. So on this point Kansas has not been silent; it has decided. You may of course still grant a right of first refusal by contract if you want to. One thing Kansas does have, and most states do not: a 2026 squatter-removal act letting an owner have a true squatter removed by law enforcement on a notarised affidavit rather than by filing an eviction case. It is narrow and the penalties for misusing it are severe, so read that entry before reaching for it — a holdover tenant is not a squatter.

title: Liens From Work a Tenant Orders
bodyText:
Kansas's mechanic's lien act never uses the words tenant, lessee or leasehold. A contractor gets a lien on the property only where the labour or materials were furnished under a contract with the owner, or with the owner's trustee, agent or spouse. A tenant who hires a plumber is not on that list, so a tenant-ordered job does not automatically reach your title.

The exposure is the word agent. Kansas has no statute answering whether a lease that consents to the tenant's alterations makes the tenant your agent for the work, so a contractor who is not paid will argue exactly that, and the lease language is what you will be arguing about.

Four other features of the act matter to a landlord. First, there is no notice of non-responsibility in Kansas. States like Oregon let an owner post a notice disclaiming the work within days of learning of it, and Florida and Kentucky let a recorded lease clause keep the owner's interest free of liens for tenant improvements. Kansas has none of those escapes, so your protection has to come from the lease and from the paperwork, not from a posted or recorded notice.

Second, you may get no warning. The warning statement a subcontractor must mail before claiming a lien applies to a home the owner lives in, or a house being built to become the owner's own residence — not to a property you rent out, so a subcontractor on your rental can file without ever notifying you first.

Third, the clocks are short: a contractor's lien statement is filed with the clerk of the district court within four months of last furnishing labour or materials, a subcontractor's or supplier's within three, and a foreclosure action must be brought within a year of the filing.

Fourth, if a lien is filed and nobody sues to foreclose it, you can petition the district court yourself for an adjudication and cancellation, and the lien is cancelled by limitation if no action is brought in time.

The cautious course when a tenant wants work done: consent in writing to that specific job and nothing more, say in the consent and in the lease that the tenant is not your agent and that your consent is not a promise to pay, require the tenant to give every contractor and supplier written notice of that before work begins, require signed lien waivers as work is paid for, and check the district court index in that county after the job ends rather than waiting for a letter that may never come.

title: Converting a Rental Building to Condominiums — Kansas Requires No Tenant Notice
bodyText: Kansas has no condominium-conversion tenant protections at all. There is no conversion notice you must give a sitting tenant, no 90-day or 60-day notice period, no offering statement, no building-condition disclosure, no right for the tenant to buy the unit first or match another buyer's offer, and no required conversion statement to print at the top of a lease. Kansas also has nothing forbidding you to convert rental housing to hotel or other transient use, or to demolish it for that purpose. Watch the vocabulary: Kansas's apartment ownership act does use the words convert and conversion, but only for a developer turning land it reserved for expansion into additional units, which must happen within seven years of recording the declaration. That has nothing to do with converting occupied rentals. So what actually governs a Kansas conversion is the ordinary law of ending a tenancy and selling a building. A fixed-term lease runs to its end; you do not get to cut it short because you recorded a declaration. A periodic tenancy ends only on the ordinary notice — seven days for week-to-week, and for month-to-month a written notice stating the tenancy ends on a rent-paying date at least 30 days after the tenant receives it. If you sell, written notice to the tenant of the conveyance relieves you of liability for later events, but you stay on the hook for the tenant's security deposit. And once the property is submitted to the act, tenants of unit owners are themselves subject to the act and to the association's declaration and bylaws, so a tenant who stays on in a converted unit inherits the association's rules whether or not the lease mentions them. One thing is now settled rather than merely absent: in 2026 the legislature barred every city and county from adopting or enforcing an ordinance requiring a landlord to grant an automatic right of first refusal to tenants, and voided any such ordinance adopted before 1 July 2026. A local conversion ordinance cannot give your tenants a purchase right. Two practical cautions. Giving tenants generous notice anyway is cheap insurance and makes the units easier to sell empty. And if the building is in a city with its own conversion or demolition permitting rules, those are local and are not resolved here.

title: No Drywall Disclosure Statute — but Your Property Manager May Owe One
bodyText: Kansas has no statute requiring you to tell a tenant that a property contains defective, corrosive or sulfur-emitting drywall, and no definition of defective drywall anywhere in Kansas law. The words drywall, wallboard, gypsum and plasterboard appear in Kansas statutes only inside case names and a controlled-substance schedule entry for gypsum weed. There is no remediation standard either. Three things fill the gap, and the third catches landlords out. First, your habitability duties. If drywall is causing a condition that breaches a building or housing code materially affecting health and safety, or that stops the premises being fit, that is a repair obligation once you are on notice, and a tenant who gives you written notice can terminate on thirty days unless you start a good-faith cure within fourteen. Second, saying nothing about a problem you know about is its own risk. Kansas's consumer protection act reaches a landlord, and concealing a known material defect to get a lease signed is the kind of conduct it is built for — quite apart from ordinary fraud. Third, and specific to Kansas: if a licensed real estate broker or salesperson is acting as your agent in letting the property, that licensee must disclose to a prospective tenant all adverse material facts the licensee actually knows, expressly including the physical condition of the property and any material defects in it. A tenant counts as a customer for this purpose. So the duty you do not personally carry may be carried by your property manager, and what you tell your manager they may have to pass on. The licensee need not inspect for the tenant's benefit or independently verify what you say, and if a qualified third party's written condition report has been given to the tenant the licensee generally need not repeat its contents — but the licensee must disclose anything they actually know that the report left out or contradicts. Practical course: if you know of a drywall problem, say so in writing before signing and describe what you know. There is no form to use and no statutory script, which means you set the wording — and a short written disclosure you can produce later is worth far more than the silence Kansas law permits.

title: No Pre-Set Deduction Schedule Rule — and What the Deposit May Actually Cover
bodyText: Kansas has no statute that either permits or forbids a lease schedule of preset deposit charges — no carpet-cleaning figure, no repainting figure, no flat cleaning fee, and no rule on nonrefundable charges taken out of the deposit. What Kansas does is limit what the deposit may be applied to, and that limit controls whatever the lease says. On termination the deposit may be applied to accrued rent and to the amount of damages you have actually suffered because the tenant did not comply with the statutory tenant duties or the lease, all itemised in a written notice delivered to the tenant.
