Those tenant duties are specific: obeying tenant obligations under building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, keeping the occupied part of the premises as clean and safe as its condition permits, removing waste, keeping plumbing fixtures clean, using the facilities and appliances reasonably, and responsibility for destruction, defacement, damage, impairment or removal caused by the tenant or anyone the tenant let in. So the test for any charge is whether it is damage you really suffered from a breach, not whether the lease put a number on it. A schedule can help if it is an honest advance estimate of the cost of repairing a real breach and you still charge only what the condition justifies. A flat charge taken from every tenant regardless of condition is the dangerous version — it is not damages you suffered, it will not survive the itemisation requirement, and no lease term can get around that, because a lease may not make either party waive rights or remedies under the Act. The downside is concrete: if you fail to comply, the tenant recovers the portion due plus damages equal to one and a half times the amount wrongfully withheld. Two further points. Normal wear and tear is not a tenant breach, so routine repainting or cleaning between tenancies is your cost of doing business unless the tenant's own act or omission caused it. And since 2026 no city or county in Kansas may adopt or enforce an ordinance limiting the amount of a security deposit you may require, and any such ordinance adopted before 1 July 2026 is null and void — so the amount is set by state law and the lease, not locally. Charge from the condition and the receipts, keep the itemised notice, and treat any schedule in the lease as an estimate you must still justify.

title: The Tenant May Not Use the Deposit as Last Month's Rent — and Loses It If They Try
bodyText: Kansas answers this directly and the answer favours you. Unless the lease says otherwise, a tenant may not apply or deduct any part of the security deposit from the last month's rent, and may not use or apply the deposit at any time in place of paying rent. If the tenant does it anyway, the statute forfeits the deposit and lets you recover the rent due as though the deposit had never been applied. That is one of the few places Kansas law hands a landlord a self-executing remedy, so it is worth understanding precisely. Three things follow. First, the rule is a default you can switch off — the opening words are 'except as otherwise provided by the rental agreement' — which means a lease term letting the tenant treat the deposit as final rent is enforceable. Almost no landlord should include one, and the library's Kansas deposit clause is drafted the restrictive way. Second, forfeiture is not a licence to go quiet. Keep sending the itemised written notice of what you are keeping and why, within the normal deadlines, and record the forfeiture as one of the items. Failing to comply with the itemisation and return duties exposes you to the withheld amount plus damages of one and a half times what was wrongfully withheld, and you do not want to be arguing about whether a forfeiture was properly claimed while that multiplier is in play. Third, Kansas has no concept of prepaid rent as a separate regulated category — no cap on how much rent you may collect in advance, no trust-account duty, and no separate-accounting duty. But do not assume money labelled last month's rent sits outside the deposit rules: Kansas defines a security deposit without regard to what it is called, so money the lease specifies and that occupancy depends on counts against the deposit cap however you label it. If you intend to hold a genuine final month's rent on top of a full deposit, get the characterisation right before you take the money. Local rules cannot help or hinder you on the amount: since 2026 no Kansas city or county may limit the size of a security deposit you require, and any such ordinance predating 1 July 2026 is void.

title: You Cannot Make the Deposit Refund Depend on Move-Out Notice — but a Demand Starts Your Clock
bodyText: Kansas has no statute letting you condition the deposit refund on the tenant giving advance notice of moving out, and no statute requiring you to put such a warning in the lease. The phrase notice of intent to vacate appears nowhere in Kansas law in connection with the deposit. A lease term making the refund depend on surrender notice would be a term by which the tenant gives up rights under the Act, which is unenforceable — and if you deliberately use a lease containing a provision you know is prohibited, the tenant can recover actual damages. What Kansas does instead is build the tenant's demand into your deadline rather than into their entitlement. Where you are keeping part of the deposit for anything other than rent, you must return the balance within 14 days after you determine the amount, and in no event more than 30 days after three things have all happened: the tenancy ended, possession was delivered, and the tenant demanded the deposit. If the tenant makes no demand within 30 days after the tenancy ends, the duty does not disappear — you must mail what is due to the tenant's last known address. So a silent tenant delays your outer deadline but never forfeits the money, and you cannot simply keep it because nobody asked. Two traps are worth naming. The first is the move-out form. If you hand a tenant a document that would serve as their written notice of intent to vacate and it carries any term not already in the lease — a deposit-forfeiture term, a cleaning charge, an inspection waiver — the document must bear a ten-point boldface warning telling the tenant that signing may bind them to terms not in their lease and that they may decline to sign and give notice another way. Without that warning the extra terms simply do not bind them. The second is the inspection. Kansas requires a joint written inventory of the premises within five days of the start of occupancy, signed in duplicate with a copy to the tenant — and requires nothing at the end. There is no move-out inspection duty, no right for the tenant to attend, and no notice you must give. Do one anyway, against your signed move-in inventory, because that document is your evidence for every figure in the itemised notice. Separately, remember the tenant's own termination notice is still due under the ordinary rules — seven days for week-to-week, 30 days ending on a rent-paying date for month-to-month — and unpaid rent from a short notice is accrued rent you may apply the deposit to. That is the lawful route to the same money, and it is nothing like forfeiting the deposit.

title: No Designated-Repairer Rule — and Nothing for One to Govern
bodyText:
Some states let a lease name who must do work a tenant has done at the landlord's expense. Kansas has no such statute, and more to the point, it has nothing for such a clause to govern: Kansas gives a tenant no repair-and-deduct right and no right to hire anyone at your expense. A tenant facing an unrepaired condition in Kansas gives written notice and may terminate, sue for damages and seek an injunction — not send you a plumber's bill. The phrase at the landlord's expense appears in the landlord-tenant act nowhere in that sense.

So a designated-repairer clause in a Kansas lease does a different job: it controls who performs work the tenant actually does, which matters where you have agreed that the tenant will handle specified repairs or maintenance.

Keep three limits in view. Shifting repair duties is itself regulated — in a building housing no more than four households with common areas you may agree in writing that the tenant performs the trash and water-and-heat duties plus specified repairs, in good faith and not to evade your obligations; in any dwelling other than a single-family residence a repair-shifting deal must be a separate signed agreement supported by real consideration, must not cover work needed to meet a building or housing code, and must not reduce what you owe other tenants, and you cannot make performing it a condition of any other lease obligation. Naming a repairer is not the same as shifting the duty, and the clause should not try to do both.

Second, some work has its own qualification rules whoever pays for it: only a licensed elevator mechanic, or someone employed and directed by a licensee, may erect, alter, maintain or dismantle an elevator; roofing contractors must hold a state registration certificate; a county or city may require licensure of HVAC contractors and master and journeyman mechanics, with a certificate of competency valid in any other Kansas county or city that licenses them; and lead-based paint and asbestos work carries its own state certification and accreditation. Those rules bind regardless of what the lease says.

Third, Kansas's 2026 digital right-to-repair act does not help a tenant fix a rental appliance. It applies to digital electronic equipment sold or leased to owners with a wholesale price of at least fifty dollars, and expressly excludes home appliances with embedded digital electronics — refrigerators, ovens, microwaves, air conditioning units and heating units — along with lighting and life-safety equipment, and reaches only equipment first made available for sale on or after 1 July 2027. Kansas legislated on the right to repair and carved out exactly what sits in a rental unit.

title: No Disaster-Guest Rule — and Why the Squatter Affidavit Is the Wrong Tool
bodyText: Kansas has no statute letting a tenant house people displaced by a disaster despite your guest or occupancy terms, none limiting how long such a stay may last, and none saying when a displaced guest becomes a tenant. Your ordinary guest, occupancy and permitted-occupant terms apply, subject to fair housing law. Kansas also has no counterpart to California's rule for disaster-displaced hotel guests: a transient stay in a hotel, motel or rooming house sits outside the residential landlord and tenant act altogether, so there is no day count after which such a guest becomes a tenant. Two Kansas features are worth knowing before an emergency arrives. First, a declared disaster does not suspend your lease. The governor's emergency powers reach suspending regulatory statutes that prescribe procedures for the conduct of state business, commandeering private property subject to compensation, compelling evacuation, controlling the occupancy of premises inside a disaster area, and making provision for temporary emergency housing. Each is exercised by executive order that must cite the specific power relied on, is reviewed by the legislative coordinating council within 24 hours, can be revoked by the legislature or that council, and is null and void once the emergency ends. So an order could in principle reach occupancy in a disaster area, but nothing in the standing law rewrites your guest limits, and the power to suspend statutes does not extend to the private rules of the landlord and tenant act. Second, and this is where landlords get hurt: do not reach for Kansas's 2026 squatter-removal affidavit against someone your tenant took in. That route requires you to swear that the person entered without authorisation and is not a tenant or holdover tenant, and the act defines a squatter to exclude anyone authorised by a tenant to occupy the dwelling. A guest your tenant invited is therefore outside the act by definition. Swearing the affidavit anyway is a class A nonperson misdemeanour, and a person wrongly removed gets possession back plus actual costs and damages, punitive damages of three times the dwelling's fair market rent, court costs and attorney fees. The lawful route is the lease: enforce your guest and occupancy terms as a tenant breach, with the ordinary notice, and evict if it comes to that. The humane and practical course in a real disaster is usually a short written variation of the guest limit, dated and time-limited, naming who is staying and until when — which protects your occupancy position without putting you in front of a judge.

title: After a Disaster: What the Act-of-God Proviso Does and Does Not Excuse
bodyText: Kansas's disaster rule for landlords is a single phrase at the front of your statutory duties. Those duties — complying with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, exercising reasonable care in common areas, keeping supplied electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning appliances including elevators in good and safe working order, providing waste receptacles and arranging removal, and supplying running water, reasonable hot water and reasonable heat — all begin with the words 'except when prevented by an act of God, the failure of public utility services or other conditions beyond the landlord's control'. Read that carefully, because it is narrower than it looks. It excuses you only while and to the extent you are actually prevented. It does not excuse delay once you can act, it does not excuse a condition you could have prevented or could now fix, and it says nothing about rent. Three things Kansas does not have. There is no clean-up or mitigation duty after a declared disaster: no statute requires you to remove debris or deal with mould, smoke residue, ash, asbestos or water damage on a timetable, or to tell the tenant in writing when it is done, or to hand over environmental test reports. There is no price-gouging law, so no cap on what you may charge after a disaster, and no local one is possible either because rent control is preempted statewide. And there is no rule about rent while a unit is inaccessible but undestroyed — no statutory abatement for a road closed or a building cordoned off. What does apply is the fire-and-casualty rule: if damage substantially impairs the use and habitability of the unit, the tenant may leave immediately and must tell you in writing within five days that they are terminating, or, where continued occupancy is lawful, may vacate the unusable part and pay rent reduced in proportion to the lost fair rental value. Two practical points. You may raise rent after a disaster despite a tenant's earlier complaint, if the increase does not conflict with a lease in effect and is made in good faith to cover expenses from an act of God — the retaliation statute names acts of God specifically. But a grossly excessive price on a new lease is exposed: the consumer protection act, which reaches landlords, treats it as an unconscionable practice when the price at the time the deal was made grossly exceeded what similar property was readily obtainable for, and the attorney general and the tenant can both act on it. Finally, an emergency declaration is not a licence to stop performing. The governor's powers are exercised by executive order citing the specific power used, reviewed within 24 hours, revocable, and void when the emergency ends; the power to suspend statutes reaches those prescribing procedures for the conduct of state business, not the private rules between you and your tenant.

title: No Drug-Free Addendum Rule — and No Faster Route Than Ordinary Eviction
bodyText: No Kansas statute requires, authorises or regulates a drug-free or crime-free lease addendum. Kansas has no drug-and-alcohol-free housing category for recovery programmes with its own required lease terms and short cure notices, no provision letting a felony charge during the term void the lease at your option, and no expedited eviction track for criminal activity. Kansas also has no drug-nuisance abatement statute in the landlord-tenant, cities, civil procedure or limited-actions chapters that would let you or a prosecutor move against a unit faster because of drug activity in it. An addendum in a Kansas lease is therefore a contract term and nothing more: it carries whatever weight the lease gives it, which means its real function is to define the breach clearly so that your notice is defensible. Use the ordinary machinery. Drug activity in a unit will usually be a material noncompliance with the lease, and the statutory tenant duties already include not engaging in, and not allowing anyone the tenant lets in to engage in, conduct that disturbs other tenants' quiet and peaceful enjoyment. The route is a written notice specifying the acts and omissions and stating that the lease terminates on a date not less than 30 days after receipt if the breach is not remedied in 14 days; the lease then ends on that date regardless of the rent-paying date. If the same or a similar breach recurs after that 14-day window, your second notice gives no cure opportunity at all — just a date not less than 30 days out. You may also sue for damages and an injunction. Three cautions. First, there is no state medical-cannabis programme in Kansas, so unlike most states your addendum has no state medical-marijuana carve-out to navigate; federal law still governs and federally assisted housing has its own required addenda and its own rules. Second, write the addendum around conduct, not status. A blanket drug prohibition applied as a screen can collide with disability protections, since a record of addiction is treated differently from current use — enforce it against what someone does on the property. Third, if the person causing the problem is someone your tenant let in, the 2026 squatter-removal affidavit is not available to you: the act excludes anyone authorised by a tenant to occupy the dwelling, and swearing otherwise is a criminal offence with treble fair-market-rent exposure. That is a tenant breach, handled through the notice above.

title: Victim Information — Kansas Makes You Collect It and Says Nothing About Keeping It
bodyText: Kansas has an asymmetry here that you should plan around. Its housing-protection statute entitles you to ask a protected person for documentation of the domestic violence, sexual assault, human trafficking or stalking — either a document signed by the victim and a physician, physician assistant, nurse or behavioural-sciences licensee declaring under penalty of perjury that in their professional judgment the incident occurred, or a court order granting the person relief. What the statute does not contain is any duty to keep that material confidential. There is no restriction on what you may do with it, no limit on how long you may hold it, no bar on passing it to anyone, and no penalty aimed at disclosure. The thousand dollars of statutory damages and the attorney fees a court may award are for violating that section, so a leak that breaches no other subsection gives the tenant nothing under it. Kansas also has no address-confidentiality scheme that binds a private landlord. The confidentiality that does exist in Kansas protective-order law is a duty on the court, not on you. In a protection from abuse case, if the court finds the plaintiff's address or telephone number needs to stay confidential to protect the plaintiff or children residing with them, that information is withheld from the public and released only to authorised court or law enforcement personnel. In a protection from stalking, sexual assault or human trafficking case the protection is stronger and automatic: the victim's address and telephone number must not be disclosed to the defendant or to the public at all. Read that second point carefully — for those purposes you are the public. Kansas tightened a criminal privacy offence in 2026, raising penalties and changing the mental state required, but that is a crime, not a landlord duty, and it does not fill this gap. Treat the material as confidential regardless. Keep it out of the ordinary tenant file and out of anything you hand to a buyer, a lender or a property manager who does not need it; keep it out of eviction pleadings and out of any conversation with other tenants; and give it to no one but your own lawyer without the tenant's written consent. The absence of a Kansas penalty is not the measure of your exposure — a disclosure that reaches an abuser can cause harm no statutory damages figure describes, and ordinary negligence and privacy claims do not disappear because the housing statute is silent. If you take part in a federally assisted housing programme, federal law imposes its own confidentiality rules on what you may do with a victim's information, and those do apply to you.

title: Deposit After a Protected-Person Termination — No Special Timing, One Real Puzzle
bodyText: Kansas gives a protected person affected by domestic violence, sexual assault, human trafficking or stalking the right to end the lease and owe no rent for the period after they vacate — but it says nothing at all about the security deposit. There is no faster return deadline, no special itemisation rule, no duty to change locks, and no lock-change fee you may charge or withhold. The ordinary deposit rules apply unchanged: where you are keeping any part of the deposit for something other than rent, return the balance within 14 days after you determine the amount and in no event more than 30 days after the tenancy ended, possession was delivered and the tenant demanded it, and if no demand comes within 30 days of the tenancy ending, mail what is due to the last known address. Four points make this work in practice. You may still apply the deposit to rent and other amounts that accrued before the tenant vacated — the protection expressly leaves that liability alone. You may not charge rent for the period after they vacated, so do not take it from the deposit: doing so exposes you both to the deposit penalty of one and a half times the amount wrongfully withheld and to a thousand dollars of statutory damages plus attorney fees and costs for violating the housing protection. The early-termination fee is different and is yours if you drafted for it: the statute lets you impose a reasonable fee of up to one month's rent, but only if the lease already contains it, and the deposit statute lets you retain part of the deposit for expenses, damages or other legally allowable charges under the lease other than rent — which is what that fee is. Itemise it in the written notice like anything else. The puzzle is the co-tenant case. When a protected person's lease terminates, the lease continues for any remaining tenants. If someone is still living there under the same lease, the tenancy has not ended and possession has not been delivered, so the deposit clock has arguably not started at all, and Kansas has no rule for apportioning a deposit between a departing protected person and those who stay. Do not guess in silence. Tell the departing tenant in writing what you are doing and why, keep the deposit intact against the continuing tenancy rather than paying out a share you may owe the others, and if the remaining tenants will pay in a replacement share, document the substitution and account to the departing tenant then. If there is any doubt, treat the safer course as accounting promptly rather than holding on, because the penalties run against withholding and not against paying early.

title: Evicting a Protected Person — What the Shield Covers, and Who Removes the Abuser
bodyText: Kansas bars you from evicting a tenant, or finding the tenant in violation of the lease, on the basis of or as a direct result of the fact that the tenant is a protected person — someone who in the preceding twelve months has been, is, or is in imminent danger of becoming a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, human trafficking or stalking. Read the shield for what it is. It is a status shield, not a performance shield, and it carries its own limit: it protects the tenant who otherwise qualifies for tenancy in or occupancy of the premises. Unpaid rent is still unpaid rent. Damage is still damage. A breach that has nothing to do with the tenant's status is still a breach, and you proceed exactly as you would with any other tenant. What you may not do is treat the violence itself, or the police coming, or the tenant's status becoming known, as the ground. Two further features matter in litigation. If you sue for rent, a tenant who was a protected person on the date they vacated and who notified you as the statute requires has an affirmative defence to rent for the period after they left, which they must establish on the balance of probabilities. And if an applicant or tenant submitted false information to claim the protection, that submission is itself a basis for denial, eviction or a lease-violation finding. Now the question landlords actually ask: can you evict the abuser and keep the victim? Kansas gives you no such power. There is no bifurcation remedy in Kansas landlord-tenant law — no provision letting you terminate one co-tenant's interest for the violence while the other stays. The statute continues the lease for remaining tenants only when a protected person ends their own tenancy, not when you want the other one out. The removal of an abusive co-tenant is done by a court, not by you: under the Protection from Abuse Act a court may grant possession of the residence or household to the plaintiff to the exclusion of the defendant and restrain the defendant from entering or remaining in it. There is a limit on that power where the parties are not married and one of them owns the home, but in a rental neither tenant owns, so the court's authority is unimpaired. The practical course is therefore to tell a victim who asks that their route is a protective order, to comply with such an order when it arrives, and to keep your own enforcement aimed at conduct and arrears rather than at the person the violence happened to. Procedurally nothing changes. There is no special notice, no special pleading and no special defence procedure for these cases: it is the ordinary three-day notice to leave the premises and the ordinary eviction action. Note one 2026 addition that applies to every residential eviction and may matter here — the court must now consider mediation, and must grant a continuance of up to fourteen days if the parties are mediating.

title: No Duty to Change the Locks for a Domestic Violence Victim
bodyText: Kansas gives a tenant who is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, human trafficking or stalking several housing protections, but a lock change is not one of them. There is no Kansas statute requiring you to change, re-key or add a lock at a victim's request, no deadline for doing it, no rule on who pays, and no statutory immunity if you do it. That is a real gap compared with other states, and it means the lease and your own practice are what govern. What Kansas protects instead is the tenancy itself: you may not deny an application, evict, or treat the lease as violated because the person is a protected person, and once a protected person gives you notice and vacates, the person stops owing rent for the period after vacating. You may charge a termination fee of up to one month's rent, but only if the lease says so. None of those rights can be waived in the lease, and a violation exposes you to statutory damages of $1,000 plus attorney fees and costs. The tool that actually removes an abuser from the home is a court order, not your locksmith. Under the protection from abuse act a judge may grant the victim possession of the residence to the exclusion of the defendant, restrain the defendant from entering or remaining there, order a law enforcement officer to evict the defendant, make provision for possession of personal property with officer assistance, and for 60 days restrain the defendant from cancelling utility service. Violating the possession order is criminal trespass, carrying a mandatory minimum of 48 consecutive hours in jail on conviction, and is also a violation of a protective order. Two limits matter to you. If the parties are not married to each other and one of them owns the residence, the court cannot grant possession to the exclusion of the owner. And no protection order affects title to real property, so an order never changes who your tenant is. An order under the separate stalking, sexual assault and human trafficking act is narrower still: it can restrain the defendant from entering the victim's residence, but it does not award possession and does not authorize an officer to evict. So handle a lock request this way. If the person to be shut out is not on the lease, you are free to change the locks and the lease's key terms let you charge the actual cost; nothing requires you to, and nothing stops you. If the person to be shut out is a co-tenant on the lease, do not change the locks on your own. Even where one tenant has vacated under the victim protections, the lease continues for the remaining tenants, so locking out someone who is still your tenant without a court order is an unlawful exclusion. The tenant can recover possession or terminate, and in either case recover the greater of one and one-half months' periodic rent or actual damages, plus the refundable part of the deposit. Ask for the court order that names the exclusion, keep a copy in the file, and act on the order's terms. Keep any charge to your documented actual cost. A fixed lock-change fee bearing no relation to what the work cost, or a charge dressed up as legal costs, invites a consumer protection problem, and a lease can never make the tenant pay either party's attorney fees.

title: Domestic Violence Citations Check
bodyText: Kansas has not moved its protection order law. Both civil acts sit exactly where they have always sat. The protection from abuse act is still in chapter 60, article 31, and the protection from stalking, sexual assault or human trafficking act is still in chapter 60, article 31a, with the same section numbers. The 2025 and 2026 legislatures both re-cited the two acts by those numbers in fee statutes, so the numbering is current, not stale. Four things did change, and each one trips up guidance written a few years ago. First, the stalking act was renamed, twice. It began as the protection from stalking act and now covers sexual assault and human trafficking as well. The section numbers never changed, so a document using the old name is citing live sections under a dead title. Use the full current name. Second, two sections of the protection from abuse act were repealed in place, not relocated. One was folded into the main orders section in 2013 and the other was dropped in 2012. The act's own opening section still describes itself as running through the repealed end section, and a later section on entering orders into the national database declares itself part of and supplemental to the act, so the act actually reaches past the range it says it covers. Do not treat that stated range as a complete list. Third, the definition of abuse was rewritten. It now turns on intimate partners or household members, which covers people in a dating relationship, people who live together or formerly lived together, and people who have a child in common, and a dating relationship is presumed if the person verifies that it exists. Fourth, and this is the one that actually moved, the criminal sections did. Kansas recodified its whole criminal code, so violation of a protective order, criminal trespass, stalking, domestic battery, assault and battery all carry new numbers. Any older citation to the repealed criminal numbers is wrong. Then there is the trap that matters most for a lease. Kansas's housing protections for victims do not borrow their definitions from either protection order act. They point to a separate definitions section in the state agencies chapter. Kansas's employment leave statute for victims, by contrast, does borrow the protection from abuse act's definition of abuse. So the state uses two different definitional anchors in two different settings, and a lease that defines domestic violence by citing the protection from abuse act is citing the wrong statute for the housing protections. If your lease or policy defines these terms, either quote the housing statute's own definitional pointer or do not define them at all and let the statute supply the meaning. Practical check: anything in your forms that names the protection from stalking act without sexual assault and human trafficking, cites the repealed criminal numbers, treats the protection from abuse act as ending at its stated last section, or defines domestic violence out of the protection from abuse act for housing purposes, needs updating. None of it changes the substance of your obligations, only whether the citation holds up.

title: What Counts as a Qualifying Document for the Victim Protections
bodyText: Kansas puts the victim protections in motion in two steps, and the second one is yours to trigger or not. Step one: the tenant or applicant gives you a statement about domestic violence, sexual assault, human trafficking or stalking. That statement alone is what qualifies the person for the protections. Step two happens only if you ask: if you request it, the tenant must then provide documentation. If you never ask, you never get documentation, and the protections still apply. Kansas allows exactly two forms of documentation, and the list is strikingly narrow. The first is a document signed by the victim and by one of four kinds of Kansas-licensed professional: a physician licensed to practice medicine and surgery, a physician assistant, a nurse, or someone licensed by the behavioral sciences regulatory board. That last category is broader than it sounds and is where most letters will come from, because social workers at every licence level, professional counselors, and marriage and family therapists are all licensed by that board. The document has to carry two signatures, the victim's and the professional's, and it must declare under penalty of perjury that the professional holds the opinion, in their professional judgment and within their scope of practice, that the incident occurred. A letter missing the victim's signature, or missing the penalty-of-perjury declaration, or giving a conclusion outside the writer's scope of practice, does not match the statute. Note too that the four boards named are Kansas boards, so a letter from an out-of-state clinician does not fit this route. The second form is a court order granting relief to the protected person relating to the alleged conduct that is the basis for the claim. A protection from abuse order or a protection from stalking, sexual assault or human trafficking order both do this. An order that denied relief does not, and neither does an order about some unrelated matter. Now the part that catches landlords out. A police report is not on the list, and neither is a letter from a domestic violence advocate or a shelter worker. Both of those do qualify a victim for time off work under Kansas's employment statute, and a still broader set qualifies for unemployment benefits, so advice written for those settings does not carry over. Do not demand a police report as the price of the protections, and do not treat the absence of one as a reason to doubt the claim. Practical handling. Decide once whether you will request documentation at all, and apply that choice the same way to everyone. If you do request it, accept either of the two statutory forms without argument, keep the document confidential and in the file, and do not ask for a second form or for underlying records. Do not demand the police report, the medical notes, the incident details, or the perpetrator's name. If what arrives is not one of the two listed forms, do not simply reject the claim: get advice before acting, because the protections attached at the statement stage and the statute does not say in terms that an unlisted document fails. Your real protection against a false claim is elsewhere: submitting false information is itself a basis for denial of tenancy, for eviction, or for finding a lease violation. Use that route, on evidence, rather than raising the documentation bar. And remember the lease cannot shift any of this. The tenant cannot waive these rights and you cannot require a waiver, so a lease clause demanding a police report, demanding notarization, setting a documentation deadline the statute does not set, or making the protections conditional on your satisfaction is unenforceable. Getting it wrong is not cheap: a court may award statutory damages of $1,000 plus reasonable attorney fees and costs.

title: No Electric Submetering Rules, and Why That Is the Risk
bodyText: Kansas has no statute on submetering electricity or gas to tenants. There is no required disclosure, no form to hand over, no billing-format rule, no cap on what you may charge, and no permission to add an administrative or service fee. The absence is not a gap the legislature overlooked. Kansas legislated submetering in 2005, for water only, and the shape of that statute is the warning. For water, a landlord supplied by a city or water district who submeters to tenants is expressly carved out of the definition of a public utility, and the furnishing is expressly not treated as a sale for resale within the state corporation commission's jurisdiction. But the carve-out is bought with conditions. You may charge the tenant only the same rate the city or water district charges you, so there is no markup. You may not charge any surcharge for installing or maintaining the meter, or for anything else related to using it. And you must give the tenant a monthly statement showing how the amount was computed, the current meter reading and the previous reading. The legislature did all of that for water and did none of it for electricity. So if you submeter and rebill electricity in Kansas, you are doing it with no statutory safe harbour. Whether that makes you a regulated public utility turns on the utilities chapter's definition, which excludes equipment operated for private use but also reaches all companies furnishing heat, light, water or power, and no Kansas statute or commission rule says which side a submetering landlord falls on, so treat this as the live risk it is rather than a settled point. What is settled is that the one express immunity Kansas wrote is limited to water furnished in accordance with that section, so it does not help you with electricity. The practical conclusion is to avoid the problem rather than disclose your way out of it. Safest is to have each unit separately metered by the utility and billed by the utility directly to the tenant, so you are never in the supply chain. Next best, where the building is master-metered and separate utility meters are not feasible, is to include the cost in the rent, which makes it rent rather than a resold utility. If you do neither and decide to submeter electricity, get advice from a Kansas utilities lawyer before you start, not after a tenant complains. Three Kansas points apply whatever you choose. First, your own duties do not move. You must keep all electrical, plumbing, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning equipment you supply in good and safe working order, and you must supply running water, reasonable hot water and reasonable heat, unless the building is not required by law to be equipped for it or the tenant's own installation generates it on a direct utility connection. A master meter does not shift the heat obligation onto the tenant. Second, what makes the tenant liable for utilities is the lease. The statute says nothing in the landlord-duty section limits a tenant's obligation to pay for utility service in accordance with the rental agreement, so if you want the tenant to pay, say so in the lease in plain terms: which utilities, in whose name the account sits, and who pays for common areas. Third, you may not interfere with or refuse access or service to a tenant by a franchised communication or cable television service. One narrow thing Kansas did add recently, and it is about generating rather than reselling. If you own a single-family dwelling or a building of two units or fewer and a retailer offers you a contract to install a distributed energy system such as rooftop solar, the retailer owes you a set of disclosures on a standard form. That right belongs to the property owner, not to a tenant, and a building of three or more units is outside it altogether.

title: No Emergency Contact Law
bodyText: Kansas has no statute requiring you to give tenants an emergency contact, a 24-hour number, or any telephone number at all. There is no posting duty and no after-hours answering duty. The word emergency does not appear anywhere in the Kansas residential landlord and tenant act. What Kansas does require is narrower than most states and is worth getting exactly right. At or before the tenancy starts you must disclose to the tenant in writing the name and address of two people: whoever is authorized to manage the premises, and an owner, or someone authorized to act for the owner, for the purpose of service of process and for receiving and receipting for notices and demands. Name and address only. A telephone number is not required, which is a real difference from states that require one, so do not assume a phone number on the lease satisfies the duty. The information must be kept current, and the duty runs against any later landlord, owner or manager, so update the lease or send a notice when your manager changes. Skipping this has a sharp consequence that catches people out. Anyone who fails to make that disclosure becomes an agent of each landlord, both for service of process and for receiving notices, and for performing the landlord's obligations under the act and the lease, including spending or making available for that purpose all the rent collected from the property. In short, the manager who never identified the owner can end up being treated as the one who has to answer for the owner's duties out of the rent. Kansas does recognise urgency in one place, though it uses different words and it points the other way. You may enter the unit without the tenant's consent in the case of an extreme hazard involving the potential loss of life or severe property damage. Ordinary entry needs reasonable hours and reasonable notice, and you must not abuse the right of access or use it to harass the tenant. Note what that provision is: a right of yours to get in, not a right of the tenant's to reach you. Nothing in Kansas law obliges you to be reachable. There is still a strong practical reason to publish an emergency number even though no statute makes you. Kansas gives a tenant no repair-and-deduct remedy and no emergency self-help. If something serious breaks, the tenant's route is a written notice specifying the breach and stating that the lease will end on a rent-paying date at least 30 days out, and you keep the tenancy alive only by adequately initiating a good faith effort to fix it within 14 days of receiving that notice. The tenant may also sue for damages and an injunction. All of that is measured from when notice reaches you, so a number that is actually answered is what lets you start the clock on your own terms and fix a problem before it becomes a termination or a lawsuit. Give tenants a repair-reporting number, say in the lease how to report after hours, and keep a written record of what was reported and when. One more caution. Cities and counties may impose contact or registration requirements through local rental licensing or housing codes. Check the ordinance where the property sits.

title: Property Taken by Eminent Domain
bodyText:
Kansas has no statute that ends a lease or abates rent when the property is taken by eminent domain. There is no provision like the ones some states have cutting off the tenant's rent on a total taking or reducing it proportionally on a partial taking, and no power in the condemnation court to cancel the lease. So the lease is what decides those questions, and if it is silent you are into unsettled territory.

Put a condemnation clause in the lease. Kansas does supply a useful default on the rent arithmetic: unless the lease says otherwise, rent is uniformly apportionable from day to day, so a clause prorating rent to the date possession is given up runs with the grain of Kansas law rather than against it.

Four Kansas points matter and none of them is obvious. First, the timetable is brutally short. Once the condemnor pays the appraisers' award to the clerk of the district court, title and the interest taken vest immediately and the condemnor is entitled to immediate possession. From that payment date, anyone with personal property on the premises has 14 days to remove it, and the clerk must notify the interested parties that the award has been paid and that the 14 days are running. Fourteen days, not months. Tell your tenant the moment you learn a payment has been made, because the clock is already going and the notice goes to parties in the case, not necessarily to an occupant nobody joined. Kansas does require the condemnor's petition to name any party in possession, so far as that party's interest is being taken — but whether your tenant's interest is being taken is the condemnor's framing, and a defect in the form of the petition that does not impair substantial rights will not invalidate the proceeding. So do not assume the court papers reached your tenant.

Second, the award is one fund and a judge divides it. Kansas does not value each interest separately. The measure of compensation is the fair market value of the property or interest if the whole is taken, and the before-and-after difference if only part is taken, and on any appeal the only question tried is that compensation — an appeal brings the damages to all interests in the tract before the court together, for one trial. Where the parties in interest disagree about how to split the appraisers' award or the final judgment, the district court determines the final distribution on the motion of any of them. A lease clause assigning the leasehold's share to the landlord settles the matter between you and your tenant, but it does not remove the court's power over distribution, so expect to show the clause rather than assume it ends the argument.

Third, relocation money is separate and it is the tenant's. Since July 2004, even with no federal funding in the project, a condemning authority that acquires property and displaces anyone must provide fair and reasonable relocation payments and assistance to the displaced person, measured by the federal relocation statute. A displaced tenant is a displaced person. If the tenant shows that money is needed before the move to make the move possible, 75 percent must be advanced, with the balance within 30 days of completion. Relocation payments are not owed until title vests in the condemning authority. Crucially, the relocation statute expressly creates no element of value or damage in the condemnation case itself, so relocation money sits outside the award and is not yours. Do not draft a clause that sweeps it in, and do not try to set it off against rent.

Fourth, a taking is not a casualty. Kansas's fire-and-casualty section gives the tenant options when the unit is damaged or destroyed by fire or casualty, and a condemnation is neither, so do not expect that section to do this work. Two related rules do still apply. If a taking leaves you unable to give the tenant possession at the start of the term, rent abates until possession is delivered and the tenant may terminate on five days' written notice and get the whole deposit back. And whenever the tenancy ends, the deposit rules apply in full, on their own timetable, whatever the lease says.

Finally, the usual caution about the clause you cannot write around. The lease may not make the tenant waive rights or remedies under the residential landlord and tenant act, may not require either side to pay the other's attorney fees, and may not exculpate or indemnify either party. A condemnation clause that allocates the award is fine. One that waives the deposit rules, the delivery-of-possession remedy, or the statutory notice requirements is not.

title: Screening Your Staff, and the Licence Most Leasing Employees Need
bodyText: Kansas has no statute requiring background checks on apartment or property-management employees. There is no mandate to screen maintenance staff who hold keys to occupied units, no sex-offender registry check requirement, and nothing resembling the apartment-employee screening laws some states have. Whether you screen is your choice, and if you do, employment law and the federal credit-reporting rules govern how, not landlord-tenant law. But there is a Kansas requirement that catches most landlords by surprise, and it does function as a compulsory background check on exactly the employees who deal with tenants. Kansas requires a real estate licence to lease property for someone else, and the definition of a broker is wide. It reaches anyone who, for compensation and as an employee of or on behalf of an owner, leases real estate, offers to lease it, negotiates or attempts to negotiate a leasing, lists property for lease, assists or directs in procuring prospects calculated to result in a lease, or assists in or directs the negotiation of a transaction intended to result in a lease. A leasing agent, a letting assistant and an on-site manager who shows units and signs tenants up are all doing those things. If you own the property yourself and do the work yourself, you are exempt, because the act does not apply to a person acting with reference to their own property. The trap is for landlords who hold property in an entity. Where a company, LLC, partnership or professional corporation owns or leases the real estate, an employee of that entity who leases it is exempt only if the employee owns 5 percent or more of the entity. An ordinary salaried leasing agent or site manager with no ownership stake, or with a stake under 5 percent, falls outside the exemption and must be licensed. Note what is not on the exemption list: there is no exemption for a resident manager or an on-site manager as such, which many states do provide. Agricultural leasing is separately exempt. Licensing is where the background check arrives. On an original application, and in connection with any investigation of an existing licensee, the Kansas real estate commission must require the person to be fingerprinted and to submit to a state and national criminal history record check, and the commission may charge a fee covering its cost. The prints go to both the Kansas Bureau of Investigation and the FBI for a search of the state and federal databases, and what comes back to the commission is adult convictions and adult non-convictions. Note who gets that information: it goes to the commission, not to you. The prints and the record information are confidential, are outside the Kansas open records act, and using or disclosing them for any other purpose is a crime and grounds for removal from office. So the licence check is not a report you can ask to see. The applicant must also be at least 18, hold a high school diploma or equivalent, pass both the national and the Kansas portions of the examination, and prove a good reputation for honesty, trustworthiness, integrity and competence. A salesperson or associate broker's application has to come with the supervising broker's own certification that the applicant is honest, trustworthy and of good reputation, which puts a signature and a judgement on you if you are that broker. So the practical position is this. Maintenance and repair staff who do not lease, show or negotiate need no licence and face no required check, and screening them is prudence rather than law. Anyone who leases units for an entity you own less than 5 percent of needs a licence, and the licence brings a fingerprint-based state and national criminal history check whether you wanted one or not. Confirm the licensing position before you hire for a leasing role, not after. One more thing about on-site staff. If an employee lives in the building and the right to live there depends on the employment, that occupancy is outside the Kansas residential landlord and tenant act altogether. The act's protections and procedures, including the eviction route it supplies, do not apply to that arrangement, so the terms of the employment agreement carry far more weight than usual. Deal with what happens to the housing when the job ends, in writing, before it ends. Finally, do not confuse two different screening questions. Kansas recently barred cities and counties from restricting how a landlord screens prospective tenants, including the use of criminal history. That is about applicants for a tenancy. It says nothing at all about screening your own employees, and it creates no duty either way.

title: No Energy Data Release Rule
bodyText: Kansas has no building energy benchmarking programme and no statute letting a lease clause authorise a utility to release a tenant's energy usage data to you. Some states have written exactly that permission into their utility law, so a sentence in the lease is enough to make the utility hand over the unit's consumption figures. Kansas has not. The word benchmark does not appear anywhere in Kansas law in an energy sense, and there is no statutory energy audit requirement for private rental property. What that means in practice is that a release clause in your lease is worth something between you and your tenant and nothing against the utility. It may record the tenant's agreement, and it may give you a contractual basis to ask the tenant to cooperate. It does not oblige the utility to give you anything, because no Kansas statute tells the utility to honour it. If you need a tenant's usage data, for an efficiency programme, a lender, a grant application or a sale, get a separate written authorisation from the tenant addressed to the utility, in whatever form that utility requires, and expect the utility to apply its own release process and its own regulator's customer-data rules. Treat the lease clause as a promise to sign that authorisation rather than as the authorisation itself. Three practical cautions. Keep any request specific. A blanket, perpetual, irrevocable consent to hand over everything, buried in a long lease, is the kind of term that invites an unconscionability argument under Kansas's consumer protection law, which does reach residential leases. Ask for the period and the purpose you actually need, let the tenant revoke, and say what you will use it for. Second, do not try to get at the data by making the utility account conditional. Kansas requires you to supply running water, reasonable hot water and reasonable heat, and you may not interfere with or refuse a tenant access to a franchised communication or cable television service. Leverage over utilities is not available to you. Third, if you submeter water, the obligation runs the other way: you must give the tenant a monthly statement showing the computation and both meter readings. One narrow exception worth knowing, and it is now confirmed rather than flagged. Kansas does have an energy audit statute, and it is about state property and state leases, not about tenants. It directs the secretary of administration to adopt rules for an energy audit at least every five years on all state-owned real property, and it bars the secretary from approving a new lease, or a renewal or extension of an existing lease, of property the state does not own unless the lessor has submitted an energy audit for that property — subject to a waiver where the secretary determines an audit is not economically feasible and gives written reasons to the legislature's joint committee on state building construction. So if you let space to a state agency, expect to produce an energy audit of the building as a condition of the lease being approved. It still gives you no route to anyone's usage data, and it has nothing to say about a residential tenancy. Nothing in Kansas's 2025 distributed energy legislation changes any of this. That law is about installing generation, not about sharing consumption. It gives disclosure rights to a property owner of a single-family dwelling or a building of two units or fewer who is offered a contract to install a system such as rooftop solar, and it lets the utility use a customer's own historic consumption to size that customer's own system. It gives a landlord no access to a tenant's data and gives a tenant no rights at all.

title: Who May Represent an LLC or Corporation Landlord in Court
bodyText: Kansas splits this question in two, and the answer flips depending on which court you are in. Get the split wrong and you either waste a filing or commit an offence. Evictions are the serious half. A Kansas eviction is an action for possession of real property, and it is brought under the limited actions code. No Kansas statute says whether a company, LLC or partnership may send a non-lawyer to court in that case. The bar comes from somewhere else: the Kansas supreme court decides, by court rule and by common law, what counts as the unauthorised practice of law, and the legislature has deferred to it. What the legislature did add is the consequence. A person not licensed or otherwise authorised by the Kansas supreme court to practise law must not commit any act the court treats as the unauthorised practice of law, must not hold out that they are admitted, and must not solicit payment for such services. A violation is an unconscionable act under the Kansas consumer protection act, and that is so whether or not a consumer or a consumer transaction is involved. The definition of who can be caught is deliberately wide: it reaches a corporation or other legal entity that knowingly commits the acts or that aids or abets someone else in committing them, and the penalties sit on top of, not instead of, the court's contempt power. So the exposure for sending your property manager to argue an eviction is not merely that the case gets dismissed. Treat an entity eviction as a job for a Kansas lawyer unless you have specific advice to the contrary. Small claims is the opposite world, and it surprises people. There, no party may be represented by an attorney before judgment at all, and a party appears instead by a full-time employee or officer, or by any person in a representative capacity, so long as that person is not an attorney. For an entity landlord this is not permission to use a non-lawyer, it is a requirement. There is a trapdoor: if any party uses a representative who is an attorney or was formerly an attorney, or is an attorney appearing for themselves, every other party becomes entitled to have an attorney appear, the court must advise them of that right, and it must grant a reasonable continuance for them to find one. Former attorneys, inactive attorneys and attorneys licensed in other states all count. Four limits decide whether small claims is even open to you. A small claim is a claim for the recovery of money or personal property only, so a claim for possession of real property cannot be brought there, which is why evictions are not a small-claims matter. The amount cannot exceed $10,000, excluding interest and costs. A claim based on a debt owed to someone else cannot be filed by you unless you are a full-time employee or officer of the person owed, which blocks a management company from suing in small claims on the owner's behalf. And no person may file more than 20 small claims in the same court in a calendar year. That last limit has teeth at both ends. Filing the action certifies that you are complying with it, a defendant may raise over-filing as a defence, and if the court finds you exceeded the limit it must dismiss with prejudice, the finding counts as an unconscionable act under the consumer protection act, and the defendant may bring a separate consumer protection claim against you. Separately, a judgment entered on something that was not a small claim, or that was filed in breach of the numerical limit, is void and unenforceable. So the working rule for a Kansas entity landlord is this. To recover possession, use the limited actions code and use a lawyer. To chase money alone up to $10,000, small claims is available, you must not use a lawyer before judgment, you must send a full-time employee or officer of the entity that is actually owed the money, and you must count your filings for the year. Where a case has both a possession claim and a rent claim, it is not a small claim, so the small-claims rules do not help you at all.

title: EV Chargers When the Tenancy Ends
bodyText:
Kansas has no statute saying who owns a tenant-installed electric vehicle charger when the tenancy ends, whether the tenant must remove it, who restores the space, or whether you must buy it. Kansas's 2026 electric vehicle legislation does not help: it governs retail electric suppliers running public fast charging stations and says nothing about landlords or tenants, and it expires in 2036. Settle it in writing before anything is installed.

There is one Kansas statute about a tenant removing improvements, and it does not apply to you. It covers farm land, where a tenant who owns substantially all the improvements may transfer the term and the improvements, and it voids a lease term requiring removal without paying fair value. That is the agricultural block of Kansas landlord law, not the residential act, so do not reason from it.

What Kansas does give you is a clear answer about what the charger is and a mandatory procedure for what happens if it is left behind, and both point the same way: the equipment is the tenant's property, not yours.

Kansas abolished the landlord's lien. A lien or security interest for the landlord in the tenant's household goods, furnishings, fixtures or other personal property is unenforceable unless it was perfected before the residential act took effect in 1975, and distraint for rent is abolished except as the abandonment procedure allows. Note the word fixtures. Kansas treats a tenant's fixtures as the tenant's property for this purpose, so you cannot simply declare an installed charger yours because it is bolted to the wall, and you cannot hold it against unpaid rent.

If the tenant abandons or surrenders the unit, or is removed by a forcible detainer action, and leaves the charger behind, you must follow the statutory route. You may take possession of the property and store it at the tenant's expense. You may sell or dispose of it only after 30 days from taking possession. At least 15 days before the sale or disposition you must publish a notice once in a newspaper of general circulation in the county where the unit is, and within seven days after publication mail a copy to the tenant at the last known address. The notice must give the tenant's name, a brief description of the property and the approximate date you intend to sell or dispose of it. Do all of that and you can sell without liability to the tenant or anyone else claiming an interest, except a secured creditor who told you about its interest before the sale, and provided you had no knowledge or notice of anyone else's claim.

During the 30 days, and at any time before the sale, the tenant may redeem the property by paying your reasonable expenses of taking, holding and preparing it for sale plus anything owed for rent or otherwise. Proceeds go in a fixed order: first your reasonable expenses of taking, holding, preparing, giving notice and selling; then whatever the tenant owes you; and you may keep any balance. A buyer who takes without knowledge that the sale breached someone's rights gets clean title.

Skipping the publication and the mailing is the common mistake, and it costs you the protection the section gives. A charger is exactly the kind of item this procedure was written for, and if yours is a Level 2 unit the value is real enough that a secured creditor may exist.

Two more Kansas points. Any restoration cost you want to recover from the deposit has to be damage rather than ordinary wear and tear, and the deposit rules apply in full on their own timetable: itemise in writing, return the balance within 14 days of working out the amount and in no event more than 30 days after termination, delivery of possession and the tenant's demand. Getting that wrong exposes you to the amount wrongfully withheld plus damages of one and a half times it. And you cannot draft around any of this. The lease may not make the tenant waive rights or remedies under the act, so a clause declaring that an abandoned charger simply becomes yours, or dispensing with the notice and sale procedure, is unenforceable, and deliberately using a term you know is prohibited lets the tenant recover actual damages. The workable approach is to agree in advance that the tenant removes the charger and makes good, or that it stays and ownership transfers to you on an agreed basis, and then to follow the statutory procedure anyway if it is simply left behind.

title: EV Charging: Kansas Legislated, but Not About Landlords
bodyText:
Kansas gives a tenant no right to install an electric vehicle charger and gives a landlord no duty to allow, provide or pay for one. It also sets no conditions you must impose if you do allow one, so there is no statutory list of requirements about licensed contractors, insurance, registration or separate metering. That is not an oversight. Kansas legislated on electric vehicle charging in 2026 and chose to regulate someone else entirely.

The 2026 act applies to retail electric suppliers, meaning anyone furnishing retail electric service, that provide, own, operate or maintain a fast charging station for direct public use. Such a supplier must offer fair, reasonable and nondiscriminatory rates and services to all entities providing similar services, and must not act so as to give its own charging station an unreasonable competitive advantage. A fast charging station means behind-the-meter equipment capable of delivering at least 50 kilowatts of direct current at 200 volts or more. The act carves out stations that existed before July 2026, stations not open to the general public that sit on the supplier's own premises and serve only its own or its employees' vehicles, and stations a supplier is required by law or by regulator order to run. The whole section expires in July 2036.

Read that against your own position. You are not a retail electric supplier, your charger is almost certainly not a fast charging station, and it is not for direct public use. So the act imposes nothing on you and gives your tenants nothing. The useful point is what it signals: the legislature looked at electric vehicle charging and deliberately addressed competition between suppliers rather than access for tenants. Do not expect a tenant right to appear by implication.

There is one Kansas rule that does reach your equipment, and it is easy to miss because it sits in agriculture law rather than property law. In 2025 Kansas brought electric vehicle supply equipment into the state's weights and measures regime. The definition is broad: a device with one or more charging ports and connectors for charging electric vehicles, including all supporting equipment necessary to operate it and the area in the immediate vicinity, including adjacent parking areas and lanes for getting vehicles in and out. The regime reaches devices used for commercial purposes. Within it, installing, repairing, adjusting or calibrating such equipment is work for a licensed service company and a licensed technical representative, the department may place a rejection tag on non-compliant equipment, and only a licensed service company or a city or county weights and measures department may remove that tag. So if you install a charger and bill tenants by the kilowatt hour, you are plausibly operating a measuring device for commercial purposes, and a lease clause that makes the tenant responsible for maintaining or calibrating it may be asking the tenant to do licensed work. Get that checked before you write it.

Since no statute sets the terms, the lease sets them, and the clause is doing all the work. Four Kansas constraints bound what you can put in it. You cannot require the tenant to waive any right or remedy under the residential landlord and tenant act. You cannot make either side pay the other's attorney fees. You cannot exculpate or limit either party's liability arising under law, or make either indemnify the other for it, with one narrow exception letting you limit your liability for fire, theft or breakage in common areas. If you deliberately use a term you know is prohibited, the tenant can recover actual damages, so this is not a harmless drafting risk. And any money you hold to secure the tenant's obligations for the charger is a security deposit, counting toward the statutory cap of one month's rent unfurnished, one and a half months if the tenant uses your furniture, plus half a month where pets are allowed. Do not treat a charger deposit as sitting outside that limit.

Finally, electrical work remains subject to building and electrical codes and permits, which are set and enforced locally in Kansas and are not covered here. Check the code where the property sits before approving an installation. If you use the library's optional charger clause, note its bracketed requirement that the tenant carry liability insurance naming you as an additional insured: whether that survives Kansas's ban on lease terms making the tenant indemnify the landlord is not settled, and the cautious course in Kansas is to leave that bracket out (see the note on exculpatory clauses).

title: No Shared-Area EV Charging Rule
bodyText:
Kansas has no statute on electric vehicle charging in shared parking at a rental property. There is no rule on reserving a space for a charger, no rule on what you may charge a tenant for the privilege, no rule on sharing a charger between tenants or allocating its running costs, and no rule requiring you to install charging in common parking. Kansas law does not mention parking spaces and charging in the same breath anywhere. Nor does its 2026 electric vehicle act help: that act governs retail electric suppliers running public fast charging stations and says nothing about landlords, tenants or shared parking, and it expires in 2036.

So this is lease and house-rules territory, and you should write it down before the first charger goes in. Decide and record who gets the space, whether it is exclusive, what the charge for reserving it is, who pays for the electricity and how it is measured, who may use the charger, who maintains it, and what happens when that tenant leaves and the next one wants the space.

Three Kansas points shape how you write it. First, the deposit cap catches more than you expect. Any money you hold to secure a tenant's obligations about a charger or a reserved space is a security deposit, and it counts toward the statutory limit of one month's rent unfurnished, one and a half months if the tenant uses your furniture, plus half a month where pets are allowed. A separate charger deposit on top of a full deposit breaches that. A genuine non-refundable charge for reserving a space is a different thing from a deposit, but label it carefully and set it by reference to something real, because a residential lease is a consumer transaction in Kansas and an unconscionable charge is actionable.

Second, you must stay inside the limits on lease terms. You cannot require the tenant to give up a right or remedy under the residential landlord and tenant act, you cannot make either side pay the other's attorney fees, and you cannot exculpate or limit either party's liability arising under law or make either indemnify the other for it, apart from a narrow allowance letting you limit your own liability for fire, theft or breakage in common areas. Be careful with a clause making a tenant responsible for all damage arising from a charger in a shared area: holding the tenant to damage the tenant actually causes is ordinary, but a clause sweeping in your own legal liability to other people is the kind that gets struck down, and deliberately using a term you know is prohibited lets the tenant recover actual damages.

Third, and least obvious, the equipment may be regulated. In 2025 Kansas brought electric vehicle supply equipment into the state's weights and measures regime, and the definition is unusually wide: it covers the device, all supporting equipment needed to run it, and the area in the immediate vicinity, expressly including adjacent parking areas and the lanes vehicles use to get in and out. That matters most in exactly the shared-parking case, because the regulated footprint is not just the box on the wall but the bay and its approaches. Where such equipment is used for commercial purposes, installing, repairing, adjusting and calibrating it is work for a licensed service company and a licensed technical representative, and the department can tag non-compliant equipment out of service. The department's technical rules have not caught up: its regulation still adopts the 2012 edition of the national weights and measures handbook, adopted long before charging equipment was brought into the regime. So if you are going to meter and bill tenants for charging in a shared lot, ask the Kansas Department of Agriculture which requirements it applies to your equipment, and take advice, before you start rather than after.

Your ordinary duties do not change because a charger is involved. You must still exercise reasonable care in maintaining the common areas, and a charger, its cabling and its bay sit in that duty. Keep the installation, the lighting, the trip hazards and the surface in the condition the rest of the lot is in. If the property is in an association, its governing documents may restrict or control charging in common parking, and those are contractual obligations you have to work within. Local zoning, parking and electrical codes may also apply and are not covered here.

title: No Hardship Stay — and the One Delay Kansas Does Require
bodyText: Kansas gives a court no power to pause an eviction because the tenant would suffer hardship. There is no hardship stay, no discretionary grace period, no payment-plan stay and no short stay of the writ while the tenant finds somewhere to go. Kansas did not merely leave the subject alone, it legislated the other way. The general rule for Kansas judgments is that nothing can be done to enforce them until 14 days have passed after entry. The limited actions code then carves evictions straight out of that rule and says an eviction judgment may be enforced as soon as it is entered. That is about as clear a legislative choice as you will see, and it is why advice written for states with hardship stays does not travel here. The machinery after judgment is quick. On your request the court must issue a writ of restitution directing anyone authorised to serve process to put you back in possession. The writ has to be executed within 14 days after the server receives it, and the server may use such reasonable force as is necessary. Before judgment the position is just as firm. If a trial is needed it must happen within 14 days after the appearance date in the summons, and a continuance is not available to the tenant on request. The tenant can only get one by filing a bond with good and sufficient security approved by the court, conditioned to pay all damages and rent that may accrue if judgment goes against them. A tenant who cannot post that bond does not get more time. There is now exactly one delay the court must grant, and it has nothing to do with hardship. Since the 2026 eviction legislation, in an eviction where the tenancy is under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, the court must consider mediation unless it finds mediation would not materially aid the parties or is impracticable. If it orders mediation and the parties are participating, the court must order a continuance of up to 14 days running from the date the mediation order was entered. Note two things about it. The word is must, not may, so this is not discretionary once the conditions are met. And it is an express exception to the bond rule, so a tenant gets this continuance without posting anything. Build the possibility of an extra fortnight into your timetable for any Residential Landlord and Tenant Act eviction, and treat mediation as a real stage rather than a formality. The other route to delay is an appeal, and it runs on money rather than need. Simply appealing does not stay anything. A stay takes effect only when the judge approves a supersedeas bond, with such surety as the judge requires, conditioned to satisfy the judgment in full with costs, interest and damages for delay. There is one alternative that matters to you: instead of a bond the court may condition a stay pending appeal on the tenant paying the periodic rent otherwise due under the lease into court as it falls due. That is the nearest thing Kansas has to an accommodation, and it is still conditioned on paying, not on circumstances. The judge hearing the appeal also keeps a general power to stay proceedings or make orders preserving the status quo during the appeal. One provision deserves your attention because it can reverse a completed eviction. If the person holding the writ receives notice from the court that proceedings have been stayed by appeal, they must immediately stop. And if the premises have already been restored to you, that person must immediately put the tenant back in possession. So a stay obtained after the writ has been executed does not simply end matters, it can undo them. Do not re-let a unit the moment you get possession if an appeal is live. Finally, a federal point that is outside Kansas law: the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act can require a court to stay an eviction against a servicemember or their dependants in some circumstances. If the tenant is in military service, take advice rather than relying on the Kansas timetable. One caution on that carve-out: the general 14-day rule sits in the appeals article and on its face applies to limited actions generally, so the two provisions read literally pull against each other. The eviction-specific rule is the better reading and is how the writ timetable reads; if a tenant's lawyer raises the 14-day rule, take advice before executing the writ on the day of judgment.

title: No Eviction Penalty Ban — but Four Limits That Do the Same Work
bodyText: Kansas has no statute banning eviction-penalty or eviction-fee clauses as such. The list of terms a Kansas rental agreement may not contain is short and closed, and an eviction charge or a notice-service charge is not on it. So a clause of that kind is not prohibited outright. That is the beginning of the answer, not the end, because four separate limits bite on it and between them they leave very little room. First, attorney fees are flatly barred. No rental agreement may provide that the tenant or the landlord agrees to pay either party's attorney fees. The ban runs both ways and there is no exception for an eviction. An eviction fee that is in substance a charge for your lawyer is void, and if you deliberately use a lease containing a provision you know is prohibited the tenant may recover actual damages. That second point is worth absorbing: the exposure is not just that the clause fails. Second, indemnity and exculpation are barred.
