No rental agreement may provide that either party agrees to the exculpation or limitation of any liability arising under law, or to indemnify either party for that liability or the costs connected with it. The only carve-out lets you limit your own liability for fire, theft or breakage in the common areas. So a fee drafted as the tenant indemnifying you against the costs of a proceeding is at risk, while a charge drafted as reimbursement of your own actual out-of-pocket loss caused by the tenant's breach is not. How you frame it decides whether it survives. Third, and this is the one landlords miss, the court already awards most of what such a clause tries to capture, and the legislature has reserved fee-setting to itself. If judgment goes for you, the court may enter judgment for the amount of the docket fee you paid. Costs are allowed as a matter of course to the party in whose favour judgment is rendered, and the statutory list of what may be taxed is broad: the docket fee; the mileage, fees and expenses of the sheriff, another officer or a private process server in serving process; publisher's charges for any publication of notices required by law; witness fees and mileage; deposition charges; postage fees for service by certified mail; the fees and expenses of mediation, conciliation, arbitration or a settlement conference that the court ordered or the parties agreed to, whether or not it worked; and convenience or administrative fees for paying by card, including electronic filing fees. That last one about mediation now matters a great deal, because in a Residential Landlord and Tenant Act eviction the court must consider mediation. The upshot is that a lease clause charging a separate eviction filing fee, service fee or mediation fee duplicates something the judgment already gives you. Collected on top, it is a double recovery. The statute also says the docket fee is the only fee or money in the nature of a fee that may be collected for the docket fee, that such a fee may only be established by an act of the legislature, and that no other authority exists to collect one. That language cuts hard against a privately invented filing surcharge. Fourth, consumer protection law reaches your fee practices. A residential lease is a consumer transaction in Kansas and a landlord is a supplier, so the rules against deceptive and unconscionable acts apply. A fixed eviction fee with no relationship to what anything actually cost, charged on top of court-awarded costs, is a live unconscionability candidate. What to do instead. Do not write a general eviction-penalty or eviction-fee clause. Let the costs regime do its work: ask the court for your docket fee and taxed costs when you win, and keep the receipts for service, postage, publication and mediation. If you want to recover a genuine out-of-pocket cost the statutory list does not reach, such as the certified-mail cost of a pre-suit notice the statute requires you to give, keep it narrow, tie it to your documented actual cost, exclude anything taxed or awarded as costs and anything in the nature of a legal fee, and frame it as reimbursement of your actual damages for the tenant's breach rather than as indemnity. Do not state a dollar total for court costs in your lease. The docket fee amounts are fixed by statute and the supreme court is separately authorised to add a surcharge for a limited period, so any figure you print will go stale.

title: Who Serves Eviction Papers, and Who Can Be Served
bodyText: Kansas has two separate delivery regimes in an eviction and they have different rules. Confusing them is a common way to lose a case on the papers. The first is the pre-suit notice to leave the premises. Before you file, you must deliver a notice to leave to the other party at least three days before commencing the lawsuit. You may deliver it by leaving a written copy with the other party, or by leaving a copy with any person over the age of 12 residing on the premises, or, if no such person is found on the premises, by posting a copy in a conspicuous place on the premises, or by mailing a copy to the other party at the address of the premises. Count the three days as three consecutive 24-hour periods beginning when the notice is delivered, posted or mailed, and if you mail it add two further days before filing. Intermediate Saturdays, Sundays, legal holidays and days the clerk's office is closed all count, which is unusual and works in your favour. You may combine this notice with any notice the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act requires, which saves a step. Note that the older statute governing service of a notice terminating a tenancy is worded differently: it allows personal service, or if the tenant cannot be found leaving a copy at the tenant's usual place of residence, or delivery to a person over 12 residing on the premises, or posting if nobody is found there, or registered or certified mail return receipt requested addressed to the tenant at the tenant's usual place of residence. The difference matters: that route mails to the tenant's usual residence, while the notice to leave is mailed to the address of the premises. If the tenant has already moved out, those are not the same place. The second regime is service of the summons once the case is filed, and here the default is the sheriff. The sheriff of the county where the action is filed serves process unless you, personally or through your attorney, elect to take responsibility for service and tell the clerk. That election is worth knowing about, because a private process server is often faster and the server's fees and mileage are recoverable as taxed costs if you win. Return receipt delivery is available and is broader than certified mail: it covers priority mail, commercial courier, overnight delivery and other reliable personal delivery services, provided you get a receipt showing to whom delivered, the date, the address and who delivered it. The court sets the appearance date at not less than three and not more than 14 days after the summons is issued. Now the question landlords ask. Can the lease name someone to accept eviction papers for the tenant? Kansas law does contemplate it. Service on an individual may be made either by serving the individual or by serving an agent authorised by appointment or by law to receive service of process, and where the agent is served by mail the papers go to the agent's usual or designated address. So an agent appointed by the tenant is a recognised route in Kansas, and a lease clause naming one is not forbidden. Treat it with care rather than as a free win. The appointment has to be a genuine one by the tenant, so do not nominate yourself, your manager or anyone under your control, and do not bury the designation. Keep the tenant's own right to be served directly intact and treat the named agent as an additional route rather than a substitute. A designation extracted in a form lease and then used to obtain a judgment the tenant never heard about is the kind of term that attracts an unconscionability challenge, because a residential lease is a consumer transaction in Kansas. Keep the named person's address current, and if the designation has gone stale serve the tenant directly. One situation to watch and not to guess at. Kansas operates an address confidentiality programme for victims of domestic violence, sexual assault, human trafficking and stalking, under which a participant uses a substitute address. The programme is run by the attorney general, not the Secretary of State, and every participant's application designates the attorney general as the participant's agent for service of process and for receiving mail; the attorney general forwards the participant's first class mail. So for a participant the attorney general is an agent authorised by law to receive service. The statute does not say how that fits with the notice-to-leave rules or whether the premises address still works, so if you learn or suspect that your tenant is a programme participant, get advice before serving, and expect to serve through the attorney general as well as by the ordinary routes. Do not simply post on the door and assume you are safe.

title: Exculpation and Indemnity Are Banned, With One Narrow Exception
bodyText: Kansas bans exculpatory and indemnity clauses in a residential lease, and the ban is wider than most landlords expect. No rental agreement may provide that the tenant or the landlord agrees to the exculpation or limitation of any liability of either party arising under law, or to indemnify either party for that liability or the costs connected with it. Read the words carefully, because four things follow. It covers exculpation and limitation alike, so capping your liability at a sum, or at the amount of the deposit, is caught just as a full waiver is. It covers indemnity separately, and it expressly reaches the costs connected with the liability, so a clause making the tenant pay your defence costs fails even if it does not make them pay the judgment. It says any liability arising under law, without distinguishing ordinary negligence from gross negligence or wilful conduct, so narrowing your disclaimer to ordinary negligence does not rescue it in Kansas the way it would in some states. And it runs both ways: a clause exculpating the tenant is just as void as one exculpating you. There is exactly one exception and it is narrow. A rental agreement may limit the landlord's liability for fire, theft or breakage with respect to the common areas of the dwelling unit. Note every limit built into that. It protects the landlord only, not the tenant. It covers only three perils, fire, theft and breakage, so it does nothing for water damage, personal injury, pests, mould or anything else. And it reaches only the common areas, so it does not apply inside the unit. A clause written to that exact shape is lawful. A clause that drifts beyond it in any direction is not. The consequences of getting this wrong come in two layers. The provision is unenforceable, so it simply fails when you need it. On top of that, if you deliberately use a rental agreement containing provisions you know are prohibited, the tenant may recover actual damages. That second layer is what makes an old form lease a live exposure rather than a harmless relic, and the damages are not limited to the exculpation clause itself. If your lease carries an inherited liability-waiver paragraph, delete it rather than relying on it being void. What you can do instead. Facts are not disclaimers. Telling the tenant that your insurance does not cover their belongings, or that you do not provide security for the parking area, states a true thing without purporting to limit your liability, and that is a real distinction worth preserving in the drafting. You may require the tenant to carry renter's insurance covering their own property and their own liability, and to show you evidence of it. Be careful before going further and requiring the tenant to name you as an additional insured. Kansas has no decision on whether that is insurance procurement, which would be fine, or indemnity in substance, which would be void. The legislature has elsewhere declared that a provision requiring one party to provide liability coverage to another as an additional insured for that other party's own negligence or intentional acts is against public policy and void, though that statute applies to construction contracts and similar agreements and expressly excludes leases. The safer course is to require insurance covering the tenant's own liability and to leave your own negligence out of it, or to take advice first. Three related points. A separate Kansas statute voids indemnity and additional-insured provisions in construction contracts, but it expressly provides that no deed, lease, easement, licence or other instrument granting an interest in or the right to possess property counts as a construction contract, even where it includes a right to repair or maintain improvements. So that statute neither helps you nor binds you here. Kansas also gives the court a general unconscionability power over a rental agreement or any clause in it, which is a second route to the same result. And the exculpation ban sits inside the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, so it does not reach arrangements the act excludes, such as transient hotel occupancy, occupancy conditioned on employment, or premises used primarily for agricultural purposes. In those settings there is no statutory ban, and the clause is still a poor idea.

title: No Expedited Deposit Procedure, and No Fee for Early Return
bodyText: Kansas has no expedited security deposit procedure. There is no mechanism by which a tenant asks you to settle the deposit early, and no authority to charge an administrative or processing fee for doing it sooner. The word expedited appears nowhere in Kansas law in a deposit context. Part of the reason is that Kansas's ordinary timetable is already short, so there is very little to speed up. Where a landlord proposes to keep part of the deposit for expenses, damages or other legally allowable charges other than rent, the balance must go back within 14 days after the amount of those charges is determined, and in no event more than 30 days after termination of the tenancy, delivery of possession and the tenant's demand. The 14 days runs from your own determination of the amount, so the practical deadline is whichever comes first. States with expedited procedures tend to be those allowing 45 days, where there is a real window to shorten. Kansas is not one of them. You may of course return the deposit sooner than the deadline, and nothing stops you settling it the week the tenant leaves. What you should not do is charge for the privilege. Kansas lets you retain from the deposit only accrued rent, the damages you have suffered by reason of the tenant's noncompliance with the statutory tenant duties and with the lease, and expenses, damages or other legally allowable charges under the lease other than rent, all itemised in a written notice to the tenant. An early-processing fee does not fit. It is not accrued rent. It is not a loss caused by the tenant's noncompliance, because asking for a prompt refund is not a breach of anything. And calling it a legally allowable charge under the lease begs the question, since nothing in Kansas law makes it allowable and a residential lease is a consumer transaction here, so an unconscionable charge is actionable in its own right. Getting this wrong is expensive in a specific way. If you fail to comply with the return rules the tenant may recover the portion of the deposit due plus damages equal to one and a half times the amount wrongfully withheld. Deduct a fee Kansas does not authorise and the deducted amount is the amount wrongfully withheld, so a small fee can carry a penalty of two and a half times itself, plus the tenant's costs of coming after it. If you want to be paid for administrative work, build it into the rent, where it is visible and lawful, rather than taking it out of the deposit at the end. Three related points worth holding on to. The deduction power reaches the lease, not just the statute: the damages you may apply the deposit to include those caused by the tenant's noncompliance with the lease, and the statute separately contemplates retention for other legally allowable charges under the lease other than rent. So genuine contractual charges are deductible even though a processing fee is not, and the difference is whether the charge answers to something the tenant actually did. The itemised written notice is not optional, whenever you keep anything. And if you have sold the property, the holder of the landlord's interest at the time the tenancy ends is bound by these rules, so a sale does not move the obligation. Finally, do not confuse timing with amount. Kansas recently barred cities and counties from limiting how large a deposit a landlord may require. That is about the size of the deposit, not about when it comes back or what you may take out of it, and it gives you no new power over either.

title: Family Child Care in Rentals
bodyText: Kansas gives a tenant no right to run a child care home in a rented dwelling, and it does not stop you refusing. Some states protect family child care against a lease or a restrictive covenant. Kansas has nothing of the kind, and it has no home-occupation statute either. So the lease decides, and if you do not want a child care business in the unit, say so in plain words rather than relying on a general residential-use clause to carry the weight. If you are willing to allow it, understand what changes, because the most important consequence is one almost nobody sees coming. The moment the unit is used as a licensed day care home, it stops being a private residence for the purposes of Kansas smoking law. Kansas defines a place of employment and a public place so as to exclude a private residence, but each definition has the same exception: unless the residence is used as a day care home. The Indoor Clean Air Act's own exemption for private homes carries the identical exception. The result is that a day care home is treated as both a workplace and a public place, and the whole state smoking ban applies inside it. Three things follow. Signs become compulsory. Whoever is the proprietor or other person in charge of the premises of a public place, or of any other area where smoking is prohibited, must post signs in a conspicuous place showing the international no smoking symbol and stating clearly that smoking is prohibited by state law. Settle in writing whether that is the tenant's job or yours before the licence is granted, because the statute speaks of the person in charge of the premises and in a rented building that is not obviously only one of you. A ten foot no-smoking zone appears around the entrances. Smoking becomes unlawful at the access points of any building not exempt from the Act, and an access point is the area within a ten foot radius outside any doorway, open window or air intake leading into it. That is worth pausing on, because the child care statute itself says nothing in its smoking subsection prohibits smoking on the premises outside the facility, specifically mentioning porches, yards and garages. Read carefully, that saving only limits that subsection. It does not disapply the Indoor Clean Air Act, so on the better reading a porch within ten feet of the door is still off limits. Treat the ten foot rule as the operative one and do not promise a smoking tenant otherwise. And if the tenant has staff, the tenant becomes an employer with real paperwork: a smoke-free workplace, plus a written smoking policy prohibiting smoking without exception in all areas of the workplace, communicated to existing employees within a week of adoption and to new ones on hiring, with a copy given to any current or prospective employee who asks. The child care rules add their own requirements to the premises. Smoking is prohibited inside the facility whenever children not related to the person keeping the home are being cared for there. The licence itself must carry a bold-print statement of that prohibition and must be posted in a conspicuous place in the facility. The home must have a fire extinguisher, kept operable and in a readily accessible location. Breaches draw civil fines, escalating for a third or later violation. The fine is assessed by the health secretary after notice and a hearing, cannot exceed five hundred dollars for each violation, and every day a violation continues counts as a separate violation — so a standing breach is not a single five-hundred-dollar event. A third or subsequent breach moves off the fine track altogether and becomes a ground on which the licence itself may be limited, modified or suspended. Two more points that affect you directly. The background rules reach everyone in the household, not just the business. Kansas restricts who may maintain, reside at, work at or volunteer at a child care facility, and it does so by defining an employee of a facility to mean a person working, regularly volunteering OR RESIDING in it — so every adult living in the unit is an employee for this purpose and comes within scope, with the health secretary entitled to court records, criminal history record information including diversion agreements held by the Kansas Bureau of Investigation, and child abuse and neglect investigation reports, and with fingerprinting for a national check. A conviction during the licence period is itself a ground for limiting, modifying or suspending the licence. The facility and its employees are not liable in civil damages to a person refused employment or discharged because of good-faith compliance with those restrictions. Those provisions were amended twice in 2026 and then reconciled; both amendments were about family foster homes rather than day care homes, but check the current text before relying on any detail. Separately, Kansas does not require a child care home licensee to live in the home, so a licence tells you nothing about who is actually residing there, and a tenant could hold a licence for premises they do not occupy. Do not read a licence as a statement of occupancy. Finally, keep two distinctions straight. A child care centre is not a child care home, and centres carry their own rules: compliance with the local jurisdiction's requirements for fire protection, water supply and sewage disposal, at least 28 square feet of indoor activity space per child excluding kitchens, passageways, storage and bathrooms, and at least 60 square feet of outdoor play space per child using it at any one time. From July 2026 those provisions are administered by the director of early childhood rather than the health secretary. And what actually counts as a day care home is fixed by state regulation rather than by statute, which matters because the whole smoking switch described above turns on that definition. Local zoning and occupancy codes may also restrict or require a permit for child care in a dwelling, and those are not covered here. Before you consent, check the zoning, tell your insurer, and put the conditions and the sign-posting duty in writing.

title: Hunting and Fishing on Rented Land
bodyText: Kansas has no statute allocating hunting or fishing rights between a landowner and a tenant. Some states reverse the default by statute and keep those rights with the owner unless the lease expressly grants them. Kansas has done nothing of the kind, so there is no rule you can fall back on and the question is answered entirely by what your lease says. If the property includes land or water where someone might hunt, fish, shoot or trap, reserve the rights in writing. That matters more than it sounds, because the default cuts against you. A lease gives the tenant possession, and possession ordinarily carries the right to use the land and to decide who comes onto it. Without a reservation you are in an argument you may well lose, and worse, you may find your tenant giving permission to other people. Say plainly that you keep all rights to hunt, fish, shoot and trap and to let others do so, that the tenant and the tenant's household and guests will not, and that the tenant will not give anyone else permission. If you want to grant the tenant some limited right, describe it: which activities, which seasons, which part of the land, and whether guests are included. Kansas criminal trespass law is the backstop, and there is a detail in it you should notice. Entering or remaining on land, in defiance of an order not to enter personally communicated by the owner or by another authorised person, is criminal trespass, and so is entering land that is posted in the manner the wildlife statutes prescribe, or posted in any other manner reasonably likely to come to the attention of intruders, or that is locked, fenced or otherwise enclosed. The phrase to watch is the owner or other authorised person. A tenant in possession is a strong candidate to be an authorised person who can order someone off, which is exactly why a lease silent on hunting can leave the tenant controlling access to your land. Kansas's hunting statutes put that beyond doubt, and this is the part that should decide how you draft. Criminal hunting in Kansas is hunting, shooting, fur harvesting, pursuing a bird or animal, or fishing on another's land without first obtaining the permission of the owner OR OF THE PERSON IN POSSESSION. The posting statute says the same thing from the other direction: a landowner OR A PERSON IN LAWFUL POSSESSION may post the land, and on posted land a hunter must carry the written permission of the owner or of the person in lawful possession. So a tenant in possession can both give hunting permission and post the land in their own right. A lease that says nothing hands that decision to your tenant, and your posted signs will not help you against someone the tenant invited. Two posting routes are available and either works. Signs saying that hunting, trapping or fishing is by written permission only; or, instead of signs, vertical purple paint marks on trees or posts around the area, each at least eight inches long, with the bottom of the mark no less than three feet and no more than five feet above the ground, readily visible to anyone approaching. Posting by paint counts as posting by written permission only. Note one carve-out: a licensed hunter following a wounded animal onto posted land is not in breach while in pursuit, but must leave if the owner or person in lawful possession tells them to. Hunting without permission, or from an adjoining public road or railway right-of-way, is a class C nonperson misdemeanour, and the court may order forfeiture of the hunting, fishing or fur-harvesting licence for up to a year on a first conviction and must do so for a year on a second. Hunting on land the person knows they are not privileged to be on, and either defying a personally communicated order to leave or entering land posted as the posting statute prescribes, is a class B nonperson misdemeanour with mandatory licence forfeiture of six months, a year, then five years. The court must notify the state wildlife department of any conviction or diversion. Three practical points. Fence or post, and keep it current, because the trespass protection that does not depend on your having a conversation with the intruder is the posting and enclosure route. Make sure the lease says who may let others onto the land, not just who may hunt, since the second question is where the trouble usually starts. And correct one assumption most landlords make. Hunting licences, seasons and methods are public regulation, and a lease cannot excuse anyone from the game laws — but on agricultural land the lease itself is what removes the licence requirement. Kansas does not require a hunting licence for a person, or a member of that person's immediate family domiciled with them, hunting on land owned by that person OR ON LAND LEASED OR RENTED BY THAT PERSON FOR AGRICULTURAL PURPOSES. So if you let land for agricultural purposes, your tenant and their household can hunt it without any licence at all, and a licence requirement is not going to be the thing that stops them. The lease is. Hunter education is a separate requirement and is not removed by the lease in the same way: a person born on or after 1 July 1957 who is sixteen or over may not hunt on land other than that person's OWN land without a certificate of completion of an approved hunter education course, with supervision rules for those under sixteen and two available deferrals. One scope point that may decide which rules apply at all. The Kansas Residential Landlord and Tenant Act does not govern occupancy under a rental agreement covering premises used primarily for agricultural purposes. So if the land, rather than the house, is the main point of the letting, you are outside the residential act altogether, and the older farm tenancy statutes and the lease govern instead, including different notice periods for ending the tenancy. If you are renting a farmhouse with acreage, work out which side of that line you are on before you rely on anything written for ordinary residential tenancies.

title: A Fee Instead of a Deposit: Kansas Leaves You Almost No Room
bodyText: Kansas has no statute authorising a non-refundable fee in place of a security deposit, and none regulating the deposit-alternative and surety-bond products now sold to landlords. There is no permission to point to, and no safe harbour. That is not the same as the practice being free, because Kansas defines its terms in a way that leaves very little space for a third kind of payment. Start with the definition of a security deposit. It is any sum of money specified in a rental agreement, however denominated, to be deposited with the landlord by the tenant as a condition precedent to occupying the unit, which sum or any part of it may be forfeited by the tenant under the terms of the agreement on the occurrence or breach of specified conditions. The words however denominated are doing deliberate work. Calling money a fee, a risk charge, a waiver payment or anything else does not take it outside the definition. If the lease specifies it, if the tenant must pay it before moving in, and if the tenant stands to lose it, Kansas is likely to treat it as a security deposit whatever it says on the invoice. Now add the second definition, which is the one that closes the door. Rent means all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement other than the security deposit. Put the two together and Kansas's scheme is binary: money the tenant pays you under the lease is either a security deposit or it is rent. There is no third box. So a fee in lieu of a deposit has to land somewhere, and both landings have consequences. If it is a security deposit, it counts against the cap, which is one month's periodic rent for an unfurnished unit, one and a half months where the tenant uses your furniture, and a further half month where pets are allowed. Taking a full deposit and a fee on top would breach the cap. It also has to be itemised and returned on the statutory timetable, and if you keep what you should not the tenant can recover it plus damages of one and a half times the amount wrongfully withheld. If instead it is rent, then it is not non-refundable in the way you intended at all: it is simply part of what the tenant pays for the tenancy, it feeds into what a month's periodic rent means for the cap, and it is exposed to the ordinary consequences of rent, including being the thing an eviction for non-payment is about. Whether a genuinely non-refundable fee satisfies the forfeiture limb of the deposit definition has not been settled in Kansas, and the argument runs both ways. A fee that never comes back is forfeited in the fullest sense, which supports treating it as a deposit. Against that, the definition speaks of money forfeited on the occurrence or breach of specified conditions, and a fee that is gone from day one is not forfeited on any condition. Until someone resolves it, the cautious course is the only sensible one: treat any such fee as a security deposit, count it against the cap, document it, and return whatever is not properly retained. Charge a fee on the footing that it escapes the cap and you are betting the one-and-a-half-times penalty on an unsettled reading. Two further points. Third-party products need separate thought. The deposit definition catches money deposited with a landlord. A premium the tenant pays directly to an insurer or surety, which you neither hold nor receive, is harder to fit into that language, so those products may sit outside the statute. But if the money passes through you, or you collect it, or you take a commission on it, you are much closer to the line, and selling an insurance product to your own tenant raises questions well beyond landlord and tenant law. Get advice before building a programme around one. And do not read the recent preemption statute as help. Kansas has barred cities and counties from limiting the amount of a security deposit a landlord may require, and voided any such local ordinance adopted before July 2026. That removes a local ceiling. It does not touch the state cap, which is where your problem is, and it creates no landlord power of any kind.

title: No All-In Pricing or Fee-Transparency Law in Kansas
bodyText: Kansas has no analogue to Colorado's Honest Pricing Act and no Minnesota-style 'Total Monthly Payment' rule. No Kansas statute requires you to advertise a single all-in price that includes mandatory fees, to state the sum of rent plus non-optional fees anywhere in the lease, to put fees on the lease's first page, to use any verbatim statutory sentence, or to offer a fee-free way to pay. There is also no Kansas junk-fee or total-price regulation that names dwelling units, and no negative-option rule reaching residential leases. The lease decides, and the Kansas rule is simply that the landlord and tenant may include terms not prohibited by the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or other law. Three real limits still apply, and they are the reason to itemize anyway. First, a residential lease is a consumer transaction under the Kansas Consumer Protection Act, and a willful failure to state a material fact, or the willful concealment, suppression or omission of one, is a listed deceptive act and practice whether or not any consumer was in fact misled. A mandatory monthly charge the tenant only discovers after signing is the standard shape of that claim. Second, the same act bars unconscionable acts and practices in connection with a consumer transaction, before, during or after it, and a term excessively one-sided in the supplier's favour is one of the circumstances a court weighs. Third, the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act lets a court refuse to enforce a lease provision it finds was unconscionable when made, enforce the rest without it, or limit its application. So the safe practice in Kansas is a matter of evidence rather than of form: name every non-optional charge in the lease itself, in dollars, state what each is for and when it is due, and do not add a mandatory charge later that the lease never mentioned. A local ordinance is a separate question. Kansas bars cities and counties from controlling the amount of rent charged, and a 2026 act voids local ordinances on four specific subjects, but neither reaches a local fee-disclosure or advertising rule, so check the city if you operate in one.

title: No Specific Rule on Fees for Services Not Provided
bodyText: Kansas has no analogue to Colorado's Honest Pricing law and no statute that specifically bars charging a tenant a fee for a service you do not actually provide. That does not make the charge safe, because three other Kansas rules reach it. First, a residential lease is a consumer transaction, and when a court decides whether a practice was unconscionable it is told to weigh, among other things, whether the consumer was unable to receive a material benefit from the subject of the transaction. A monthly charge for something the tenant never gets is the plainest version of that. The same act also makes it a deceptive act and practice to offer services without intending to supply them, or to represent that services have uses or benefits they do not have, whether or not any tenant was in fact misled. Second, a court may refuse to enforce a lease provision it finds was unconscionable when made, enforce the rest of the lease without it, or limit how it applies. Third, if the charge is for something you are required to supply in the first place, the statutory duties take over. You must keep in good and safe working order every electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning appliance you supply or are required to supply, maintain the common areas with reasonable care, provide and arrange removal of waste receptacles, and supply running water, reasonable hot water and reasonable heat. If you do not, the tenant has a damages and injunction claim, and a termination route after written notice. If you willfully cut off electric, gas, water or another essential service, the tenant may recover possession or terminate and take the greater of actual damages or one and a half months' rent. Practical rule: make every fee in the lease correspond to something real, describe what the tenant gets for it, and stop charging when the service stops. Billing a tenant for a service you are already obliged to supply is a separate problem, because it does not buy the tenant anything.

title: Which Fire Code Applies, and to Which Buildings
bodyText: Your Kansas lease obligations include complying with applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, and that duty outranks the landlord's other statutory maintenance duties where they conflict. The fire code those words point to is the Kansas fire prevention code. It is not in the statutes. It is the body of rules and regulations the state fire marshal adopts, published in the Kansas Administrative Regulations, and the statute lets those rules incorporate by reference specific editions, or parts of editions, of nationally recognized fire prevention codes, which Kansas defines by example as the National Fire Protection Association's codes and American National Standards Institute standards. In 2026 the legislature directed the state toward the International Fire Code, 2024 edition: it told the fire marshal that a rulemaking updating the Kansas fire prevention code with that edition, with appropriate amendments, is exempt from the usual economic impact statement, gave the attorney general 120 days to review the proposed rules, and left the rules subject to legislative ratification. Check the fire marshal's current regulations for the edition actually in force before you rely on an edition number. Two points matter more to a landlord than the edition does. First, scope. The fire marshal's rules on exits and fire escapes, on fire control, detection and extinguishing equipment, and the catch-all safeguards rule all expressly reach apartment houses, and all three expressly do not apply to buildings used wholly as dwelling houses containing no more than two families. So a single-family rental or a duplex sits outside those rules, while a three-unit building and up sits inside them. Second, uniformity. The Kansas fire prevention code has uniform force and effect throughout the state, and no city or county may enact or enforce any ordinance, resolution, rule or regulation inconsistent with it. The exceptions are narrow: a municipality keeps its power to regulate the use of land by zoning or fire district regulations, and to regulate fireworks. If you think a local requirement conflicts with the state code, the statute makes the state fire marshal the one who decides, after a hearing, with court review afterwards. Enforcement reaches you, not just the building. The fire marshal, the marshal's deputies and the chief of any organized municipal fire department enforce the code; a violation is a class B misdemeanor and each day it continues after written notice is a separate violation; the fire marshal can also impose an administrative penalty of up to $1,000 per violation, appealable first to the marshal and then to court; and the attorney general or the county or district attorney can get an injunction where the violation continues or is an immediate hazard. Older buildings get some protection: the marshal's rules must let facilities that were in service before the rules took effect, and that do not strictly conform, stay in service, unless the marshal determines the facility is a distinct hazard to life or property, and that determination can be appealed. As of 2026-10-24 the fire marshal has not carried that direction out: K.A.R. 22-1-3 still adopts the International Fire Code 2006 edition and the International Building Code 2006 edition, and K.A.R. 22-1-2 accepts in the alternative the 1997 Uniform Building Code or the 2006 IBC with a certificate of occupancy. Those 2006 editions are the standard in force.

title: Fire Sprinklers: No Statutory Duty, and a Ban on City Mandates for Small Dwellings
bodyText: No Kansas statute requires a residential landlord to install fire sprinklers or to retrofit an existing rental with them, and there is no Kansas sprinkler-disclosure duty. What Kansas has instead is a prohibition pointed at local government. No city or county may adopt or enforce any ordinance, order, code, standard or rule requiring a multi-purpose residential fire protection sprinkler system or any other fire sprinkler system in a residential structure, and no city or county may require one as a condition of approving a building permit or a plat. Read the definition before you rely on it, because it is narrower than it sounds: a residential structure for this purpose is a single-family dwelling, a multi-family dwelling of two attached living units or less, or a manufactured home. A triplex, a fourplex and an apartment building are not covered, so a local sprinkler requirement reaching those is not barred by this statute. Anyone may still install sprinklers voluntarily, and the statute says so expressly. Above the two-unit line, the question is regulatory rather than statutory. The legislature has given the state fire marshal authority to make rules on the installation and maintenance of equipment intended for fire control, detection and extinguishment in buildings where people work, live or congregate, expressly including apartment houses, and has told the marshal those rules do not apply to buildings used wholly as dwelling houses containing no more than two families. Whether and when those rules call for sprinklers in a particular building is answered by the Kansas fire prevention code and the building code editions the marshal accepts, not by any statute, and it typically turns on occupancy, height, construction type and the date of the building permit. Do not assume a sprinkler system is optional in a larger or newer building because no statute names one. Practical course: if the building has a system, say so in the lease, keep it maintained and inspected, and tell tenants plainly not to hang anything from a sprinkler head or block one, because a damaged head floods the building and the cost lands on whoever caused it. If the building has none, do not represent that it does.

title: Firearms: No Kansas Statute Either Way, and Cities May Not Fill the Gap
bodyText:
Kansas has no statute on firearms in a residential tenancy, in either direction. Nothing makes a lease firearm rule unenforceable against a tenant, the way Ohio and Tennessee do for licence holders, and nothing requires you to allow a firearm in the unit, in a tenant's vehicle in the parking area or anywhere else you control. Kansas also has no parking-lot firearm statute reaching property owners, so the sentence that Louisiana and Mississippi leases must carry about locked private vehicles has no Kansas counterpart, and copying it into a Kansas lease would state a rule Kansas does not have.

The general Kansas rule applies instead: the landlord and tenant may include in a rental agreement terms and conditions not prohibited by the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or other rule of law. A firearm rule is not on the act's list of prohibited terms.

Two limits are worth knowing. The first is that a city or county cannot help you and cannot stop you. Kansas bars every city and county from adopting or enforcing any ordinance, resolution or regulation, and any agent of one from taking administrative action, governing fees, licences or permits for, or the commerce in or the sale, purchase, transfer, ownership, storage, carrying, transporting or taxation of, firearms or ammunition or any component. Any such ordinance adopted before 1 July 2015 is null and void. The exceptions are about the city's own employees, public buildings, police officers acting in their duties, and sales tax. So a Kansas city cannot pass a firearm ordinance that overrides your lease, and it cannot pass one that forces a firearm rule on your property either.

The second is the state constitution: a person has the right to keep and bear arms for the defense of self, family, home and state, for lawful hunting and recreational use, and for any other lawful purpose. That right runs against government, not against a private landlord's lease, and no Kansas court has been shown to apply it to a lease term, so treat a flat possession ban as a business decision with an untested legal edge rather than as safe ground.

The narrow, defensible rule is the one most landlords actually want: no unlawful discharge, and safe and lawful storage. Both are enforceable as ordinary lease terms and neither depends on a Kansas statute that does not exist. If you intend a broader ban, put it in the lease in plain words before signing rather than imposing it later as a rule change, and apply it to every tenant the same way.

title: No Flood Disclosure Statute, but a Licensed Agent Still Has to Speak
bodyText: Kansas has no flood disclosure statute for residential rentals. There is no required notice, no state model form, no 12-point rider, no separate signature line, and no tenant right to terminate after a flood loss, so nothing resembling the California, Texas or Florida regimes applies here. Kansas also has no general residential property condition disclosure statute for sellers, let alone for landlords. That is not the whole answer, and a row that stopped there would be wrong. If a licensed real estate broker or salesperson is involved in the rental, the licensee has a disclosure duty that runs to the prospective tenant directly. A landlord's agent owes a customer no duty except that the licensee shall disclose to any customer all adverse material facts actually known by the licensee, including environmental hazards affecting the property that the law requires to be disclosed, the physical condition of the property, and any material defects in the property. A prospective tenant is a customer. A transaction broker owes the same disclosure to a prospective tenant. Known repeated flooding, a unit below grade that takes water, or a property inside a mapped special flood hazard area is the kind of fact that lands in that category, and an intentional failure to disclose it is also grounds for discipline against the licence. Note the limit in the other direction too: Kansas does not require a licence to rent out residential property, because the licensing act defines a lease as one for nonresidential use, so an owner managing their own rentals is outside that duty. Two more things reach a landlord who is not using an agent. A residential lease is a consumer transaction under the Kansas Consumer Protection Act, and the willful failure to state a material fact, or the willful concealment, suppression or omission of one, is a deceptive act and practice whether or not the tenant was actually misled. Separately, flood risk is a land-use subject in Kansas, not a disclosure subject: cities and counties may establish flood plain zones and restrict the use of land in them, subject to approval by the chief engineer of the division of water resources and to the minimum requirements of the national flood insurance act. The practical course: find out whether the property sits in a special flood hazard area, say so in the lease in writing if it does or if you know the property has flooded, and tell the tenant plainly that renters insurance does not cover flood damage and that the tenant's own belongings are the tenant's own risk.

title: Telling a Prospective Tenant About a Pending Foreclosure
bodyText: No Kansas statute requires you to tell an applicant or a tenant that the property is in foreclosure, that a notice of default has been recorded, or that a foreclosure sale is set. Kansas has nothing like Nevada's pre-lease written disclosure, Minnesota's notice of the end of the redemption period, Arizona's notice of possible foreclosure, or Vermont's duty on an owner served with a foreclosure complaint. There is also no Kansas form, no signature requirement and no tenant right to terminate because of a foreclosure. One exception matters in practice. If a licensed real estate broker or salesperson is involved in the rental as the landlord's agent, or acting as a transaction broker, that licensee must disclose to a prospective tenant all adverse material facts actually known to the licensee, including any material limitation on the client's ability to perform under the terms of the contract. A pending foreclosure on the very property being leased is the clearest example of that: it is a known limitation on the landlord's ability to deliver the term being promised. The duty is the licensee's, so it bites when you use a brokerage, and not when you rent out your own property yourself, because Kansas does not license residential renting. A second exception is general rather than specific. A residential lease is a consumer transaction under the Kansas Consumer Protection Act, and the willful failure to state a material fact, or the willful concealment, suppression or omission of one, is a deceptive act and practice whether or not the tenant was in fact misled. Signing a tenant to a twelve-month term on a property you know is weeks from a sheriff's sale is the scenario that provision was written for. What the law gives you instead of a disclosure rule is time, and knowing the timetable is what lets you answer a tenant honestly. Kansas foreclosure is judicial and is followed by a statutory redemption period. The owner may redeem within twelve months of the sale, and keeps the right to possession in the meantime, but that period drops to three months where default occurred before a third of the original debt was paid, and a court can shorten or extinguish it on 21 days' notice if the property has been abandoned or is not occupied in good faith. So a tenancy does not end at the sale. Practical course: if a foreclosure is pending and you are signing a new tenant, say so in writing before signing, set out the dates, and do not take a long term or a large deposit you may not be able to stand behind.

title: When a Tenant Can Still Undo a Termination by Paying or Curing
bodyText: Kansas gives a tenant a short cure window before termination and nothing at all after it. Know which window you are in, because Kansas has no pay-and-stay right at the courthouse door. For unpaid rent, you may terminate only after serving a written notice of the nonpayment and of your intention to terminate if the rent is not paid within three days. Those three days are three consecutive 24-hour periods, running from the moment you hand the notice to the tenant, hand it to a person over 12 living at the premises, or post it conspicuously on the property. If you mail it instead, the tenant gets two extra days from the date of mailing. Pay inside that window and the tenancy continues. For any other material breach of the lease, or a breach of the tenant's statutory duties that materially affects health and safety, the notice is different: it must specify the acts and omissions and state that the agreement terminates on a date at least 30 days out if the breach is not remedied in 14 days. If the breach can be fixed by repair, by paying damages or otherwise, and the tenant adequately initiates a good faith effort to fix it before the date in the notice, the agreement does not terminate. But if the same or a similar breach happens again after that 14-day period, your next notice can terminate in 30 days with no chance to cure. Once the cure window closes, Kansas offers the tenant no statutory redemption. There is no Maine-style right to reinstate by paying arrears before the writ issues, no Vermont-style second chance, no New Hampshire-style payment to stop the case, and no California-style election-of-forfeiture trap in the notice. After termination you serve a three-day notice to leave the premises, which may be combined with the statutory notice you already gave, then file. One new thing does slow the case down. Since 2026, in an eviction governed by the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, the court must consider mediation unless it finds mediation would not aid the parties materially or is impracticable, and if the parties are participating in mediation the court must order a continuance of up to 14 days from the date the mediation order is entered. That is a delay, not a redemption: it does not revive a terminated tenancy. Two separate things also called redemption, so you do not confuse them with the tenancy. If the tenant leaves property behind, or is removed by a writ and leaves property behind, the tenant may redeem that property during the 30 days before you sell it, by paying your reasonable costs of taking, holding and preparing it for sale plus anything owed for rent or otherwise. And accepting rent after a breach can waive the breach, which is the opposite problem.

title: Codes Frozen to a Named Edition, and Why the Current Edition May Not Be the One That Applies
bodyText: Several Kansas requirements are measured against an outside code fixed at a particular edition rather than against whatever the publisher has most recently issued. Reading the current edition of one of those codes can give you the wrong answer. The most important rule is the general one about locally adopted codes, and it works in your favour as often as against you. When a Kansas city puts a model or standard code into an ordinance by reference, or a county into a resolution, the ordinance or resolution must name the code, the organization that produced it and the year or edition. From then on, the publisher amending the code or issuing a new revision does not change what applies locally. The incorporated edition stays in force until the city or county repeals the ordinance, amends it, or incorporates a later code. So the edition your city adopted, not the edition on sale today, is the one that governs your building. The reverse is true for state material a local government incorporates: if the legislature amends an incorporated statute, or a state agency changes an incorporated regulation, the incorporated version stops being effective until the local government re-adopts it. Four more Kansas freezes are worth knowing. First, fire. A building is deemed to comply with the Kansas fire prevention code if it conforms to one of four named building code editions, has a certificate of occupancy and meets the fire code's special requirements that the building code does not cover. The four are old: the 1976 or 1979 Uniform Building Code, the 1975 or 1978 BOCA Basic Building Code, the 1976 or 1979 Standard Building Code, and the 2000 International Building Code. The state fire marshal can unfreeze the list by rule, by specifying later editions of those or other nationally recognized building codes that give equivalent protection. Second, the fire code itself. The marshal's rules may incorporate specific editions, or parts of editions, of nationally recognized fire prevention codes, and in 2026 the legislature named the International Fire Code, 2024 edition, as the edition the Kansas fire prevention code is to be updated to, with a streamlined rulemaking path. Confirm the edition actually adopted before relying on a number. Third, small new houses. Since 2026, for new single-family residences under 2,500 square feet of livable floor area on their own lot with its own legal description, every Kansas city and county must allow construction under the 2018 International Residential Code, in one of three permitted versions, and any part of a local building code that conflicts is void as applied to that property. That is a frozen floor a local government may not raise. Fourth, accessibility. Kansas did not incorporate an outside accessibility standard for dwellings; it wrote the dimensions into the statute itself, with a 32-inch clear door opening, a 36-inch accessible route, ramp and threshold limits, reinforced bathroom walls and reach ranges for controls. The practical consequence is that those numbers change only when the legislature changes them, not when a national standard is revised. As of 2026-10-24 the fire marshal has not carried that direction out: K.A.R. 22-1-3 still adopts the International Fire Code 2006 edition and the International Building Code 2006 edition, and K.A.R. 22-1-2 accepts in the alternative the 1997 Uniform Building Code or the 2006 IBC with a certificate of occupancy. Those 2006 editions are the standard in force.

title: No Good-Cause Eviction Law, So No Coverage Notice to Give
bodyText: Kansas has no good-cause or just-cause eviction law, so there is no Kansas notice telling a tenant whether the unit is covered by one, no statutory form, and no reason you must state when you decline to renew. New York requires a landlord to append a prescribed notice to every lease saying whether the good cause eviction law applies and, if it does, which permitted reason supports a non-renewal; Kansas has nothing of the kind, and neither has it an exempt-unit coverage notice like the District of Columbia's or a protected-tenant notice like Connecticut's. To end a periodic tenancy you give the statutory notice and nothing else. A week-to-week tenancy ends on written notice given at least seven days before the termination date stated in the notice. A month-to-month tenancy ends on written notice stating that the tenancy terminates on a periodic rent-paying date not less than 30 days after the notice is received; a tenant in military service whose orders require it needs give only 15 days. A fixed term of more than 30 days is not a month-to-month tenancy merely because rent is payable every 30 days, and it simply ends at the end of its term. No reason has to be given in any of those notices, and no reason has to be given for declining to renew. Three limits still apply, and none of them is a good-cause rule. You may not retaliate by raising rent or cutting services after the tenant has complained to a code-enforcement agency about a violation materially affecting health and safety, complained to you about one of your statutory duties, or joined or organized a tenants' union; a tenant who is retaliated against has a defence to a possession action. Fair housing law applies. And ending a fixed-term tenancy early still needs a ground, because that is contract law, not tenure protection. One point of drafting care: if you hand the tenant a document that would operate as the tenant's notice of intent to vacate and it contains any term not already in the lease, the statute requires a ten-point boldface warning, and without that warning the tenant's signature does not bind them to the extra terms. Finally, local law. Kansas's 2026 preemption of city and county rental ordinances covers four specific subjects and good-cause eviction is not among them, so a Kansas city is not barred from adopting one. Check the city if you operate in one.

title: Passing a Local Government Fee On to the Tenant
bodyText:
No Kansas statute authorizes a landlord to pass a local government fee through to a tenant, and none forbids it. Kansas has no rental registration or rental licensing statute at all, so unlike Indiana there is no state provision telling you how to notify the tenant and collect, and unlike Maryland there is no court surcharge that a lease is barred from shifting. The question is therefore one of contract: the landlord and tenant may include terms and conditions not prohibited by the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or other rule of law, and a reimbursement term is not among the terms the act prohibits.

Three Kansas-specific cautions. First, do not draft the reimbursement as an indemnity. No rental agreement may provide that either party is exculpated from liability or holds the other harmless, and a clause framed as the tenant indemnifying the landlord against government charges risks being unenforceable, with actual damages if you deliberately use a provision you know is prohibited. A plain reimbursement of a stated, notified amount is not that.

Second, think about whether the reimbursement is rent. Kansas defines rent as all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement other than the security deposit, which on its face is broad enough to swallow a fee reimbursement, but no Kansas statute settles whether a non-rent charge can support the three-day pay-or-quit notice, and an eviction resting on an unpaid fee rather than unpaid rent is untested here. Do not assume you can evict over it.

Third, the fee has to be real and the notice has to come first. Charge the actual amount the government actually assessed, in writing, and keep the assessment.

Where the fees themselves come from is local. A Kansas city levying a fee or charge for revenue under its constitutional home rule power must do it by ordinance passed by a two-thirds vote of the members-elect, published twice, not effective for 60 days, and subject to a referendum if enough electors petition in that window. Two recent state laws push in your favour on development-side costs rather than rental ones: a local government may not charge an additional filing fee when you resubmit a single-family building permit application after a denial, and in a city or county that has opted into the 2026 third-party review scheme, the regulatory authority may not impose an additional fee for a third-party review or inspection triggered by its own delay. Neither creates a tenant pass-through. Local fee ordinances vary, so check your city.

title: Passing a Government Fine On to a Tenant: Use a Damages Claim, Not an Indemnity Clause
bodyText: Kansas has no statute that bars passing a government fine on to a tenant, and none that authorizes it. Texas has a statute on the point and Kansas does not. But Kansas has something most states do not, and it should change how you draft. No rental agreement may provide that either party agrees to the exculpation or limitation of any liability of either party arising under law, or to indemnify either party for that liability or the costs connected with it. The only exception is that a tenant may agree to limit the landlord's liability for fire, theft or breakage in the common areas. A fine, a citation or a nuisance-abatement charge that a city, county or state agency imposes on you is a liability of yours arising under law. A lease clause saying the tenant will reimburse you for it reads squarely as an agreement to indemnify you for that liability and for the costs connected with it, and a provision prohibited by that section is unenforceable. Worse, if you deliberately use a lease containing a provision you know is prohibited, the tenant can recover actual damages. No Kansas court decision has been found applying that provision to a government fine, so treat this as a serious risk rather than a settled rule, but do not assume the common clause works here. The good news is that you do not need the clause. Kansas already gives you the remedy. A tenant must comply with the obligations building and housing codes impose primarily on tenants where they materially affect health and safety, keep the occupied part of the premises clean and safe, remove waste, use the facilities reasonably, not disturb other tenants, and is expressly responsible for any destruction, defacement, damage, impairment or removal of any part of the premises caused by the tenant or by anyone or any animal on the premises with the tenant's permission. If the tenant breaches that, you may recover damages and obtain injunctive relief, and separately you may bring a claim for actual damages for breach of the rental agreement, which you can file even before the lease term ends. A fine you actually paid because of what the tenant did is provable actual damage flowing from the tenant's breach. That route survives the prohibition because it rests on the tenant's own breach rather than on a promise to indemnify you. Two practical notes. Nuisance abatement in Kansas lands on the owner by design: a city may abate a nuisance on a lot at the cost and expense of the owner after an order and at least ten days, and if the owner does not pay within 30 days of the notice of cost, the city assesses the amount against the parcel and collects it on the tax roll like a tax. And association fines are a different subject with a different answer, because they arise from private covenants rather than from law.

title: No Guarantor Statute, So the Guaranty's Own Words Decide
bodyText:
Kansas has no residential-lease guarantor statute. Nothing limits a guarantor to the original term, nothing requires a guaranty to state a maximum amount or an end date, and nothing conditions a guarantor's liability for a renewal on the renewal keeping the same parties or not raising the rent. Texas has a statute of that kind and Kentucky requires a free-standing guaranty to state a maximum and an end date; Kansas has neither, so the guaranty's own words decide, read against ordinary contract law and against the common-law rule that a material change to the underlying obligation can release a guarantor who never agreed to it.

One Kansas rule does apply, and it is the important one. No action may be brought to charge a party on a special promise to answer for the debt, default or miscarriage of another person unless the agreement, or a memorandum or note of it, is in writing and signed by the party to be charged or by someone that party authorised in writing. A guaranty of a tenant's lease is exactly that kind of promise, so get it in writing and get the guarantor's signature. The simplest way is to have the guarantor sign the lease itself, which also makes the guaranteed obligations unambiguous.

Because nothing in Kansas fills the gaps for you, write the scope into the guaranty: the maximum total amount, whether it covers renewals, extensions and a month-to-month continuation, and whether it covers rent increases made under the lease. If the guaranty is silent about renewals and you later extend or raise the rent, you are relying on an unsettled common-law argument, which is a poor place to be.

Three further Kansas points. You do not have to sue the tenant first: Kansas provides that in all cases of joint obligations and joint assumptions, suits may be brought and prosecuted against any one or more of those who are liable, and the lease can say so expressly. Releasing one person who is jointly or severally liable does not discharge the others beyond the share the released person owed. And the guaranty sits inside the lease, so the lease's limits reach it: a guaranty may not make the guarantor pay either party's attorney fees, may not authorise a confession of judgment, and may not operate as an indemnity for a liability the law places on you.

title: Guests Have No Statutory Rights in Kansas, but the 2026 Squatter Route Is Closed Against Them
bodyText:
The Kansas Residential Landlord and Tenant Act says nothing about guests. There is no Kansas provision giving a tenant a right to have social guests, family, tradespeople, delivery people or suppliers of goods and services, no non-waivable guest right for buildings of three or more households as Pennsylvania has, no ban on guest fees as New Mexico has, and no statutory definition of a guest or default day limit as Montana has.

Guests appear in the Kansas statute only in the other direction, as the tenant's responsibility. The tenant is responsible for any destruction, defacement, damage, impairment or removal of any part of the premises caused by the tenant or by any person or animal on the premises at any time with the tenant's express or implied permission or consent, and the tenant must not allow such a person to engage in conduct that disturbs other tenants' quiet and peaceful enjoyment. The same idea runs the other way too: a tenant cannot terminate for a condition caused by a person or animal on the premises with the tenant's permission.

So your guest policy is a matter of lease drafting, and Kansas supplies neither a floor nor a ceiling for it. Set the limit in the lease, apply it evenly, and do not charge a separate guest fee without saying so in the lease, because an unstated mandatory charge is where consumer-protection exposure starts.

One 2026 development matters and it cuts against the landlord. Kansas's removal of squatters act lets an owner have an unauthorised occupant removed by law enforcement on a notarised affidavit, without an eviction case. That route is not available against a tenant's guest. The act defines a squatter as a person occupying a dwelling who is not entitled to occupy it under a lease or rental agreement and who is not authorised by a tenant to occupy it, and it expressly excludes a tenant who holds over in a periodic tenancy. A person your tenant let in is authorised by a tenant, so they are not a squatter, and the affidavit itself must state that the person is not a tenant or a holdover tenant. Getting that wrong is expensive: a knowingly false affidavit is a class A nonperson misdemeanour, and a person wrongly removed may recover possession, actual costs and damages, punitive damages of triple the fair market rent of the dwelling, court costs and reasonable attorney fees.

The lawful routes against an overstaying guest are the ordinary ones: treat the overstay as the tenant's breach of the lease and serve the statutory notice, or, where the person is there against your communicated order and without the tenant's authority, criminal trespass.

Also worth knowing: if the occupancy is transient occupancy in a hotel, motel or rooming house, the Act does not apply at all, and a different body of law governs guests there.

title: Kansas's Materiality Test: Materially Affecting Health and Safety
bodyText: Kansas filters habitability complaints through one phrase repeated across the Act: materially affecting health and safety. Your first duty is to comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, and where that duty is greater than any other duty on the statutory list, it governs. The tenant's mirror duty is to comply with the obligations those codes impose primarily on tenants, again only where they materially affect health and safety. The remedy track uses the same filter, with one asymmetry worth knowing. A tenant may serve the 30-day termination notice for a material noncompliance by you with the rental agreement, or for a noncompliance with your statutory duties materially affecting health and safety. So a breach of the lease has to be material; a breach of the statutory duty list has to materially affect health and safety, which is a narrower gate. Either way the tenant must deliver a written notice specifying the acts and omissions constituting the breach, and the agreement does not terminate if you adequately initiate a good faith effort to remedy within 14 days. Separately, and regardless of materiality, the tenant may recover damages and get an injunction for any noncompliance with the lease or your statutory duties. Three other thresholds use their own words. Retaliation protection attaches when the tenant has complained to a code-enforcement agency about a violation materially affecting health and safety. Fire or casualty gives the tenant an immediate exit only where the damage impairs the use and habitability of the unit substantially. And the tenant's own side of the line runs the same way: you may terminate for a material noncompliance by the tenant with the lease, or for a noncompliance with the tenant's statutory duties materially affecting health and safety, with a 30-day notice and a 14-day cure, and no cure at all if the same or a similar breach recurs. What Kansas does not have is a floor or a list. There is no Kansas provision excluding breakage, malfunctions or conditions that do not materially affect the physical health or safety of an ordinary renter, as Wyoming has; no catalogue of serious defects, as Maryland has; and no schedule of conditions always deemed to endanger health or safety, as Massachusetts has. Kansas sets the standard and leaves the application to the facts and to the local code. So the practical answer to a tenant framing a minor problem as a habitability failure is not a statutory list you can point to; it is whether the condition materially affects health and safety, and whether a local code requires something you have not done.

title: You Can Move Who Performs a Duty, Not Whether the Duty Exists
bodyText:
Kansas draws a line that some states do not, and it is the whole answer to this question. A written agreement can move who performs certain of your statutory duties. Nothing in a Kansas lease can make the duty itself disappear.

Compare Wyoming, where the sentence requiring operational electrical, heating and plumbing with hot and cold running water ends with the words unless otherwise agreed upon in writing by both parties, so a signed lease can agree there need not be hot water. Kansas's duty section contains no such escape. The phrase unless otherwise agreed does appear elsewhere in the Act, which shows the drafters knew how to use it: it governs a landlord's release on sale, a manager's release on termination of management, the tenant's duty to occupy only as a dwelling, and the effect of accepting late rent. It appears nowhere in the duty section.

The only exceptions to your duties are built into the statute and turn on facts, not on agreement. All of the duties are suspended when performance is prevented by an act of God, a failure of public utility services or other conditions beyond your control. The water and heat duty does not apply where the building is not required by law to be equipped for that purpose, or where the unit is so constructed that heat or hot water is generated by an installation within the tenant's exclusive control supplied by a direct public utility connection. Those are conditions of the property, not clauses you can write.

What a written agreement can do is reassign performance, and Kansas gives two routes with different conditions depending on the building. That mechanism is the subject of its own guidance and its own optional agreement in this library, so use those rather than drafting from scratch.

Three limits apply whichever route you use. The agreement has to be made in good faith and not to evade your obligations. It cannot cover work needed to cure a failure to comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, which stays yours. And it cannot be turned into leverage: you may not treat the tenant's performance of a separate maintenance agreement as a condition of any obligation under the lease.

One more rule closes the loop. No rental agreement, assignment, conveyance, trust deed or security instrument may permit the receipt of rent free of the obligation to comply with your statutory duties, so the duty follows the rent no matter how the paperwork is arranged.

title: No Presumptions Run Against You on Condition or Repair Time
bodyText: No Kansas statute presumes that you breached a duty about the condition of the property, and none presumes that you took too long to fix something. There is no Kansas equivalent of California's presumed habitability breach where an inspector has cited the property and the condition remains unabated, no Maryland-style rebuttable presumption that more than 30 days from notice is an unreasonable time to repair, and no Massachusetts-style presumption that proof of a code violation entitles the tenant to a defence or that written notice of an inspection proves you knew. Kansas has the general machinery for presumptions in its evidence code and simply does not apply any of it to habitability. The practical consequence is that the ordinary burden stays where it starts. A tenant who says the unit breaches your duties has to prove it, and a tenant who wants to end the tenancy over it has to deliver a written notice specifying the acts and omissions constituting the breach and stating that the agreement will terminate on a periodic rent-paying date not less than 30 days after the notice is received. You keep the tenancy alive by adequately initiating a good faith effort to remedy the breach within 14 days. Do not mistake three other things for presumptions. First, a defence is not a presumption: if you retaliate by raising rent or cutting services after the tenant complained to a code-enforcement agency, complained to you about your statutory duties, or joined or organised a tenants' union, the tenant gets the unlawful-exclusion remedies and a defence in your possession action, but the tenant still has to prove the retaliation. The statute also tells you when you may still sue for possession: where the code violation was caused primarily by the tenant's own lack of reasonable care or that of someone on the premises with the tenant's consent, where the tenant is in default in rent, or where complying with the code needs alteration, remodelling or demolition that would effectively deprive the tenant of the unit. Second, a waiver rule is not a presumption: in your action for possession for nonpayment, or your action for rent while the tenant is in possession, the tenant must counterclaim for anything recoverable under the lease or the Act or the counterclaim is deemed waived, and the court may order rent paid into court and then decide what each party owes. Third, documentation is not a presumption, but it is the next best thing: the joint written inventory you and the tenant must complete within five days of occupancy is the record that decides most condition disputes in practice, so complete it, sign it and keep it.

title: No Required Fitness Statement, and No Kansas Warranty of Habitability to State
bodyText: Kansas does not require your lease to say that the property will be delivered fit for habitation. Maryland requires exactly that sentence, or else a statement of the agreed condition; Kansas requires nothing of the kind, and the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act prescribes no lease content on condition at all. There is a deeper point, and it is the one to carry. Kansas has no warranty of habitability. The words fit for habitation, habitable condition and condition permitting habitation appear nowhere in the Act, and the implied warranty of habitability exists in Kansas's annotated statutes only as a law-review citation, never as a rule. What you owe instead is a short, enumerated list: comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, exercise reasonable care in maintaining the common areas, keep in good and safe working order every electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning appliance including elevators that you supply or are required to supply, provide and maintain waste receptacles on the grounds and arrange removal unless a government entity does it, and supply running water, reasonable amounts of hot water at all times and reasonable heat. Those duties are excused when prevented by an act of God, a failure of public utility services or other conditions beyond your control, and the water and heat duty has its own limits where the building is not required by law to be equipped for it or the unit generates its own on a direct utility connection.
