The code duty outranks the rest: where it imposes a greater duty than any other item on the list, it governs. So do not write a lease statement that the unit is fit for habitation, and above all do not write one saying the unit complies with all applicable laws and codes. Kansas gives you no credit for the promise and you may be held to it as a contract term you did not have to make, on top of a breach claim under the statute. Say instead what Kansas actually requires of you and what the tenant actually agreed to. Two Kansas rules do bite at the start of the term. At the commencement of the term you must deliver possession of the premises in compliance with the rental agreement and with your statutory duties. And within five days of the initial date of occupancy or delivery of possession, you and the tenant must jointly inventory the premises and complete a written record of the condition of the premises and of any furnishings or appliances provided, both of you signing duplicate copies and the tenant getting one. That inventory, not a fitness recital, is where the condition of the unit should be documented.

title: The Habitability Duties Cannot Be Waived, Though Some Can Be Shifted
bodyText: A Kansas lease cannot waive your habitability duties, and the line between an unlawful waiver and a lawful shift of who performs the work is the whole of this subject. The prohibition is flat. No rental agreement may provide that the tenant or the landlord agrees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. Your duties under the Act are the tenant's rights under it, so a lease term saying the tenant accepts the unit as is and releases you from the statutory duties, or gives up the written-notice-and-terminate remedy, the damages and injunction remedy, or the counterclaim, is caught. A provision prohibited by that section is unenforceable, and if you deliberately use a lease containing a provision you know is prohibited, the tenant may recover actual damages. Two more rules back it up. No rental agreement, assignment, conveyance, trust deed or security instrument may permit the receipt of rent free of the obligation to comply with your statutory duties, so the duty follows the rent through any paperwork. And a court may refuse to enforce a lease provision it finds was unconscionable when made, or a settlement in which a party waived or agreed to forego a claim or right under the Act that was unconscionable when made, enforcing the remainder without it or limiting its application. Now the other half, because it is just as real. The same statute that creates the duties permits a written agreement to move performance of some of them to the tenant, and that is not a waiver. For a dwelling providing a home for not more than four households having common areas, a written agreement may put the waste-removal duty and the running-water, hot-water and heat duty on the tenant, along with specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodelling, if the transaction is genuinely in good faith and not a way of evading your obligations. For any dwelling unit other than a single-family residence, a separate written agreement signed by both parties and supported by adequate consideration may put specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodelling on the tenant, but only if it is in good faith and not to evade, only if the work is not needed to cure a failure to comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, and only if it does not diminish or affect what you owe other tenants. And you may not treat the tenant's performance of that separate agreement as a condition of any obligation under the lease. Hold both halves at once. Shifting a named task by a proper written agreement is lawful. Writing that the tenant waives the duty, or releases you from it, or gives up a remedy for it, is not, and attempting it can cost you actual damages.

title: No Contamination Disclosure Statute, but a Licensed Agent Must Still Speak
bodyText: No Kansas statute requires a landlord to tell a tenant that the property is or was contaminated. There is no Kansas counterpart to Missouri's disclosure for property contaminated with radioactive or other hazardous material, none to Iowa's written notice before the tenancy begins when the property appears on the federal CERCLIS list, none to Mississippi's brownfield status statement in an instrument conveying an interest, and none to the Massachusetts requirement that a recorded notice of activity and use limitation be incorporated into the lease. Kansas's one contaminated-property statute runs the other way: the contaminated property redevelopment act exists to let real property with environmental contamination be purchased without the purchaser becoming liable for cleanup costs, and to fund municipal redevelopment. It protects buyers; it says nothing to tenants. Two things still reach you. First, if a licensed real estate broker or salesperson is involved in the rental as your agent or as a transaction broker, the licensee must disclose to a prospective tenant all adverse material facts actually known. Read that list carefully, because its first item is circular and the next two are not. Environmental hazards are only covered where another law requires them to be disclosed, which in Kansas usually means federal law. But the physical condition of the property, and any material defects in the property, carry no such qualifier. Known soil or groundwater contamination, a buried tank, or a prior methamphetamine manufacture that left residue is a material defect and a condition of the property, so a licensee who knows of it must say so whatever the environmental limb does, and an intentional failure is grounds for discipline against the licence. Kansas does not license residential renting, so this bites when you use a brokerage and not when you manage your own property. Second, a residential lease is a consumer transaction under the Kansas Consumer Protection Act, and the willful failure to state a material fact, or the willful concealment, suppression or omission of one, is a deceptive act and practice whether or not the tenant was in fact misled. That is the provision that reaches an owner who knows and says nothing. One federal duty does apply by its own force: for most housing built before 1978 you must give the lead-based paint disclosure and pamphlet. The practical course is simple. If you know the property has been contaminated, or is subject to a recorded environmental restriction on how it may be used, say so in writing before signing and attach what you have. The cost of saying it is nothing; the cost of a tenant proving you knew and concealed it is not.

title: County Sanitary Codes — No Duty to Hand Tenants the Rules
bodyText: Kansas has no statewide health-district rental code and no law requiring you to give a tenant a copy of health-department rental rules on request, to post a notice of occupants' rights, or to refer a tenant to a health agency. What Kansas does have is county sanitary codes. In any county served by a local health department, the county commissioners may adopt a sanitary code by resolution, and the subjects a sanitary code may cover expressly include housing, trailers and trailer courts, insects and rodents, refuse storage, collection and disposal, water supply, sewage and sewage disposal, and food handling. A sanitary code may provide for permits, licenses and reasonable fees. The local health department administers the code unless the commissioners designate another county agency, which they may do for sewage and sewage disposal. Violating a sanitary code provision is a misdemeanor carrying a fine of up to $200 for each offense, with each day a separate offense, prosecuted by the county attorney — or, in a county that handles the matter under its code for enforcement of county codes and resolutions, under that code's penalties and by the county counselor. So whether any health rules apply to your rental is a county-by-county question: find out whether your county has adopted a sanitary code and what it says about housing. Two practical consequences. First, your lease duty to comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety picks up whatever your county's sanitary code requires, so a county housing provision becomes a landlord duty under the rental act as well as a county offense. Second, Kansas has no statutory pest-control duty in the rental act — if a pest duty binds you, it comes from a county sanitary code's insects-and-rodents provisions, from the lease itself, or from a code provision your general code-compliance duty picks up.

title: Heat: a Duty to Supply "Reasonable Heat," With No Number Attached
bodyText: Unless prevented by an act of God, a failure of public utility services or another condition beyond your control, you must supply running water, reasonable amounts of hot water at all times, and reasonable heat. Kansas sets no minimum indoor temperature, no heating season and no outside-temperature trigger — "reasonable" is the whole of the standard, and there is no implied warranty of habitability behind it to fill the gap, so the enumerated duty is all there is. Two statutory exceptions, and only two: the duty does not apply if the building containing the dwelling units is not required by law to be equipped for that purpose, or if the unit is built so that heat or hot water is generated by an installation within the tenant's exclusive control and supplied by a direct public utility connection. Supplying heat and paying for the fuel are different questions: the statute expressly does not abrogate the tenant's obligation to pay for utility service under the rental agreement, so you can put the gas or electric bill on the tenant and still owe the duty to supply reasonable heat. You must also keep every heating, ventilating and air-conditioning appliance you supply, or are required to supply, in good and safe working order and condition. You can shift the heat-and-water supply duty to the tenant only in the narrow way the statute allows. In a building providing a home, residence or sleeping place for no more than four households with common areas, you and the tenants may agree in writing that the tenant performs the waste-removal and water-and-heat supply duties, but only if the deal is made in good faith and not to evade your obligations. In any dwelling unit other than a single-family residence, an agreement that the tenant will do specified repairs, maintenance, alterations or remodeling must be in a separate written agreement, signed, supported by adequate consideration, made in good faith, not covering work needed to cure a building- or housing-code violation, and not cutting into what you owe other tenants — and you may not make performance of it a condition of any obligation under the lease. Nothing else works: a lease term by which the tenant gives up a right or remedy under the rental act is unenforceable, and deliberately using a lease you know contains a prohibited term exposes you to the tenant's actual damages. Never use heat as leverage. If you willfully diminish services by interrupting electric, gas, water or other essential service, the tenant can recover possession or terminate, and in either case recover the greater of one and one-half months' periodic rent or actual damages. Separately, a Kansas Corporation Commission rule governs when a regulated utility may disconnect service in cold weather; check it before any winter shutoff. One equipment point: under the boiler safety act, heating boilers located in private residences or in apartment houses of fewer than five family units are exempt from the certificate-inspection, certificate and fee requirements — which means a heating boiler in an apartment house of five or more units is not exempt and carries annual certificate inspection, an inspection certificate valid for no more than 14 months, and cease-and-desist exposure if it is operated without one.

title: Renting a Home That Is in an Association
bodyText:
Kansas does have an association statute, and it is the Kansas uniform common interest owners bill of rights act. It applies to any common interest community containing 12 or more units that may be used for residential purposes, whether created before or after January 1, 2011, and its provisions are mandatory: they apply despite anything to the contrary in the declaration or bylaws and cannot be varied or waived by agreement.

Three things about it matter to you as a landlord. First, the rights it creates run to unit owners, not to renters — it says in terms that owning a unit does not include holding a leasehold interest, so your tenant has no standing under it and you are the one who must deal with the association.

Second, it says nothing at all about leasing. There is no statutory power for a Kansas association to approve your lease or your tenant, no cap on an approval fee, no limit on the tenant information an association may demand, no statutory right for an association to collect rent directly from your tenant when you are behind on assessments, and no statutory rule on rental restrictions in a declaration. Whatever power the association has over your renting comes from the recorded declaration and bylaws and from your contract with it — read them, because the statute will not help you.

Third, there is one protection your tenant gets indirectly: an association may suspend a non-paying owner's rights, but it may not deny the owner or any other occupant access to the unit, and it may not withhold a service it provides if withholding it would endanger anyone's health, safety or property.

Association rules have procedure attached. Before adopting, amending or repealing a rule the board must give all owners notice of its intention, the text, and a date on which it will act after considering comments, and must send a copy of the new rule afterwards. A rule affecting use of or behavior in a residential unit may be adopted only to implement a provision of the declaration, or to regulate behavior or occupancy that violates the declaration or adversely affects other owners' use and enjoyment — and every rule must be reasonable. An association also may require that a dispute with it go to non-binding alternative dispute resolution before anyone files suit, and in a court action to enforce the act, the declaration or the bylaws, the court may award reasonable attorney's fees and costs to either side.

Outside that act, three other Kansas rules reach associations. In a condominium under the apartment ownership act, each apartment owner must comply strictly with the bylaws, the rules adopted under them, and the covenants, conditions and restrictions in the declaration or the deed, enforceable by the board or by an aggrieved owner; in a townhouse development, each unit owner must comply with the declaration's covenants, conditions and restrictions. A restrictive covenant that prohibits a political yard sign of less than six square feet from 45 days before an election to two days after it is void and unenforceable. And no association's declaration or governing document may contain a restrictive covenant that violates the Kansas act against discrimination — the board had to remove any such covenant, must delete one within 30 days of written notice from the human rights commission or the city or county, and an inactive association's prohibited covenant can be released by the city or county by recorded certificate, with attorney's fees available to the prevailing party in an enforcement action.

Finally, two drafting cautions. Do not write the tenant's association obligations as an indemnity: Kansas voids a lease term by which either party agrees to indemnify the other for a liability arising under law, so recover an association fine from the tenant as your actual damages for the tenant's breach of a lease promise, not as the tenant's indemnity. And do not put an attorney-fee clause in the lease — the fee award in an association case comes from the association statute, not from your lease, and a lease fee clause is void in Kansas whichever way it runs.

title: No Home-Business Right — the Default Runs Your Way
bodyText: Kansas has no statute making a home-based business a permitted use of a rental dwelling, and nothing that stops a lease from limiting or prohibiting one. The default actually runs in your favour: unless the parties agree otherwise, the tenant must occupy the dwelling unit only as a dwelling unit. So silence in the lease is already a residential-use rule, and your lease's residential-use clause restates and sharpens it rather than creating it. Kansas also lets the parties put into a rental agreement any terms and conditions not prohibited by the rental act or another rule of law, so you can go the other way just as freely — permit quiet work from home, permit a named business, or permit business use on conditions about customer visits, deliveries, signage, employees, parking and insurance. Put whichever choice you make in writing, because "unless otherwise agreed" means an oral or implied agreement can change the default, and a landlord who has knowingly let a business run for a year has a harder argument than one whose lease says what is allowed. Nothing in Kansas law protects a tenant's home child care, home office or cottage business against the landlord: Kansas has no analogue of the states that make a no-impact home-based business a permitted use, and no analogue of the states that bar an association from restricting a renter's home child care. Two things are outside your lease and you should check them before you say yes. Local zoning decides whether a home occupation is permitted at all, and what conditions ride on it. And if the business is child care, the tenant needs a state child care licence, and licensure brings its own requirements into your property — smoking is prohibited inside the facility while unrelated children are being cared for, the licence must be posted conspicuously and must itself state that ban in bold print, and the home must have an operable fire extinguisher in a readily accessible location. Licensure also changes your smoking analysis: the Kansas indoor clean air act normally exempts a private home, but not when the home is used as a day care home, so a unit you had treated as exempt stops being exempt. Last, do not assume a short-term-rental operation is a settled question: the 2026 act that suspended municipal limits on regulating short-term rentals ran only from 15 May to 25 July 2026 and that window has closed, so municipal short-term-rental regulation is back in ordinary operation.

title: No Early Exit for Illness, Age or a Move Into Care
bodyText: Kansas gives a tenant no right to end a fixed-term lease early because of illness, disability, age or a move into a nursing home, assisted living or senior housing. There is no Kansas equivalent of the statutes that let a tenant terminate on a doctor's certificate, on acceptance into public or subsidized senior housing, or on relocation for care. A tenant who has to move for health reasons therefore stays on the lease unless you agree otherwise. The contrast tells you this is a choice and not an oversight: in the same sentence that sets the ordinary 30-day notice for a month-to-month tenancy, the legislature wrote in a shorter exit — not more than 15 days' written notice — for a tenant in the military service of the United States whose termination is necessitated by military orders, and elsewhere it wrote a full early-termination right for a tenant who is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, human trafficking or stalking. It wrote nothing for infirmity. What actually governs is the lease plus three background rules. A month-to-month or week-to-week tenant needs no special right: written notice of 30 days to a periodic rent-paying date, or seven days for week-to-week, ends the tenancy. If a fixed-term tenant leaves anyway, you are not simply entitled to the rest of the term — on abandonment you must make reasonable efforts to re-rent at a fair rental, and the agreement is treated as terminated on the date you had notice of the abandonment if you fail to make those efforts or accept the abandonment as a surrender; for a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy the term for this purpose is deemed a month or a week. And a request to be released early may arrive as a disability accommodation request under the Kansas act against discrimination, which requires reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices or services when necessary to afford a person with a disability equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling — handle such a request on its own terms rather than treating it as a lease question only. Because this is one of the commonest hardship requests a landlord gets, decide your policy in advance and write it down: an early-termination option with a stated notice period and a stated fee is an ordinary lease term in Kansas, and having one is better than improvising when a tenant's family calls.

title: Talking It Out Before Court — What Kansas Law Does and Doesn't Do
bodyText:
No Kansas statute requires a landlord and tenant to try to settle informally, to mediate, or to meet before filing, and none specifically authorizes or regulates a lease clause that asks for it. The lease decides, within one hard limit: a Kansas rental agreement may not provide that either party waives or foregoes rights or remedies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. A pre-suit clause that delayed a statutory notice, extended a statutory deadline, or made a tenant give up a remedy would be unenforceable, and if you deliberately used a lease containing a term you knew was prohibited, the tenant could recover actual damages. So write the clause as a courtesy and not as a gate: exclude possession actions, say that it does not delay or limit any notice, deadline or remedy the law gives, and say that nobody has to accept any proposal.

Kansas does have a general mediation framework if you use it. Under the dispute resolution act, mediation means intervention by an impartial third party with no decision-making power who helps the parties define issues and reach resolution.

Three features matter to a landlord. Everything said in a proceeding conducted by a neutral under the act is confidential: no admission, representation or statement made in the proceeding is admissible as evidence or subject to discovery, the neutral cannot be made to disclose it, and the privilege is the parties' as well as the neutral's — subject to narrow exceptions for ethics complaints, mandatory child-abuse reports, stopping an ongoing or intended crime or fraud, other statutory or court-ordered disclosures, and reporting a threat of physical violence.

If the parties settle, the agreement may be put in writing and signed, must set out the settlement and each party's future responsibilities, and, where a court referred the case, may be presented as a stipulation and is enforceable as a court order once approved. And the clock stops: during the process any applicable statute of limitations is tolled from the date the parties jointly agree in writing to participate until the neutral officially terminates the proceeding, for no longer than 60 days without everyone's consent.

Avoiding a court-ordered mediation without just cause or excuse is evidence of bad faith, and on a finding of deliberate and intentional avoidance the court may order that party to pay the other side's reasonable attorney fees directly related to the mediation — a rare Kansas route to a fee award, since a fee clause in the lease itself is void.

Separately, in an eviction action under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act the court must now consider mediation unless it finds mediation would not materially aid the parties or is impracticable, and must order a continuance of up to 14 days from the mediation order where the parties are participating; that change is covered in the eviction-record note and is not repeated here.

title: No Duty to Hand Over Open Code or Condemnation Orders — With One Exception
bodyText: Kansas requires no landlord to tell an applicant or a tenant about an outstanding inspection order, code-violation notice or condemnation proceeding, and requires no copies to be handed over. There is no Kansas equivalent of the statutes that make you give an applicant a copy of a cited inspection order or a condemnation declaration, and no Kansas pre-lease code-violation disclosure form. The exception that does bite: if a licensed real estate broker or salesperson is acting as your agent or as a transaction broker in the letting, that licensee must disclose to a customer — and a customer expressly includes a tenant — all adverse material facts actually known to the licensee, including the physical condition of the property, any material defects in the property, and any environmental hazards the law requires to be disclosed. An open condemnation or repair order is the clearest kind of known material defect. The duty is the licensee's, not yours, and an ordinary Kansas landlord renting their own property is not a licensee and owes no such duty — but if you use an agent, assume the order will be disclosed and plan accordingly. Kansas handles the problem a different way: it gives the occupant notice directly rather than routing it through you. When a city's enforcing officer certifies that a structure is unsafe, dangerous or abandoned, the governing body must set a hearing by resolution, publish it once a week for two consecutive weeks with at least 30 days between the last publication and the hearing, and mail a copy by certified mail, marked deliver to addressee only, to the owner, the owner's agent, each lienholder of record and any occupant of the structure. So your tenant is a person the city must notify of the condemnation hearing, and you should expect them to receive it. Two practical consequences. First, silence is not safety: an open order usually means an actual condition, and Kansas makes you comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, and lets a tenant who gives written notice of a noncompliance materially affecting health and safety terminate if you do not remedy it. Second, if you do choose to disclose — and disclosing is often the better course — do not let the disclosure be framed as the tenant accepting the condition or waiving anything, because a lease term by which a party waives or foregoes a right or remedy under the rental act is unenforceable.

title: The Move-In Inventory Is Required, But Skipping It Carries No Statutory Penalty
bodyText:
Kansas has the duty but not the penalty. Within five days of the initial date of occupancy or upon delivery of possession, you and the tenant must jointly inventory the premises, complete a written record detailing the condition of the premises and any furnishings or appliances provided, sign duplicate copies as an indication that the inventory was completed, and give the tenant a copy. That is a flat statutory requirement — and the statute that imposes it attaches no sanction at all. There is no Kansas rule that failing to do the inventory, or failing to give the required copy, costs you the right to deduct from the deposit, forfeits any part of the deposit, or triggers damages.

Kansas also has no move-out inspection and no inspection-notice duty of any kind: nothing requires you to offer the tenant a final walk-through, to notify the tenant of a right to be present, or to tell the tenant about inspection rights when the deposit is paid.

Do not read that as permission to skip it. The practical penalty is evidentiary and it is severe. The signed inventory is normally your only contemporaneous proof of what the unit looked like at move-in, and without it you are arguing about damage from memory against a tenant who may have photographs. And the money penalty in Kansas is tied to the deposit accounting rather than to the inspection: on termination you may apply the deposit to accrued rent and to the damages you suffered from the tenant's noncompliance with the tenant-duties section and with the rental agreement, all as itemized in a written notice delivered to the tenant, and you must return the balance within 14 days after you determine the amount and in no event more than 30 days after termination, delivery of possession and the tenant's demand — with the deposit mailed to the tenant's last known address if no demand is made within 30 days. If you fail to comply with that, the tenant recovers the portion due plus damages equal to one and a half times the amount wrongfully withheld.

So the inventory is what lets you defend an itemization, and the itemization is where the statutory exposure actually sits. Do the inventory, keep the signed copy, and give the tenant theirs.

title: Evictions Are Jury-Triable on Demand — and No Jury Waiver Is Offered
bodyText: Start with the surprise: a Kansas eviction can be tried to a jury. Eviction suits are brought under the code of civil procedure for limited actions, and every lawsuit filed under that code is tried by the court unless one of the parties demands a jury, with the demand made on or before the date of the pretrial conference. A limited-actions jury is six people unless the parties agree on fewer. In an ordinary district court case the right of trial by jury declared by section 5 of the Kansas bill of rights, or given by statute, is preserved to the parties inviolate, and a party demands it by serving a written demand — which may be in a pleading — no later than 14 days after the last pleading directed to the issue is served, and filing it; a party who does not do that waives the jury, though the court may set a waiver aside in the interest of justice or where it resulted inadvertently. Now the lease question. Kansas has no statute that authorizes a jury-trial waiver in a residential lease, and none that forbids one. The rental act's ban on lease terms by which a party agrees to waive or forego rights or remedies under that act does not by its own words reach a jury waiver: the jury right comes from the Kansas constitution and from the procedure codes, not from the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, which contains no jury provision at all. So the ban is not the obstacle. The obstacle is that nothing in Kansas law makes a pre-dispute contractual jury waiver effective. The statutes describe one route to waiver — failing to make a timely demand — and describe the right itself as preserved inviolate, and whether a lease signed long before any dispute can override that is a question Kansas statutes do not answer. For that reason this library offers no Kansas jury-waiver clause. If you have one in a form lease, understand what it may and may not do: it cannot keep a tenant from demanding a jury if a court declines to enforce it, and a waiver drafted broadly enough to cut off the tenant's ability to assert a defence or remedy under the rental act would run into the waiver ban after all, with the clause unenforceable and actual damages available if you used it deliberately knowing it was prohibited. The safer course is to leave it out and, if the eviction timetable is your real concern, note that a jury demand in an eviction must come by the pretrial conference and that the trial itself must be held within 14 days of the appearance date.

title: No Key-Control Mandate — the Word "Key" Isn't in Kansas Tenancy Law
bodyText: Kansas requires nothing about keys. No statute makes you adopt a written key-control policy, keep a key log, limit master-key holders, deactivate electronic credentials, or background-check staff who can get into units — at any size of complex. Kansas also sets no threshold by unit count or county population the way Nevada does, and it imposes no duty to supply locks or keys in the first place, because the landlord's duty list in Kansas is a short enumerated one and locks are not on it. There is no implied warranty of habitability behind that list to add a security duty either. So key control in Kansas is entirely a matter of your own policy and your lease. Treat it as risk management rather than compliance, and the sensible practice is the same everywhere: issue keys against a signed receipt, keep a record of who holds what, keep master keys under single-person control, re-key when keys go missing or staff leave, and treat electronic codes the same way you treat metal. Two Kansas rules do shape how a key gets used once you hold one. Entry is limited: you may enter at reasonable hours, after reasonable notice, to inspect, make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations or improvements, supply necessary or agreed services, or show the unit to prospective or actual purchasers, mortgagees, tenants, workmen or contractors — and without consent only in an extreme hazard involving potential loss of life or severe property damage. You may not abuse the right of access or use it to harass the tenant. Holding a key is not permission to enter; it is only the means. Second, a key is not a self-help remedy: changing the locks to exclude a tenant is an unlawful exclusion, and your 2026 options against a genuine squatter do not extend to anyone who is a tenant or a holdover. On charging for keys, your lease may recover the actual cost of re-keying when a tenant fails to return keys or needs a replacement; keep it tied to actual cost rather than a fixed fee.

title: Deliberately Using a Term You Know Is Banned Costs You the Tenant's Actual Damages
bodyText: Kansas does attach a penalty to using a prohibited lease term, and it has two separate layers that are easy to run together. The first layer is automatic and fault-free: any provision on the prohibited list that appears in a rental agreement is simply unenforceable. You do not have to have known anything; the clause has no effect. The second layer is the penalty, and it requires two things at once. If a landlord deliberately uses a rental agreement containing provisions known by that landlord to be prohibited, the tenant may recover the actual damages the tenant sustains. So the tenant must show both that the use was deliberate and that you knew the provisions were prohibited — carelessness or inheriting someone else's form is not, by itself, enough. But the knowledge element is a one-way door. Once you have been told that a term is void in Kansas — by a lawyer, by a tenant's letter, by a court in an earlier case, or by guidance like this — reusing the same form lease is deliberate use of a term known to be prohibited. That is the realistic way landlords get caught: a national form carrying an attorney-fee clause or a broad indemnity, used again after the problem was pointed out. Note three limits that work in your favour. The penalty runs only against the landlord: the prohibited-terms list binds both parties, but only a landlord's deliberate use triggers damages, and a tenant has no matching exposure. The remedy is actual damages only — there is no multiplier, no statutory minimum, no penalty figure and no fee award, which stands out because Kansas uses a one-and-a-half-times measure elsewhere in the same act for wrongful exclusion, wrongful withholding of a deposit and a wilful holdover. And the tenant must prove real loss; a void clause that was never enforced against the tenant may have caused none. One procedural trap cuts the other way. In an action for possession based on nonpayment of rent, or an action for rent while the tenant is in possession, the tenant must counterclaim for any amount recoverable under the rental agreement or the act or the counterclaim is deemed waived — so a prohibited-term damages claim will usually land inside your own eviction case, and the court may order rent paid into court and determine the net amount due to each side. Fix the form before you file.

title: What a Kansas Tenant Can Do When You Breach
bodyText: Kansas gives a tenant a short, closed set of remedies against a landlord, and the shape of it is as important as the content: the tenant's route is notice, then termination or a lawsuit — never self-help with the rent. The main remedy is notice and termination. If there is a material noncompliance by you with the rental agreement, or a noncompliance with the statutory duty list that materially affects health and safety, the tenant may deliver written notice specifying the acts and omissions constituting the breach and stating that the agreement will terminate on a periodic rent-paying date not less than 30 days after you receive it. You have a cure window inside that: if the breach can be remedied by repairs, payment of damages or otherwise, and you adequately initiate a good faith effort to remedy it within 14 days after receiving the notice, the agreement does not terminate. The catch is repetition — if the same or a similar breach happens after that 14-day period, the tenant may serve a fresh notice describing the breach and the agreement terminates as that notice says, with no second cure window. The tenant cannot use this route for a condition caused by the tenant, or by any person, animal or pet on the premises with the tenant's express or implied permission. On termination you must return the portion of the deposit the tenant is entitled to. Separately and in addition, the tenant may recover damages and obtain injunctive relief for any noncompliance with the rental agreement or with your statutory duties — that remedy stands on its own and does not require the 30-day notice. Three specific breaches carry their own rules. If you fail to deliver possession at the start of the term, rent abates until possession is delivered, and the tenant may either terminate on at least five days' written notice, in which case you return all of the deposit, or demand performance, sue for possession against you or anyone wrongfully in possession, and recover damages; if the failure to deliver was wilful and not in good faith, the aggrieved party recovers the greater of one and a half months' periodic rent or one and a half times actual damages. If you unlawfully remove or exclude the tenant, or wilfully diminish services by interrupting electric, gas, water or another essential service, the tenant may recover possession or terminate and, either way, recover the greater of one and a half months' periodic rent or actual damages. If you enter unlawfully, enter lawfully but in an unreasonable manner, or make repeated otherwise-lawful demands for entry that unreasonably harass the tenant, the tenant may get an injunction against recurrence or terminate, and recover actual damages. Now what Kansas does NOT give, because it matters more than the list: there is no repair-and-deduct right, no rent withholding, no rent escrow, no general rent-abatement remedy outside the failure-to-deliver and casualty situations, and no tenant lien on your property of the Texas kind. A Kansas tenant who stops paying rent because of a defect is simply in default. Two procedural points. In an action for possession for nonpayment, or an action for rent while the tenant is in possession, the tenant must raise any claim recoverable under the lease or the act as a counterclaim or it is waived — so these claims usually arrive inside your own eviction. And accepting late rent without reservation, or accepting non-rent performance that varies from the lease, waives your right to terminate for that breach unless you agree otherwise after the breach has occurred.

title: No State Insurance Mandate — and No Registration Tied to One
bodyText: Kansas does not require a residential landlord to carry liability insurance, in any amount, for any kind of property. There is no Kansas equivalent of the New Jersey scheme that sets a minimum coverage figure, requires the certificate to be registered with the municipality each year and fines owners who do not comply. There is also no Kansas state rental registration of any kind to hang an insurance condition on, so the pairing other states use does not exist here. Carrying coverage is still the obvious course, and the practical pressure comes from somewhere other than the statute book: your lender will require it, and if the property is in an association the governing documents may. Two association rules are worth knowing because they can reach you as an owner. If you own a condominium unit under the apartment ownership act, the manager or board must obtain insurance on the property against fire and other hazards when the declaration, the bylaws, a majority of the apartment owners or a first mortgagee of record requires or requests it, written in the manager's or board's name as trustee for the owners in their declared percentages, with the premiums a common expense — and that is without prejudice to your right to insure your own unit for your own benefit. If you own a townhouse unit, the declaration must require each owner to maintain fire and extended coverage insurance to the full replacement value of the unit, excluding land, foundation and excavations, with proceeds payable to the association or its nominee as insurance trustee, and the declaration may put that coverage into one blanket policy as a common expense, in which case each owner must be given a memorandum of coverage approved by the commissioner of insurance. Neither is a liability-insurance mandate — both are property and casualty coverage — but both are real obligations that a Kansas landlord in an association may already be under. Finally, do not try to substitute lease language for coverage. Kansas voids a lease term by which either party agrees to the exculpation or limitation of any liability arising under law, or to indemnify the other for that liability or its costs, with one narrow exception: the agreement may limit your liability for fire, theft or breakage with respect to common areas. Insurance is how you manage the rest of the risk, because the lease cannot.

title: No State Landlord Registration — but Cities May License, Within Limits
bodyText: Kansas has no statewide landlord registration, no rental licence and no rental registry. There is nothing to file with the county assessor, nothing to renew, and no fee. An out-of-state owner does not have to employ a Kansas-licensed broker or designate an in-state agent for tenant communications — Kansas has no counterpart to the states that require either. An out-of-state company is different: before doing business in Kansas it must register with the Secretary of State and keep a Kansas registered office and resident agent, and until it registers it may not maintain any action, including an eviction (K.S.A. 17-7931, 17-7934, 17-76,126, 17-7307) (see "Out-of-State Owners: Companies Must Register Before Suing"). What Kansas requires instead is a disclosure to your tenant rather than a filing with the government: in writing, at or before the tenancy begins, you must give the name and address of the person authorized to manage the premises and of an owner or a person authorized to act for the owner for service of process and for receiving notices and demands. That substitutes for registration in practice, and it has teeth, so treat it as the Kansas version of this duty. Local law is a different matter, and it is the part worth checking. Kansas law assumes cities and counties may adopt residential property licensing ordinances, because it legislates about them — and it legislates one firm limit. No city or county may adopt, enforce or maintain a residential property licensing ordinance or resolution that includes a requirement for periodic interior inspections of privately owned residential property for code violations unless the lawful occupant has consented to those inspections. Note whose consent that is: your tenant's, not yours, so you cannot sign the tenant into a routine inspection programme. The limit does not apply to mixed-use residential and commercial property, and it does not stop a city or county from doing plan reviews, periodic construction inspections or final occupancy inspections required by building permits. The same section runs the other way too: any lawful occupant of privately owned residential housing may ask the city — or the county, if the property is in the unincorporated area — to inspect for code violations at any time, without your involvement. So whether you must register is a city-by-city question; state law sets a ceiling on what the ordinance may demand. One thing not to assume: the 2026 act that voided a range of local rental ordinances did not touch registration. It reaches only four subjects — refusing a tenant because of a housing-choice-voucher or other voluntary-participation source of income, restricting what screening information a landlord may use or request, capping security deposits, and requiring an automatic right of first refusal for tenants. A local registration or licensing requirement is outside all four and survives.

title: No Cap on Residential Late Fees — and Why That Is Not a Free Hand
bodyText:
Kansas sets no cap on a residential late fee. There is no dollar maximum, no percentage of rent, no mandatory grace period and no daily limit anywhere in the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, and no statute requires you to wait any number of days before charging one. Rent is due on the day the lease says, and whatever late fee the lease sets is what applies.

That the silence is deliberate, rather than an oversight, is clear from the chapter the rental act sits in. Kansas capped late fees for a storage unit: an operator of a self-service storage facility may impose a reasonable late fee for each month an occupant does not pay rent when due, not to exceed $20 a month or 20 percent of the monthly rental amount, whichever is greater — may charge more only if it is reasonable, with the burden of proving reasonableness on the operator — and may collect no late fee at all unless it is stated in the rental agreement or an addendum. The legislature wrote that for a locker and wrote nothing for a home.

Three real constraints remain, and the first is the one to plan around. The rental act has its own unconscionability provision: if a court finds as a matter of law that a rental agreement or any provision of it was unconscionable when made, it may refuse to enforce the agreement, enforce the rest without the unconscionable provision, or limit that provision's application to avoid an unconscionable result — and the same applies to a settlement in which a party waives or foregoes a claim or right. If unconscionability is raised by a party or by the court on its own motion, both sides get a reasonable opportunity to present evidence about the setting, purpose and effect of the agreement. That is an in-the-act remedy, so it is the constraint that actually bites on an outsized or compounding late fee.

Second, consumer protection law reaches a landlord's fee practices as a backstop, since a residential lease is a consumer transaction and you are the supplier, but treat it as a backstop rather than a ceiling: where the rental act itself speaks to the subject, the specific statute may displace a consumer-protection claim built on the same conduct.

Third, a late fee must be in the lease to be charged at all, because nothing but the lease creates it.

Practical drafting: set the amount and any grace period expressly, keep it proportionate to the rent rather than escalating daily without limit, and do not treat the absence of a cap as an invitation. Separately, do not assume an unpaid late fee is rent — Kansas has no statute saying whether it is, and your three-day pay-or-quit notice runs on unpaid rent.

title: Crime-Free Lease Clauses, Police Cooperation, and the Common-Nuisance Report That Protects Your Building
bodyText:
Kansas has no crime-free lease statute. Nothing requires or regulates a crime-free or drug-free addendum, no statute obliges you to give officers access to a rental or to hand over tenant information, no statute makes you report a tenant to the police, and nothing obliges you to report to a child-protection investigator the way some states do; Kansas's child-abuse and adult-abuse reporting duties bind only listed professionals, and anyone else may report (K.S.A. 38-2223, 39-1431).

One general rule does reach you: when someone dies, or a body is found, and the death is suspected to be from violence, unlawful means, suicide or accident, or came suddenly to someone in apparent health or not regularly attended by a doctor, the statute says the coroner shall be notified by the attending doctor, the police, the embalmer "or by any other person", so if you find a tenant dead, call the police or the coroner at once (K.S.A. 22a-231).

The phrase "crime-free" does not appear anywhere in Kansas law. Kansas also has no statute barring a local nuisance or crime-free-housing ordinance that penalizes a property for calls for service, and no state-level protection for a tenant who calls the police — so if your city runs such a programme, that is a city question. One related limit does exist at state level: cities and counties are prohibited from adopting or enforcing ordinances that restrict where a registered offender may live, apart from residential licensing or zoning of correctional placement residences. That bars one common crime-free ordinance device, and it says nothing about your own tenancy decisions as a private landlord.

There is no duty to report, but Kansas gives you a powerful reason to report anyway, and it is the most important thing on this subject for a landlord to know. Kansas declares a list of activities to be common nuisances where real property is used to carry them on or is permitted to be used for them: any violation of a law regulating controlled substances, commercial gambling, dealing in or possessing gambling devices, promoting obscenity, promoting the sale of sexual relations, commercial sexual exploitation of a child, habitual unlicensed sales of liquor or of cigarettes and tobacco products, a felony committed for or in association with a criminal street gang, and unlawful use of pyrotechnics in a place of public assembly. The controlled-substance limb carries no requirement that the conduct be habitual.

Only the attorney general or a city, county or district attorney may bring the abatement action; you cannot bring it and you are not a party to it by right, though the property itself may be named as a defendant, in which case the summons is served on the owner or whoever is in possession — so you may have to appear to protect the building.

What is at stake for you is the building. On a final judgment that the property is being or has been used for one of those activities, the court may order the house, room, building or other structure closed and padlocked for up to two years; may require you, or the lessee, tenant or occupant, to post a bond conditioned on not using or permitting the use of the property unlawfully for two years, the whole of which may be recovered as a penalty if any condition is broken; may assess a civil penalty of up to twenty-five thousand dollars; and must make the costs of the action, including a fee for the prosecuting attorney, a lien on the real property. The padlock order and the costs lien both turn on the same two findings: that the owner knew or should have known of the nuisance, and that the owner did not make a bona fide attempt to abate it.

Kansas then tells you what counts as evidence of a bona fide attempt — a written report, filed by you or at your direction with the local law enforcement agency, stating that you suspect the property is being used for one of those activities. So if you suspect it, report it in writing, report it early, and keep your copy.

A second route runs alongside. If a person is arrested for one of those activities, a prosecutor may petition the court to decide whether the activity occurred on your property; you may be given notice of the hearing, which is held within thirty days of notification, or within seven days in the pyrotechnics case. A finding on the balance of the evidence that an unlawful act occurred voids any lease under which a tenant holds possession and returns the right of possession to you, and you may then evict. If you do not commence eviction proceedings within thirty days of that determination, the prosecutor may move against the property itself. That remedy is expressly in addition to anything the residential landlord and tenant act gives you, not a substitute for it.

Finally, maintaining or assisting in the maintenance of one of these nuisances is itself a class A nonperson misdemeanor, and a defendant may be fined up to twenty-five thousand dollars on top of the sentence — so a landlord who knowingly lets the activity continue is exposed personally, not only through the property.

The other place Kansas law puts a landlord and law enforcement in the same procedure is the 2026 Removal of Squatters Act, and it is a trap as much as a tool. An owner or the owner's agent may ask a law enforcement agency in the county to remove an unauthorized person by filing a notarized affidavit stating six things: that the affiant is the owner or the owner's agent; that a person has entered and is remaining unlawfully; that the person was not authorized to enter; that the person is not a tenant or a holdover tenant; that the affiant has asked the person to vacate and they have not; and that the person is not an immediate family member of the owner.

You must also post notice at the dwelling telling the person they have no right to occupy and must vacate immediately, giving the street address of the agency where the affidavit will be delivered, and attach a copy with the date and time of delivery. The agency verifies record ownership and, at least 24 hours after receiving the affidavit, serves a notice to vacate immediately, by hand delivery to any unauthorized occupant or by posting on the front door, and tries to identify everyone in the dwelling. The officer may charge up to $50 to process the affidavit.

Now the trap: knowingly filing a false affidavit is a class A nonperson misdemeanor, and on a wrongful removal the occupant can have possession restored and recover actual costs and damages, punitive damages of triple the fair market rent of the dwelling, court costs and reasonable attorney fees. The act does not reach a tenant or a holdover in a periodic tenancy. If there is any doubt whether the person is a tenant, use an eviction action and not the affidavit.

For an unauthorized person who is not an occupant at all, criminal trespass remains available: entering or remaining in a structure knowing one is not authorized, in defiance of an order to leave personally communicated by the owner or another authorized person, or where the property is posted, locked, fenced or otherwise secured, is a class B nonperson misdemeanor.

title: No Lead-Safe Certificate — but Lead Work Needs a Licence, and You Are Not the Exempt Owner
bodyText: Kansas issues no lead-safe certificate for a rental unit. There is no state certificate, registry or compliance statement showing a unit is lead-safe, nothing to attach to a lease, and no routine state inspection that produces one. The only state lead order is reactive: when a child's elevated blood lead level is traced to a property, the Department of Health and Environment can issue a lead hazard control notice requiring the owner to make the property lead-safe by a set date. What Kansas does regulate is who may do lead work. Under the residential childhood lead poisoning prevention act, a business entity or public agency may not engage in a lead-based paint activity unless it holds a licence from the secretary of health and environment, and no individual may engage in lead-based paint activities without a certificate from the secretary, which requires completing an accredited training programme and passing a third-party exam. To be licensed, a business must make sure every employee or agent who will do lead work is certified, satisfy the secretary that it can comply with the applicable EPA, OSHA and state requirements, follow the secretary's regulations, and allow the secretary's representatives to enter and inspect a habitation at any reasonable time with the owner's consent or under a search warrant. Read the exemptions carefully, because the one people assume covers them does not cover a landlord. An individual may do lead-based paint activities without a certificate only in a residential dwelling that the individual both owns and resides in — owning a rental you do not live in is outside it. The other exemption is for a business or public agency doing the work in a nonresidential dwelling it owns or leases. Either way, the work must still be done in accordance with state and federal guidelines or statutes. So if you are renovating or abating a rental you do not live in, you are hiring licensed and certified people, not doing it yourself under the owner exemption. Two cautions. First, the regulations the statute waited for are in force. The Department of Health and Environment certifies lead inspectors, risk assessors, abatement workers and supervisors and project designers, licenses the firms that employ them, and sets work-practice standards for inspection, risk assessment and abatement. The regulations also reach paid renovation, which the statute's own list does not: renovation of housing built before 1978 done for compensation must be done by a renovator the department has certified, working for a renovation firm the department has licensed, under the federal renovation work practices, which Kansas has adopted as its own rule with the department in the EPA's place. Minor repair and maintenance that disturbs six square feet or less of painted surface per component, and emergency repairs, are outside it. Second, the lease disclosure is still federal. Federal law separately requires pre-1978 housing disclosure before a lease, and nothing in the Kansas act or its regulations replaces it. For paid renovation, check that your contractor holds the department's renovator certificate and renovation firm licence.

title: No Kansas Lead Notice on Top of the Federal One
bodyText:
Kansas adds no state lead notice to a residential lease. There is no Kansas pamphlet or brochure you must hand over at signing, no state lead-hazard notification form, no duty on you to tell a tenant that a lead hazard has been identified in the unit, and no state tenant-rights notice of the kind several other states require alongside the federal disclosure.

If a child's elevated blood lead level is traced to your property, it is the Department of Health and Environment that notifies you and the occupants, by a lead hazard control notice requiring you to make the property lead-safe by a set date, and you may not use the investigation's findings or the notice to the occupants' detriment. Kansas has no statute at all that requires a landlord to notify anyone about lead.

The federal rule still applies in full and is the only lead notice in a Kansas lease: before renting pre-1978 housing you must give the Lead Warning Statement, disclose known lead-based paint and lead-based paint hazards or state that you have no knowledge of any, list and provide any available records and reports or state that you have none, obtain the tenant's acknowledgment of receipt and of the federally approved pamphlet, and certify accuracy. Your lease's lead-based paint disclosure clause does that work; nothing in Kansas law modifies it.

One Kansas provision is worth knowing about because it may become a notice duty, but it is not one today on the face of the statute. The state's childhood lead poisoning prevention act directs the secretary of health and environment to adopt rules about distributing lead hazard information to owners and occupants of housing before renovation activities in housing, and to adopt rules on notification and record keeping for lead-based paint activities generally.

The department has used those powers, and the duty it created falls on the renovator, not on you: no more than 60 days before paid renovation in a pre-1978 unit, the renovator must give the owner and an adult occupant the lead pamphlet and a renovation notice and document delivery, and for work in the common areas of a multifamily building must give a pamphlet and notice to each unit. Kansas adopted these rules as its own version of the federal renovation rule, so hire a renovator certified by the department and expect your tenants to receive that notice.

The rest of the act is about surveillance and public health rather than landlords: it lets the secretary investigate childhood lead poisoning, build a data system, educate health care providers, recommend screening and testing intervals (with a written religious objection by a parent or guardian overriding screening of a child), issue health advisories, help local health departments identify and follow up elevated blood lead levels, and run a public education programme. None of that reaches you as a landlord.

title: Kansas Dictates No Lease Contents — It Fills the Gaps Instead
bodyText: Kansas requires no particular contents in a residential lease. No statute says a lease must contain named terms, a notice of tenant rights, a statement of the law, a minimum type size or any prescribed language. It does not even require a lease to be in writing, except that a lease or interest in land for more than one year must be in writing signed by the party granting it. The rental act's only word on contents is permissive: the landlord and tenant may include terms and conditions not prohibited by the act or another rule of law, including rent, the term, and provisions governing the parties' rights and obligations. That the silence is a choice is clear from the two neighbouring Kansas acts that do prescribe contents — a mobile home park rental agreement in a park with five or more homes must contain a notice that the tenant has rights under that act and that copies are available from the landlord on request, and a self-service storage rental agreement must contain a specified bold-type statement and must ask the occupant to designate an alternative contact. The legislature wrote content requirements twice in the same chapter and wrote none for a home. What Kansas does instead is supply defaults when your lease is silent, and you should know them because they are what you get if you leave something out. With no agreement on rent, the tenant pays the fair rental value for use and occupancy. Rent is payable without demand or notice at the time and place agreed; unless you agree otherwise, it is payable at the dwelling unit, periodic rent falls due at the beginning of any term of a month or less and otherwise in equal monthly instalments at the beginning of each month, and rent is uniformly apportionable day to day. If the lease does not fix a definite term, the tenancy is week-to-week for a roomer who pays weekly rent and month-to-month in every other case. Signatures are not everything either: if you never sign a written lease the tenant signed and delivered to you, knowingly accepting rent without reservation makes it as effective as if you had signed, and the mirror rule binds a tenant who takes possession and pays rent on a lease you signed; an agreement given effect that way is good for only one year however long its stated term. Three real limits on content do exist. The prohibited-terms list voids a waiver of rights or remedies under the act, a confession of judgment, any attorney-fee clause, and exculpation, liability limitation or indemnity except a limit on your liability for fire, theft or breakage in common areas. No lease, assignment, conveyance, trust deed or security instrument may permit rent to be received free of your statutory duty list. And there is one true formatting rule, though it is not about the lease itself: if you give the tenant a document that would be their written notice of intent to vacate and it contains any terms not in the lease, it must carry a specified warning in no smaller than ten-point boldface telling the tenant the signature may bind them to additional terms and that they may decline to sign — and without that warning, the tenant's signature does not bind them to the additional terms. Separately, federal law requires the lead-based paint disclosure elements for pre-1978 housing to be in the lease or attached to it; that is a federal requirement, not a Kansas one.

title: Kansas Never Makes You Give the Tenant a Copy of the Lease
bodyText:
Kansas does not require you to give a tenant a copy of the signed lease. Not at signing, not on request, not ever. There is no delivery duty, no deadline, no penalty and no defence a tenant can raise to enforcement of the lease because they never received one.

The sharpest proof is inside the rental act itself: the act does require you to give the tenant a copy of one document, the move-in inventory, and it says nothing about the lease. The legislature knew how to require a copy and required it for the inventory only.

Two other Kansas statutes point the same way. A lease-purchase agreement — rent-to-own — must be accompanied by a copy given to the consumer. And in a mobile home park, park rules are enforceable against a tenant only if, among other conditions, the prospective tenant is given a copy of them before the rental agreement is entered into. The residential rental act has no comparable provision and in fact has no rules-and-regulations section at all, so your house rules bind a Kansas tenant as contract terms, through the lease, rather than through any statutory notice condition.

None of that makes withholding a copy sensible. Give every tenant a fully signed copy as a matter of course, because the lease is what you will rely on in an eviction or a deposit dispute, because a tenant who has never seen the document is a tenant who will dispute its terms, and because several of your statutory obligations are performed through the lease. Keep proof that you gave it.

The library offers an optional clause in which the tenant acknowledges receiving a copy of the lease and of any written rules and in which you promise a fully signed copy promptly after all parties sign — in Kansas that clause is purely evidentiary, since no statute compels it, which is exactly why having it is worth something.

Two related duties are real and should not be confused with a lease copy. You must give the tenant a copy of the joint move-in inventory, completed within five days of the initial date of occupancy or delivery of possession. And you must disclose in writing, at or before the tenancy begins, the name and address of the person authorized to manage the premises and of an owner or a person authorized to act for the owner for service of process and for receiving notices and demands.

title: No Initials Requirement — but One Kansas Notice Formality Does Exist
bodyText: No Kansas statute requires a tenant to initial a particular lease term, including a notice period longer than the law requires, for that term to bind the tenant. The tenant's signature on the lease is all Kansas asks for. Kansas does impose one notice formality, but it attaches to a different document: if you hand the tenant a form to sign as their written notice of intent to vacate and that form adds terms that are not already in the lease, Kansas law requires a specific warning in at least 10-point boldface type, and without it the added terms do not bind the tenant even if they sign. Two cautions before you lengthen the notice period in the lease itself. First, the 30-day notice to end a month-to-month tenancy belongs to the tenant as well as to you, and Kansas voids any lease term by which either party gives up a right or remedy under the residential landlord and tenant act — so a term making the tenant give more notice than the statute requires may not be enforceable, and initials will not rescue it. Second, a tenant in military service whose orders require it needs give you only 15 days. Initials are still worth collecting beside an unusual term: they are evidence the tenant saw it, which is a different thing from a statutory requirement.

title: Recording a Lease with the Register of Deeds — Optional in Kansas
bodyText: Kansas has no lease registry and does not require you to record a residential lease anywhere. Recording is permissive: a written instrument that conveys real estate, or by which real estate may be affected, may be recorded with the register of deeds of the county where the property sits, and a lease is such an instrument — the recording statute speaks of the lessor and the lessee by name. To be recorded the instrument must be signed by the party granting it and acknowledged before a notary, so an ordinary unnotarized lease will not be accepted as it stands. Recording is not an empty formality. From the moment it is filed, a recorded instrument gives notice of its contents to everyone, and later buyers and mortgage lenders take the property on notice of it. An unrecorded lease is valid between you and the tenant, and against anyone who actually knows about it, but not otherwise — so if you sell or mortgage the property, an unrecorded long lease may not bind the new owner or lender. For the ordinary one-year residential tenancy almost no Kansas landlord records, and nothing in the residential landlord and tenant act turns on whether you did. Think about recording, or recording a short memorandum of the lease instead of the whole document, when the term is long, when there is a purchase option, or when the tenant has paid for something they need protected against a future owner. Recording is also not what makes a long lease enforceable in the first place: a lease of more than one year must be in writing and signed by the party granting it, and that rule is separate from recording.

title: No Lease-Type Parity Rule
bodyText: Kansas has no statute requiring the same rent or the same terms for a month-to-month tenancy and a fixed-term lease, and none capping how far the two may differ. You may price a twelve-month lease below a month-to-month, charge a month-to-month premium, or attach a condition to one lease type and not the other. Kansas law puts terms in the hands of the parties: landlord and tenant may agree to any terms the residential landlord and tenant act and other law do not prohibit. What you cannot do is use the difference to discriminate on a Kansas protected ground, or to retaliate. Three rules apply whichever lease type you use, and none of them creates parity. First, if the agreement does not fix a definite term, the tenancy is week-to-week for a roomer paying weekly rent and month-to-month otherwise. Second, the notice to end a tenancy is set by the statute and differs by tenancy type, not by what the lease says: seven days for week-to-week, and thirty days ending on a rent-paying date for month-to-month, with fifteen days enough from a tenant in military service whose orders require it. Third, a term that makes the tenant give up a right or remedy under the act is unenforceable, so you cannot price a shorter notice or a waived protection into either lease type. Cities and counties cannot close the gap either: Kansas forbids any local ordinance that would control the amount of rent charged for privately owned residential property.

title: No Lease Type-Size Rule — One Document Is the Exception
bodyText: Kansas sets no minimum type size for a residential lease and has no evidence rule shutting you out of relying on a lease, or part of one, because the print is small. Kansas does set type sizes, but for other kinds of paper: car-rental collision damage waivers, loan broker disclosures, door-to-door sales confirmations, insurance-benefit assignments, credit-services agreements, and cigarette packaging. One landlord-tenant document is the exception, and it is not the lease. If you hand the tenant a form to sign as their written notice of intent to vacate and it carries terms that are not already in the lease, Kansas requires a set warning in at least 10-point boldface type, and without it those added terms do not bind the tenant even if they sign. Print the lease legibly anyway. Kansas lets a court refuse to enforce a rental agreement or any provision of it that was unconscionable when made, and buried small print is the kind of fact a court weighs when it looks at the setting, purpose and effect of the agreement. A residential lease is also a consumer transaction under the Kansas consumer protection act, which reaches deceptive and unconscionable supplier conduct.

title: Time Limits to Sue a Tenant for Rent or Damage
bodyText: Kansas has no special deadline for landlord-tenant claims. The general limitation periods apply. A suit on a written lease — unpaid rent, late fees, charges and damages the lease makes the tenant answerable for — must be brought within five years. A suit on an oral or implied agreement, including an oral month-to-month tenancy or a claim for the fair rental value of the premises where there is no written lease, must be brought within three years, and the same three years applies to a claim created by a statute rather than by the lease. A claim for injury to your property that does not arise on the lease has its own shorter clocks: two years for taking, detaining or injuring personal property, two years for trespass on the land, and two years for other non-contract injury. A claim on a statutory penalty must be brought within one year. The clock runs separately for each month's rent, from the day that installment fell due, so an old tenancy can be partly in time and partly out. Two things restart or pause it. A part payment of principal or interest restarts the full period from the date of the payment. A written acknowledgment of the debt, or a written promise to pay, does the same — but only if it is in writing and signed by the person you want to charge, so a verbal promise or a text you cannot tie to the tenant will not do. And if the tenant leaves Kansas, or absconds or conceals themselves, that time does not count against you, unless you know where they are and can serve them. Because a part payment restarts the clock, keep the date and amount of every payment a former tenant makes. Note that the deadline to sue is a separate question from how long an eviction judgment stays on the tenant's record: Kansas now lets a tenant apply to expunge an eviction judgment after three years, and that expungement does not cancel the debt or stop you suing for it.

title: Agreed Damages for a Tenant's Breach
bodyText:
No Kansas statute and no Kansas regulation addresses a lease term that fixes in advance what a tenant owes for breaking the lease. There is no safe-harbour figure to copy and no cap to stay under.

Four Kansas rules shape what such a term can do. First, what the statute gives you is actual damages: on termination you may claim possession, rent, or both, and you have a separate claim for actual damages for breach of the lease.

Second, you must mitigate — if the tenant abandons the unit you must make reasonable efforts to re-rent it at a fair rental, and if you do not, the lease is treated as terminated on the date you knew of the abandonment. That duty is part of the residential landlord and tenant act, so a clause saying you need not re-rent, or that the tenant owes the whole unexpired term regardless, is unenforceable.

Third, the court may refuse to enforce any lease provision that was unconscionable when it was made, or cut it down to avoid an unconscionable result.

Fourth, a residential lease is a consumer transaction under the Kansas consumer protection act, and a charge that is excessively one-sided in your favour, or grossly out of line with the market, is the kind of thing that act reaches — though how far that act operates where the landlord-tenant act already covers the ground is not settled.

Practical course: tie any agreed figure to a real estimate of what the breach will actually cost you, say in the lease that it is an estimate of damages and not a penalty, keep it modest against a realistic re-letting loss, and credit the tenant with rent you recover from a new tenant. Never take the figure out of the security deposit as a matter of course: the deposit may be applied only to accrued rent and the damages you have actually suffered, itemised in writing.

title: No Lockout for Unpaid Rent, and No Way to Buy One in the Lease
bodyText: Some states let a landlord change the locks on a tenant who is behind on rent if the lease opts in, with advance notice and round-the-clock key access. Kansas has nothing of the kind. No Kansas statute permits a lock change, a lockout, or any other self-help recovery of the unit for unpaid rent, on any notice and on any terms, and no lease clause can create the right. A Kansas landlord may not recover or take possession of the dwelling unit by action or otherwise, including by willfully cutting off electricity, gas, water or another essential service, except where the tenant has abandoned or surrendered it or where the landlord-tenant act itself permits. Because that is a provision of the act, a lease term by which the tenant agrees to a lockout is a term giving up a right under the act, which Kansas makes unenforceable — and if you knowingly use a lease containing a term you know is prohibited, the tenant can recover their actual damages for that alone. Lock the tenant out, or cut a service, and the tenant may either get possession back or end the tenancy, and either way recover the greater of one and a half months' periodic rent or their actual damages, plus the recoverable part of the deposit if they terminate. The tenant does not have to give you any warning period first. Kansas's 2026 squatter-removal route is not an alternative: a squatter is defined to exclude anyone occupying under a lease, anyone a tenant has authorised to be there, and a tenant holding over in a periodic tenancy, and a knowingly false affidavit is a class A nonperson misdemeanour that also exposes you to treble the fair market rent as punitive damages, costs and the tenant's attorney fees. For unpaid rent the route is the statutory one: the three-day notice, then an eviction action.

title: No Meth-Contamination Disclosure Duty — With One Real Exception
bodyText: Kansas has no methamphetamine or drug-lab disclosure statute for rental property. An ordinary Kansas landlord renting out their own home has no statutory duty to tell a prospective tenant that the property was once used to make meth, no duty to report contamination, no cleanup standard to meet and no habitation ban to observe. Kansas legislates on meth as a criminal and public-health subject, not a property-disclosure one: the only meth statute that touches commerce is a logging system for sales of precursor chemicals, and the state has funded remediation of sites law enforcement identifies as hazardous without imposing any duty on an owner. One real exception. If a licensed real estate broker or salesperson is acting in the transaction — as your agent or as a transaction broker — that licensee must disclose to a prospective tenant all adverse material facts they actually know, expressly including any material defects in the property, its physical condition, and any environmental hazards the law requires to be disclosed. A tenant counts as a customer for that duty. Note carefully what the exception is not.
