Kansas has no property-manager licence, and the licensing act defines a lease as one for non-residential use and exempts a person dealing with their own property, so renting out your own home does not make you a licensee and does not bring the duty on you. The duty exists because a licensee is in fact acting. Three practical points even without a duty. Knowingly concealing a serious contamination you are aware of risks a fraud or consumer-protection claim rather than a disclosure penalty. Your duty to comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety still applies, and a local health or housing authority may act on a contaminated property. And if you disclose at all, disclose accurately: a half-true statement is worse than silence.

title: No Military Air Zone Disclosure
bodyText: Kansas requires no disclosure to a tenant about a nearby military installation, an air installation compatible use zone, a noise zone or an accident potential zone, and gives a tenant no right to end the lease on that ground. This is not a gap Kansas overlooked. Kansas legislated on exactly this subject in 2010 and chose to put the duties somewhere else. It declares that land inside a jointly developed air installation compatible use zone study area, a joint land use study area, an army compatible use buffer or an environmental noise management plan is a state area of interest vital to national security, and it then imposes duties only on the military installation and on the adjacent city or county: to meet annually, to agree which parts are critical areas, to notify each other of regulations and development proposals, and to weigh noise above 65 day-night level, light and electrical emissions, bird attraction and structures near approach and departure surfaces before deciding a development proposal. None of that reaches a landlord or a lease, and the final decision on planning, zoning and land use stays with the municipality. Two practical points. If a licensed real estate broker or salesperson is acting in the transaction, that licensee must disclose to a prospective tenant the adverse material facts they actually know about the physical condition of the property — which is a licensee's duty, not a landlord's, and renting out your own home does not make you a licensee. And a city or county near an installation may have adopted its own zoning or notice rules; those are local, and you would need to check the locality. Disclosing voluntarily costs you nothing and heads off a tenant who did not expect the noise.

title: Minors as Tenants and as Eviction Defendants
bodyText: Kansas has no bar on naming a minor in an eviction case, and no penalty for doing it. Several states now dismiss the case, seal it, or make the landlord pay the minor's legal fees; Kansas does none of that. What Kansas does instead is make it harder to serve a minor properly. Service on a minor must reach two people, not one: the minor personally, and either a guardian or conservator in Kansas if the minor has one, or the minor's father, mother or other person having the minor's care or control or with whom the minor resides. If neither can be served, you need a court order setting another way. A limited-action eviction follows those same rules. Once the case is on foot, the court must appoint a guardian ad litem, or make another protective order, for a minor who is unrepresented. So naming a child who merely lives with your tenant does not strengthen your case; it adds a second service to get right, a guardian ad litem, and a chance the whole thing is delayed. The practical course is to name only the people who are actually your tenants. On whether a minor may be your tenant at all: Kansas's residential landlord and tenant act sets no minimum age and nothing in it stops a minor signing a lease. Capacity comes from Kansas's general law of minority instead, and it is more favourable to a landlord than most people expect. Minority runs to eighteen, except that a person sixteen or over who is or has been married counts as an adult in all matters relating to contracts, property rights, liabilities and the capacity to sue and be sued — so a married sixteen- or seventeen-year-old has full capacity to take a lease and can sue and be sued on it like anyone else. An unmarried minor is bound by contracts for necessaries and by their other contracts as well, and can escape only by disaffirming within a reasonable time after turning eighteen and at the same time giving back all the money or property they received under the contract that is still in their hands. And a minor cannot disaffirm at all where, because of the minor's own misrepresentation about being of age or because the minor had been carrying on business as an adult, you had good reason to believe the minor could contract. So a Kansas lease with a minor is not a nullity: it binds unless and until it is disaffirmed, and a false statement of age on the application forecloses disaffirmance. Two practical consequences. Keep the application question about date of birth, keep the signed application, and keep anything the applicant told you about their age — that record is what defeats a later attempt to walk away. And take an adult co-signer or guarantor anyway where you can, because disaffirmance only requires the minor to restore what is still in hand, which may be nothing, and because a guarantor's own promise is an adult's contract and stands on its own feet. Kansas also has no statute letting an unaccompanied or homeless minor contract for housing, as some states do.

title: What the Three-Day Nonpayment Notice Must Say and How to Serve It
bodyText:
Kansas prescribes no form of words for a nonpayment notice — there is no sentence you must copy and no state form to attach. It does prescribe the substance. The notice must be in writing, it must be given by the landlord, and it must state two things: that the rent is unpaid, and that you intend to terminate the tenancy if the rent is not paid within three days. A demand for rent that does not say you intend to terminate is not the statutory notice.

Count the three days as three consecutive 24-hour periods, not as business days, so weekends and holidays are inside the count. The clock starts at the moment of delivery or posting if you hand the notice to the tenant, hand it to someone over 12 who lives at the premises, or post it conspicuously on the premises. If you mail it instead, allow the tenant two more days from the date of mailing. Do not file until the period has run; if the tenant pays inside it, the tenancy continues.

The lease cannot shorten the three days, waive the notice, or let the tenant agree in advance to go without it, because Kansas voids any lease term by which either party gives up a right or remedy under the residential landlord and tenant act. Before filing you also need the separate three-day notice to leave the premises that the eviction statute requires — but Kansas lets one document do both jobs, and a single notice drafted to satisfy both saves a step.

Three practical points. Acceptance of late rent without reservation waives your right to terminate for that breach, so do not take the money and file anyway unless the tenant has agreed otherwise after the breach. The nonpayment track is separate from the 14-day cure and 30-day termination route for other breaches. And once you sue for possession for nonpayment, the tenant must bring any counterclaim in that action or lose it, and the court may order rent paid into court while it works out who owes what.

title: Kansas Has No Nonrefundable Deposit — and Nothing to Disclose
bodyText: Kansas has no statute allowing a nonrefundable deposit and none requiring you to tell a tenant that a deposit, or part of one, will not be returned. There is nothing to disclose because there is no such category. Kansas's definitions leave no room for a third kind of money. A security deposit is any sum specified in a rental agreement, however denominated, that the tenant must deposit as a condition of occupying the unit and that the tenant may forfeit on the terms the lease sets. Rent is every other payment the tenant makes to you under the lease. So a charge is one or the other. Calling money a nonrefundable deposit or fee changes nothing: the definition is blind to what you call it, and if occupancy depends on the money and it is forfeitable, it is a deposit. That matters, because a deposit counts against the cap of one month's periodic rent for an unfurnished unit, a month and a half if the tenant uses your furniture, with another half month allowed if pets are permitted. It must be itemised in a written notice if you keep any of it, and the balance returned within 14 days of working out the amount and in no event more than 30 days after the tenancy ends, possession is delivered and the tenant demands it. Get that wrong and the tenant recovers the amount due plus damages of one and a half times what was wrongly withheld. If a charge really is not a deposit — not required for occupancy and not forfeitable on a breach — then under the definitions it is rent, and you should set it out in the lease as the charge it is rather than as a deposit. Do not use a nonrefundable label to get a pet charge or a cleaning charge over the cap. Kansas gives a specific pet allowance inside the cap, which is the lawful way to charge more for a pet.

title: No Separate Nonrefundable-Deposit Notice
bodyText: Kansas has no rule requiring a separate written notice, handed over when you collect the deposit, saying that part of it will not be returned. The reason is that Kansas has no nonrefundable deposit to give notice of. Money the lease specifies, that the tenant must put down to get the unit and may forfeit on the terms the lease sets, is a security deposit whatever you call it — the definition is blind to the label. Every other payment the tenant makes under the lease is rent. There is no third category, so there is nothing a separate notice could describe. Do not hand a tenant a notice of this kind. A written statement that a slice of the deposit is nonrefundable claims a right Kansas does not give and may mislead the tenant about the money they are entitled to get back. Kansas does require one separate document around move-in, and it is a different thing entirely: within five days of the first day of occupancy or on delivery of possession, you and the tenant must jointly inventory the premises, complete a written record of the condition of the premises and of any furnishings or appliances you provide, sign duplicate copies, and give the tenant a copy. That record is what supports a deduction later. The deposit itself must be itemised in a written notice if you keep any of it, with the balance returned within 14 days of determining the amount and in no event more than 30 days after the tenancy ends, possession is delivered and the tenant demands it.

title: Out-of-State Owners: Companies Must Register Before Suing
bodyText: Kansas does not require an out-of-state individual landlord to appoint an agent who lives in Kansas, and an individual has nothing to file with the Secretary of State to rent out a Kansas home from elsewhere. An out-of-state company is different (see below). Kansas also has no rent-withholding rule: a tenant paying rent to an out-of-state owner withholds no Kansas income tax. What Kansas requires instead applies to every landlord, in state or out. At or before the tenancy begins you must disclose to the tenant in writing the name and address of the person authorized to manage the property, and the name and address of an owner or of a person authorized to act for the owner both for service of process and for receiving and receipting for notices and demands. That information must be kept current, and the duty binds any later landlord, owner or manager. The person named may be out of state; Kansas does not say otherwise. The sanction for not disclosing is pointed: anyone who fails to comply becomes the agent of each landlord for service of process and for receiving notices and demands, and for performing the landlord's obligations under the act and the lease, spending the rent collected to do it. So a management company that does not disclose can find itself answerable as the landlord. Two related points. Being out of state does not keep you out of a Kansas court: owning, using or possessing real estate in Kansas submits a person to the jurisdiction of Kansas courts for claims arising from it, whether or not they are a resident, and process may be served outside the state. And if you hold the property through an out-of-state LLC or corporation, it must register with the Secretary of State before doing business in Kansas, naming a Kansas registered office and resident agent and consenting to service on the Secretary of State. Kansas's list of activities that are not doing business does not include owning or renting out real property (only property acquired by collecting debts or foreclosing), so assume renting is doing business. Until it registers, the company may not maintain any action in Kansas, including an eviction, although its leases remain valid and it may defend a suit (K.S.A. 17-7931, 17-7932, 17-7934, 17-76,126, 17-7307). Having a registered agent is not the same as a landlord's disclosure, and it does not discharge it.

title: How Kansas Notices Must Be Delivered — and Why Email Will Not Do
bodyText:
Kansas sets the delivery method notice by notice, and the lists are not the same.

For a three-day nonpayment notice, the clock starts on delivery or posting if you serve the tenant, hand it to someone over 12 who lives at the premises, or post it conspicuously on the premises; if you mail it, allow two more days.

For a notice terminating a lease or tenancy, Kansas allows service on the tenant, or if the tenant cannot be found, leaving a copy at the tenant's usual place of residence, delivering a copy to a person over 12 residing on the premises, or, if nobody is found there, posting conspicuously, or registered mail or certified mail with return receipt requested — and the return receipt, or an affidavit of the person who mailed it, is your proof.

For the pre-filing notice to leave the premises, you may leave a written copy with the other party, leave a copy with a person over 12 residing on the premises, post conspicuously if nobody is found, or mail a copy to the premises address; that three-day period runs as three consecutive 24-hour periods, weekends, holidays and days the clerk's office is shut are counted in, and mailing adds two days.

None of those lists includes email, text or a tenant portal. Kansas has no landlord-tenant electronic notice regime at all — no consent rule, no pre-consent disclosure, nothing. The general electronic transactions act applies to a lease like any other contract, but it rescues nothing here, because it says in terms that where another law requires a record to be sent by a specified method, the record must be sent by that method. So electronic delivery is available for routine communications the parties agree to handle that way, and not for the notices the statutes route.

Three cautions. A party who has agreed to electronic dealings may refuse further electronic dealings, and that right cannot be waived by agreement, so a lease cannot lock a tenant into email. If you send an electronic record in a form the recipient cannot print or store, it is unenforceable against them. And the lease cannot substitute its own delivery method for a statutory one, because a term giving up a right or remedy under the residential landlord and tenant act is unenforceable.

Which of those lists governs a particular termination notice is not always clear from the statutes. The course that works under every reading is to use a method that appears on every list: hand the notice to the tenant, or to a person over 12 who lives at the premises, and keep a signed record of who delivered it, when and to whom; if you also mail it, use certified mail with return receipt and allow the two extra days.

title: What You May and May Not Charge a Tenant for a Notice or an Eviction
bodyText:
No Kansas statute lets you charge a tenant a notice-service fee, and none forbids it.

Four limits decide what a charge of that kind can look like. First, attorney's fees are out. No Kansas lease may provide that either party pays the other's attorney's fees, the provision is unenforceable, and if you knowingly use a lease containing a term you know is prohibited the tenant can recover their actual damages for that alone. A fee that is really a lawyer's charge in disguise falls under this.

Second, indemnity is out. No lease may make either party indemnify the other against a liability arising under law, or against the costs connected with it, apart from limiting the landlord's liability for fire, theft or breakage in common areas. A charge drafted as the tenant covering your exposure is at risk; a charge drafted as reimbursement of what the tenant's own breach actually cost you is not.

Third, the court already handles court costs, and the legislature has reserved fee-setting to itself. The filing fee in a limited action is set by statute, and if you win the court may enter judgment for it in your favour. The statute says that fee is the only fee that may be collected for the docket fee, that it may be set only by an act of the legislature, and that no other authority exists to collect a fee. The taxable costs list already covers a process server's expenses, publication charges, certified-mail postage, mediation costs whether or not the mediation worked, and electronic filing and card fees. So charging the tenant separately for anything the court awards is a double recovery.

Fourth, a residential lease is a consumer transaction under the Kansas consumer protection act, which reaches unconscionable supplier conduct and treats a grossly excessive price and an excessively one-sided bargain as factors. How far that act operates where the landlord-tenant act covers the same ground is not settled, so treat it as a real risk rather than a fixed ceiling.

The safe shape, if you want such a clause, is reimbursement of your actual documented out-of-pocket cost of serving a notice the statute requires, itemised when you charge it, excluding attorney's fees and anything taxed as costs, and framed as damages for the tenant's breach rather than as indemnity.

title: A Kansas Lease Cannot Waive or Shorten the Notice
bodyText: Some states let a lease say the tenant gives up the notice to quit. Kansas has no such permission, and for a tenancy under the residential landlord and tenant act a waiver clause would not work. Kansas voids any lease provision by which either party agrees to waive or forgo a right or remedy under that act, the provision is unenforceable, and if you knowingly use a lease containing a term you know is prohibited the tenant can recover their actual damages for that alone. The three-day nonpayment notice, the 14-day cure and 30-day termination notice for other breaches, and the seven-day and 30-day notices for ending a week-to-week or month-to-month tenancy are all rights under the act. Treat each as a floor you can lengthen but not cut. The separate notice to leave the premises that you must deliver at least three days before filing an eviction case sits in the eviction statute rather than in the landlord-tenant act, and the eviction statute is written in mandatory terms, with no provision letting the parties agree otherwise. The cautious course, and the one we recommend, is to treat it as unwaivable too. Kansas does dispense with a notice to quit in some situations, but by statute rather than by agreement, and the difference matters. No notice to quit is necessary where the time for the termination of the tenancy is specified in the contract, where a tenant at will commits waste, in the case of a tenant by sufferance, or where no landlord and tenant relationship exists. So for a fixed-term lease that simply runs out, you do not need a notice ending the tenancy — the lease ends on its own date. That is the statute operating, not a waiver clause, and it does not excuse you from the pre-filing notice to leave the premises. Do not put a waiver-of-notice clause in a Kansas lease. It buys you nothing and creates exposure.

title: Nuisance in Kansas: No Landlord Receivership, but the City Can Bill You
bodyText: Kansas has none of the heavy landlord-side nuisance machinery some states use. There is no nuisance receivership taking your rents, no padlock or building-closure order, no statute making you a necessary defendant in a neighbour's abatement suit, and no drug-nuisance statute letting a court escrow rent or terminate the lease. Nothing in the residential landlord and tenant act mentions nuisance at all, so a nuisance is a ground for ending a tenancy only if the lease or the act's own breach provisions make it one. What Kansas has instead is two things. The first is an ordinary injunction. A private party — a neighbour — may enjoin the continuance of a common nuisance affecting their personal rights, and an injunction may also be granted in the name of the state, brought by the attorney general, the county attorney for a nuisance in the county, or the city attorney for one in the city. The second is the one that costs money. A city may have any nuisance removed or abated from a lot within the city at the cost and expense of the owner. The city orders the owner or the owner's agent to abate within a period of up to ten days, extendable if the owner shows due diligence, served by certified mail with return receipt or personally, and the owner may request a hearing before the period runs out. If the owner does not comply, the city abates it and bills the owner; if the bill is not paid within 30 days of notice, the cost, including the cost of giving notice, is either collected as a debt or assessed against the lot and put on the county tax roll. A nuisance assessment therefore attaches to your property, not to your tenant. So the practical route is contractual, not statutory: keep a lease term requiring the tenant not to create a nuisance, respond to a city abatement order inside the time it gives you, ask for the hearing if you need one, and recover from the tenant as damages for breach what their conduct actually cost you. Note two limits. If the nuisance comes from farmland, a separate Kansas act presumes that farming consistent with good agricultural practices, and established before the surrounding uses, is not a nuisance unless it has a substantial adverse effect on public health and safety; it limits damages to measures such as the loss in the property's market or rental value, and only a person with an ownership interest in the affected property may sue for private nuisance. And exactly what counts as a nuisance is mostly set by city ordinance, which you would need to check locally.

title: Where Kansas Law Lets Your Lease Decide
bodyText: The Kansas Residential Landlord and Tenant Act sets a default for several things and then lets the lease change it. A silent lease takes the default, and on most of these the default is the one you would not have chosen. (1) Rent: unless the lease says otherwise, rent is payable at the dwelling unit, periodic rent is payable at the beginning of each month (or of any term of a month or less), and rent is apportionable day to day. Say in the lease where and how rent is paid if you want anything else. (2) Term: unless the lease fixes a definite term, the tenancy is week-to-week for a roomer who pays weekly rent and month-to-month in every other case. (3) Rent amount: with no agreement at all, the tenant owes the fair rental value of the unit, not a figure you can set later. (4) Deposits: you may take the higher 1 1/2 month deposit only if the lease provides for the tenant to use your furniture, and the extra half-month pet deposit only if the lease permits pets. You may also keep deposit money for damages from breach of the lease itself, and for expenses, damages or other legally allowable charges other than rent, only to the extent the lease provides for them, so unwritten charges have nothing to attach to. (5) Last month's rent: the tenant may not apply the deposit to the last month's rent unless the lease says they may; leave that term out and the statutory bar protects you. (6) Use: unless the lease says otherwise, the tenant must occupy the unit only as a dwelling. The lease may also require the tenant to tell you about any anticipated absence longer than seven days, and if the lease does not say so there is no such duty and no damages remedy if the tenant disappears. (7) Shifting your own duties: by a written agreement you may have the tenant handle trash removal and heat or hot water, but only where the building houses four households or fewer; and in anything other than a single-family residence you may have the tenant do specified repairs, maintenance, alterations or remodeling only under a separate signed written agreement supported by its own consideration, entered in good faith, not covering work needed to meet building and housing codes, and not reducing what you owe other tenants. You may not make performance of that separate agreement a condition of the lease. (8) Sale or change of manager: unless the lease says otherwise, selling the property in good faith to a bona fide purchaser releases you from liability for later events once you give the tenant written notice, though you stay liable for the deposit; the same release applies to a manager who gives written notice that the management has ended. (9) Waiver: accepting late rent without reservation waives your right to terminate for that breach, and you can preserve the right only by a separate agreement made after the breach, not by a clause written into the lease in advance. (10) Entry: your right of entry covers "necessary or agreed" repairs and services, so whatever the lease defines as agreed work widens what you may enter to do. Anything the act does not prohibit may go in the lease, but nothing in the lease can waive a right or remedy the act gives the tenant.

title: No Ordnance, Demolition or Shared-Meter Disclosure — and Who Does Give the Tenant Notice
bodyText: Kansas requires none of the three pre-signing disclosures some states impose. There is no duty to tell an applicant or tenant about a former military ordnance or munitions training site near the property, however close it is and however much you know about it. There is no duty to disclose that you have applied for a demolition permit, to state the earliest approximate demolition date, or to say when you expect to end the tenancy. And there is no duty to disclose that the tenant's gas or electric meter also serves areas outside the unit. None of these is a Kansas lease term, so nothing has to appear in the lease and no form exists. What Kansas does instead on demolition is give the occupant notice through the city, not through you. A city acting on an unsafe, dangerous or abandoned structure must set a hearing at which the owner, the owner's agent, lienholders of record and any occupant may appear and show cause, publish the resolution once a week for two consecutive weeks, let at least 30 days pass after the last publication, and mail a copy by certified mail marked deliver-to-addressee-only. Under the parallel municipal unfit-for-habitation ordinance scheme, the complaint is served on the owner, every mortgagee of record and all parties in interest including persons in possession. So your tenant learns of a condemnation or demolition proceeding from the municipality on the municipality's timetable, which may be the first you hear that the tenant knows. Two practical points follow. First, demolition is not a free exit: ending the tenancy still takes the ordinary Kansas termination notice, and the only place Kansas names demolition in the landlord-tenant act is as an answer to a retaliation defence, where you may bring a possession action if complying with the building or housing code requires alteration, remodeling or demolition that would effectively deprive the tenant of the use of the unit — and bringing that action does not release you from damages for your own noncompliance. Second, if a licensed real estate broker or salesperson is acting as your agent or as a transaction broker in the letting, that licensee must disclose known adverse material facts to a customer, and a customer expressly includes a tenant; an owner renting their own property is not a licensee and owes no such duty. Shared and submetered utilities are a separate subject with their own Kansas rules; see the Kansas submetering and water-meter-charge entries rather than treating this as the place that answers them.

title: Facilities Kansas Does and Does Not Make You Supply
bodyText:
Kansas's landlord duty list is closed and short, and nothing outside it is implied. You must comply with applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety; exercise reasonable care in maintaining the common areas; keep in good and safe working order all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning appliances, including elevators, that you supply or are required to supply; provide and maintain common receptacles for ashes, garbage, rubbish and other waste and arrange for removal, unless a governmental entity provides them; and supply running water, reasonable amounts of hot water at all times, and reasonable heat. You may not block a tenant's access to a municipally franchised communication or cable television service.

That is the whole list. Beyond it, Kansas requires no window or door screens, no locking mail receptacle, no telephone jack or inside telephone wiring, no specified lighting of halls or stairways, no minimum number of fixtures per household, and no extra standards keyed to buildings with three or more units. If you want those things, they come from the local building and housing code, from the lease, or not at all.

Three qualifications matter. First, the duty on appliances is triggered by supply: if you provide a dishwasher, a window air conditioner, a garbage disposal or a washer, you have taken on a statutory duty to keep it in good and safe working order even though no statute required you to provide it in the first place, so think before you leave an appliance in the unit.

Second, elevators are named in the duty list, and separately no one may erect, alter, replace, inspect, maintain, remove or dismantle an elevator in Kansas, including in a private residence, unless they are a licensed elevator mechanic, contractor or inspector or work under one, and no mechanic may inspect their own work. Hiring an unlicensed handyman for an elevator is unlawful, not merely unwise.

Third, you may shift some of these duties only within narrow limits: trash and the water/heat duties only by written agreement and only where the building houses four households or fewer, and specified repairs, maintenance, alterations or remodeling only in a unit other than a single-family residence, by a separate signed written agreement supported by its own consideration, in good faith, not covering code-compliance work, and not reducing what you owe other tenants — and you may not make performance of it a condition of the lease.

Smoke detectors are a separate Kansas duty with its own rules and are covered by the Kansas smoke-detector entries.

title: No Parking-Rules Notice Statute — the General Rules Statute Is What Binds You
bodyText: Kansas has no parking-specific notice statute. Nothing requires you to hand a tenant your parking or towing rules before the lease is signed, nothing prescribes a heading or typeface for a parking paragraph, nothing limits the vehicle information you may ask for, and nothing makes a parking permit run only as long as the lease. Kansas never enacted anything resembling the Texas multiunit parking-rules rule. What governs instead is the general landlord-rules statute, and it does more work here than landlords expect. A parking rule binds the tenant only if it promotes the convenience, safety, peace or welfare of the tenants, preserves your property from abusive use, or fairly distributes services and facilities held out to tenants generally; is reasonably related to that purpose; applies to all tenants in the premises equally; is explicit enough to fairly tell the tenant what to do or not do; is not adopted to evade your own obligations; and — the point that matters most for parking — the tenant has notice of it at the time the tenant enters into the rental agreement. So although no statute orders pre-signing delivery, a parking rule the tenant first sees after signing is unenforceable against that tenant unless it clears the next hurdle: a rule adopted after signing that substantially modifies the rental agreement binds the tenant only if the tenant consents to it in writing. Kansas sets no advance-notice period for a rule change. The practical consequences: attach the parking rules to the lease or set them out in it, have the tenant sign for them, and treat a mid-term change that reassigns spaces, takes parking away or adds a charge as needing written consent, not a posted notice. Towing is a separate subject with its own Kansas answer; see the Kansas towing entry. Note only that a tower who takes a vehicle at the direction of the property owner gets a first and prior lien on it for the full value of the service, and that where a vehicle is left behind at the end of a tenancy the abandoned-property procedure in the landlord and tenant act, not a tow, is the route that protects you.

title: What a Kansas Lease Cannot Waive — and Who Falls Outside the Act Entirely
bodyText: Kansas's non-waiver rule is one line and it is the broadest thing in the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act: no rental agreement may provide that the tenant or the landlord agrees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under the act. It runs both directions, so it protects you as well as the tenant, and it is not limited to a named right. Every duty and every remedy the act creates is swept in — the habitability duties, the deposit cap and the 14-day and 30-day return deadlines, the notice periods for terminating, the three-day nonpayment notice, the tenant's fire-and-casualty termination, the retaliation bar, the remedies for unlawful removal or exclusion, the abandoned-property procedure. A clause shortening any of them, or having the tenant agree in advance not to use one, is unenforceable, and if you deliberately use a rental agreement containing a provision you know is prohibited the tenant may recover actual damages. Three things make this larger than it first looks. First, you cannot get around it by routing the rent elsewhere: no rental agreement, assignment, conveyance, trust deed or security instrument may permit the receipt of rent free of the obligation to comply with the landlord's duties. Second, even outside the prohibited list, a court may refuse to enforce a lease or any provision of it that was unconscionable when made, and may do the same to a settlement in which a party waived or agreed to forego a claim or right under the act or the lease — so a signed release after the dispute is not automatically safe either. Third, and most important in practice, the act cannot be waived by agreement but whole arrangements sit outside it to begin with, and that list is longer than the statute says. The act does not govern residence at an institution incidental to detention or to medical, geriatric, educational, counseling or religious service; occupancy by a purchaser under a contract of sale; occupancy by a member of a fraternal or social organization in a structure operated for the organization; transient occupancy in a hotel, motel or rooming house; occupancy by an employee whose right to occupy is conditional on employment in and about the premises; occupancy by a condominium owner or a holder of a proprietary lease in a cooperative; or premises used primarily for agricultural purposes. The act also does not apply to a pre-1975 rental agreement, though it does apply to any renewal, extension or modification, nor to a person who enters and remains without a rental agreement and without the landlord's knowledge, knowing they are not authorized, once the landlord has personally communicated an order to leave. And since 2026 a further exclusion sits outside the act's own scope section: occupancy by a squatter is excluded from the residential landlord tenant act, and removing a squatter does not require an eviction action under it. Two warnings about that last one. It is a definition with teeth pointed at you: a tenant who holds over in a periodic tenancy is not a squatter, and using the squatter affidavit route against a tenant or holdover is a class A nonperson misdemeanor and exposes you to restored possession, actual costs and damages, punitive damages of triple the fair market rent, court costs and attorney fees. And every one of the scope exclusions is prefaced by the words "Unless created to avoid the application of this act" — a tenancy dressed up as something on that list to escape the act stays inside it.

title: No No-Notice Entry for Scheduled Services — and You Cannot Write One In
bodyText:
Some states let a landlord enter without notice for regularly scheduled services — filter changes, pest treatment, yard work — if the right is conspicuously written into the lease. Kansas has no such provision, and more to the point it is not something you can create by drafting. Kansas's entry right already covers scheduled services: you may enter at reasonable hours, after reasonable notice, to make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations or improvements and to supply necessary or agreed services. The words "or agreed" are what a scheduled-services clause is for — the lease is what makes a recurring filter change or quarterly pest treatment an "agreed" service, and once it is agreed the statutory entry right reaches it.

What the lease cannot do is remove the notice. Reasonable notice at reasonable hours is a right the act gives the tenant, and no rental agreement may provide that the tenant agrees to waive or forego a right or remedy under the act; a no-notice entry clause is therefore unenforceable, and deliberately using a provision you know is prohibited exposes you to the tenant's actual damages.

Kansas also has no mechanism like Wisconsin's separately captioned nonstandard rental provisions, so there is no form of conspicuous drafting that buys you an exception. The only consentless entry Kansas allows is for an extreme hazard involving the potential loss of life or severe property damage — narrower than a general emergency.

Two further Kansas points shape how you should run a service schedule. Kansas fixes no number of hours, so the notice you promise in the lease is in practice the standard you will be held to; pick a period and keep to it. And repeated demands for entry that are otherwise lawful can themselves be the violation if they have the effect of unreasonably harassing the tenant, which is a real risk with a frequent service rota: the tenant may then obtain an injunction or terminate the lease and recover actual damages.

If the tenant refuses access you have a remedy — an injunction to compel access or termination, with actual damages in either case — but you have to go and get it; you may not simply let yourself in.

title: No Pesticide Notice to Tenants — What Kansas Regulates Instead
bodyText: Kansas imposes no pest-control notice duty on a landlord. You need not tell a tenant before a pesticide is applied, need not give a new tenant a copy of a periodic pest-control service contract or the operator's notice, need not post a sign or hand over a caution statement, and need not name the pest, the product or the application schedule. Kansas never enacted anything like the California pre-signing and 24-hour pesticide notices. What Kansas does regulate is the applicator, not the landlord: pest control technicians are registered and trained under the Kansas pesticide law, and anyone inspecting for wood-destroying insects in connection with a real estate transaction or a loan secured by real estate must hold a valid certification authorising use of restricted-use pesticides for that purpose — doing it without one is a deceptive act or practice under the Kansas Consumer Protection Act. Neither of those is a tenant-notice rule, and neither attaches to you. Four practical consequences. First, if you hire a licensed company, the Kansas pesticide regulations put the information duty on the company, and it is information after the fact, not advance notice: when a pesticide is applied in an apartment house or other multiple-tenant building, the company must make information about the pesticide available to the owner or manager, and information about a treated home available to that tenant on request. Nothing requires notice before treatment, so if advance notice matters to your tenants, put it in the lease or in the pest-control contract. Second, you still need a lawful way in. Kansas lets you enter at reasonable hours after reasonable notice to make necessary or agreed repairs and supply necessary or agreed services, which is what a treatment visit is, so the notice you actually owe is entry notice, not pesticide notice. Third, where a pest duty exists at all in Kansas it comes from a local code, not from the state: county commissioners served by a local health department may adopt a sanitary code covering, among other things, insects and rodents, housing, trailers and trailer courts, and your statutory duty is to comply with applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety — which is defined broadly enough to pull such a local rule into the lease. Whether your county has one, and what it says about treatment and notice, is a local question to check, not a state one. Fourth, nothing here gives the tenant an inspection or treatment right; Kansas has no bed bug statute and no general warranty of habitability, so the allocation of pest responsibility between you and the tenant is whatever the lease makes it.

title: No Pets-and-Eviction Fact Sheet to Hand Over
bodyText: Kansas publishes no state fact sheet on caring for pets through an eviction and requires you to give a tenant nothing of the kind, at signing or at any later point, even when you know the tenant has a dog or cat. Kansas never enacted anything like Maryland's requirement to include a link to the agriculture department's fact sheet with the lease. Kansas's eviction statutes also contain no special rule for an animal left in the unit, and that gap is worth planning around rather than ignoring. Where Kansas does mention animals in the landlord and tenant act, it does so only to put responsibility on the tenant: the tenant is responsible for destruction, defacement, damage, impairment or removal of any part of the premises caused by any person, animal or pet on the premises with the tenant's express or implied permission, and must not allow any person, animal or pet on the premises with that permission to disturb other tenants' quiet and peaceful enjoyment. A tenant also cannot terminate for a condition caused by an animal or pet that was there with their permission. Nothing in the act tells you what to do with a living animal found in a unit after a writ is executed. The abandoned-property procedure in the act is written for household goods, furnishings, fixtures and other personal property, and it gives you 30 days of storage before sale or disposal — a timetable that cannot responsibly be applied to an animal. So if you know or suspect an animal is in the unit, raise it with the sheriff before the writ is executed and contact the local animal control officer or shelter; do not store, release or dispose of the animal yourself. Kansas's animal cruelty law is a criminal statute of general application and it does not exempt a landlord.

title: Pet Money in Kansas: Deposit, Rent, and Nothing in Between
bodyText:
Kansas gives you one express pet allowance and no others. If the lease permits the tenant to keep or maintain pets in the unit, you may demand and receive an additional security deposit not exceeding half of one month's rent. It stacks on top of the ordinary cap, so an unfurnished pet-friendly unit allows up to one and a half months' rent in deposit, and a furnished pet-friendly unit up to two. That allowance is the lawful way to charge more for a pet, and it is only available because the lease permits pets — if your lease is silent or bans pets, the half-month is not available to you at all.

Everything else about pet money follows from a definition problem rather than from any pet statute. Kansas has no pet deposit, pet fee or pet rent statute; those three phrases appear nowhere in Kansas law. What Kansas has instead are two definitions that leave no third category. A security deposit is any sum specified in the lease, however denominated, that the tenant must deposit as a condition of occupying the unit and that the tenant may forfeit under the lease's terms. Rent is every other payment the tenant makes under the lease. So money the tenant pays you is one or the other, and the label on it decides nothing.

Work it through. A refundable pet deposit is plainly a security deposit, counts against the cap and must be itemised and returned on the statutory timetable. A one-off "nonrefundable pet fee" that the tenant must pay to move in and does not get back is a security deposit too, because it is a condition precedent to occupancy and is forfeited — so it eats the half-month allowance and the rest of the cap, and calling it nonrefundable does not save it. Monthly pet rent is different: it is not a condition precedent to occupancy and is not forfeited on a breach, so it falls outside the deposit definition and is therefore rent. Kansas does not cap rent and has preempted local rent control, so pet rent is not limited in amount — but it is rent for every other purpose, which means nonpayment of it is nonpayment of rent and runs on the three-day notice, and it belongs in the rent clause rather than the deposit clause.

The practical rule is simple: if you want more than the half-month, take it monthly as rent, state it in the lease, and never try to reclassify an up-front, forfeitable payment as a fee.

One category is carved out entirely. A legally blind person accompanied by a guide dog, a person who is deaf or hard of hearing accompanied by a hearing assistance dog, and a person with a disability accompanied by a service dog each have the right to that dog in the acquisition and use of rental residential housing without being required to pay an extra charge for it — so no pet deposit, no pet fee and no pet rent. The person remains liable for damage the dog does to the premises. Kansas's own definition does not treat a dog present for comfort, protection or personal defence as an assistance dog, but federal fair housing law treats assistance animals more broadly, so do not use the narrower state definition to charge for an animal a federal accommodation covers.

title: No Plain-Language or Readability Law for Kansas Leases
bodyText: Kansas has no plain-language statute, no readability test and no consumer-contract act that reaches residential leases. There is no requirement that a lease use short words and sentences, avoid Latin or legal terms, use personal pronouns, be divided and captioned by section, meet a reading-score threshold, or be set in a minimum type size. Nothing like Minnesota's Plain Language Contract Act, Pennsylvania's Plain Language Consumer Contract Act or Hawaii's division-and-caption rule exists here, and no dollar ceiling or exemption question arises because there is no statute to apply. The absence is deliberate rather than accidental: Kansas does impose a readability duty elsewhere, on car rental companies, whose rental agreements may not contain a collision damage waiver unless it is written in simple and readable words with common meanings and is understandable and its terms are prominently displayed. The legislature knew how to write such a rule and did not write one for leases. Kansas legal scholarship surveyed readability statutes in 1980 and proposed a model; none was enacted for residential tenancies. The only typography requirement anywhere in Kansas's landlord and tenant act is narrow and specific: if you hand a tenant a document that would serve as the tenant's written notice of intent to vacate and it contains terms not in the lease, the document must carry a prescribed warning in no less than ten-point boldface type telling the tenant the signature may bind them to additional terms and that they may decline to sign and give notice another way. Without that statement, a signature does not bind the tenant to the extra terms. Two things do still discipline how a Kansas lease is written, and neither is a readability rule. A court may refuse to enforce a lease or any provision of it that was unconscionable when made, or limit its application, and the parties get a chance to put in evidence of the setting, purpose and effect — a lease written to be impenetrable is evidence in that inquiry. And the Kansas Consumer Protection Act reaches a landlord as a supplier in a consumer transaction, where deceptive and unconscionable practices include taking advantage of a consumer's inability to understand the transaction's language. That reach is qualified: Kansas authority treats the landlord and tenant act as the specific statute taking precedence over the broader consumer act on subjects the former addresses, so the consumer act is at its strongest exactly where the tenancy act is silent, as it is here. Write the lease to be understood because it is good practice and because of those two doctrines, not because a statute scores it.

title: No Statement of Consumer Restrictions to Put in the Lease
bodyText: Kansas requires no statement of consumer restrictions in a lease. There is no front-page or any-page block in which you must list what the tenant could lose, no obligation to itemise every waiver or landlord-protective term, no readability test the lease must pass, no attorney general preapproval procedure for a lease form, and no dollar ceiling above which such a rule stops applying — because there is no such rule in the first place. The words statement of consumer restrictions, consumer restrictions and notice to consumer do not appear anywhere in Kansas law. Kansas never enacted a plain-language consumer contract act of the Pennsylvania kind, and nothing in the Kansas landlord and tenant act or the Kansas Consumer Protection Act requires a lease to summarise itself. You may of course include a plain summary of the tenant's main obligations if you want to, and doing so is good practice, but understand what it does and does not do: it is a drafting choice, not compliance with anything, and it does not cure a term that Kansas prohibits or make an unenforceable clause enforceable. The one place where failing to spell something out carries real risk is not a disclosure rule but a general one. A Kansas court deciding whether a lease or any provision of it was unconscionable when made will consider, among other circumstances the landlord knew or had reason to know, whether the landlord took advantage of the tenant's inability to protect their own interests because of physical infirmity, ignorance, illiteracy, inability to understand the language of an agreement or a similar factor, and whether the transaction the landlord induced the tenant to enter was excessively one-sided in the landlord's favour. So a lease that buries its one-sided terms is exposed through unconscionability, not through a missing statement. That reach has a limit worth knowing: Kansas authority treats the landlord and tenant act as the specific statute taking precedence over the broader consumer act where the two overlap, so the consumer act bites hardest on subjects the tenancy act does not address.

title: No Candidate or Canvasser Access Right — and the One Political Sign Rule That Is Not About Leases
bodyText: Kansas gives political candidates, campaign workers and voter-registration canvassers no right of access to a multi-unit building, and imposes no corresponding duty on you. There is no Kansas equivalent of Minnesota's candidate-access statute, and no requirement to designate a voter information area in a building where unit entrances are behind a locked door. Access to locked lobbies, corridors and other common areas is yours to control, and a no-soliciting rule applied evenhandedly to everyone is an ordinary landlord rule. A tenant may of course invite anyone, including a candidate, to their own unit. Two Kansas points sit near this subject and are easy to misread. First, Kansas does void a restriction on political yard signs, but it does so in restrictive covenants, not in leases: a covenant provision banning the display of political yard signs under six square feet during the period from 45 days before an election to two days after it is against public policy and void, and that applies to covenants already in existence. The statute speaks to restrictive covenants running with land, so it does not by its terms strike a yard-sign term in a lease — but if the property is in a covenanted subdivision, your lease cannot enforce as a private term what the covenant itself could not impose, and in a covenanted property the safer course is to allow a sign inside those limits rather than to ban one. Second, Kansas protects tenant organising, which is political activity of a different kind. You may not retaliate by increasing rent or decreasing services after a tenant has organised or become a member of a tenants' union or similar organisation, and a tenant hit with retaliation may recover the greater of one and a half months' rent or actual damages, may terminate the lease, and has a defence in a possession action. You may still raise rent in good faith to meet increased costs of operation such as tax rises, utility rate increases or acts of God, if the increase does not conflict with a lease in effect.

title: No Tenant Right to a Window or Portable Air Conditioner — but Watch What You Supply
bodyText: Kansas gives a tenant no right to install a portable or window-mounted cooling device, and imposes no notice duty on you if your lease restricts or bans them. The phrases window unit, window-mounted and portable cooling device appear nowhere in Kansas law. There is no Kansas equivalent of Washington's rule requiring a lease that restricts window units to say so, and none of Oregon's rule that a restriction is unenforceable unless it is in writing and limited to specified grounds. So whether a tenant may put an air conditioner in the window is purely a lease question. Write the answer into the lease either way, because nothing supplies a default: say whether tenant-installed cooling devices are allowed, what kind, how they must be mounted and vented, who pays for the electricity, that the tenant must remove the device and repair any damage at the end of the tenancy, and that nothing may block an exit or a required opening. The tenant is already responsible by statute for damage to the premises caused by the tenant or by anyone there with the tenant's permission, so a badly mounted unit that falls or leaks is on them — but a written term makes that easier to enforce and lets you refuse before the damage happens rather than after. Two cautions. First, Kansas has no cooling duty of any kind: nothing requires you to provide air conditioning and no statute sets a maximum indoor temperature. But if you supply a cooling appliance, you must keep it in good and safe working order, because the duty attaches to what the landlord supplies, not to what the law requires. Leaving a window unit in the unit for the next tenant quietly creates that duty. Second, do not use a supplied air conditioner as leverage — see the Kansas confirmed-absences entry on habitability, which records the unresolved question whether cooling is an 'other essential service' whose willful interruption triggers the Kansas penalties; the statutes name electric, gas and water and do not name cooling, so treat the point as unsettled and assume it counts. Separately, if a local building or fire code restricts how a window unit may be installed, compliance with applicable codes materially affecting health and safety is your statutory duty, and L. 2026, ch. 74, s 2 smooths the way for the state fire marshal to update to the 2024 edition of the International Fire Code — an update not yet made, because K.A.R. 22-1-3 still adopts the 2006 International Fire Code and the 2006 International Building Code.

title: No Tenant Solar Right — and a Kansas Statute That Points the Other Way
bodyText: Kansas gives a tenant no right to install a solar device, portable or otherwise. There is no plug-in or balcony solar right, no notice-and-reasonable-restrictions procedure, no wattage allowance, no commencement date, and no rule voiding a lease term that bans tenant solar. The phrases plug-in solar, balcony solar and portable solar appear nowhere in Kansas law. Kansas also has no statute voiding instrument restrictions on solar energy systems of the kind some states use to reach lease terms — its solar statutes do the reverse. Kansas says that no person other than the surface owner of a tract has the right to use the land to produce wind or solar generated energy unless the lawful owner of the surface estate grants that right by lease or easement for a definite period, and it preserves any otherwise enforceable restriction on using land for solar production. Kansas also requires any easement for exposure of a solar energy device to be created in writing and recorded, with the angles and the terms of termination stated. So in Kansas the starting position is that a tenant generates solar power on your property only if you grant the right, and a lease term requiring your prior written consent for any solar installation is both lawful and the sensible default. Write it in, and if you do consent, deal in the same term with mounting and penetrations, weight and wind loading, electrical connection and who pays for the power, insurance, removal at the end of the tenancy, and restoration of the building. Kansas did legislate on distributed energy in 2025, and it is worth knowing what that act does, because it protects you rather than the tenant. It requires a distributed energy retailer to register and, before contracting, to hand the customer a separate disclosure document in at least 10-point type, in the language used in the sales process, covering the system's major components and expected useful life, a generation guarantee with a remedy, the total aggregate cost in bold highlighted type separately acknowledged in writing, the ownership and transferability of tax credits and incentives, and a bar on blank spaces that could later be filled in. But the customer it protects is defined as a property owner of a single-family dwelling or a multifamily dwelling of two units or fewer. A tenant is not a distributed energy customer, and neither is the owner of a larger building. If you are approached to put solar on a one- or two-unit rental you own, those disclosures are yours to demand.

title: Kansas Size Thresholds: Three, and Only One Counts Your Portfolio
bodyText: Kansas has no general small-landlord concept. The residential landlord and tenant act applies in full to every landlord whatever the size of the holding: there is no exemption, no tiered duty, no reduced notice, and no deposit, entry or termination rule that turns on how many units you own. The phrase small landlord appears nowhere in Kansas law. Only three thresholds exist, and you have to match each to the duty in front of you. First, and the only one that counts your portfolio rather than the building, is the fair-housing exemption. Most of the Kansas Act Against Discrimination does not apply to the sale or rental of a single family house by an owner, but only if two conditions are both met: the owner does not own or have any interest in more than three single family houses at any one time, and the house is rented without a real estate broker, agent or salesperson or the facilities of anyone in the business of renting dwellings. Read them conjunctively — using an agent forfeits the exemption even for an owner of one house, and owning a fourth house forfeits it even if you never use an agent. If the owner does not live in the house and was not its most recent resident, the exemption covers only one sale in any 24-month period. The exemption also never reaches the discriminatory-advertising prohibition, which applies to everyone. A second fair-housing exemption turns on the building rather than the portfolio: rooms or units in a building with living quarters for no more than four families living independently, where the owner actually maintains and occupies one of them as the owner's residence. Second, the duty-shifting thresholds in the tenancy act turn on the building too. You may agree in writing that the tenant performs your trash-removal and water-and-heat duties only where the dwelling unit or units provide a home for not more than four households having common areas; and you may agree that the tenant performs specified repairs, maintenance, alterations or remodeling only in a unit other than a single family residence, and then only under a separate signed written agreement with its own consideration, in good faith, not covering code-compliance work, and not reducing what you owe other tenants. Third, the fair-housing accessibility standard turns on the building and its date: for covered multifamily property first occupied on or after January 1, 1992 — buildings of four or more units with one or more elevators, and ground-floor units in other buildings of four or more units — the public and common use portions must be readily accessible, with the doorway and interior requirements that follow. One point about what Kansas has taken off the table for cities. A 2026 act bars any city or county from adopting or enforcing an ordinance limiting the amount of a security deposit a landlord may require, restricting a landlord's use of income-qualifying methods, credit scores, credit reports, eviction history, property damage history or criminal history, forbidding refusal to lease because of a housing choice voucher or another voluntary-participation housing assistance programme, or requiring an automatic right of first refusal; any such ordinance adopted before July 1, 2026 is null and void. So a locally invented portfolio-size rule in those four areas is void. The act runs only against cities and counties and creates no duty for you, and it does not preempt local rules outside those four limbs.

title: No End-of-Term Possession Bond — but Three Real Bonds Run Through a Kansas Eviction
bodyText: Kansas has nothing like the end-of-term possession bond some states allow, under which a tenant binds themselves to deliver possession on the last day of the term and authorises a confessed judgment if they do not. No Kansas statute creates one, and you cannot write one into a lease: Kansas flatly bars any rental agreement providing that the tenant or the landlord authorises any person to confess judgment on a claim arising out of the rental agreement. Such a term is unenforceable, and if you deliberately use a lease containing a provision you know is prohibited the tenant may recover actual damages. Three bonds that do exist are worth knowing, because two of them are the tenant's and one is yours. First, the tenant's continuance bond. An eviction trial is held within 14 days after the appearance date in the summons, and no continuance is granted unless the defendant asking for it files a bond with good and sufficient security approved by the court, conditioned for the payment of all damages and rent that may accrue if judgment goes against them. That has been the single most useful provision in the landlord's hands, and in 2026 it gained an exception you must know about: where the underlying rental agreement is governed by the residential landlord and tenant act and the parties are participating in mediation, the court shall order a continuance of not more than 14 days from the date the mediation order is entered — with no bond. The same 2026 act requires the court, in an eviction on a lease governed by the act, to consider mediation unless it finds that mediation would not aid the parties materially or is impracticable. So the realistic sequence now is that the court raises mediation at the appearance, orders it, and the tenant gets 14 more days without posting anything. Plan your timeline on that basis. Second, the tenant's stay-on-appeal bond. An appellant wanting a stay must get a supersedeas bond approved by the judge from whom the appeal is taken, conditioned for satisfaction of the judgment in full with costs, interest and damages for delay. In a case about real property the court may instead condition the stay on the timely payment into court of the periodic rent otherwise due under the rental agreement, which is often what happens. Third, your own bond. If you want immediate possession before the case is over, you move for it, the court holds a hearing on evidence, and if the judge is satisfied that immediate possession is in the interest of justice and will properly protect all parties, the order issues only on your giving an undertaking to the tenant, in an amount and with sureties the court sets, conditioned to pay damages if the tenant wins. Finally, do not try to substitute the 2026 squatter affidavit route for any of this. A tenant who stays past the end of the term is a holdover, not a squatter; the act says so, a knowingly false affidavit is a class A nonperson misdemeanour, and a wrongly removed person recovers possession, actual costs and damages, punitive damages of triple the fair market rent, court costs and attorney fees.

title: What You Must Do With Property Left After a Writ of Restitution
bodyText:
Kansas runs post-eviction property through the same section as abandonment, and the statute says so: it applies where the tenant abandons or surrenders possession and leaves things behind, and equally where the tenant is removed as a result of a forcible detainer action under the Kansas eviction statutes and fails to remove property after possession is returned to you. It reaches household goods, furnishings, fixtures and any other personal property in or at the dwelling unit.

The procedure is mandatory if you want protection, and the periods are exact. You may take possession of the property and store it at the tenant's expense. You may sell or otherwise dispose of it only upon the expiration of 30 days after you take possession of the property. At least 15 days before the sale or other disposition you must publish once, in a newspaper of general circulation in the county where the dwelling unit is located, a notice of your intention to sell or dispose of the property. Within seven days after publication you must mail a copy of the published notice to the tenant at the tenant's last known address. The notice must state the tenant's name, a brief description of the property and the approximate date on which you intend to sell or dispose of it. Publication and mailing are both required; they are not alternatives.

Meet those requirements and you may sell or dispose without liability to the tenant or to anyone else claiming an interest — with one exception that catches landlords out: a secured creditor who gives you notice of its interest before the sale, and the protection only holds where you have no knowledge or notice that someone other than the tenant claims an interest.

Throughout the 30 days, and at any time before sale or disposition, the tenant may redeem the property by paying your reasonable expenses of taking, holding and preparing it for sale, plus any amount due from the tenant for rent or otherwise. Proceeds are applied in a fixed order: first your reasonable expenses of taking, holding, preparing for sale or disposition, giving notice and selling or disposing; then any amount due from the tenant for rent or otherwise; and only then may you keep the balance, free of liability to the tenant or anyone else except a secured creditor who gave notice. A buyer who takes without knowledge that the sale violates a third party's ownership or security interest takes free and clear.

Five things Kansas does not give you. There is no inventory duty, no duty of care and no bailment standard written into the statute, but equally no statute relieving you of them, so do not assume the Colorado-style no-duty rule; store the goods somewhere dry and keep a record. There is no landlord immunity statute for executing a writ. There is no post-writ pet animal procedure at all, and the 30-day storage timetable cannot sensibly be applied to a living animal, so involve the sheriff and local animal control before the writ is executed. There is no separate ejectment route with a warehouse-storage option. And there is no self-help: you may not hold the goods as a lien, because a lien or security interest in the tenant's household goods, furnishings, fixtures or other personal property in the landlord's favour is unenforceable unless it was perfected before 1975, and distraint for rent is abolished except as this same section allows.

On the writ itself, it is executed within 14 days after the person named in it receives it, that person may use such reasonable force as is necessary, and if a stay on appeal comes through after the premises were restored to you, the tenant goes back in.

A tenant who returns after the writ is in criminal trespass territory, as a person entering or remaining who knows they are not authorised and does so in defiance of an order to leave personally communicated by the owner, or on premises locked or secured against entry — a class B nonperson misdemeanour. That is a matter for law enforcement, not for you. And do not reach for the 2026 squatter affidavit against a former tenant: a holdover in a periodic tenancy is not a squatter, a knowingly false affidavit is a class A nonperson misdemeanour, and a wrongly removed person recovers possession, actual costs and damages, punitive damages of triple the fair market rent, court costs and attorney fees.

title: No Private Well Testing or Results Disclosure — but the County May Have Rules
bodyText: Kansas has no private well testing act. If the rental's drinking water comes from a private well, no Kansas statute requires you to test it on any schedule, to test it before letting, to give a tenant the results of any test you did do, to give a new tenant the most recent results, or to post results at a seasonal rental. There is no Kansas analogue to New Jersey's Private Well Testing Act or to Oregon's exempt-well notice. There is also no state disclosure that the water source is a well at all. Four things still bear on it. First, your general duty: you must supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times. That is a supply duty, not a quality standard, and Kansas sets no potability standard in the landlord and tenant act — but a well that stops producing is a failure of that duty. Second, the duty that does the real work is compliance with applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, and in Kansas that is where well rules live. A county served by a local health department may adopt a sanitary code, and the subjects such a code may cover expressly include water supply, sewage disposal, insects and rodents, refuse, and housing. A 2026 act confirmed that although counties may not regulate the transfer or appropriation of water, nothing stops a county using zoning or sanitary code requirements to regulate the location or use of domestic water wells. So the question whether your well must be tested, and on what cycle, is a county question, and the answer may differ between two properties you own in different counties. Find out before you let the property, and do not assume that because the state is silent the subject is unregulated. The Department of Health and Environment's water well regulations govern how a well is built, disinfected and plugged rather than how often it is tested: a well producing drinking water must be disinfected when it is built or repaired, and the landowner must plug a well that has been abandoned. Third, if you have had the water tested and the results are bad, say so. A licensed real estate broker or salesperson acting as your agent or as a transaction broker must disclose known adverse material facts to a customer, and a customer expressly includes a tenant. An owner letting their own property is not a licensee and owes no such duty — but a known contaminated supply is also a candidate for a deceptive or unconscionable practice under the Kansas Consumer Protection Act, and silence about a known hazard is not a safe position just because no statute names the disclosure. Fourth, if you do test, say in the lease who arranges and pays for testing and treatment and how results are shared, because nothing supplies a default.

title: What Kansas Bars a Tenant From Doing — and What Happens If They Do It
bodyText: Kansas has no separate list of prohibited tenant acts with its own penalties. It has a single duties section, and the two prohibitions in it are worded as responsibility rather than as a ban, which changes how you enforce them. The tenant is responsible for any destruction, defacement, damage, impairment or removal of any part of the premises caused by an act or omission of the tenant or by any person or animal or pet on the premises at any time with the tenant's express or implied permission or consent. Read that carefully, because it is wider than the clause most leases use. There is no intent or negligence qualifier — the tenant is responsible for damage whether or not anyone was at fault — and it reaches a guest, a visitor's dog or a child's friend, so long as they were there with the tenant's express or implied consent. Do not narrow it in your lease to damage the tenant caused intentionally or negligently; that gives away a defence Kansas does not give. The tenant must also not engage in conduct, or allow any person, animal or pet on the premises with their permission to engage in conduct, that will disturb the quiet and peaceful enjoyment of the premises by other tenants. Note the limit on that one: the protected group is other tenants, not neighbours generally and not you, so a single-family rental with no other tenants gives you nothing to enforce under this limb unless your lease says more. The rest of the section is positive duties — comply with the building and housing code obligations imposed primarily on tenants that materially affect health and safety, keep the occupied part clean and safe, remove waste, keep plumbing fixtures clean, and use the electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances in a reasonable manner. Enforcement runs through the general machinery, not through a penalty attached to the act. For a material noncompliance with the lease, or a noncompliance with the tenant duties section materially affecting health and safety, you serve a written notice specifying the acts and omissions and stating that the lease terminates on a date not less than 30 days after receipt if the breach is not remedied in 14 days; if the same or a similar breach recurs after that 14-day period, your second notice terminates in not less than 30 days with no chance to cure. You may also recover damages and obtain injunctive relief for any noncompliance, whether or not it is material. Three further points. Refusing access is handled separately: if the tenant refuses to allow lawful access you may obtain an injunction to compel access or terminate the lease, and recover actual damages either way — but you must go and get that remedy rather than letting yourself in. Damage to the deposit is handled separately too: the deposit may be applied to accrued rent and to damages from the tenant's noncompliance with the duties section and with the lease. And conduct that is also a crime — deliberate damage, or returning to the property after you have told the person to leave — is a matter for law enforcement under Kansas's criminal statutes, not something your lease converts into a private penalty.

title: No Written-Promise Rule, But a Written Promise Binds You
bodyText: Kansas has no statute requiring a promise to clean, repair or improve a unit to be put in writing, to carry a completion date, or to be given before the lease is signed. Wisconsin has that rule; Kansas does not, and there is no Kansas form and no penalty for an undated promise. What Kansas gives you instead is ordinary contract law plus two statutory hooks worth knowing. First, you and the tenant may include in the rental agreement any term that the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act and other law do not prohibit, so a promised repair written into the lease or into a signed addendum becomes a lease term. Second, once it is a lease term, not keeping it is material noncompliance by the landlord with the rental agreement: the tenant may deliver a written notice specifying the acts and omissions and stating that the agreement terminates on a periodic rent-paying date not less than 30 days after receipt. The tenancy then ends on that date unless you adequately initiate a good-faith effort to remedy the breach within 14 days of receiving the notice. If the same or a similar breach happens again after that 14-day window, the tenant may give a fresh 30-day notice and you get no second cure period. Separately, and whether or not the tenancy is terminated, the tenant may recover damages and obtain injunctive relief for any noncompliance with the rental agreement. An unwritten promise is a worse position, not a safe one: it may still be enforceable, but you will be arguing about what was said, and a lease of land for more than one year has to be in writing signed by the party granting it. So write every promise down, describe the work item by item, and give each item a date. Kansas already requires a record you can use for this. Within five days of the initial date of occupancy or delivery of possession, you and the tenant must jointly inventory the premises, complete a written record of their condition and of any furnishings or appliances provided, sign duplicate copies, and give the tenant a copy. Note the promised work and its dates there. One last point: if a licensed real estate broker or salesperson is acting in the transaction, that licensee's own misrepresentation exposure is governed separately and is not your promise.

title: No Chemical-Exposure Warning Law, and Do Not Copy California's
bodyText: Kansas has nothing resembling California's Proposition 65. There is no state list of chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm, no duty to warn a tenant or an applicant that a unit may expose them to such a chemical, no prescribed warning words, no posting rule and no private enforcement bounty. The phrase known to the state to cause cancer does not appear anywhere in Kansas law. Where Kansas does prescribe a cancer warning, it writes it for a sale rather than a lease.
