Every contract for the sale of residential real property must contain set language telling the buyer that the property may present exposure to dangerous concentrations of indoor radon gas that may place occupants at risk of radon-induced lung cancer, describing radon as a class-A human carcinogen and the leading cause of lung cancer in non-smokers, stating that Kansas law requires sellers to disclose information known to them showing elevated radon concentrations, and pointing to testing and mitigation. That is a sale requirement. The legislature did not extend it to leases, which is why a Kansas landlord owes no radon warning. Kansas deals with hazardous substances by licensing the work rather than by warning the occupant. Asbestos projects run under a certification, licensing and notification regime, and lead-based paint activities under a certification regime of their own; both bind the people who do the work, not a landlord talking to a tenant. Kansas also has a successor-corporation asbestos liability act and a block of asbestos-claim procedure sections in its civil code, and none of them creates a warning owed to an occupant. Two things still bite. Federal law requires the lead-based paint disclosure and pamphlet for most housing built before 1978, and that is the one chemical warning a Kansas residential landlord genuinely owes. And if you know of a specific hazard at the property, silence carries risk without any warning statute: the Kansas Consumer Protection Act reaches deceptive and unconscionable practices, and a licensed broker or salesperson actually acting in the transaction must disclose known adverse material facts, including environmental hazards required by law to be disclosed and material defects in the property. The practical course is simple. Do not paste a Proposition 65 warning into a Kansas lease. It announces a legal standard Kansas does not have, invites questions you cannot answer from Kansas law, and an inaccurate warning is worse than none. Give the federal lead disclosure where it applies, disclose in writing any specific hazard you actually know about, and keep a copy of what you gave and when.

title: No Property-Tax-Portion-of-Rent Statement
bodyText: Kansas requires no statement telling a tenant what share of the rent goes to property taxes. There is no annual July statement, no statement on a rent change, no prescribed form, and no lease alternative to giving one. Some states impose that duty; Kansas has not. Kansas mentions property taxes in its landlord-tenant law exactly once, and it is a permission rather than a duty. The retaliation statute bars you from increasing rent after a tenant has complained to a code-enforcement agency about a violation materially affecting health and safety, has complained to you of a breach of your statutory duties, or has organised or joined a tenants' union; but you may still increase the rent despite such a complaint if the increase does not conflict with a lease agreement in effect and is made in good faith to compensate you for expenses incurred as a result of acts of God, public utility service rate increases, property tax increases or other increases in costs of operations. So a property tax rise is a recognised reason to raise rent in Kansas, and the statute neither requires you to show the tenant your tax bill nor says how much of the rise you may pass on. Two practical points follow. If you want rent to track your tax bill, that is a lease drafting question, not a disclosure question, and the library's rent escalation clause is where to do it; write the calculation into the lease so a later increase does not conflict with it. If a tenant asks what portion of the rent is tax, answering is a courtesy and nothing obliges you to, but if you do answer, answer accurately, because a false statement about a charge is the kind of thing the Kansas Consumer Protection Act reaches. Note too that Kansas's own property tax relief programmes live in the tax statutes rather than in landlord-tenant law and are claimed by the person entitled to them, so a tenant asking you for a figure for such a claim is asking a favour, not enforcing a duty. Check the current rules with the Kansas Department of Revenue rather than relying on a landlord-side note for them.

title: No Separate Ban on Asking, But Your Application Form Is Regulated
bodyText: Kansas has no statute separately prohibiting you from asking an applicant about a protected characteristic or from keeping a record of one. Nebraska and Minnesota make the inquiry and the record unlawful in their own right; Kansas did not adopt that structure, and the words inquiry and record appear nowhere in its housing discrimination provisions. What Kansas prohibits is the decision and the document. It is unlawful to make, print, publish, disseminate or use, or cause to be made, printed, published, disseminated or used, any notice, statement, advertisement or application, with respect to the sale or rental of real property, that indicates any preference, limitation, specification or discrimination based on race, religion, color, sex, disability, familial status, national origin or ancestry, or an intention to make one. Read the word application in that list carefully, because it does most of the work here: a rental application form whose questions signal a preference or a limitation on one of those grounds is itself unlawful, whether or not you ever act on the answer. Note too that ancestry is a Kansas ground in addition to national origin. An oral question at a showing, or a note in your own file, is not automatically a violation in Kansas the way it is in Nebraska, but it is evidence of discrimination in any complaint that follows, and there is rarely a lawful reason to ask. Keep your application to what you actually screen on. Two practical points. First, the application and advertising rule is the one provision that survives the Kansas small-landlord exemptions, so a landlord otherwise outside the state act still may not use a discriminatory application form or advertisement. Second, disability is where the gap matters most: the Kansas provisions tell you what you must permit and accommodate but contain no inquiry ban, and the restriction on asking whether a person has a disability or how severe it is comes from federal fair housing law, which applies to Kansas property on its own terms. On local law, Kansas's 2026 preemption stops a city or county from restricting your ability to use, consider or request income-qualifying methods, credit scores, credit reports, eviction history, property damage history or criminal history under your customarily applied criteria, so no Kansas city can ban those questions. It says nothing about protected-class questions, so a city is not barred from legislating there; check the city if you operate in one.

title: No Use-Restriction Statute, So Write the Restriction Into the Lease
bodyText: Kansas has no statute limiting a residential tenancy to a purpose stated in the lease, and none giving you a special remedy when the tenant uses the property for something else. North Dakota lets a landlord whose lease states a purpose either hold the tenant responsible for the safety of the property during any other use or treat the contract as rescinded; Kansas has nothing like it. But Kansas does keep the old criminal-law provisions that reach a lease of premises used for a prohibited purpose, and they are stronger than most landlords expect. They are in the criminal procedure code, under the heading of common nuisances, and they do three things to a landlord. A use restriction in a Kansas lease is therefore an ordinary lease term, and it is enforced the ordinary way, so write it plainly and specifically. If the tenant materially breaches it, serve a written notice specifying the acts and omissions and stating that the tenancy will terminate on a date not less than 30 days after receipt if the breach is not remedied within 14 days. The tenancy does not end if the tenant adequately begins a good-faith effort to cure before the date in the notice, but if the same or a similar breach happens again after those 14 days you may serve a fresh notice terminating in not less than 30 days with no chance to cure, and either way you may also recover damages and obtain injunctive relief. Some use restrictions are backed by the statutory tenant duties whether or not your lease says anything: the tenant must keep the part of the premises they occupy as clean and safe as its condition permits, use the electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning facilities and appliances in a reasonable manner, answer for destruction, defacement, damage, impairment or removal of any part of the premises caused by the tenant or by anyone the tenant lets in, and not engage in or allow conduct that disturbs other tenants' quiet and peaceful enjoyment. First, a listed activity can void the lease outright. Kansas declares a list of unlawful activities, and the use of real or personal property in carrying them on, to be common nuisances: commercial gambling, dealing in or possessing gambling devices, promoting obscenity, promoting the sale of sexual relations, commercial sexual exploitation of a child, any violation of a law regulating controlled substances, habitual unlicensed liquor or tobacco sales, a felony committed for or with a criminal street gang, and unlawful use of pyrotechnics. If someone is arrested for one of those on your property, the attorney general or the city, county or district attorney may ask the court for a hearing on whether the activity is or has been occurring there. You may be given notice of it, and the hearing is normally held within thirty days. If the court finds by a preponderance of the evidence that an unlawful act occurred, that finding renders void any lease under which the tenant holds possession and the right of possession reverts to you, so you may evict. That is a statutory lease-voiding route and it sits in addition to anything the residential landlord and tenant act gives you. Do not treat it as a windfall, because of the second thing. If you do not start eviction proceedings within thirty days of that determination, the prosecutor may move on to a petition to enjoin the nuisance against the property itself — and the judgment in such a case can order the building closed and padlocked for up to two years, require you to post a bond that the property will not be used unlawfully for two years with the whole amount recoverable if you breach it, and impose a civil penalty of up to twenty-five thousand dollars on any or all defendants. Costs, including a fee to the prosecuting attorney, become a lien on the real property. Those consequences attach where the court finds the owner knew or should have known of the nuisance and did not make a bona fide attempt to abate it. Third, and this is the practical protection, the statute tells you what counts as a bona fide attempt. Evidence of one includes, and is not limited to, filing a written report with the local law enforcement agency, by you or at your direction, that you suspect the property is being used for one of those activities. So if you suspect it, report it in writing, keep the copy, and start the eviction promptly. Reporting and acting is what stands between you and the padlock, the bond, the penalty and the lien. Note two limits. The property itself, real or personal, can be named as a party defendant and summons served on the owner or person in possession, and anyone claiming an interest may intervene — so you may have to appear to protect your own building. And the ordinary civil nuisance track is separate and is not a lease remedy: a private party may enjoin the continuance of a common nuisance affecting their personal rights, and an injunction may also be granted in the name of the state at the suit of the attorney general, a county attorney or a city attorney. That abates the nuisance; it does not end the tenancy. Where purpose does decide something in Kansas is whether the residential landlord and tenant act governs the arrangement at all. Unless created to avoid the act, it does not reach occupancy under a rental agreement covering premises used by the occupant primarily for agricultural purposes, residence at an institution incidental to detention or to medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious or similar service, occupancy by a member of a fraternal or social organization in a part of a structure operated for the organization, transient occupancy in a hotel, motel or rooming house, occupancy by an employee whose right to occupy is conditional on employment in and about the premises, occupancy by a condominium owner or a holder of a cooperative proprietary lease, or occupancy by a purchaser under a contract of sale. A 2026 act added one more that is not in that list: occupancy by a squatter is excluded from the act, and removing a squatter does not require an eviction action. So settle what the occupancy is for before you assume the act's notices and remedies are the ones that apply.

title: No Recycling Notice Duty; What Kansas Requires Is Waste Receptacles
bodyText:
Kansas imposes no duty to tell tenants where or how to recycle on the premises. Oregon requires that notice; Kansas has no equivalent, and no Kansas statute mentions a tenant and recycling in the same breath.

What Kansas requires instead is plainer. Except where a governmental entity provides them, you must provide and maintain on the grounds, for the common use of all tenants, appropriate receptacles and conveniences for the removal of ashes, garbage, rubbish and other waste incidental to the occupancy of the dwelling unit, and you must arrange for their removal. The duty is about receptacles and collection, and it says nothing about separating recyclables. The tenant's side is the matching one: the tenant must remove from the dwelling unit all ashes, rubbish, garbage and other waste in a clean and safe manner.

That receptacle duty is one of the few you may shift. In a dwelling providing a home, residence or sleeping place for not more than four households having common areas, you and the tenants may agree in writing that the tenant will perform it, provided the arrangement is in good faith and not a way of evading your obligations.

Whether recycling exists at all where your property sits is a local question, and local law is worth checking rather than guessing. Kansas lets a municipality, meaning any county, city, township or other political or taxing subdivision, establish an organized collection service, which is a system for collecting solid waste, recyclables or both, by franchise or by moving from multiple haulers to a single contracted hauler for a defined geographic area. That statute applies to every municipality whatever stage its collection system has reached. So the practical answer is that your city or county decides whether there is recycling and who hauls it, and nothing in state law makes you explain the scheme to a tenant.

If you do provide recycling, treat it as a contract matter rather than a statutory notice: say in the lease or the house rules which containers are for what, where they go and on which day, and keep that consistent with whatever your hauler actually accepts. That protects you under the clean-and-safe waste duties on both sides, which are the duties Kansas will actually enforce.

title: Redemption in Kansas Means the Property, Not the Tenancy
bodyText: Kansas gives a tenant no right to redeem a tenancy by paying after it has been terminated. There is no pay-at-the-courthouse-door right of the Virginia or West Virginia kind, no obligation to accept full payment up to judgment as in Colorado, and no statute letting a charity's or agency's cheque stand as the tenant's payment. Kansas's cure windows all close before termination and are covered in the note on cure and forfeiture. What redemption means in Kansas is the right to buy back real property after a judicial or tax sale, and that matters to you in two ways. After real property is sold under execution, special execution or order of sale, the defendant owner may redeem it within 12 months of the sale by paying what the holder of the certificate of purchase paid, plus that holder's allowed expenses, interest, costs and taxes to the date of redemption, and the owner is entitled to possession in the meantime. Several exceptions change the clock. The period is three months, not twelve, where the default happened before one-third of the original debt had been paid; it returns to twelve months if the court finds all mortgages and liens total less than one-third of the property's market value; and a three-month period may be extended by three more if the owner involuntarily lost their primary source of income after the sale. A court may shorten or extinguish the period altogether, after a hearing on not less than 21 days' notice, if it finds the property abandoned or not occupied in good faith. Outside agricultural land and one- or two-family dwellings held by natural persons as their residence, a mortgagor may agree in the mortgage to a shorter period or waive redemption entirely. Redemption does not reach oil and gas leaseholds, and lien creditors get their own window once the owner's exclusive period ends. Two points bear directly on renting. First, the property can be rented during redemption: the defendant owner keeps possession and may keep tenants and collect rent, and if the court appoints a receiver to protect the premises against waste, the receiver may rent, control and manage them, with the income, after the receiver's fees, repairs, waste prevention, real estate taxes and insurance, going to whoever would otherwise be entitled to possession. Second, there is a real trap for anyone who buys a distressed house and rents it out. If a person acquires a one- to four-family dwelling, including a condominium or cooperative, or any interest in one including an equity or redemption interest, where the loan is in default at purchase or goes into default within the next year, fails to notify the mortgage holder or certificate holder in writing within 21 days of the purchase, and fails to apply the rent to the mortgage as payments come due, then the former owner, that person's own tenant, and the mortgage or certificate holder may each bring a civil action. The recovery is all actual damages, court costs and attorney fees plus all rents received, and it applies whether or not the buyer is obligated on the loan. Tax sales run on their own clock. Real estate bid off by the county for delinquent taxes or special assessments is held two years, or one year if it is an abandoned building and the land accommodating it, and the owner or record-title holder, their heirs, devisees, executors, administrators, assigns or any mortgagee may redeem by paying the sale amount with accrued interest, later delinquent taxes and assessments with interest, and the costs and expenses of sale and redemption. A homestead, and other real estate outside that category, is held three years and may be redeemed partially year by year, which pushes back when tax foreclosure may begin. If the period runs out unredeemed, the property goes to tax foreclosure and sale. Last point: say nothing to a tenant about who will end up owning the property. Kansas has no statute making you disclose a pending foreclosure and none deciding whether the lease survives the sale.

title: No Religious or Cultural Display Right, and the Religious Freedom Act Binds Government, Not You
bodyText: Kansas gives a tenant no statutory right to display a religious or cultural item on a door, doorpost, entry or window, and gives you no statutory duty to allow one. Several states have a mezuzah or religious-object statute; Kansas has none, and the words mezuzah, doorpost and doorframe appear nowhere in its statutes. The question is decided by your lease and house rules, by fair housing law, and, if you are a government landlord, by a statute that does not reach private owners. Start with the statute that looks relevant and is not. Under the Kansas preservation of religious freedom act, government may not substantially burden a person's civil right to exercise of religion even where the burden results from a rule of general applicability, unless it shows by clear and convincing evidence that applying the burden furthers a compelling governmental interest and is the least restrictive means of doing so; a person burdened may raise it as a claim or a defence and a court may order injunctive relief, a protective order, mandamus or prohibition, declaratory relief, actual damages, and costs and attorney fees. But government there means the executive, legislative and judicial branches and any agency, board, commission, department, district, authority or other subdivision of state and local government, as well as any person acting under colour of law. A private landlord is not government and owes nothing under that act. A municipal housing authority is, and should treat a refusal to allow a religious display as a decision it may have to justify by that standard. Kansas's one cultural-display statute is narrower still: no state agency or municipality may prohibit an individual from wearing traditional tribal regalia or objects of cultural significance at a public event, meaning an event held or sponsored by a state agency or municipality such as an award ceremony, a graduation or a meeting of a governing body. That is about wearing, at public events, and has nothing to say about a rental unit. What does reach a private landlord is fair housing. Religion is a Kansas protected class, and so are national origin and ancestry. You may not discriminate in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental because of any of them, and an advertisement, notice, statement or application indicating a preference or limitation on those grounds is itself unlawful. A neutral rule is lawful on its face. A rule enforced against one faith's observance while other attachments are tolerated is where complaints come from. Federal fair housing law applies on top, and accommodation requests under it should be handled on their merits. Treat this as a drafting question. If you want to control what goes on doors, balconies and windows, put a neutral rule in the lease, apply it to everyone, allow small removable items that cause no damage, and write down your reason on the rare occasion you say no. And remember that a rule adopted after the tenant signs, which effects a substantial modification of the rental agreement, is unenforceable against that tenant unless the tenant consents to it in writing, so a display ban invented mid-tenancy will not bind an existing tenant.

title: No Concession Statute, So Write the Concession Into the Lease
bodyText:
Kansas has no statute about rent concessions. Nothing requires you to state a free month, a move-in discount, a credit or a rebate in the lease, nothing regulates how a concession is advertised, and nothing says what happens when it ends. Illinois has a concession statute and Washington reaches concessions through its rent-increase cap and its ban on confidentiality terms; Kansas has neither mechanism. The parties may include in the lease any term the residential landlord and tenant act and other law do not prohibit, including rent, so a concession is simply a term you agree.

Put it in the lease anyway, and put the whole of it there.

Three Kansas points make that worth doing. First, Kansas has no rent cap and no rent-increase notice statute, so the end of a discount is not a regulated rent increase, but on a periodic tenancy any change to what the tenant actually pays has to ride on the termination notice. If the concession is written into the lease with its own end date, the rent simply reverts as agreed and you need no notice at all. If it is not written down, stopping it mid-tenancy means terminating the tenancy on the statutory notice and offering a new one, which is a slower and riskier route.

Second, if you want the concession to be repaid on default, say so expressly; without that sentence you have given it away. Think carefully before adding it, because an unstated clawback of a concession already enjoyed looks like a penalty, and Kansas courts can refuse to enforce an unconscionable lease term.

Third, do not let a concession be used to disguise something the statute controls. The security deposit cap is one month's rent unfurnished, one and a half months where the tenant uses your furniture, plus half a month where pets are permitted, and it is measured against the rent; a nominal rent propped up by a concession is a poor basis for a deposit calculation. Keep the stated rent honest and show the concession separately.

The library's rent concession clause is the place to record each period of free or reduced rent, each credit or rebate, and the rental periods it applies to.

title: No Bar on Demanding Rent for a Defective Unit, But Two Statutory Abatements
bodyText: Kansas has no statute barring you from demanding or collecting rent, raising rent, or serving a pay-or-quit notice because a unit has code violations or is unfit. California bars all four where defined conditions exist; Rhode Island suspends the rent outright under a code repair order; Maryland stops a foreclosure purchaser collecting rent until it makes inquiry and serves a notice. Kansas has none of those. The words do not appear: nothing in Kansas law says a landlord may not demand or collect rent, and nothing ties a bar on collecting rent to a violation, an unfit finding or a code order. Your right to serve a three-day notice for nonpayment is unaffected by the condition of the unit. Two statutory abatements do exist and are worth knowing, because they are real exceptions to the general position. First, if you fail to deliver possession of the dwelling unit, rent abates until possession is delivered, and the tenant may either terminate on at least five days' written notice, in which case you must return the whole deposit, or demand performance, sue for possession against you or anyone wrongfully in possession, and recover damages; a wilful and bad-faith failure exposes the party at fault to the greater of one and a half months' periodic rent or one and a half times actual damages. Second, after a fire or casualty that substantially impairs the use and habitability of the unit, a tenant who stays where continued occupancy is lawful may vacate the unusable part, and the tenant's liability for rent is reduced in proportion to the diminution in the fair rental value of the unit. Beyond those two, condition does its work in court rather than before it. In an action for possession based on nonpayment, or an action for rent where the tenant is in possession, the tenant must counterclaim for anything recoverable under the lease or the act or lose it; the court may order the rent paid into court, determines what each side is owed, pays the net amount to whoever is owed it, and if no rent remains due after that offset, judgment may be entered for the tenant in the possession action. So a badly maintained unit does not stop you demanding the rent; it can stop you winning the eviction. Two further limits sit beside this. If you unlawfully remove or exclude the tenant, or wilfully cut off electricity, gas, water or another essential service, the tenant may recover possession or end the lease and recover the greater of one and a half months' periodic rent or actual damages. And you may not retaliate by raising rent or cutting services after a protected complaint. Practical course: fix the condition and keep collecting rent in the ordinary way, rather than assuming either that you may ignore the defect or that you must stop billing.

title: No Escalation Rule, But the Retaliation Safe Harbour Makes the Clause Worth Having
bodyText:
Kansas has no rent-escalation statute. There is no index rule, no cap, no limit on how often rent may change and no required notice period for a change. Whether rent can change during a fixed term is decided entirely by your lease, and if the lease says nothing the rent is fixed for the term.

One Kansas provision makes an escalation clause worth having rather than merely permitted. You may not retaliate by increasing rent after the tenant has complained to a government agency responsible for enforcing a building or housing code about a violation materially affecting health and safety, has complained to you of a violation of your statutory duties, or has organised or become a member of a tenants' union or similar organisation. The statute then gives you a safe harbour, and it is narrow. You may still increase the rent despite such a complaint if the increase does not conflict with a lease agreement in effect and is made in good faith to compensate you for expenses incurred as a result of acts of God, public utility service rate increases, property tax increases or other increases in costs of operations.

Read the two conditions together, because that is where the clause earns its place. The increase has to be cost-based, not market-based; Kansas's safe harbour is narrower than the market-rate safe harbours some states give. And it must not conflict with the lease in effect, so where the lease fixes rent for the term a mid-term increase conflicts with it and the safe harbour does not reach it. A rent-change term agreed at signing is what keeps a later increase from conflicting with the lease.

Two clause shapes work here and both are offered: a schedule of changes or an index formula fixed in advance, and an optional mid-term increase on written notice with a fee-free exit for the tenant. If you prefer an escalation tied to your costs, the categories the safe harbour names are a sensible model to draft to.

On a periodic tenancy you need no escalation clause at all, because rent changes by giving the statutory termination notice and offering a new tenancy at the new rent. And no Kansas city, county or township may impose a rent cap on you, subject to the limited exceptions covered in the note on rent control.

title: No Rent-Increase Notice Statute, and the 60-Day Rule You Have Read About Is the Mobile-Home Rule
bodyText:
Kansas has no rent-increase notice statute. There is no cap on how much rent may rise, no limit on how often, and no notice period set by law for an increase as such.

Ignore the 60 days you will see quoted for Kansas. That figure is real but it belongs to the Mobile Home Parks Act, which requires each tenant to be notified in writing of any rent increase at least 60 days before the effective date and forbids an effective date sooner than the expiration of the original rental agreement or any renewal or extension of it. That act governs mobile home spaces, not ordinary residential rentals, and quoting it in an ordinary lease will mislead both sides.

For a fixed-term lease, the rent is whatever the lease says for the term, and you cannot raise it mid-term unless the lease itself provides for it. For a periodic tenancy, a rent change rides on the termination notice: you end the existing tenancy and offer a new one at the new rent. A week-to-week tenancy ends on written notice given at least seven days before the termination date stated in the notice. A month-to-month tenancy ends on written notice stating that the tenancy terminates on a periodic rent-paying date not less than 30 days after the notice is received. Count that carefully, because it is the most commonly botched step in Kansas. The 30 days run from receipt, not from posting, and the date you name has to be a rent-paying date, so in practice a change for the first of next month usually needs to go out well before the start of this one. A fixed term of more than 30 days is not a month-to-month tenancy merely because rent is payable every 30 days.

Three limits apply to the increase itself. You may not retaliate by increasing rent after the tenant has complained to a code-enforcement agency about a violation materially affecting health and safety, has complained to you about one of your statutory duties, or has organised or joined a tenants' union; the only escape is the statute's narrow safe harbour, which requires that the increase not conflict with the lease in effect and be made in good faith to recover cost increases from acts of God, utility rate rises, property tax rises or other operating costs. Fair housing law applies. And if you give the tenant a document that would operate as the tenant's own notice of intent to vacate and it carries any term not already in the lease, including a new rent, it must contain the statutory warning in ten-point boldface type, and without it the tenant's signature does not bind them to the added terms.

One related trap: you cannot raise rent by house rule. A rule or regulation adopted after the tenant enters the rental agreement that effects a substantial modification of the agreement is unenforceable against the tenant unless the tenant consents to it in writing.

Finally, two things Kansas does not have. There is no emergency rent freeze and no price-gouging law reaching rent, so nothing caps what you may charge during or after a declared disaster. And no county, city or township may impose rent control on your property, subject to the exceptions set out in the rent-control note.

title: Installments Are Allowed by Agreement, and They Move the Three-Day Clock
bodyText:
Kansas has no statute on splitting rent into instalments and none saying whether a scheduled instalment counts as a partial payment. Oregon has both; Kansas has neither.

What Kansas gives you is a default you can contract out of. Rent is payable without demand or notice at the time and place the parties agreed. Unless otherwise agreed, rent is payable at the dwelling unit, at the beginning of any term of one month or less and otherwise in equal monthly instalments at the beginning of each month, and rent is uniformly apportionable from day to day. The words unless otherwise agreed are what let you set a different schedule, and the act separately confirms that the parties may include any term it and other law do not prohibit, rent among them. So an instalment schedule is lawful, and the library's instalment clause is where to put it.

Understand what a schedule does to your remedies, because this is the part landlords get wrong. You may terminate if rent is unpaid when due and the tenant fails to pay within three days after written notice of the nonpayment and of your intention to terminate. Those three days are three consecutive 24-hour periods running from delivery to the tenant, delivery to a person over 12 living at the premises, or conspicuous posting; add two days if you serve by mail.

If the lease makes rent payable in instalments, when due means each instalment's own date, so a missed instalment starts a clock on that instalment rather than on the whole month, and you must be able to show what was due when. Write each instalment amount and date into the lease and keep the late charge tied to the rental period, so a second instalment in the same month cannot generate a second late charge unless you intended that.

Two further cautions. Kansas has no statute telling you what a partial payment does, so the effect of accepting one is a matter of waiver, and accepting money after a breach or after a termination notice can undo the notice; the note on accepting late rent explains how to reserve your position. And rent is not a licence to collect ahead: whatever schedule you set, the security deposit caps are measured against the rent and the tenant may not apply the deposit to the last month unless the lease says otherwise.

title: No Duty to Give a Rent Receipt, Including for Cash
bodyText: Kansas does not require you to give a tenant a receipt for rent, in cash or in any other form. There is no cash-receipt duty, no record-book requirement, no penalty for failing to give one, and nothing making a missing receipt a defence to a nonpayment case. Kansas also has no presumption of the kind Puerto Rico and Guam have, under which a receipt for a later payment is evidence that earlier ones were made. Rent is simply payable, without demand or notice, at the time and place the parties agreed; if they agreed nothing, it is payable at the dwelling unit, at the beginning of any term of a month or less and otherwise in equal monthly instalments at the beginning of each month. That Kansas made a choice here rather than overlooking the subject is clear from where its one lessor receipt rule sits. The Kansas consumer lease-purchase agreement act requires a lessor to provide the consumer a written receipt for each payment made by cash or money order. But an agreement under that act is one for the use of personal property by a natural person primarily for personal, family or household purposes, for an initial period of four months or less renewing with each payment, which lets the consumer become the owner. That is the rent-to-own furniture and appliance statute. It does not reach a dwelling, and nothing like it was written for residential rent. Give receipts anyway. The reason is evidentiary, not legal: a cash payment with no receipt leaves neither side a record, and in a dispute about whether rent was paid the gap cuts against whoever carries the burden on that point. If you take cash, hand over a written, dated receipt naming the property, the period the payment covers, the amount received and any balance still owing, and keep a copy. Better still, require a traceable method of payment in the lease and stay out of the argument altogether. Two related points live elsewhere: accepting rent after a breach or after a termination notice can waive the breach or create a new tenancy, and that is covered in the notes on accepting late rent and on holdovers.

title: No Rent-Reporting Rule, But Know Where the Credit Reporting Act Bites
bodyText: Kansas neither requires, forbids nor regulates a landlord's reporting of rent payments to a credit bureau. There is no mandatory offer of positive rent reporting like California's, no state rent-reporting programme a tenant cannot be made to join like Nevada's, and no duty to notify a tenant in writing before reporting late rent like Puerto Rico's. Whether you report is a business decision. What does apply is the Kansas fair credit reporting statute, and it is worth knowing where its duties fall, because they are not where most people assume. Its obligations run against consumer reporting agencies and against users of consumer reports. The act contains no section imposing duties on a person who furnishes information to an agency, so if you report rent your exposure comes from federal credit reporting law and from ordinary liability for an inaccurate statement, not from the Kansas act. Three parts of that act still matter in practice. A consumer reporting agency generally may not report adverse items older than seven years, with suits and judgments running seven years from entry or until the governing limitation period expires, whichever is longer, and bankruptcies fourteen years; those limits fall away for very large credit transactions, large life policies and higher-salary employment screening. If a tenant disputes an item and tells the agency, the agency must reinvestigate within a reasonable time and record the current status. And the state adverse-action notice is narrower than people expect: it is triggered when credit, insurance or employment is denied or made more expensive because of a consumer report, and a rental application is none of those three, so the state duty does not attach to a tenancy denial. Federal law is what reaches tenant screening. Think about the second direction too. A delinquency you report becomes a record the tenant can dispute, and from 2026 the court record behind it has a clock the credit record does not. A tenant who was the defendant in a residential eviction may apply electronically to expunge the judgment at no cost, and the court must grant it once three years have passed since judgment, any money judgment owed to you is shown satisfied, and no further residential eviction judgment has been entered in that period. You get 30 days after service to object, and if you do not object the court decides without a hearing and presumes any money judgment satisfied. An unsatisfied money judgment is not expunged unless you agree. Expungement does not satisfy or extinguish the debt and does not stop you suing separately for unpaid rent or damages. A public housing authority may still ask for three years of eviction judgment history for active applicants for federal housing assistance. So report only what you can document, correct it promptly if it is wrong, and if you intend to report at all, say so in the lease.

title: No Tax on Ordinary Rent; the Transient Guest Tax Starts at 28 Days
bodyText: Ordinary residential rent in Kansas carries no state or local rent tax. The tax to know about is the transient guest tax, and it turns on two things: a 28-day line and the kind of place. A transient guest is a person who occupies a room in a hotel, motel or tourist court for not more than 28 consecutive days. Hotel, motel or tourist court means a structure containing rooms furnished to provide lodging, held out to the public as a place where sleeping accommodations are sought for pay, with more than two bedrooms furnished for guests. A house or an apartment let on a lease is neither of those things. An accommodations broker is a business keeping an inventory of two or more rooms, in one or more locations, offered for pay for not more than 28 consecutive days. The tax is local rather than state. A county or city may levy a transient guest tax of up to 2 percent of the gross receipts derived from transient guests for sleeping accommodations, exclusive of charges for incidental services or facilities, in a hotel, motel or tourist court. A county of more than 300,000 people, and cities inside it, work under a parallel act capped at the same 2 percent but requiring approval at an election. Either way the tax is paid by the guest to the business, the business must collect it and pay it over to the Department of Revenue, and nothing is levied until the city or county passes an ordinance or resolution. No county may levy inside the corporate limits of a city in that county that is already levying, and no city in a county that is already levying may levy at all. In practice: if you rent a dwelling on a lease, the transient guest tax does not reach you. If you run short stays, a vacation rental or rooms let by the night, it may, and the test is the 28 consecutive days together with whether what you operate answers the statutory description of a hotel, motel or tourist court. Put that question to the Kansas Department of Revenue and to your city or county before you start, not after. One 2026 change, and what is left of it. For the FIFA World Cup, Kansas temporarily widened transient guest, from 15 May to 25 July 2026, to reach a guest occupying one or more individual rooms within a dwelling or residential unit offered as a place of accommodation, or such a dwelling or unit in whole or in part, while excluding a permanent guest or a person contracting for more than 28 consecutive days within that period where the contract was intended for long-term or permanent occupancy. The same act barred municipalities from limiting the number or duration of short-term rental permits during the window and required applications to be processed within 15 calendar days, with a deemed approval if they were not. That window has closed. The permanent definition was re-enacted in the same act and is unchanged in substance: not more than 28 consecutive days, in a hotel, motel or tourist court. Nothing from the World Cup provisions survives for an ordinary rental. Finally, the state sales tax, and the short answer is that it does not reach a house or an apartment let on a lease. Kansas sales tax reaches sales and leases of tangible personal property and a list of named services. A lease of real property is neither, so it is outside the tax from the start. The twenty-eight-day line appears here too, but it is doing a different job: the definition of a sale excludes the sale of the use of tangible personal property used as a dwelling by way of a lease or rental for a term of more than twenty-eight consecutive days, and the exemptions separately exempt all leases or rentals of tangible personal property used as a dwelling where it is leased or rented for more than twenty-eight consecutive days. Those are about property that is personal rather than real — a manufactured home is the usual case — so a short let of such a unit can be taxable where a longer one is not. On the services side the one that matters is the renting of rooms by hotels and by accommodation brokers, both defined by cross-reference to the lodging and the transient-guest statutes rather than by the tax chapter. That is the same boundary as the transient guest tax, approached from the other direction, and it is another reason the question to settle first is whether what you operate is a lodging business at all. These definitions sit in the tax chapter rather than in landlord-tenant law and they change often, so confirm the current text with the Department of Revenue before relying on it for an unusual arrangement.

title: Kansas Bars Local Periodic Interior Inspections Without the Occupant's Consent
bodyText: Kansas has no state rental inspection programme, no rental registration scheme and no inspection districts. It has the opposite: a statute telling cities and counties what they may not do. No city or county may adopt, enforce or maintain a residential property licensing ordinance or resolution that includes a requirement for periodic interior inspections of privately owned residential property for city or county code violations unless the lawful occupant has consented to those interior inspections. Three limits on that protection are in the statute itself. It does not apply to inspections of mixed-use residential and commercial property. It does not stop a city or county from conducting plan reviews, periodic construction inspections or final occupancy inspections required by building permits. And it bars only periodic interior inspections under a licensing ordinance, so it does not touch an inspection prompted by a complaint, a warrant, or an exterior or common-area look. The same statute gives the tenant a right you do not control: any lawful occupant of privately owned residential housing may ask the city, or the county if the property is in an unincorporated area, to inspect for code violations at any time. A tenant who is unhappy with a repair can invite the inspector in, and you cannot stop that. Do not treat your lease as the occupant's consent. The consent the statute speaks of is the occupant's, and a signed lease term agreeing in advance to future city inspections has not been tested in Kansas, so it is not something to rely on. A clause obliging the tenant to cooperate with a lawful inspection is fine as a contract term, but get the occupant's actual consent when an inspection is proposed. Your own right of entry is separate and does not carry an inspector in with you: you may enter at reasonable hours after reasonable notice to inspect, make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations or improvements, supply necessary or agreed services, or show the unit to prospective or actual purchasers, mortgagees, tenants, workmen or contractors; without consent only in case of an extreme hazard involving potential loss of life or severe property damage; and never abusively or to harass. Two recent acts speed permits up rather than creating inspections. A local government must approve or deny a building permit application and give written notice within 60 days of a complete application, must say within 15 days if an application is incomplete, and if it misses the 60 days the application is deemed approved. Separately, a 2026 act lets a political subdivision opt in, by ordinance or resolution of its governing body, to a regime allowing third-party review of development documents and third-party development inspections when the authority misses 30 days; it is opt-in locality by locality and not a statewide entitlement. Everything else about inspections is local. Kansas's 2026 preemption of local rental ordinances covers only source of income, screening criteria, deposit caps and rights of first refusal, so it does not stop a city from regulating rental housing in other ways. Check your city and county. Kansas does not say whether a clause in the lease can be that consent. Do not rely on a lease term for it: if your city runs a periodic inspection programme, ask the occupant for separate written consent before each inspection.

title: No Right to End the Lease Because a Repair Costs Too Much
bodyText: Kansas gives you no right to refuse a repair and end the tenancy because the work would cost too much. Wyoming has that right; Kansas does not, and there is no cost threshold, no written election, and no move-out window of the kind Wyoming prescribes. The Kansas statute that sets your duties names its own excuses and cost is not one of them: your duties apply except when you are prevented by an act of God, the failure of public utility services, or other conditions beyond your control. An expensive repair is within your control, so the duty stands. If you do not perform, the tenant may give you a written notice specifying the breach and stating that the tenancy ends on a periodic rent-paying date not less than 30 days later, and the tenancy ends unless you adequately begin a good-faith effort to fix the problem within 14 days of receiving the notice; the tenant may also sue for damages and an injunction. What you do have is three lawful exits, none of them cost-based. One, fire or casualty: if the unit or premises are damaged or destroyed by fire or casualty to an extent that substantially impairs the use and habitability of the unit, the tenant may vacate at once and end the lease by written notice within five days, or stay and pay reduced rent for the part still usable. That statute gives the tenant the choice, not you, so if you want your own casualty exit you must write it into the lease. Two, the term: a fixed-term lease simply expires, and a periodic tenancy ends on the statutory notice, seven days for week-to-week and 30 days running to a rent-paying date for month-to-month, with no reason given. Three, a government order: a city or county acting under its unsafe-structure ordinance can order a building repaired, vacated, closed or demolished, and the cost becomes a lien on the property. That is the local authority's decision about the building, not a private right to walk away from a lease, and it is the local code you should be watching, not a repair-cost rule. Plan repairs as a cost of holding the property, and if you cannot carry them, end the tenancy the ordinary way or sell.

title: Nothing to Opt Out Of: Kansas Has No Repair Escrow or Repair-and-Deduct
bodyText: Kansas has no small-landlord exemption notice for tenant repair remedies, for the simple reason that it has no repair remedies to be exempt from. Ohio lets a landlord who is party to rental agreements covering three or fewer dwelling units escape the rent escrow remedy by giving the tenant notice of that fact; Kansas has no escrow remedy, no repair-and-deduct right, no unit-count threshold and no notice that would disapply anything. Do not put an Ohio-style notice in a Kansas lease: it would tell a tenant their remedies are cut off when no such remedies exist, and it invites an argument that you tried to waive rights the act does not let you waive. What a Kansas tenant has instead is a single route and two court-based ones. If there is material noncompliance by you with the lease, or a noncompliance with your statutory duties that materially affects health and safety, the tenant may deliver a written notice specifying the acts and omissions and stating that the agreement will terminate on a periodic rent-paying date not less than 30 days after you receive it; the tenancy does not end if you adequately initiate a good-faith effort to remedy within 14 days of receipt, but a repeat of the same or a similar breach after that window lets the tenant give a fresh 30-day notice with no cure period. Separately, and whether or not the tenancy ends, the tenant may recover damages and obtain injunctive relief for any noncompliance. And in an action for possession for nonpayment, or an action for rent where the tenant is in possession, the tenant must counterclaim for anything recoverable under the lease or the act or waive it, the court may order rent paid into court, and if nothing remains due after the offset, judgment may be entered for the tenant. None of that depends on how many units you own. Size does matter in Kansas, but in the other direction, and it is a permission rather than an exemption. In a dwelling providing a home for not more than four households having common areas, you and the tenants may agree in writing that the tenant performs the waste-receptacle and water-and-heat duties and specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodelling, if done in good faith and not to evade your obligations. For any dwelling other than a single-family residence, a separate signed written agreement supported by adequate consideration may give the tenant specified repairs and maintenance, provided the work is not needed to cure a building or housing code violation and the agreement does not affect your duties to other tenants. You may not make performance of that separate agreement a condition of anything else in the lease. That is the whole of the Kansas size story, and it shifts work forward by agreement rather than switching off a remedy by notice.

title: Kansas Requires One Lease Disclosure, and the Penalty for Missing It Is Unusual
bodyText:
Kansas has one required lease disclosure and a short list of documents around it. That is the whole state-law picture, so do not expect the kind of pre-signing checklist Virginia or Wisconsin imposes.

The disclosure: at or before the commencement of the tenancy, you, or whoever is authorised to enter into the rental agreement on your behalf, must disclose to the tenant in writing the name and address of the person authorised to manage the premises, and the name and address of an owner of the premises or of a person authorised to act for the owner for service of process and for receiving and receipting for notices and demands. The information must be kept current, and the duty runs against a successor landlord, owner or manager.

The penalty is worth taking seriously because it is not a fine. A person who fails to comply becomes an agent of each landlord for service of process and for receiving and receipting for notices and demands, and for performing the landlord's obligations under the act and under the rental agreement, spending or making available for that purpose all rent collected from the premises.

Two documents go with the tenancy rather than being disclosures. Within five days of the initial date of occupancy or delivery of possession, you and the tenant must jointly inventory the premises, complete a written record of their condition and of any furnishings or appliances provided, sign duplicate copies and give the tenant a copy. At the other end, if you keep any part of the deposit you must give an itemised written notice.

There is also exactly one form of words Kansas prescribes, and it is not in the lease: a document that would operate as the tenant's notice of intent to vacate and that contains terms not in the rental agreement must carry the statutory ten-point boldface warning, or the tenant is not bound by the added terms.

Now what Kansas does not require. There is no state lease form, no required first page, no state summary of rental terms and no statement of tenant rights. There is no coverage notice telling a tenant whether a just-cause or rent-increase law applies, because Kansas has neither law. There is no state disclosure duty for mold, radon, bed bugs, methamphetamine contamination, flood history or a pending foreclosure; each of those has its own note. And a residential lease need not be in writing at all unless the term exceeds one year.

Two things fill part of the gap, and neither is Kansas landlord-tenant law. Federal law requires the lead-based paint disclosure and pamphlet for most housing built before 1978, and that duty is real whatever the state statutes say. And where a licensed real estate broker or salesperson is in fact acting in the transaction, that licensee must disclose to a customer, which includes a tenant, all adverse material facts actually known, including environmental hazards required by law to be disclosed, the physical condition of the property, material defects in the property and material defects in the title.

Read that limit carefully. Kansas has no property-manager licence; the licensing act defines lease as renting for nonresidential use, and a person dealing with their own property is exempt from the act. So the duty attaches because a licensee is acting, not because someone is a landlord, and an ordinary Kansas owner renting out their own house owes nothing under it.

title: No Rights Guide Delivery Duty
bodyText: Kansas does not require you to give a residential tenant a state-published guide to landlord and tenant rights, before signing or at renewal, and requires no signed acknowledgment of one. No Kansas statute directs any state agency to prepare, publish or distribute such a guide for residential tenancies, and no Kansas statute requires a lease to carry a summary of the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or a statement that the tenant has rights under it. The Legislature plainly knows how to impose that duty: in the separate mobile home parks act it requires that a rental agreement for a space in a park harboring five or more mobile homes contain a notice telling the tenant that the tenant has certain rights under that act and that copies of the act may be obtained from the landlord on request. The residential act's matching section, which otherwise repeats the same opening words, has no such subsection. The one brochure duty in Kansas real estate law runs the other way: a real estate licensee must furnish a prospective buyer or seller with the commission's 'real estate brokerage relationships' brochure at the first practical opportunity, and acknowledgment of receipt goes in any contract for sale. That duty is owed to buyers and sellers, not to tenants, and only where a licensee is acting. The only thing Kansas makes you disclose in a residential tenancy is the name and address of the person managing the premises and of the owner or the owner's agent. You may of course hand a tenant a plain-language summary of the act or a copy of the act itself, and doing so is good practice, but nothing turns on it and no penalty attaches to leaving it out.

title: No Code Variance Notice
bodyText: Kansas has no state rule requiring you to give a tenant a copy of, or attach to the lease, a variance or exemption from a sanitary, health or housing code in effect for the property. Kansas has no state sanitary code for dwellings at all. What it has is county sanitary codes: the commissioners of a county served by a local health department may adopt one by resolution, after review and approval by the secretary of health and environment and a published public hearing, and housing is expressly a subject such a code may cover. That act contains no variance mechanism of any kind, and so no notice duty attached to one. It also does not reach incorporated cities, or premises in single ownership of more than ten acres used only for agricultural purposes, so in a city the applicable code is the city's own. Violating a county sanitary code is a misdemeanor carrying a fine of up to $200, and each day is a separate offense. Whatever code applies, complying with it is your duty as landlord anyway, because the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act makes you comply with the requirements of applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, and that duty overrides your other maintenance duties where it is the greater one. The nearest Kansas thing to a code variance is on the fire side: the state fire marshal may grant an exemption from a specific requirement of the fire regulations, but only on a written request showing that enforcement would cause unnecessary hardship or that the exemption is needed to use a new method or equipment of recognized adequacy meeting fundamental safety standards. The statute says exactly where the written particulars of that exemption go: a copy is kept in the fire marshal's office. It says nothing about telling the people who live in the building. So no statute makes you hand it over. Two cautions. A county sanitary code or a city housing code is a local enactment and may write in its own variance procedure with its own notice conditions, so read the variance itself and follow its terms. And a variance excuses you against the code authority, not against your tenant: the uncorrected condition can still be a breach of your statutory maintenance duties and can still support a retaliation defense if you react to a tenant who reports it. The safe course is to give the tenant a copy of any variance or exemption in effect and attach it to the lease even though Kansas does not require it.

title: Seasonal and Vacation Rentals
bodyText: Kansas has no seasonal-tenancy rules. There is no seasonal lease category, no shorter or longer deposit deadline for one, no deposit exemption for a vacation or recreational rental, and no separate eviction track for a seasonal tenant. If you rent a cabin, a lake house or any other dwelling for a season to someone who lives in it, that is an ordinary tenancy under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, with the full deposit cap and return deadlines, the habitability duties, the notice periods and the eviction procedure. The one thing the act does carve out is transient occupancy in a hotel, motel or rooming house, and those are not loose descriptions - Kansas defines each of them. A hotel is a building held out to the public as offering sleeping accommodations for pay primarily to transient guests with four or more rooms used for guests, whatever it calls itself, including a cabin camp, tourist cabin or motel. A rooming house takes eight or more guests and keeps no common food-preparation facilities; a boarding house is the same but with them. A single house rented for a season is none of these, so the carve-out does not reach it. Where short-term renting does change your position is licensing, and this catches people out. A guest house - a building held out to the public for sleeping accommodations for pay to transient or permanent guests, taking no more than seven guests in no more than three rooms - is a lodging establishment under the state lodging inspection act. It does not need a lodging license, but it can be inspected if the Department of Agriculture receives a complaint about it, and it is subject to temporary closure. Go above that, to four or more rooms held out primarily to transient guests, and you are running a hotel: operating a lodging establishment without a valid license from the secretary of agriculture is unlawful, the license must be displayed conspicuously and it is not transferable to another person or location. Two further points. Kansas briefly preempted local short-term-rental regulation in 2026 for the World Cup, barring any city or county from capping permit numbers or rental durations and deeming an unanswered permit application approved after 15 calendar days, but that ran only from 15 May to 25 July 2026 and has lapsed, so your city or county may regulate short-term rentals again and you should check its code. And the transient guest tax turns on 28 consecutive days, not on whether the stay is seasonal.

title: Kansas Does Not Say Where to Hold the Deposit
bodyText: Kansas puts no rules at all on how you hold a residential security deposit. There is no escrow requirement, no trust account, no requirement that the money sit in a separate account or in a federally insured institution, no bar on commingling it with your own funds, no surety or guarantee bond you may post instead, no duty to tell the tenant which bank holds it, and no duty to pay the tenant interest or to account for interest you earn. There is no small-owner exemption either, because there is nothing to be exempt from. The money is simply yours to hold, subject to the duty to account for it and return it when the tenancy ends. This is a deliberate gap, not an oversight. Kansas wrote exactly those duties into its mobile home parks act: there, deposits must be held for the tenant in a federally insured bank, credit union or savings and loan, may not be commingled with the landlord's personal funds, may sit in a common or interest-bearing trust account, and any interest earned belongs to the landlord. The residential act's deposit section was written from the same template, has the same itemized-notice rule, the same 14-day and 30-day deadlines and the same penalty, and contains no holding subsection whatever. Two other Kansas trust-fund rules exist and neither reaches you. For commercial real estate, escrow funds including security deposits must be held in this state in a licensed broker's trust account. And a real estate broker must keep a separate designated trust account for down payments, earnest money and other trust funds received in a real estate transaction, and may not keep interest on an interest-bearing trust account without the written consent of all parties. But Kansas's real estate licensing act defines a lease, for its own purposes, as a rent or lease for nonresidential use, and exempts a person acting with reference to their own property, so neither rule governs a residential deposit you take on your own rental. Hold it separately anyway. Not because a statute says so, but because the penalty for getting the return wrong is the withheld amount plus damages of one and a half times whatever you wrongfully kept, the person who holds your interest in the premises when the tenancy ends is bound by the deposit section, and a deposit you cannot produce is a deposit you cannot show you were entitled to keep. If you operate in a city or county, check its code: the 2026 state law voiding local deposit rules reaches only ordinances that limit the deposit amount, not ordinances about how a deposit is held.

title: Deposit Rights Cannot Be Waived, but Two Parts of the Deposit Rule Are the Lease's to Set
bodyText: A Kansas lease cannot take away the tenant's security deposit rights, but the rule that does the work is not in the deposit section. Kansas has no deposit-specific nonwaiver clause of the Colorado, Maryland or Massachusetts kind. What it has is one general sentence covering the whole Residential Landlord and Tenant Act: no rental agreement may provide that the tenant or the landlord agrees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under the act. The deposit section sits inside that act, so its mandatory parts are swept in. A clause shortening the return deadline, dropping the itemized written notice, raising the cap, or having the tenant give up the one-and-a-half-times penalty is unenforceable, and if you deliberately use a lease containing a provision you know is prohibited, the tenant may recover actual damages. Note what the Kansas penalty is and is not: actual damages, not Maryland's attorney's fees and not the Massachusetts forfeiture of your right to keep any part of the deposit or to counterclaim. The bar runs in both directions too, so it protects you from a clause you would later want to disown. Two parts of the Kansas deposit rule are different, because the statute itself hands them to the lease. First, the deposit may be applied at the end of the tenancy not only to accrued rent and to damage from the tenant's breach of the statutory tenant duties, but to damage from breach of the rental agreement, and the statute expressly contemplates retention for expenses, damages or other legally allowable charges under the lease, other than rent. So what you may deduct is partly a drafting question, and a charge you never put in the lease is a charge you will struggle to justify keeping. Second, the bar on a tenant using the deposit as the last month's rent applies except as otherwise provided by the rental agreement, so you may agree to let the tenant do it. If you do not, and the tenant does it anyway, the deposit is forfeited and you may recover the rent due as if it had never been applied. Those two openings are the statute's own, not waivers, and using them is not a breach of the nonwaiver rule. One more thing to watch. A signed release after a deposit dispute is not automatically safe: a court may refuse to enforce a settlement in which a party waived or agreed to forego a claim or right under the act or the lease if it was unconscionable when made.

title: No Deposit Standards Disclosure
bodyText: Kansas does not require you to post or disclose the standards you use to set deposit amounts, and does not require you to use the same standard for every tenant. There is no Kansas analogue to the South Carolina rule that catches a landlord of more than four adjoining units who sets deposits by differing standards, and no unit-count threshold of any kind in the Kansas deposit section. Three real limits still bound how you set them. First, the statutory caps apply to every tenant whatever your standard is, so a standard that produces a figure above the cap is simply unlawful. Second, fair housing law governs the difference between tenants: it is unlawful in Kansas to discriminate against any person in the terms, conditions or privileges of rental of real property because of race, religion, color, sex, disability, familial status, national origin or ancestry, and a deposit is a term of the rental. Note what is on that Kansas list and what is not. There is one narrow exemption from the Kansas act for the rental of a single family house by an owner who owns no more than three of them and rents without a broker, and for rooms or units in a building of no more than four families where the owner lives in one of them, but that exemption does not reach discriminatory advertising, and federal fair housing law has its own scope that may still reach you. Third, a court may refuse to enforce a lease provision it finds was unconscionable when made. Kansas does have one place where a deposit standard is written into statute, and it is not about disclosure. A municipal housing authority that is wholly or partly federally subsidized and sets rent solely by the tenant's income may set deposits by a schedule based on the bedroom size of the unit instead of by the ordinary caps, and if it does, it must provide a deferred payment plan letting the tenant pay the deposit in reasonable increments over time. That is a power given to housing authorities, not a duty on a private landlord. The practical course is to write your criteria down and apply them uniformly, because nothing requires you to publish them but a differing deposit you cannot explain by a written, consistently applied standard is the easiest kind of discrimination claim to bring. One local note: a 2026 state law voids any city or county ordinance that limits the amount of a security deposit, but it says nothing about an ordinance requiring you to disclose how you calculate one, so check your city or county.

title: No Security Device Rule
bodyText: Kansas has no security-device statute of any kind. It does not require you to fit a deadbolt, a keyless bolting device, a door viewer or peephole, a window latch, a sliding-door pin lock or a handle latch. It does not require a peephole in multi-unit buildings of any construction date. It does not require you to rekey or change the locks between tenancies, or on request, and it does not make the lock on the door something you must supply at all. There is no Kansas list of devices like Texas's, no inoperable-lock reporting scheme like California's, and no tenant right to have the locks changed after domestic violence. The words themselves are absent from the Kansas statute book: deadbolt, peephole, door viewer, rekey, window latch, locking device and security device each appear nowhere in it. What fills the gap is your lease and your local code. Your statutory duty is to comply with the requirements of applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, and that duty overrides your other maintenance duties where it is the greater one, so if your city or county code requires locks on exterior doors, the code requirement becomes your duty as landlord through the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. Check the code where the property is. Your separate statutory duty to exercise reasonable care in the maintenance of the common areas is the one that most plausibly reaches a broken lock on a shared building entrance, though no Kansas statute says so in terms. Note what your maintenance duty does not cover: the list of things you must keep in good and safe working order is electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning appliances, including elevators, and a lock is not among them. The contrast with life-safety hardware is instructive and worth knowing, because it shows the omission is deliberate. Kansas does legislate hardware inside dwellings, in detail, for smoke detectors: the owner supplies and installs them, and inside rental units the occupant tests and maintains them after taking possession. The Legislature simply never did the same for locks. Two practical points. Because nothing requires you to supply a lock, the lease is where the key and lock arrangement has to live, including who may rekey, who pays and what happens to a lock the tenant changes. And whatever your lock policy is, you may not use it to get possession: Kansas separately bars a landlord from recovering or taking possession other than by action, including by willfully diminishing services, and gives the tenant a direct money remedy if you do.

title: No Senior Housing Work Card
bodyText: Kansas does not require a work card, a sheriff-issued permit or a criminal background check for anyone you employ in rental housing, including housing intended and operated for people 55 and older. There is no Kansas analogue to the Nevada rule that bars employing a person who works 36 or more hours a week with access to all units in 55-and-older housing unless they hold a current sheriff-issued work card. The phrase does not appear in Kansas law at all. Kansas does recognise senior housing, but only for one purpose and with no staffing consequence. Its fair housing act's familial-status provisions do not apply to housing provided under a state or federal program specifically designed and operated to assist elderly persons, or to housing for older persons, which it defines as a community intended for and at least 80 percent occupied by at least one person 55 or older per unit while providing significant facilities and services designed to meet the physical or social needs of such persons, or a community intended for and occupied solely by persons 62 or older. Qualifying as senior housing therefore buys you an exemption from the familial-status rules; it does not attach any duty about who you may hire. Kansas does require criminal history checks in other settings, and knowing which ones shows where the line falls. Real estate licensees and appraisers are checked as part of licensure, and child care facility staff are checked under the licensing law for those facilities. Apartment maintenance and management staff are not on that list, in senior housing or anywhere else. So screening your own staff is an ordinary employment decision. Screen anyone who will hold keys to occupied units, because nothing requires it and nothing protects you if you do not. If you run the check yourself, the consumer-report rules apply to how you obtain and use it, and separately note that Kansas law lets a person whose conviction has been expunged state that they have never been convicted, with limited exceptions, so an expunged record is not something you can treat as disclosed.

title: Kansas's Military Notice Rule Is a Shortened Notice, Not a State SCRA
bodyText: Kansas has no state Servicemembers Civil Relief Act and no state lease-termination right for servicemembers. What it has is narrower and easy to misread: a shortened notice period for ending a periodic tenancy. Under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, either side may end a month-to-month tenancy by written notice effective on a rent-paying date at least 30 days after the other side receives it, except that no more than 15 days' written notice by a tenant is needed where the tenant is in the military service of the United States and termination is necessitated by military orders. The same 15-day rule appears again in Kansas's older general landlord-tenant sections, for a tenancy at will or a tenancy from one period to another of three months or less. Read the limits carefully. It runs one way only, so it is a right the tenant has and not a shortcut for you. It applies to periodic tenancies, so it does nothing for a fixed-term lease. It requires military orders that necessitate the termination, not merely military service. And it says military service of the United States, so a National Guard member on state active duty is outside it unless federalized. Kansas has not extended servicemember protections to the Guard on state orders the way some states have, and its militia and veterans chapter, which runs to licensure, insurance, benefits and military justice, contains no landlord-tenant provision at all. For anything beyond the shortened notice, the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act is the authority, and it is where a fixed-term lease termination, the stay of proceedings and the protection against default judgment come from. Kansas does acknowledge it in one procedural place worth knowing if you are in court: written contact with the court by a servicemember defendant, or by an attorney for the defendant, invoking protection under the federal Act is not an entry of appearance. So a letter asserting those rights in your eviction case does not amount to the tenant appearing. Three further things Kansas does not do. There is no rule requiring a servicemember's rental application to be decided within any number of days. There is no eviction stay keyed to a rent ceiling. There is no Kansas bar on contacting a tenant's military unit or chain of command about unpaid rent, as California has, though doing so invites a federal problem. And military status is not one of Kansas's housing protected classes, which are race, religion, color, sex, disability, familial status, national origin and ancestry, so a Kansas state-law discrimination claim on that ground does not exist.

title: No Sex Offender Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Kansas does not require a lease to carry a sex offender registry notice and does not require you to tell a tenant or applicant about a registered offender in the building or nearby.
