There is no Kansas analogue to the California registry-notice paragraph, and the Kansas Offender Registration Act puts its duties on offenders and on registering law enforcement agencies, not on landlords. Kansas also has no rule the other way: nothing bars you from looking at the public registry or from considering what you find, as California does for its Megan's Law data. One qualification that is not about you renting your own place. Where a real estate licensee is in fact acting as the landlord's agent in the transaction, that licensee owes a duty to disclose to a customer, and a tenant counts as a customer, all adverse material facts actually known about the property. But read the list the statute gives: environmental hazards required by law to be disclosed, the physical condition of the property, material defects in the property, material defects in title, and any material limitation on the client's ability to perform the contract. Those are facts about the property, not about who lives in the neighbourhood, and the Kansas Attorney General has read the duty exactly that way. Note also that Kansas has no property-manager licence: its real estate licensing act defines a lease, for its own purposes, as a rent or lease for nonresidential use, and exempts a person acting with reference to their own property. So an ordinary Kansas landlord renting their own property is not a licensee and owes no such duty at all. Two practical points. The registry is public, so a tenant can check it as easily as you can, and pointing them to it is the safe response to a question rather than making a representation of your own. And if you do say something, say it accurately: a false statement about the premises or a half-answer that misleads can expose you under Kansas's consumer protection act even though no statute required you to speak in the first place. One local note: Kansas bars a city or county from requiring you to hand over a list of your tenants' names, except where that is necessary to comply with the Kansas Offender Registration Act, and except for 30 days after a citation for a public health, safety or welfare violation on the property.

title: Offender Residency Restrictions Are Preempted, and the Occupancy Decision Is Yours
bodyText: Kansas has taken offender residency restrictions away from local government. Since 1 June 2006, cities and counties have been prohibited from adopting or enforcing any ordinance, resolution or regulation establishing residential restrictions for offenders as the Kansas Offender Registration Act defines them. So there is no Kansas proximity rule you have to apply, no distance from a school, park, playground or child care centre that disqualifies your property, and no city that may impose one on you. That is a positive statement of Kansas law, not a gap. The prohibition has one exception, and it is about institutions rather than ordinary rentals. A city or county may still run a residential licensing or zoning program for correctional placement residences that includes regulations for housing offenders. A correctional placement residence is a facility providing residential services to people placed there instead of or before prison, on conditional release before a hearing, under a sentence of confinement of not more than a year, in a privately operated facility housing parolees, on a deferred sentence in a community corrections facility, or under court-ordered or voluntary alcohol or drug treatment. The statute says expressly that it does not include a single or multi-family dwelling or a commercial residential building that houses staff and people other than those. So an ordinary rental is not a correctional placement residence and the exception does not reach it. Kansas also does not make it a crime or a civil offence to lease to a registered offender, and it does not punish knowingly letting two registered offenders live in the same dwelling, as a Birmingham ordinance does under Alabama law. There is no Kansas lease-statement safe harbour to collect, because there is no Kansas offence to be safe from. Nothing in the preemption statute restricts your own tenancy decisions. You may ask, you may check the public registry and you may decline an applicant on that basis, because criminal history is not a protected characteristic under Kansas's fair housing classes, which are race, religion, color, sex, disability, familial status, national origin and ancestry. A 2026 state law reinforces the point from the other direction by voiding any city or county ordinance that restricts your ability to use, consider or request criminal history when applying your customarily applied criteria. Apply your criteria consistently and in writing, and keep federal fair housing guidance on blanket criminal-history exclusions in mind, because that is a federal question.

title: No Single-Family Occupancy Notice and No First-Page or Relative-Font Rule
bodyText: Kansas requires no single-family-residence occupancy notice in a lease. There is no Kansas analogue to the Nevada rule that makes a landlord of a single-family residence put a notice about unlawful-occupancy presumptions at the top of the first page in a font at least twice the size of any other font in the lease. Kansas has neither half of that rule: no occupancy-presumption notice, and no placement or relative-font requirement anywhere in its landlord-tenant law. Nothing in Kansas law tells you what must appear on a lease's first page, and nothing measures one part of a lease against the size of another. Kansas does define a single family residence, but only to work its own machinery, not to trigger a disclosure. It means a structure maintained and used as a single dwelling unit, and a unit that shares one or more walls with another still counts if it has direct access to a street or thoroughfare and shares no heating facilities, hot water equipment or any other essential facility or service with another unit. That definition matters because the rule letting you agree that the tenant will do specified repairs, maintenance, alterations or remodelling is available for any dwelling unit other than a single family residence, so a single-family rental is outside it. It does not require you to say anything. Kansas does have things to say about unauthorised occupants, and the point worth taking is that it never asks you to warn the tenant about them in the lease. A person who enters and remains in a dwelling unit without a rental agreement and without your knowledge, knowing they are not authorised, is outside the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act once you have personally told them to leave, and may be prosecuted for criminal trespass. A 2026 act adds an affidavit route for removing a squatter by law enforcement rather than by eviction, and excludes squatter occupancy from the act. None of that is a disclosure duty. One Kansas type-size rule does exist in landlord-tenant law and it is not about the lease: a document you give the tenant that would serve as their written notice of intent to vacate, if it carries terms not in the lease, must bear a set warning in at least ten-point boldface type, or the added terms do not bind the tenant. Put your occupancy terms in the lease because they are worth having, not because Kansas makes you, and set them out plainly.

title: No Shoreline Access Disclosure
bodyText: Kansas has no statute requiring a lease of waterfront property to carry a notice about public access along the shore, and no public shoreline access right for such a notice to describe. The word shoreline does not appear in Kansas's statutes at all. Kansas is landlocked, so there is no tidal shore and no public trust right of passage of the kind Rhode Island now makes landlords disclose. Nothing requires you to tell a tenant about public access to a lake, reservoir or river, about an easement across the property, about riparian rights, or about how far public use may extend. Two related things are worth knowing if your rental fronts water. First, Kansas's general water law and its state park, lake and reservoir rules sit outside landlord-tenant law and outside this answer; a federal reservoir shoreline is governed by the federal agency that manages it, and if your property adjoins one, the access question is decided by that agency's rules and not by your lease. Second, Kansas does have a recreational use statute that works in your favour and in your tenant's. It exists to encourage owners to make land and water areas available to the public for recreation by limiting their liability. An owner who makes all or any part of the land available to the public for recreational purposes owes no duty of care to keep that part safe for entry or use for recreation, and no duty to warn of a dangerous condition, use, structure or activity. Recreational purposes expressly include swimming, boating, fishing, water skiing, hunting, camping, picnicking and hiking. Owner is defined broadly enough to include a tenant, lessee or occupant, so a tenant who opens the water to others is covered as well as you. And an owner who does take steps to make the premises safe or to warn people is not deprived of the protection. The protection has limits set out in the act, and it does not apply where an admission price or fee is asked in return for permission to enter. So the sensible lease provision for a waterfront rental is not a disclosure Kansas requires but a term you write: say plainly who may use the water and the bank, whether guests may, whether swimming or boating is permitted, who is responsible for a dock or boat, and that the tenant is not to charge anyone for access.

title: Shorter Notice for Showings: Specify It, You Cannot Waive It
bodyText:
Kansas has no procedure letting a tenant waive or shorten the entry notice for showings, and no separate-signed-document route like Delaware's. Nothing in Kansas law mentions a signed addendum or a separate written instrument for this or any other tenancy purpose.

But Kansas is not a state where there is nothing to waive either, so do not treat it as one. Showing the property is one of the purposes the entry statute expressly covers: the landlord has the right to enter at reasonable hours, after reasonable notice, to exhibit the dwelling unit to prospective or actual purchasers, mortgagees, tenants, workmen or contractors. The notice obligation is a standard rather than a clock, and that standard is a right under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. No rental agreement may provide that the tenant agrees to waive or forego rights or remedies under the act, and a provision that does is unenforceable.

So the distinction that matters in Kansas is between specifying and waiving. A lease term saying that during the last stretch of the term, or after either side gives notice of termination, showings may be made on a stated shorter notice within stated hours is a specification of what reasonable notice means for that purpose, and that is a sensible thing to put in the lease. A term saying the tenant gives up the right to reasonable notice, or that any notice at all is unnecessary, is a waiver, and it will not hold. Keep the shorter notice short of nothing, keep it tied to the end of the tenancy and to daytime hours, and keep it in the lease rather than extracted later.

Two other Kansas points shape how this plays out. Kansas has no duty on the tenant not to unreasonably withhold consent to entry; that phrase appears nowhere in Kansas law. What Kansas gives you instead is a remedy you have to go and get, and separately a penalty on you for over-using the right: a lawful entry made in an unreasonable manner, and repeated demands for entry that are otherwise lawful but have the effect of unreasonably harassing the tenant, are both violations. A showing schedule that is lawful entry by entry can still be the violation if the pattern is harassing.

title: Government Shutdowns and Rent
bodyText: Kansas has no law delaying rent or eviction for a tenant affected by a federal, state or tribal government shutdown. There is no Kansas analogue to Nevada's rule making a rent-due date unenforceable against a shutdown-affected government worker, no extra time to pay, no defence to a nonpayment eviction, no bar on late fees, and no proof-of-status procedure for a tenant to invoke. Kansas is not silent on federal shutdowns in general. It legislated about one, once, and for a different purpose: because the 2013 federal shutdown delayed death gratuity payments to the survivors of more than twenty-five service members, Kansas now has the adjutant general pay the death gratuity for an eligible Kansas military service member killed while a federal shutdown is in progress, with reimbursement once the federal government reopens. That is the whole of Kansas's shutdown law, and it has nothing to do with rent. So the ordinary rules apply without modification. Rent is payable at the time and place agreed, without demand or notice. If rent is unpaid when due, you may terminate if the tenant does not pay within three days after your written notice of the nonpayment and of your intention to terminate, counted as three consecutive twenty-four-hour periods from delivery or posting, with two extra days if you serve the notice by mail. Nothing in that machinery bends for a furloughed tenant. What you do have is discretion, and it is worth using. A written payment plan or a short written extension of the due date for a tenant whose pay has stopped costs far less than an eviction, and Kansas's three-day notice remains available if the plan fails. If you do agree to wait, put it in writing and say what it does not do, because accepting rent late without reserving your position can undercut a termination you later rely on. And if a case is filed, note that Kansas eviction procedure now has two court-side pressure valves that did not exist before 2026: the court is to consider mediation in an action on a residential tenancy unless mediation would not materially aid the parties or is impracticable, and where the parties are participating in mediation the court is to order a continuance of not more than fourteen days from the mediation order.

title: No Owner-Occupancy Rental Limit, and Kansas Is Moving the Other Way
bodyText: Kansas has no law limiting the rental of a home in a single-family zone to an owner who lives on the lot. There is no Kansas analogue to the Kentucky rule that bars leasing a single-family home in a traditional single-family zone unless the owner primarily lives in one of the homes on the lot, and no Kansas statute ties your right to rent to where you live. The phrase single-family zone does not appear in the Kansas statutes at all. Kansas law in 2026 ran firmly the other way, which is worth knowing because it is the opposite of an owner-occupancy limit. A new act requires that proposed housing developments meeting its definition, including single-family homes, townhouses and accessory dwelling units, be approved as a matter of right without discretionary review by a planning commission or zoning board, with the application deemed approved if it is not denied within 30 days, or 60 days where a subdivision plat is needed, or 90 days for a plat of more than 40 single-family homes. The same act goes further and provides that, notwithstanding any law to the contrary, all land within a city's corporate limits that is zoned for any type of residential use is to be considered zoned for single-family residential use in addition to whatever other zoning the city has adopted, leaving the city only reasonable setback, development, performance, utility, subdivision, street-connection, grading and platting regulations. It also takes an owner-initiated rezoning to a single-family residential district outside the protest-petition process. None of that creates a right to rent, and none of it restricts one. Zoning in Kansas is still a delegated local power. Cities and counties zone under state enabling legislation that protects the public health, safety and welfare and that expressly does not prevent additional local laws on the same subject so long as they do not conflict with the act, and the list of things a zoning ordinance may do is open-ended. So the practical risk is local, not state. Two local devices to watch, because Kansas does not preempt either: how your city defines a family or caps unrelated occupants in a dwelling, and any owner-occupancy condition a city attaches to an accessory dwelling unit. Check the code where the property sits before you assume you may rent the whole house to unrelated tenants. Note too that occupancy limits sit outside Kansas fair housing law, which does not limit the applicability of reasonable local, state or federal restrictions on the maximum number of occupants permitted in a dwelling.

title: No Smart-Access Law, but the Privacy Crime Is Real
bodyText: Kansas has no statute regulating smart locks, keypads, key fobs, biometric readers or app-based entry in rentals. There is no Kansas analogue to Washington's coming rules, so no tenant right to demand an alternative key that uses no biometrics and no phone app, no duty to publish or hand over a written privacy policy, no limits on what access data you may collect or how long you may keep it, and no rule about who may see the entry log. Kansas also has no biometric privacy act of its own. So the technology is a lease question, and the lease is where to settle who holds codes, who may add or remove a user, what happens to a tenant's app access at the end of the term, and who pays for a lost fob. Two things are not lease questions, and both matter more than the absence of a smart-lock statute. First, an access log is not notice. Whatever the lock, your right to enter still depends on reasonable notice at reasonable hours for a permitted purpose, and you may not abuse the right of access or use it to harass the tenant. Being able to unlock a door remotely changes nothing about when you may. Entry without the tenant's consent is permitted only in case of an extreme hazard involving the potential loss of life or severe property damage, and a remote-unlock capability is not an emergency exception. Second, monitoring inside the unit can be a crime, not merely a breach of the lease. Kansas's breach-of-privacy offence reaches entering with intent to listen surreptitiously to private conversations in a private place, or to observe the personal conduct of a person entitled to privacy there, and separately reaches installing or using, outside or inside a private place, any device for hearing, recording, amplifying or broadcasting sounds originating in that place that would not ordinarily be audible without it, in each case without the consent of the person entitled to privacy. A private place is one where a person may reasonably expect to be safe from uninvited intrusion or surveillance, which a rented home plainly is. Those offences are class A nonperson misdemeanors. Note the asymmetry: the audio limb is broad, while the separate camera limb is narrow and aimed at filming a person nude, in a state of undress or under their clothing, which is a felony. So a camera or an audio-capable doorbell or smart speaker pointed into a tenant's living space is a risk you should simply not take. Get written consent for anything that records inside the unit, keep cameras outside and pointed away from windows and doors, and do not use a smart access system as a monitoring tool.

title: Kansas Bans Smoking in Your Enclosed Common Areas and Makes You Post Signs
bodyText:
Kansas has no statute about tobacco smoke drifting between units, and a lease clause making the tenant waive drift claims against you will not hold here. But Kansas does have real smoking law for a multi-unit building, and it puts two affirmative duties on you that are easy to miss.

The Kansas Indoor Clean Air Act makes it unlawful, with no requirement of a culpable mental state, to smoke in an enclosed area including restrooms, lobbies, hallways and other common areas in public and private buildings, condominiums and other multiple-residential facilities. The ban also reaches access points, meaning the area within a ten-foot radius outside any doorway, open window or air intake of a covered building, so smoking just outside your front door or under a window is unlawful even though it is outdoors. Enclosed area has a technical meaning: space between a floor and ceiling enclosed on all sides by solid walls, windows or doorways running floor to ceiling, which leaves a genuinely open breezeway outside the ban while an interior hallway or stairwell is squarely inside it. Private homes and residences are exempt, so the inside of a tenant's unit is not covered, with one exception: a residence used as a day care home.

Then comes the duty nobody expects. The proprietor or other person in charge of the premises of a public place, or any other area where smoking is prohibited, must post or cause to be posted in a conspicuous place signs displaying the international no smoking symbol and clearly stating that smoking is prohibited by state law. Your enclosed common areas are an area where smoking is prohibited, so the signs go up, and posting them is your job as the person in charge.

There is a second duty if you have staff. An employer is anyone who employs one or more individuals, and a place of employment includes stairwells and hallways under the employer's control that employees use in the course of employment. So if a maintenance or management employee works in your enclosed common areas, those areas are a place of employment, smoking there is separately unlawful, and you must provide a smoke-free workplace and adopt and maintain a written smoking policy prohibiting smoking without exception in all areas of the place of employment, communicate it to current employees within one week of adopting it and to new employees on hiring, and give a written copy to any current or prospective employee who asks.

Know the gaps, because they are where your lease has to do the work. Smoking under this Act means possession of a lighted cigarette, cigar, pipe or burning tobacco in another form or a device designed for tobacco. Vaping and electronic cigarettes are outside it, and so is cannabis. Nothing in the Act reaches inside a tenant's unit, and nothing in it gives a tenant a remedy against you for a neighbour's smoke. That is why a smoke-free-building rule belongs in every lease, covering vaping and cannabis as well as tobacco, rather than being left to the statute.

Finally, do not copy a smoke-drift waiver from another state. Kansas forbids a rental agreement in which either party agrees to the exculpation or limitation of any liability arising under law, or to indemnify the other for it, and the only exception is a clause limiting your liability for fire, theft or breakage with respect to common areas. Smoke drift is none of those three, so the waiver is unenforceable, and if you deliberately use a lease containing a provision you know is prohibited the tenant may recover actual damages. Disclose the risk instead of trying to waive it, and remember that your duty to exercise reasonable care in maintaining the common areas does not disappear because the Act is a criminal statute.

One local point: a Kansas city may regulate smoking more strictly than the state does, so check the city's ordinance.

title: No Late-Benefit Eviction Defense or Continuance
bodyText: Kansas gives a tenant no special defense, continuance or reinstatement right when rent is late because a Social Security, SSI, public assistance or housing voucher payment was delayed or interrupted through no fault of the tenant. The ordinary nonpayment rules apply: the three-day notice to pay or vacate, and then the eviction action. In an eviction trial a Kansas court may not grant the tenant a continuance at all unless the tenant files a bond with security approved by the court, conditioned on payment of all damages and rent that may accrue if judgment goes against the tenant. The one new exception is mediation: in an eviction on a residential rental agreement the court must consider mediation unless it would not materially aid the parties or is impracticable, and if the parties are participating in mediation the court must order a continuance of not more than 14 days from the date of the mediation order. Nothing in that depends on why the rent was late. Separately, and only after judgment, Kansas exemption law limits what a landlord can actually collect: federal pension money received within the three months before an execution, attachment or garnishment is released on the tenant's affidavit that it is needed for support, and wage garnishment is capped. Landlord may of course agree in writing to wait for a delayed benefit payment, but is not obliged to.

title: No Special District Statement Required in a Kansas Lease
bodyText: No Kansas statute requires a residential lease to state that the property sits inside a special district, or to have the tenant acknowledge district charges, rules or plans. Kansas has many such districts - general improvement districts, community improvement districts, business improvement districts, self-supported municipal improvement districts, transportation development districts, tax increment financing districts and benefit districts - but every one of them reaches the property owner, not the tenant. A special assessment is levied as a special tax on the land, collected with the general property taxes, and paid by the owner of the assessed parcel. A community improvement district sales tax is a retailers' sales tax on taxable retail sales inside the district; it does not attach to residential rent. Landlord may include a statement identifying the district and disclaiming responsibility for district actions, but it is a contract term, not a required disclosure, and Landlord should not word it so that Tenant appears to take on an assessment the statute places on the owner. If Landlord wants to pass a district assessment through to Tenant, the lease must say so plainly - nothing in Kansas law does it automatically.

title: No Sprinkler Disclosure Duty in Kansas
bodyText: Kansas has no sprinkler-disclosure statute. Nothing requires a Kansas residential lease to state whether the building has a maintained and operative sprinkler system, to say when it was last inspected, or to post a warning sign because a building has none. The New York lease notice and the Maryland high-rise lease notice and entrance sign have no Kansas counterpart. Kansas legislated about sprinklers in one direction only, and it points at local government rather than at landlords: no city or county may adopt or enforce any ordinance, order, code, standard or rule requiring a multi-purpose residential fire protection sprinkler system or any other fire sprinkler protection system in a residential structure, or require one as a condition of a building permit or plat. That ban is narrower than it sounds. A residential structure for this purpose means a single-family dwelling, a multi-family dwelling of two attached living units or less, or a manufactured home, so a triplex, a fourplex and an apartment building fall outside the preemption and may be reached by a local requirement. Anyone may install sprinklers voluntarily, and the statute says so expressly. Practical course: a statement of whether the building has a sprinkler system is optional in Kansas, but if Landlord makes one it must be accurate, because a false statement about a fire-safety feature is a misrepresentation a tenant can act on. Do not represent that a building is sprinklered when it is not, and do not imply a system is inspected or monitored unless it is.

title: Leases Longer Than One Year Must Be in Writing
bodyText: Kansas has a statute of frauds, and it reaches leases. No lease, estate or interest in land exceeding one year in duration may be granted or assigned except by deed or note in writing, signed by the party granting or assigning it or by an agent whose authority is itself in writing, or by act and operation of law. A separate provision adds that any agreement not to be performed within one year of the making, and any contract for the sale of land or an interest in it, is unenforceable unless the agreement or a memorandum of it is in writing and signed by the party to be charged, or by a person that party authorized in writing. Two practical consequences. First, an agent signing a lease of more than one year for an owner needs written authority, not just the owner's say-so, and so does anyone assigning such a lease. Second, a lease over a year that is not in a signed writing does not create the term the parties intended. A person in possession of real property with the owner's assent is presumed to be a tenant at will, and in a residential tenancy the Kansas Residential Landlord and Tenant Act then supplies the term: unless the rental agreement fixes a definite term, the tenancy is week-to-week for a roomer paying weekly rent and month-to-month in every other case, and rent is the fair rental value if nothing was agreed. A month-to-month tenancy is terminated by written notice stating the tenancy ends on a rent-paying date at least 30 days after the notice is received; a week-to-week tenancy takes seven days' written notice. A tenant who holds over at the end of a lease of a year or more with the landlord's assent becomes a tenant from year to year. Kansas has no recording requirement that makes a long lease void, and no notarial acknowledgment requirement for a lease to be valid between the parties. Practical course: put every lease of more than one year in writing and have it signed by the party to be bound; if an agent signs for the owner, get the agent's authority in writing too; and do not rely on an oral renewal or extension that pushes the total term past a year.

title: Kansas's Money Limits at a Glance
bodyText: These are the money limits Kansas sets for a residential tenancy, whatever the lease says. Security deposit: no more than one month's periodic rent for an unfurnished unit; up to 1.5 months' rent if the tenant uses Landlord's furniture; plus up to another half-month's rent if pets are permitted - so a furnished, pet-friendly unit tops out at two months. A municipal housing authority that is federally subsidized with income-based rent may instead use a bedroom-size schedule and must offer a deferred payment plan. Deposit penalty against Landlord: the withheld portion plus damages equal to 1.5 times the amount wrongfully withheld. Holdover damages: if the tenant's holdover is willful and not in good faith, not more than 1.5 months' periodic rent or 1.5 times actual damages, whichever is greater. Failure to deliver possession, if willful and not in good faith: the same 1.5 months' rent or 1.5 times actual damages formula, and it runs against either party. Unlawful lockout or cutting off essential services: not more than 1.5 months' periodic rent or the tenant's actual damages, whichever is greater. Prohibited lease terms: if Landlord deliberately uses a lease containing a term Landlord knows the statute forbids, the tenant recovers actual damages - there is no multiplier and no fixed penalty. Bounced rent check: the service charge may not exceed $30, and the statutory claim is the check amount plus costs, the service charge, interest, collection costs and the greater of treble damages capped at the check amount plus $500, or $100. Court-level caps that decide where a claim can be filed: a small claim is one of $10,000 or less, and the limited actions code may be used for an unsecured contract debt without limit but for a secured contract debt or a non-contract claim only up to $25,000. What Kansas does not cap: there is no late-fee cap, no application-fee cap, no cap on a pet fee as distinct from the pet deposit, no interest requirement on a deposit, and no general cap on what Landlord may recover for actual damage to the unit. A city or county may not fill those gaps with a local ordinance limiting the amount of a security deposit. One caution outside the lease: Kansas's statute capping noneconomic damages in personal injury actions is still printed in the statute book, but the Kansas Supreme Court has held it unconstitutional, so do not rely on it as a ceiling on an injury claim by a tenant or guest.

title: No Radiator Cover Requirement in Kansas
bodyText: Kansas has nothing on steam radiator covers. No statute requires Landlord to install an insulating cover on a steam radiator when a tenant asks, and none requires a radiator-cover rider on the lease, an annual written notice or a posted notice in the common area. The New Jersey scheme has no Kansas counterpart. What Kansas does require is the general duty: Landlord must maintain in good and safe working order and condition all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning appliances supplied or required to be supplied by Landlord, and must comply with applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety. A radiator that leaks steam, will not shut off, or is broken is a heating appliance out of good and safe working order, so that duty reaches it; whether a working but uncovered radiator must be covered is a building and housing code question, not a statutory one. Practical course: in a unit with uncovered steam radiators, especially one rented to a household with young children, fit covers anyway and say in the lease or the move-in condition record that they are there and must not be removed. Kansas law does not oblige Landlord to do it, but the cost is small against a scald injury, and the health-and-safety code limb of Landlord's duty is where such an injury would be argued.

title: Stigmatized Property: No Kansas Rule, and the One Duty That Can Still Apply
bodyText: Kansas has no psychologically-impacted-property or stigmatized-property statute. There is no Kansas rule requiring Landlord to tell a prospective tenant that a death, suicide, homicide or other felony occurred at the property, that a former occupant had a serious or communicable illness, or that a registered sex offender lives at or near the property - and equally no Kansas safe harbour saying those facts need not be disclosed, no three-year death window, and no immunity statute of the Arizona kind. There is also no Kansas duty to answer truthfully if the tenant asks; that is left to the general law against fraud and misrepresentation. One duty does cut across this, and it must be stated precisely. If a licensed real estate broker or salesperson is acting in the transaction, that licensee must disclose to a customer all adverse material facts actually known to the licensee, including the physical condition of the property and any material defects in it, and a tenant counts as a customer. The Attorney General has read that duty as reaching adverse information about the premises known to the broker, but not information about who resides in the area - so not neighbourhood sex-offender information. Two limits make this narrow for most landlords. The duty belongs to the licensee, not to Landlord, and Kansas has no property-manager licence: the licensing act defines lease as renting for nonresidential use, and it exempts a person acting with reference to that person's own property. So an ordinary Kansas landlord renting out their own place is not a licensee and owes no such duty. Practical course: say nothing voluntarily that Kansas does not require, never answer a direct question falsely, and if a licensee is involved in the letting, expect the licensee's own disclosure duty to apply to adverse material facts about the property itself.

title: No Duty to Supply a Stove or Refrigerator
bodyText:
Kansas does not require Landlord to supply a stove or a refrigerator. There is no Kansas habitability provision of the California kind making a working stove and refrigerator part of what Landlord must provide. Kansas mentions them in one place only, and for a different purpose: the Act defines a major kitchen facility as a refrigerator, stove and sink, and uses that definition to decide who is a roomer - a person occupying a dwelling unit that lacks a major bathroom and kitchen facility, in a structure where one or more major facilities are shared with other units.

That classification matters because a roomer who pays weekly rent has a week-to-week tenancy terminable on seven days' written notice, rather than the month-to-month tenancy and 30-day notice that apply in every other case. So a unit with no kitchen of its own may put the occupant in the roomer category, with a shorter notice period, rather than creating any duty to install appliances.

What Kansas does require is maintenance of what Landlord actually supplies: Landlord must maintain in good and safe working order and condition all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning appliances, including elevators, supplied or required to be supplied by Landlord.

Read that list carefully. It is written by category of system, and it does not say "and other appliances", so whether a supplied refrigerator or kitchen range falls inside it is not spelled out - an electric refrigerator or range is naturally an electrical appliance, while a gas range is not obviously on the list at all. Treat the duty as applying and keep supplied kitchen appliances working.

Separately, the tenant's own duty is broader on its face: the tenant must use in a reasonable manner all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances in the premises.

Practical course: list exactly which appliances are included and whether Landlord maintains them, and if an appliance is at the property but not supplied by Landlord, say so in writing on the move-in record rather than leaving it to be argued later.

title: Renting to Students in Kansas
bodyText: Kansas has no student-housing regime. There is no licence to rent to students, no required student-housing certification clause in the lease, no inspection scheme and no special rent, deposit or termination rule for a student tenant. A college student renting a private house or apartment in Kansas is an ordinary tenant and the Kansas Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies in full. Three boundaries are worth knowing, because each takes a letting outside the Act rather than creating a student rule. First, residence at an institution, public or private, is outside the Act if it is incidental to the provision of educational services - that is what puts a university's own residence hall outside the Act. Second, occupancy by a member of a fraternal or social organization in the portion of a structure operated for the benefit of the organization is outside the Act, which is the fraternity and sorority house exclusion. Third, transient occupancy in a hotel, motel or rooming house is outside the Act. All three are prefaced "Unless created to avoid the application of this act", so a private landlord cannot dress an ordinary student letting up as one of them. One classification does bite on an ordinary student rental: a person occupying a dwelling unit that lacks a major bathroom and kitchen facility, in a structure where one or more major facilities are shared with other units, is a roomer, and a roomer who pays weekly rent has a week-to-week tenancy ending on seven days' written notice instead of the usual 30. Practical course: use the ordinary lease. Where several students share, name every occupant and make all signers jointly and severally liable, because Kansas supplies no student-specific default on who owes the rent. Age is not an obstacle - a Kansas tenant reaches majority at 18 - and whether a city may limit the number of unrelated people in a dwelling in a single-family zone is a local question.

title: Subsidy Inspections and Refusing a Voucher Tenancy
bodyText: Kansas has no statute about a subsidy-program inspection, in either direction. There is no Kansas rule requiring Landlord to accept a housing-authority inspection, no special eviction procedure for a subsidized tenant who refuses one, and no Kansas source-of-income protection that would make declining a voucher tenancy unlawful. Kansas law goes the other way on the second point: no city or county may adopt or enforce an ordinance or resolution prohibiting landlords from refusing to lease privately owned single-family, multi-unit residential or commercial property to a person because that person's source of income to pay rent consists, in whole or in part, of a payment from or through the housing choice voucher program or any successor program, or any other housing assistance program in which landlord participation is voluntary - and any such ordinance adopted before 1 July 2026 is null and void. So a Kansas landlord may decline to participate in a voluntary assistance program, including because of the inspection it would bring, and no Kansas city can forbid it. Note the limits: that statute binds cities and counties only, it creates no duty on Landlord, and its voucher limb reaches programs in which landlord participation is voluntary. It does not touch what a program requires of a landlord who has already signed up - once Landlord signs a housing assistance payments contract, the program's own inspection terms and federal rules govern, and Kansas law does not override them. If a tenant refuses access, Kansas uses one ordinary rule for every tenancy: Landlord may enter at reasonable hours after reasonable notice to inspect, repair or show the unit, and may enter without consent only in an extreme hazard involving potential loss of life or severe property damage. If the tenant refuses lawful access, Landlord may obtain injunctive relief to compel access or terminate the rental agreement, and in either case recover actual damages. There is no two-refusals-in-30-days trigger and no expedited subsidized-housing track.

title: No Subsidy Proration Rule
bodyText: Kansas has no special rule for prorating rent when a housing subsidy pays part of the rent and part of the unit becomes unusable. One general rule covers every tenancy, subsidized or not: where fire or casualty damages the property enough to substantially impair its use and habitability and continued occupancy is lawful, the tenant may vacate the unusable part, and in that case the tenant's liability for rent is reduced in proportion to the diminution in the fair rental value of the dwelling unit. Rent is accounted for as of the date of vacating. Kansas does not say whether that proportional reduction is measured against the full contract rent, including the part a subsidy pays, or only against the tenant's own share - the statute speaks of the tenant's liability for rent and of the unit's fair rental value, and no Kansas statute resolves the gap. Colorado answers it by statute; Kansas does not. The cautious course is to treat the reduction as a proportion of the unit's whole fair rental value and to apply it to the tenant's share in the same proportion, so the tenant gets the benefit of the reduction on the part of the rent the tenant actually pays, and to notify the housing authority at once rather than adjusting the subsidy portion unilaterally. If the property is under a housing assistance payments contract, that contract and the program's own rules govern what happens to the subsidy payment when a unit fails inspection or becomes partly unusable, and Kansas law does not override them. Note too that the Kansas casualty right has no tenant-fault exception, so it is available even where the tenant caused the damage, and it cannot be taken away by the lease.

title: No Subsidy Late-Fee Rule
bodyText: Kansas has no rule about late fees on the part of the rent a housing subsidy pays. There is no Kansas ban of the Colorado kind on charging a late fee for the subsidy-paid portion, no cap measured on the tenant's own share as in Connecticut, and in fact no late-fee cap for a residential tenancy at all. The late fee is whatever the lease says, subject only to the court's power to refuse to enforce an unconscionable provision, to enforce the remainder without it, or to limit its application to avoid an unconscionable result. Nor may a city or county fill the gap in one related respect: no city or county may adopt or enforce an ordinance prohibiting Landlord from refusing to lease to a person because that person's source of income to pay rent is in whole or part a housing choice voucher or any other housing assistance program in which landlord participation is voluntary, and any such ordinance adopted before 1 July 2026 is void. That statute binds cities and counties only; it creates no landlord duty, and it says nothing about late fees. The practical risk runs the other way. A tenant whose own share arrived on time has not failed to pay anything, and charging that tenant a late fee because a housing authority's payment was slow invites an unconscionability challenge and, if the amount is pressed, an argument that the fee is a penalty. The safe course is to write the lease so that the late fee attaches only to Tenant's own share of the rent, to say so expressly, and never to charge a fee for a delay in a payment Tenant does not control. Watch one more trap: accepting late rent without reservation waives the right to terminate for that breach, so reserve rights in writing when accepting a late payment. If the property is under a housing assistance payments contract, that contract and the program's rules govern fees on the subsidy portion, and Kansas law does not override them.

title: Code Repair Orders, and No Receivership for an Occupied Rental
bodyText: Kansas has no housing receivership for an occupied substandard rental. No city, county, tenant or neighbourhood group can have a receiver appointed to collect the rents and fix up a building a landlord is neglecting. What Kansas gives a city instead is a condemnation and repair-or-demolish power, and it is worth knowing how it runs. When the enforcing officer files a written statement that a structure is unsafe or dangerous, or is abandoned property, the governing body must by resolution fix a time and place at which the owner, the owner's agent, any lienholders of record and any occupant of the structure may appear and show cause why it should not be condemned and ordered repaired or demolished. Notice is published once a week for two consecutive weeks, at least 30 days must pass between the last publication and the hearing, and a copy goes by certified mail to each owner, agent, lienholder and occupant, marked deliver to addressee only. Note that the tenant is notified directly and may appear - Landlord should expect an occupied building's tenants to learn of the proceeding from the city, not from Landlord. After the hearing, if the structure is unsafe or dangerous the resolution must direct it to be repaired or removed and the premises made safe and secure, and must fix a reasonable time to begin. If Landlord does not begin in time or does not prosecute the work diligently, the city may raze and remove the structure itself, sell the salvage, and recover the balance of its cost either as a debt or as a special assessment certified onto the county tax rolls against the parcel. That is a lien on the property, so it follows ownership. A separate route exists for abandoned property only - residential real estate with two years of delinquent taxes that has been continuously unoccupied by anyone legally in possession for 90 days. A nonprofit housing organization may petition the district court for temporary possession to rehabilitate and then lease it; the owner may defeat the petition by filing a rehabilitation plan and bringing the property into code compliance and the taxes current within 90 days, extendable once. Because the definition requires the property to be unoccupied, that route cannot reach a tenanted building. Local code enforcement is where this actually happens, and it is a local question. Practical course: respond to a condemnation notice at once and start the ordered work inside the stated time, because the city's alternative is demolition at Landlord's cost secured against the land.

title: Passing On Property Tax Increases
bodyText:
Kansas has no statute about passing a property tax increase on to a residential tenant. Nothing permits it expressly and nothing forbids it, and Kansas sets none of the content requirements other states impose: no requirement that the clause state the tenant's exact share, no requirement to refund a proportionate part of any abatement, and no deposit-deduction rule that makes the right depend on the lease invoking it.

The general rule is the one the Act states: Landlord and Tenant may include in the rental agreement terms and conditions not prohibited by the Act or other rule of law, including rent, the term of the agreement and other provisions governing the parties' rights and obligations. A tax pass-through is not on the Act's list of prohibited terms, which covers only waiver of rights under the Act, confession of judgment, either party's attorney's fees, and exculpation or indemnity.

Two Kansas points shape how such a clause should be written. First, rent in Kansas means all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement other than the security deposit, so a tax share is rent - which means it is reached by the three-day notice for nonpayment of rent, and it counts in the periodic rent the deposit cap is measured against.

Second, a court may refuse to enforce a rental agreement provision that was unconscionable when made, enforce the remainder without it, or limit its application to avoid an unconscionable result.

So the protections other states require by statute - a stated percentage that is the unit's true share, the tax bill and the calculation shown, no liability for Landlord's own late-payment penalties and interest, and a proportionate refund of any abatement - are the right way to draft the clause in Kansas even though no statute compels them. They keep the amount objective, which is what makes the clause defensible.

No Kansas city may fill the gap the other way either: no political subdivision may enact, maintain or enforce any ordinance or resolution that would have the effect of controlling the amount of rent charged for the lease of privately owned residential property.

title: Cable and Communication Service Access
bodyText: Kansas does have a telecom-access rule, and it sits in an unexpected place: the end of the landlord's duty to supply water and heat. Landlord shall not interfere with or refuse to allow access or service to a tenant by a communication or cable television service duly franchised by a municipality. That is the whole of it, and it is a landlord duty under the Act, so a lease term purporting to waive it would be a waiver of a right under the Act and unenforceable. Note what Kansas does not have. There is no ban on Landlord taking a payment from a provider for access to the building, no ban on charging tenants different rent according to whether they take a service, no requirement that the provider or tenant bear installation and removal costs or indemnify Landlord, no bulk-billing opt-out, and no satellite-dish rule. There is also a wording problem worth knowing about, and it is narrower than it first looks. The duty is written around a service duly franchised by a municipality. For a telephone or other communication provider that phrase is still live: Kansas cities still franchise businesses using the streets, and the statute restraining municipalities from changing their relationship with telecommunications providers expressly contemplates city franchise and right-of-way ordinances and sets up an access-line fee a city may charge a local exchange provider. The problem is confined to the cable television limb. Since 1 July 2006 anyone seeking to provide cable or video service in Kansas must apply to the state corporation commission for a state-issued video service authorization, only the state is the exclusive franchising authority, and a municipality is forbidden to require a video provider to obtain a separate franchise. Municipal cable franchises that were in effect on that date continue until they expire, are terminated or are modified, so some providers still hold one. But a provider that entered the market afterwards cannot obtain a municipal franchise at all, because the law forbids the city to require one. Reading the duty as reaching only municipally franchised providers would therefore not merely narrow it; it would make its precondition impossible for every new entrant. That is a strong reason to doubt the narrow reading, but no Kansas court has decided it. The cautious course is to treat the duty as covering any lawfully authorized cable, video or communication provider a tenant has asked for, and not to refuse access on the ground that the provider's authorization came from the state rather than the city. Landlord may still impose reasonable, non-obstructive conditions about where and how equipment is installed - that is ordinary property management, not interference - and should put those conditions in the lease rather than refusing access and arguing about it later.

title: Tenancies at Will, and Which Rule Actually Governs a Home
bodyText: Kansas has a tenancy-at-will presumption: any person in possession of real property with the owner's assent is presumed to be a tenant at will unless the contrary is shown. Two more old rules fill it in. Where rent is reserved payable at intervals of three months or less, the tenant is deemed to hold from one period to another equal to the interval between payment days, unless there is an express contract to the contrary. And an occupant without special contract of any lands is liable for the rent to the person entitled to it. For a residential tenancy, though, the rule that governs is the Kansas Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, not the tenancy-at-will sections. The Act supplies the term directly: unless the rental agreement fixes a definite term, the tenancy is week-to-week for a roomer who pays weekly rent and month-to-month in every other case. So a residential occupant who moves in with no written lease does not stay a tenant at will in any practical sense - the Act converts the arrangement into a periodic tenancy, and termination follows the Act's own notice rules: seven days' written notice to end a week-to-week tenancy, and for a month-to-month tenancy written notice stating that the tenancy ends on a periodic rent-paying date not less than 30 days after the notice is received. A rental agreement for a definite term of more than 30 days is not a month-to-month tenancy even if rent is reserved payable every 30 days. The older sections still matter in three places. First, for an arrangement the Act does not govern. Second, a tenant who holds over at the end of a lease of a year or more with Landlord's assent becomes a tenant from year to year, and a year-to-year tenancy other than a farm tenancy is ended by at least 30 days' written notice given before the year expires. Third, no notice to quit is necessary where the lease itself specifies the time of termination, where a tenant at will commits waste, in the case of a tenant by sufferance, or where no landlord-tenant relation exists at all. Practical course: always fix a definite term in writing. An oral or open-ended arrangement becomes month-to-month by operation of the Act, Landlord cannot shorten the 30-day notice by agreement in a way that waives the tenant's rights under the Act, and the notice must land on a rent-paying date.

title: Tenant Bankruptcy
bodyText: Kansas has no rule of its own on what happens to a tenancy when the tenant files for bankruptcy. Nothing in the Kansas Residential Landlord and Tenant Act mentions bankruptcy, nothing suspends or accelerates an eviction because of a filing, and nothing says what becomes of the security deposit or of pre-filing rent. The Act does not even contain the supplementary-principles provision some states have, by which general principles of law including bankruptcy are said to supplement the statute - Kansas simply left the subject out. Federal bankruptcy law governs instead, of its own force. It decides whether Landlord may serve a notice, start or continue an eviction, collect rent that accrued before the filing, or enforce a lease term that ends the lease because of the bankruptcy. Treat a bankruptcy filing as a stop sign: do not serve a notice, file, proceed to judgment or enforce a writ against a tenant who has filed without getting advice first, because acting in the face of the federal stay can expose Landlord to sanctions, and a lease clause making bankruptcy itself a default is of doubtful effect. One Kansas rule does bear on what Landlord can collect. Kansas has opted out of the federal exemption list: an individual debtor in bankruptcy may not elect the federal exemptions, and must use the Kansas ones instead, with the single exception of the federal subsection covering certain benefits and awards. So Kansas's own exemptions - the homestead, the personal-property list, pension and benefit money, and the wage-garnishment cap - are the measure of what a landlord's judgment can actually reach. Two other Kansas points are worth knowing because they shape the claim rather than the bankruptcy. A landlord's lien or security interest in the tenant's household goods, furnishings, fixtures or other personal property is unenforceable unless it was perfected before the Act took effect, and distraint for rent is abolished except for the abandoned-property procedure. So a Kansas landlord has no lien to assert in the tenant's bankruptcy and is an unsecured creditor for unpaid rent.

title: Tenant Information: No Disclosure Ban, but a Breach Duty
bodyText: Kansas has no statute limiting what a landlord may disclose about a tenant, a former tenant, an applicant or a household member. There is no Kansas list of confidential tenant information, no consent requirement, no ban on passing an applicant's criminal history to anyone else, and no general consumer data-privacy act. The Oregon and Maryland rules have no Kansas counterpart. Three Kansas rules do reach tenant data, and they are worth knowing. First, breach notification. A person who conducts business in Kansas and owns or licenses computerized data that includes personal information must, on becoming aware of a security breach, conduct a good-faith, reasonable and prompt investigation into the likelihood that the information has been or will be misused, and if misuse has occurred or is reasonably likely, must notify the affected Kansas resident as soon as possible and without unreasonable delay. Personal information means the consumer's first name or initial and last name linked to an unencrypted and unredacted Social Security number, driver's licence or state ID number, or financial account or card number with any access code. A breach means unauthorized access and acquisition of unencrypted or unredacted computerized data that compromises its security and that causes or is reasonably believed likely to cause identity theft. If more than 1,000 consumers must be notified, the nationwide consumer reporting agencies must be told too, and the attorney general enforces. Landlord who keeps application files with that data is inside this duty, and it applies only to computerized data. Kansas also has a front-end rule that covers paper too: anyone who collects or keeps personal information in the ordinary course of business must use reasonable procedures and practices to protect it, and must shred, erase or otherwise make unreadable any record containing it once the record is no longer to be kept; only the attorney general enforces it (K.S.A. 50-6,139b). Second, consumer reports. A consumer reporting agency may furnish a report only for the listed purposes, which include a legitimate business need in connection with a business transaction involving the consumer, and an ordinary report may not carry suits and judgments more than seven years old, arrest or conviction records more than seven years after disposition, release or parole, or any other adverse item more than seven years old. Third, surveillance. Kansas makes it a crime to breach privacy, which includes entering with intent to listen surreptitiously to private conversations in a private place or to observe the personal conduct of a person entitled to privacy there, and installing or using a device to hear, record, amplify or broadcast sounds originating in a private place without the consent of the person entitled to privacy. A tenant's home is a private place. Practical course: collect only what is needed, keep it in as few places as possible, treat a lost laptop or a hacked portal as triggering the investigate-and-notify duty, say nothing about a tenant to a third party without a reason you could defend, and never put a camera or microphone where it reaches inside a dwelling.

title: Flags, Signs and Displays: What Kansas Does and Does Not Protect
bodyText: Kansas gives a tenant no statutory right to display a flag, a sign or anything else at a rental, and requires nothing about displays in a lease. There is no Kansas equivalent of the Nevada flag-display right or of the required lease notice that goes with it. As between Landlord and Tenant, a lease rule on signs, flags, banners and window displays governs - so if Landlord wants to control what appears on doors, windows, balconies and lawns, the lease is the only place to say so, and if the lease says nothing Landlord has no statutory handle. Two Kansas rules do protect displays, and both run against covenants and associations rather than against Landlord. First, a provision of a restrictive covenant that prohibits the display of political yard signs smaller than six square feet, during the period beginning 45 days before an election and ending two days after it, is against public policy and void and unenforceable, including in covenants that existed when the statute took effect. Second, in a common interest community of 12 or more residential units, an association rule regulating display of the United States flag must be consistent with federal law, and the association may not prohibit display on a unit or on a limited common element adjoining a unit of the Kansas flag or of signs regarding candidates for public or association office or ballot questions; the association may set reasonable time, place, size, number and manner rules that do not conflict with the political-yard-sign statute. There are three further limits on that association rule, and they are worth knowing because they are limits a landlord can point to. A rule affecting the use of or behaviour in units that may be used for residential purposes may be adopted only to implement a provision of the recorded declaration, or to regulate behaviour in or occupancy of a unit that violates the declaration or adversely affects other owners' use and enjoyment of their units or the common elements. An association may adopt and enforce construction, design and aesthetic standards by rule only if the declaration so provides. And every rule must be reasonable. So a display rule invented by the board with no footing in the declaration, or one aimed at nothing beyond taste, is outside the association's rulemaking power. Note the limits: holding a leasehold is not ownership for that Act, so a tenant is not a unit owner and the Act gives tenants nothing directly - though the flag and sign protection is written by location, covering display on a unit, rather than by who displays it. Practical course: if the property is in an association, do not promise Tenant more control over signs than the association allows, and do not include a lease rule banning a small political yard sign in the election window where a covenant could not, because a term Landlord cannot enforce is worse than no term. Two more things sit outside this. The federal rule on displaying the United States flag is what the association's flag rule must be consistent with, and it is federal law rather than Kansas law, so check it directly before relying on a flag restriction anywhere. And a city or county sign ordinance may restrict what can go up at the property regardless of what the lease, the covenants or the association say; that is local law and is not resolved here. Fair housing law separately protects religious expression, and any blanket display ban should be applied evenhandedly for that reason.

title: Housing for Your Employees
bodyText:
Kansas has no statute requiring an employer-landlord to give an employee a signed disclosure of the conditions for occupying and vacating the housing, and none requiring Landlord to offer a rental agreement when the job ends.

The rule that matters is scope. The Kansas Residential Landlord and Tenant Act does not govern occupancy by an employee of a landlord whose right to occupancy is conditional upon employment in and about the premises - so a resident manager, caretaker or maintenance employee housed as part of the job is outside the Act. Read the qualifier carefully, because three things have to be true: the occupant must be Landlord's employee, the right to occupy must be conditional on that employment, and the employment must be in and about the premises. An employee who simply rents from the employer at arm's length, or whose job has nothing to do with the property, is an ordinary tenant with the Act's full protection. And every exclusion in that list is prefaced by the words unless created to avoid the application of the Act, so papering an ordinary tenancy as employee housing fails and leaves Landlord exposed to the Act's deposit cap, notice rules and remedies.

When the Act does not apply, the older general tenancy law does, and it is less favourable to the occupant than most landlords expect it to be in one respect and more generous in another. Where premises are furnished or let by an employer to an employee, the tenancy ceases and determines ten days after written notice to vacate. That is a short notice period compared with the Act's 30 days, but it still requires written notice - so an employer may not simply change the locks when the job ends, and the self-help rules still bite.

Kansas has no employee-housing or farm-labour housing code and no migrant-housing standards; its migrant-worker statutes concern paying wages directly to the worker rather than to a crew chief, and registering crew chiefs with the state employment service. There is no Kansas analogue of the sponsored-guest-worker rent filing some jurisdictions require.

Practical course: decide at the outset which regime applies and write the lease to match. If the housing is genuinely part of the job, say so, identify the duties in and about the premises, and state that occupancy ends with the employment and on ten days' written notice. If it is not, use the ordinary lease and follow the Act.

title: No Duty to Forward Legal Papers; Attornment to a Stranger Is Void
bodyText: Kansas law does not require a tenant to tell you about, or hand over, papers in a lawsuit or other proceeding to recover the property. If you want that duty, it has to come from the lease, and the library's notice-of-proceedings clause supplies it. Kansas does, however, protect your position in two ways without any help from the lease. A tenant's attornment to a stranger -- recognizing someone else as landlord -- is void and does not affect your possession, unless you consented to it or it was made under a judgment or a court order or decree. And if you sell or convey the property or any interest in it, the conveyance is valid without the tenant attorning to the buyer; but rent the tenant pays to you before the tenant has been given notice of the sale is good against the buyer, so give the tenant prompt written notice of a sale and tell the tenant where rent is to be paid from then on.

title: No Kansas Rule on Claiming Against a Tenant's Insurance
bodyText: Kansas has no statute on whether you may make a tenant claim on the tenant's own renter's insurance, or whether you may file a claim against that policy yourself, and no statute barring an insurer from subrogating against a tenant. Requiring renter's insurance in the lease is lawful in Kansas and the lease does that separately. Two Kansas rules still limit how far you can go. A rental agreement may not make either party agree to the exculpation or limitation of the other's liability arising under law, or to indemnify the other for it, except that the tenant may agree to limit your liability for fire, theft or breakage in the common areas of the dwelling unit; if you deliberately use a lease containing a term you know is prohibited, the tenant can recover actual damages. And your own repair and maintenance duties are set by statute and cannot be waived, so do not treat a tenant's insurance claim as a condition of doing a repair you owe. If you want to recover from the tenant for damage the tenant caused, use the statutory security-deposit and damages route, not the tenant's policy, unless the tenant agrees in writing at the time.

title: Tenant Portals and Electronic Dealings
bodyText:
Kansas has no statute on tenant portals as such. Nothing requires you to publish a printable paper application, nothing bars you from taking rent through an online portal, and nothing caps a portal or card convenience fee on rent.

Three Kansas rules still shape how you may use one. First, Kansas's electronic transactions act applies only to transactions where both you and the tenant have agreed to deal electronically, it does not require anyone to use an electronic record or signature, and a party who has agreed to one electronic transaction keeps a right to refuse other electronic transactions that cannot be waived by agreement. So do not write the lease as though the tenant has given up the ability to go back to paper, and keep at least one non-electronic way to pay rent and to reach you.

Second, an electronically signed lease and electronic notices are fully effective where both sides have agreed, so a portal is a sound way to run the tenancy with a willing tenant.

Third, a notice terminating the tenancy is different: Kansas prescribes how it is served -- on the tenant, or at the tenant's usual place of residence, or on a person over 12 years of age residing on the premises, or by posting conspicuously on the premises, or by registered or certified mail return receipt requested. A portal message is not one of those methods, so serve a termination notice the statutory way even if everything else runs through the portal.

title: Tenant Records: No Ledger Duty, but a Duty to Protect and Shred
bodyText: Kansas imposes no duty to give a tenant a rent ledger, a payment history or access to the tenant's file, and no duty to keep tenancy records for any set period. If you want a records-access or copy-charge rule, it has to come from the lease. What Kansas does regulate is how you look after the personal information in those files. If you collect, maintain or possess another person's personal information in the ordinary course of business -- which a landlord taking rental applications does -- you must implement and maintain reasonable procedures and practices appropriate to the nature of the information and exercise reasonable care to protect it from unauthorized access, use, modification or disclosure. And when you no longer intend to keep a record containing personal information, you must take reasonable steps to destroy it, or arrange for its destruction, by shredding, erasing or otherwise making the personal identifying information unreadable or undecipherable. Personal information means a person's name together with a Social Security number, a driver's licence or state ID number, or a financial account or card number. Unlike the breach-notification duty, this one is not limited to computerised data, so paper application files are inside it. Each violation is an unconscionable act under the Kansas Consumer Protection Act, the attorney general has exclusive enforcement authority and there is no private right of action. There are two narrow affirmative defences, one of which depends on having a bona fide written or electronic records-management policy that your staff have been trained on, so a short written retention-and-shredding policy is worth having. Two record duties you do owe the tenant sit elsewhere: the itemised written notice of what you deduct from the security deposit, and compliance with any court order for records in an eviction case.

title: A Kansas Tenant Has No Repair Remedy That Touches the Rent
bodyText: Kansas gives a tenant no repair-and-deduct right, no rent withholding, no rent escrow and no rent-abatement remedy for disrepair. None of those exists in Kansas law at all, so a tenant who stops paying, pays less, or pays a repair bill out of the rent because you have not fixed something is simply in default, and you may proceed for nonpayment. The two places Kansas lets rent go to the court are both judicial and neither is a tenant self-help route: in your own action for possession for nonpayment, or an action for rent while the tenant is in possession, the court may order the tenant to pay accrued and accruing rent into court and then determine what each party is owed; and on appeal from an eviction judgment the court may condition a stay on the tenant paying the periodic rent into court instead of posting a bond. What a tenant with a repair complaint actually has is the written-notice and termination route, a damages and injunction action, a counterclaim inside your eviction, and a complaint to the city or county code officer. Two consequences for you. First, do not write the lease so that a capped repair allowance, a repair-and-deduct limit or an arbitration-style repair process becomes the tenant's only remedy: a rental agreement may not have either party waive or forgo rights or remedies under the Act, such a provision is unenforceable, and deliberately using a lease with a term you know is prohibited exposes you to the tenant's actual damages. Second, if the tenant complains to a building or housing code agency about a violation materially affecting health and safety, or complains to you about one of your statutory duties, you may not retaliate by raising the rent or cutting services; a good-faith increase to cover acts of God, utility rate rises, property tax rises or other cost increases is still allowed, and you may still bring a possession action if the violation was caused mainly by the tenant's lack of reasonable care, the tenant is in default in rent, or compliance would require alteration, remodelling or demolition that would deprive the tenant of the unit.

title: Tenants Who Organize Are Protected From Retaliation
bodyText: Kansas protects a tenant who organizes or becomes a member of a tenants' union or similar organization. You may not retaliate against that tenant by increasing the rent or decreasing services. The same protection covers a tenant who has complained to a government agency responsible for enforcing a building or housing code about a violation at the property that materially affects health and safety, and a tenant who has complained to you about one of your statutory landlord duties. If you do retaliate, the tenant may recover possession or terminate the lease and, either way, recover the greater of one and a half months' periodic rent or actual damages, and the tenant also has a defence to any action you bring for possession -- so an eviction or a non-renewal aimed at an organizer can be defeated on that ground. Two things are still permitted. You may raise the rent even after one of those events if the increase does not conflict with a lease in effect and is made in good faith to cover expenses from acts of God, public utility rate increases, property tax increases or other increases in your costs of operation. And you may still bring a possession action if the code violation was caused mainly by a lack of reasonable care by the tenant or by a person, animal or pet on the premises with the tenant's consent, or the tenant is in default in rent, or compliance with the code would require alteration, remodelling or demolition that would effectively deprive the tenant of the unit -- though bringing that action does not release you from damages for the underlying breach. What Kansas does not give is an affirmative organizing right: there is no statutory right for a tenants' group to meet in a common room, to distribute literature door to door, to canvass the building or to be given tenant contact details. Whether to allow those things is yours to decide, so long as the decision is not retaliation for organizing. Do not put a term in the lease barring tenants from forming or joining a tenants' organization; a lease may not have the tenant waive or forgo rights or remedies under the Act, such a term is unenforceable, and deliberately using a lease with a term you know is prohibited exposes you to the tenant's actual damages.

title: No Statement of Tenant Rights Has to Go With a Kansas Lease
bodyText: Kansas requires no statement, summary or pamphlet of tenant rights to be given with a residential lease. There is no state-agency form to attach, no page-by-page acknowledgment to collect, no renewal reminder to send, and nothing that has to be provided before you may sue. This is a deliberate choice rather than an oversight: Kansas does require that notice in its separate mobile home park act, where a rental agreement in a park harbouring five or more mobile homes must contain a notice telling the tenant that the tenant has certain rights under that act and that copies of the act may be obtained from the landlord on request. The ordinary residential act's equivalent section, which covers the same ground -- what the agreement may contain, what rent is owed without one, when rent is payable and what the tenancy period is -- has no such subsection. If you want to hand a new tenant a plain-language summary of Kansas landlord-tenant law, you may, and many landlords do; just be careful that anything you write is accurate, because a summary you supply becomes something the tenant can hold you to, and nothing in it can cut down the tenant's rights under the Act.

title: Screening in Kansas: Unregulated by the State, and Protected From Local Rules
bodyText: Kansas has no tenant-screening statute. There is no conditional-offer rule, no look-back limit on criminal or rental history, no cap on how income may be tested, no reusable or portable screening report scheme, no state adverse-action or denial-notice duty and no statutory negligence shield for renting to someone with a criminal record. In 2026 the legislature went further and protected screening from local regulation: no Kansas city or county may adopt or enforce an ordinance or resolution restricting your ability to use or consider income-qualifying methods, credit scores, credit reports, eviction history, property damage history or criminal history, or to request that information, when you do so to decide whether to lease according to your customarily applied criteria. Any ordinance of that kind adopted before July 1, 2026 is null and void.
