Note the shape of that protection: it binds cities and counties, not you, it creates no duty and no defence against anything else, and it is written around criteria you apply customarily -- so write your criteria down, apply them to every applicant the same way, and keep the records. Four real limits remain. First, fair housing. The Kansas Act Against Discrimination makes it unlawful to refuse to rent, or to discriminate in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental, because of race, religion, color, sex, disability, familial status, national origin or ancestry; federal law adds its own duties, and a facially neutral screening rule that falls hardest on a protected group can still be unlawful in effect. Second, eviction history ages out. From 2026 a tenant may apply to expunge an eviction judgment at no cost once three years have passed, the money judgment is satisfied and there is no further eviction judgment in that period, so older eviction records will progressively disappear from what you can find. Third, criminal records that have been expunged. Once a Kansas court orders expungement the person is treated as not having been arrested, convicted or diverted, the custodian of the records may not disclose them, and the person may say they were never arrested or convicted when applying for employment, a licence or another civil right or privilege. Do not penalise an applicant for answering no, and do not try to dig an expunged record out. Fourth, what a screening report may lawfully contain. Kansas limits a consumer reporting agency to a seven-year window for arrests, indictments and convictions measured from disposition, release or parole, seven years or the statute of limitations (whichever is longer) for suits and judgments, seven years for collections and for any other adverse item, and fourteen years for bankruptcies. Those limits bind the agency rather than you; the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act is what imposes duties on you as a user of a report, including having a permissible purpose and giving an adverse-action notice.

title: The Seven Statutory Tenant Duties in Kansas, and What They Leave Out
bodyText:
Kansas puts seven duties on a residential tenant by statute, and they are the whole of it. The tenant must:
- comply with the obligations building and housing codes impose primarily on tenants where those materially affect health and safety
- keep the part of the premises the tenant occupies and uses as clean and safe as the condition of the premises permits
- remove ashes, rubbish, garbage and other waste from the dwelling unit in a clean and safe manner
- keep all plumbing fixtures in the unit or used by the tenant as clean as their condition permits
- use all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, in a reasonable manner
- be responsible for any destruction, defacement, damage, impairment or removal of any part of the premises caused by an act or omission of the tenant or by any person, animal or pet on the premises with the tenant's express or implied permission
- not engage in, or allow such a person, animal or pet to engage in, conduct that will disturb the quiet and peaceful enjoyment of the premises by other tenants.

Two more sit outside that list. Unless otherwise agreed the tenant must occupy the unit only as a dwelling unit, and the lease may require the tenant to tell you about any anticipated absence over seven days, no later than the first day of it -- that duty only exists if the lease creates it, and a willful failure gives you actual damages.

Note what Kansas does not include. There is no statutory wear-and-tear standard, so 'ordinary wear and tear' in your lease is a contract term, not a statutory line. There is no tenant duty to report pests, to test or maintain smoke detectors, to keep utilities on, or to give notice at the end of the tenancy beyond what the lease requires. And Kansas has no treble-damages waste statute: the only waste rules are that a tenant at will who commits waste may be put out without a notice to quit, and that a tenant appealing an eviction must give a bond conditioned on not committing or suffering waste.

One asymmetry is worth knowing, because it cuts against you. The tenant's duty covers 'other facilities and appliances', but your own maintenance duty is written as a closed list of electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning appliances, including elevators, that you supply or are required to supply. So for a supplied appliance outside those categories -- a refrigerator, range, washer, dryer, dishwasher or microwave -- the tenant owes a reasonable-use duty but your statutory repair duty is at best arguable. If you supply such an appliance, say in the lease who repairs and replaces it rather than leaving it to the statute.

title: Changing Lease Terms Mid-Tenancy in Kansas
bodyText: Kansas has no term-change-notice statute. Nothing in Kansas law lets you serve a notice that of itself rewrites the lease, as several neighbouring states allow, and nothing sets a notice period for a rent increase, a fee increase or any other change of terms. During a fixed-term lease you cannot change a term at all without the tenant's agreement. In a periodic tenancy the route is termination and re-letting: give written notice that the tenancy will end on a periodic rent-paying date not less than thirty days after the tenant receives it for a month-to-month tenancy, or at least seven days before the termination date for a week-to-week tenancy, and offer a new tenancy on the new terms. A tenant who stays on and pays the new rent has accepted the new tenancy; a tenant who does not is simply out at the end of the notice. Watch three things. A rental agreement for a definite term of more than thirty days is not a month-to-month tenancy even if rent is payable at thirty-day intervals, so that route is not open for it. House rules are not a way around this: a rule is enforceable only if its purpose is to promote the convenience, safety, peace or welfare of tenants, to preserve your property from abusive use or to distribute services fairly, it is reasonably related to that purpose, it applies to all tenants in the premises equally, it is explicit enough to tell the tenant what to do, it is not for the purpose of evading your own obligations, and the tenant had notice of it when entering the rental agreement -- and a rule adopted later that effects a substantial modification of the rental agreement is unenforceable unless the tenant consents to it in writing. A rent or fee increase is a substantial modification, so it cannot be imposed as a house rule. And a change of terms must not be retaliation: you may not raise the rent or cut services after the tenant has complained to a code agency about a violation materially affecting health and safety, complained to you about your statutory duties, or organized or joined a tenants' union, though a good-faith increase to cover acts of God, utility rate rises, property tax rises or other cost increases is still allowed if it does not conflict with a lease in effect.

title: No Exemption Notice to Give in Kansas
bodyText: Kansas requires no notice telling a tenant that a property is exempt from rent limits, from a just-cause eviction rule or from a tenant purchase right. Nothing like California's exemption statement exists here, and there is nothing for such a notice to be about: Kansas has no statewide rent cap, no just-cause requirement and no tenant right to buy, and it bars cities and counties from creating a local rent cap or requiring an automatic right of first refusal. Kansas also has no two-tier scheme of covered and exempt rental property of the kind some states use. The one place Kansas does set out what a tenancy is and is not covered by is the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act's own scope, and it imposes no notice duty either: you do not have to tell a tenant that the Act does not apply to the arrangement. If an arrangement sits outside the Act -- occupancy incidental to institutional care or schooling, a purchaser under a contract of sale, a member of a fraternal or social organization in a structure the organization operates, transient occupancy in a hotel, motel or rooming house, an employee whose occupancy is conditional on employment about the premises, a condominium owner or cooperative proprietary lessee, premises used primarily for agricultural purposes, a pre-Act agreement, or an unauthorized occupant who has been personally ordered to leave -- say so plainly in the written agreement for your own sake, since the Act's protections and its remedies both turn on the point and the exclusions are read against an arrangement created to avoid the Act.

title: No Rent-Cap, Just-Cause or Tenant-Purchase Notice in Kansas
bodyText: Kansas requires no lease notice of a rent cap, a just-cause eviction rule or a tenant right to buy, because it has none of those things. There is no statewide rent cap or rent stabilization, and Kansas law forbids any county, municipality or township from enacting, maintaining or enforcing an ordinance that would have the effect of controlling the rent charged or the purchase price agreed for privately owned residential or commercial property -- with narrow exceptions for property the political subdivision itself owns and for a voluntary agreement an owner makes in exchange for grants or incentives. Kansas has no tenure-based or any other just-cause requirement for ending a tenancy. It has no tenant opportunity to purchase and no tenant right of first refusal of any kind, and no condominium-conversion notice or purchase right for a tenant whose building is converted. In 2026 the legislature made the point again from the other direction: no Kansas city or county may adopt or enforce an ordinance requiring landlords to grant an automatic right of first refusal to tenants, and any such ordinance adopted before July 1, 2026 is null and void. So there is nothing for the lease to disclose here. If you do give a tenant a contractual right of first refusal or a purchase option, that is your own bargain; write it carefully, because no statute supplies terms, notice periods or remedies for it.

title: No Kansas Landlord-Tenant Statute Is Set to Expire
bodyText: As of October 24, 2026, none of Kansas's core landlord-tenant statutes carries a repeal or expiration date. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, the security-deposit rules, the prohibited-terms section, the notice and termination sections, the retaliation bar and the eviction procedure all run indefinitely, and Kansas has no tenant-protection act on a clock to watch, because it has no rent cap, just-cause regime or tenant purchase right in the first place. Most of the Act is in fact unamended since 1975. Three dated items from the 2026 session are worth noting, none of them a sunset of a tenant protection. The short-term-rental window has already closed: for the period May 15, 2026 through July 25, 2026 only, municipalities could not limit the regulation or duration of short-term rentals or vacation properties and had to process permit applications within fifteen calendar days, and a transient-guest tax definition was modified for the same period. The electric-vehicle charging rules for retail electric suppliers expire on July 1, 2036 -- they impose nothing on landlords in any event. And the digital right-to-repair act applies only to digital electronic equipment first made available for sale in Kansas on or after July 1, 2027, which is a start date rather than an expiry, and it binds manufacturers rather than landlords. The practical point for you is the opposite of a sunset watch: the new 2026 acts on eviction expungement, squatter removal and local preemption are permanent, and the ones that matter to a Kansas landlord are not going to lapse on their own.

title: No Lease Translation Duty, but Consumer Law Still Reaches a Lease the Tenant Cannot Read
bodyText: Kansas has no lease-translation duty. Nothing requires you to translate a lease, an addendum or a notice into another language, however you advertised or negotiated, and Kansas publishes no official translated landlord-tenant notices. There is no minimum type size for lease text either. One Kansas rule still bears on this, and it is worth taking seriously. The Kansas Consumer Protection Act reaches a residential lease: a consumer transaction includes a lease of property for value to a consumer, property includes real estate, and a supplier includes a lessor who in the ordinary course of business solicits, engages in or enforces consumer transactions. The Act forbids a supplier from engaging in any unconscionable act or practice in connection with a consumer transaction, before, during or after it, and the first factor the court is told to weigh is whether the supplier took advantage of the consumer's inability to protect their own interests because of physical infirmity, ignorance, illiteracy, inability to understand the language of an agreement or a similar factor. Kansas also shows what it thinks of the problem elsewhere: in a door-to-door sale the contract or receipt and the cancellation notice must be in the same language, Spanish for example, as that principally used in the oral sales presentation. So although nothing compels a translation, handing an English lease to a tenant you negotiated with in another language is the kind of conduct the unconscionability factor is written for. The safe course where you have dealt with an applicant in another language is to give a written translation of the whole lease before signing, keep a copy of what you gave, and have the signing witnessed by someone who can confirm the tenant understood -- not because a statute says so, but because it removes the strongest unconscionability argument against your lease.

title: Barring a Non-Tenant From the Property in Kansas
bodyText: Kansas criminal trespass gives you a workable way to keep a non-tenant out. It is a crime to enter or remain on land or in a structure by a person who knows they are not authorized or privileged to be there, where any one of three things is true: the person is there in defiance of an order not to enter, or to leave, that was personally communicated to them by the owner or another authorized person; the premises are posted under the state's posting statute or in any other manner reasonably likely to come to the attention of intruders, or are locked, fenced, otherwise enclosed, or shut or secured against passage or entry; or the person is there in defiance of a protection-from-abuse or protection-from-stalking restraining order that has been personally served on them. Criminal trespass is a class B nonperson misdemeanor, and a violation of the restraining-order limb carries at least 48 consecutive hours' imprisonment. Two practical points follow. The order to leave is most useful when it is personally communicated and you can prove it, so give the ban in writing, hand it over or have it served, keep a dated copy and a witness, and tell the police what you gave and when. And both limbs turn on the person knowing they are not authorized, so a ban is weak against someone a tenant has invited in: a tenant's guest is normally there with authority, and you cannot use a trespass warning to override a tenant's right to have guests. Keep the ban aimed at common areas and at people with no tenant inviting them. Note the line between a trespasser and an occupant. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act does not apply to a person who enters and remains in a dwelling unit without a rental agreement and without your knowledge, knowing they are not authorized, where an order to leave has been personally communicated to them by you -- that person may be prosecuted for criminal trespass. Separately, Kansas's 2026 squatter-removal procedure defines a squatter as a person occupying a dwelling who is not entitled to occupy it under a lease or rental agreement and is not authorized by a tenant, and expressly does not include a tenant holding over in a periodic tenancy. Anyone a tenant authorised is outside both routes. Using either against a real tenant or a holdover is a serious mistake.

title: No Truth-in-Renting Notice in Kansas
bodyText: Kansas has no truth-in-renting law. No statute requires your lease to carry a notice saying that the lease must comply with state law or that the tenant may want to consult a lawyer, none prescribes a type size for lease text, and there is no state-published truth-in-renting statement to hand over or post. Kansas does require two things at the start of a tenancy, and they are the nearest equivalents. First, you or whoever signs the lease on your behalf must disclose to the tenant in writing, at or before the tenancy begins, the name and address of the person authorized to manage the premises and the name and address of an owner, or someone authorized to act for the owner, for service of process and for receiving notices and demands. That information must be kept current, it binds a successor landlord, owner or manager, and anyone who does not give it becomes an agent of each landlord for service of process, for receiving notices and demands, for performing the landlord's obligations under the Act and the lease, and for spending the rent collected on doing so. Second, within five days of the initial date of occupancy or on delivery of possession, you or your designated representative and the tenant must jointly inventory the premises and complete a written record of the condition of the premises and of any furnishings or appliances provided; duplicate copies are signed by both to show the inventory was done, and the tenant gets a copy. One other statement is mandatory, but only in a narrow case: if you give a tenant a document that would be the tenant's written notice of intent to vacate and it contains terms not in the lease, it must carry a prescribed warning in no less than ten-point boldface type, and without it the tenant's signature does not bind them to those extra terms.

title: Charging Separately for Parking: No Unbundling Rule, but a Separate Charge Is Rent
bodyText:
Kansas has no unbundled-parking law. No Kansas statute requires you to offer parking separately from rent, forbids you from doing so, regulates a separate parking agreement or addendum, caps what you may charge for a space, or gives a tenant a right of first refusal to a space built for the property. Whether parking comes with the unit, costs extra, or is not offered at all is left to the lease.

What Kansas does control is what a separate parking charge counts as. Under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, rent means all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement other than the security deposit, and the rental agreement includes the lease, any addendum to it, and rules you adopt for the tenant's use and occupancy of the premises. So a parking charge payable to you under any of those is rent in Kansas whatever the lease calls it, and three things follow. First, the security deposit you may demand for an unfurnished unit is capped at one month's periodic rent, so a monthly parking charge inside the rental agreement enlarges the figure the cap is measured against. Second, if the tenant does not pay it, that is unpaid rent, and the Act's three-day written notice is the route to termination rather than the longer notice and cure period that applies to other material breaches. Third, you cannot label the charge as not rent in order to escape either consequence, because a rental agreement may not provide that the tenant waives or foregoes rights or remedies under the Act, and a term that does is unenforceable.

Moving parking into a genuinely separate agreement, outside the rental agreement for the dwelling unit, takes the charge outside that definition, but it also takes it outside the Act's remedies, and it does not take the parking area outside the Act. Premises under the Act includes grounds, areas and facilities held out for the use of tenants generally or the use of which is promised to the tenant, so a parking area you advertise to tenants or promise to this tenant is part of the premises either way. Unlawfully removing or excluding a tenant from the premises lets the tenant recover possession or terminate and, in either case, recover the greater of one and a half months' periodic rent or actual damages. Decide deliberately which structure you want, write it plainly into the lease, and do not withdraw promised parking mid-term without a lease term that allows it.

If you allocate spaces by rule rather than by naming them in the lease, the rule is enforceable against the tenant only on the Act's conditions, one of which is that its purpose is to make a fair distribution of services and facilities held out for the tenants generally. A rule adopted after the tenant signs that substantially modifies the rental agreement is unenforceable unless the tenant consents in writing, so moving a tenant from included parking to a paid space mid-term needs that written consent. Cities and counties may still have parking ordinances of their own; a 2026 Kansas act voids several kinds of local rental ordinance, but an unbundling mandate is not one of them, so check the local code rather than assuming the subject is preempted.

title: Interest on Unpaid Amounts
bodyText:
Kansas gives you interest on money a tenant owes you without any lease language. Creditors are allowed 10% a year when no other rate of interest is agreed upon, for any money after it becomes due, and also for money due and withheld by an unreasonable and vexatious delay of payment or settlement of accounts. So unpaid rent, and damages beyond the security deposit once the amount is ascertained, carry the 10% legal rate whether or not the lease mentions interest at all.

Agreeing to a different rate is where Kansas turns dangerous, and the cautious course is not to try. Kansas voids a provision in a contract for the payment of money that in effect makes any interest or charges, or any higher rate of interest or charges, accrue as a penalty for any default. A term that switches on only when the tenant defaults, or that steps a rate up once the tenant is late, is the kind of provision that language is aimed at, so do not draft one. Separately, a rate stipulated in a written instrument for the payment or forbearance of money may not exceed 15% a year unless another statute allows more, and the consequence of exceeding it falls entirely on you: you forfeit all the interest contracted for above the limit, you forfeit a further sum equal to that excess, which is deducted from the principal and lawful interest you are owed, the tenant may set both up as a defense or counterclaim in your own collection suit, and the tenant also recovers a reasonable attorney fee. That fee award comes from the interest statute rather than from the lease, so the rule that no rental agreement may make either party pay the other's attorneys' fees gives you no protection from it.

Whether those two limits reach a residential lease, rather than only a loan or a credit sale, has not been settled in Kansas. Treat them as if they do. If you want the lease to say anything about interest, the cautious form is a single rate, at or below 15% a year, running on any amount from the date it becomes due, never described as a penalty and never applying only on default. Simpler still, say nothing: the 10% legal rate needs no lease term and cannot be attacked as a penalty.

After judgment, two rates matter. A judgment in a limited action, which is where an eviction and most landlord damage claims are filed, bears 12% a year. A judgment under the general code of civil procedure bears a rate that changes each July 1 and is four percentage points above the New York Federal Reserve discount rate, published each July by the Secretary of State in the Kansas Register. But if your lease does specify a rate of interest, that rate continues until full payment and the judgment bears the contract rate, which must be specified in the judgment. A rate you write into the lease therefore displaces the statutory judgment rate, up or down, which is one more reason to choose it deliberately rather than copying a figure from another state's form.

title: Leasing as a Life Tenant (No Usufruct in Kansas)
bodyText:
Usufruct is a civil-law interest, and Kansas property law does not use it. The word appears nowhere in the Kansas Statutes, so the civil-law rules that a lease granted by a usufructuary ends when the usufruct ends and that an undisclosed usufructuary owes the tenant the losses caused by that ending simply do not arise in Kansas. The Kansas equivalent is a life estate, most often a surviving spouse who holds the home for life while children hold the remainder.

No Kansas statute says what happens to your lease when your life estate ends. The general Kansas rule on conveyances is that every conveyance of real estate passes all the estate of the grantor unless an intent to pass a lesser estate expressly appears or is necessarily implied, which is the principle behind the usual proposition that you cannot give a tenant a longer right of possession than you hold yourself. But Kansas courts have dealt with a deceased life tenant's lease, and in at least one old decision the remainderman took the rent under that lease rather than the lease simply falling with the life estate. Treat the point as unsettled and do not promise the tenant either answer. The cautious course is to write into the lease what happens if your estate ends during the term, whether the tenancy ends then or continues with rent payable to whoever holds the property, so neither side is left relying on an unsettled rule.

The Kansas statutes that do touch a life tenant's lease all cut the same way. Rents from lands granted for life or lives may be recovered as other rents, so you sue for rent as any landlord would. An occupant of land without a special contract is liable for the rent to any person entitled to it, so if your estate ends mid-term the tenant does not get free occupancy and the remainderman can look to the tenant for rent. And a person holding an estate in remainder or reversion may sue for waste or trespass injuring the inheritance notwithstanding an intervening life estate, so damage done during your tenancy is the remainderman's claim as well as yours. Document the condition of the property at move-in and move-out for that reason, not only for the deposit.

The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies to you in the ordinary way. Landlord under the Act means the owner, lessor or sublessor of the dwelling unit, and owner means a person in whom is vested all or part of the legal title, so a life tenant who rents out the home is a landlord carrying the Act's full duties. You must disclose to the tenant in writing, at or before the tenancy begins, the name and address of the person authorized to manage the premises and of an owner of the premises, or someone authorized to act for the owner, for service of process and for receiving and receipting for notices and demands. That information must be kept current and the duty is enforceable against any successor landlord, owner or manager. If nobody makes that disclosure, the person who failed to becomes the landlord's agent for service of process and for performing the landlord's obligations out of the rent collected, which is a poor position to leave a remainderman in.

Two practical steps. First, say in the lease that you hold the property for life rather than in fee, and say what happens to the tenancy if your estate ends during the term. No Kansas statute makes you disclose the nature of your estate and none penalises you for staying silent, so the risk you are managing is a dispute, not a fine. Second, remember that security deposits follow the property: the holder of the landlord's interest in the premises at the time the tenancy ends is bound by the deposit rules. Arrange for the deposit and its written itemisation to pass to whoever then holds the landlord's interest, rather than leaving a remainderman to answer for money they never received.

title: Apportioning Utilities Among Tenants: No Kansas Formula Rule, but a Hard Cap on Water
bodyText:
Kansas has no ratio-utility-billing (RUBS) statute, no required or forbidden allocation formula, and no disclosure duty for the method you use to divide a master-metered bill. Who pays for a utility is left to the lease: the landlord's duty section says in terms that nothing in it abrogates, limits or otherwise affects a tenant's obligation to pay for any utility service in accordance with the rental agreement. So if you apportion a master-metered bill by square footage, by occupancy, by fixture count or by any other method, Kansas law does not prescribe the method, does not cap an administrative fee, and does not require you to show the tenant the formula. Say in the lease exactly what is apportioned and how, because the lease is the only rule.

Water is the exception, and the limit is strict. If a city or water district supplies water to the building and you furnish that water to a tenant through a separate meter measuring the tenant's use, Kansas law lets you bill the tenant for it without becoming a regulated public utility, but only on three conditions: you charge the tenant at the same rate the city or water district charges you, you charge no surcharge for the installation or maintenance of the meter or for any other purpose related to its use, and you give the tenant a monthly water statement showing how the amount owed was computed together with the tenant's meter reading for that period and for the prior period. There is no markup, no administrative or billing fee, and no meter-rental charge in that arrangement. Exceed the city's rate, and the statutory protection drops away: the arrangement can then be treated as a sale of water for resale within the state corporation commission's jurisdiction, and you can be arguing that you are not a public utility.

Two practical consequences. First, you may install separate meters if you want to: no city or public water supply system in Kansas may prohibit installing a separate water meter for each dwelling unit in a multi-unit building in place of a master meter for the whole building. Second, the safe harbor covers water only. Kansas's public-utility definition reaches companies furnishing heat, light, water or power, and the landlord exemption the legislature wrote in 2005 names only a landlord supplied water by a city or water district. If you submeter and resell electricity or gas, there is no comparable Kansas statute saying you are not a public utility, so treat that as an unsettled arrangement and get advice before building it into a lease. Where a city regulates a utility operating wholly within it, the power to regulate rates and service sits with the city, so a local ordinance may add rules a state search will not show.

title: A Separate "Utility Deposit" Is Just a Security Deposit in Kansas
bodyText:
Kansas has no separate utility-deposit statute. There is no Kansas rule like Wyoming's, where a deposit identified as a utility deposit is returned on its own timetable once the tenant proves the utility bills are paid. What Kansas has instead is a definition that swallows the label. A security deposit is any sum of money specified in a rental agreement, however denominated, to be deposited with the landlord by the tenant as a condition precedent to occupancy. So money you call a utility deposit, a utility reserve or a billing deposit is a security deposit if the lease specifies it and occupancy depends on it. Three consequences follow, and all of them bite.

First, it counts against the cap. You cannot create extra room by splitting the money into two names: the total of everything the lease requires before occupancy has to stay inside the one month's rent limit for an unfurnished unit, the one and a half months where the tenant uses your furniture, and the extra half month where pets are permitted. Second, it comes back on the ordinary deposit timetable, not a utility timetable: itemize in a written notice anything you keep, return the balance within 14 days of determining the amount and in any event within 30 days of termination, delivery of possession and the tenant's demand, and mail it to the last known address if no demand comes within 30 days. Unpaid utility charges the tenant owes you under the lease are a legitimate deduction, because the statute lets you retain for expenses, damages or other legally allowable charges under the rental agreement other than rent. Third, getting it wrong costs one and a half times the amount wrongfully withheld, plus the amount itself. The practical advice is to take one deposit, inside the cap, and deduct unpaid utilities from it at the end, rather than holding a second pot of money you cannot lawfully hold.

The deposit the utility itself takes is a different thing, and Kansas does regulate it. A public or municipally owned utility may not collect a deposit as security for service bills unless it keeps a separate account showing the date, the depositor and the amount, and pays the customer interest at the rate the state corporation commission sets; the deposit must at all times be reasonable and based on the value of the maximum service rendered, and it may be applied to accrued bills or to bills due when service is discontinued. A municipality may require only a single deposit covering all of its utility services, and it may not exceed the expected average bills for a three-month period. A municipality may not refuse to contract with a tenant for service, except where that person already owes it unpaid utility charges. Note also that a deposit or refund a utility owes a subscriber is presumed abandoned one year after it becomes payable, which is a much shorter clock than the five years that applies to a deposit refund you owe a former tenant — so if a utility holds a deposit in your name on a unit you no longer serve, claim it inside a year.

For utilities the state corporation commission regulates, the detailed deposit rules are in the commission's billing standards, adopted by commission order rather than in the statutes. A utility may require a deposit from a new residential customer only for an unsatisfactory or too-short credit history, an undisputed unpaid account from the last five years (three if the agreement was oral), or tampering with a meter in the last five years. A residential deposit may not exceed the customer's projected average bills for two months, and the customer may pay it in equal installments over at least four months. The utility must credit or refund it with interest after 12 months if the customer paid 10 of the last 12 bills on time and left no undisputed bill unpaid more than 30 days past due, and must refund it, less unpaid bills, when service ends. Instead of a cash deposit, the utility must accept the written guarantee of another residential customer with no deposit on file and 10 of their last 12 payments on time, and the guarantor's liability is capped at the deposit amount.

title: No Utility Disclosure Has to Be Attached to a Kansas Lease
bodyText:
Kansas requires no utility disclosure document attached to or delivered with a lease. There is no required attachment explaining how an apportioned or shared-meter bill is calculated, no water submeter certificate to file with a board of health or copy to the tenant, no notice that a utility tariff carries energy-efficiency or renewable-energy charges, and no utility cost history or average-bill statement. The only written disclosure the Kansas Residential Landlord and Tenant Act requires at or before the start of a tenancy is a narrow one: the name and address of the person authorized to manage the premises, and the name and address of an owner or of someone authorized to act for the owner for service of process and for receiving notices and demands. That information has to be kept current, it binds a successor landlord, owner or manager, and the penalty for omitting it is pointed — whoever fails to give it becomes the landlord's agent for service of process and for performing the landlord's obligations under the Act and the lease, spending the rent collected from the premises to do it. Nothing in that list touches utilities.

The one other document Kansas makes you produce at the start is the joint inventory: within five days of the initial date of occupancy or on delivery of possession, you and the tenant jointly inventory the premises, complete a written record of the condition of the premises and of any furnishings or appliances provided, sign duplicate copies, and give the tenant a copy. That is a condition record, not a utility disclosure, though it is the natural place to record the condition of a furnace, water heater or appliance you supply.

There is one recurring utility disclosure in Kansas, and it is monthly rather than attached to the lease. If a city or water district supplies water to the building and you furnish it to the tenant through a separate meter, you must give the tenant a monthly water statement showing how the amount owed was computed, together with the tenant's meter reading for that period and for the prior period. That duty runs for the life of the tenancy; handing it over once at signing does not discharge it.

So the practical position is that any utility information in a Kansas lease is there because you put it there. Spell out which utilities the tenant pays, which you pay, how anything shared is divided, and what the tenant should expect to arrange in their own name — not because a statute compels the disclosure, but because the lease is the only place the arrangement exists. Kansas does legislate utility disclosure, but it aims at the provider rather than the landlord: a distributed energy retailer must give a property owner a separate disclosure document before contracting, and an electric utility must disclose its compensation formula to a parallel-generation customer. Nothing comparable runs from landlord to tenant.

title: Learning Before a Tenant's Utility Is Cut Off
bodyText:
Kansas has no statute that lets a tenant authorize a utility to warn you before the tenant's own service is disconnected, and no statute requiring a utility to copy a landlord or owner on a tenant's shutoff notice. There is no Kansas equivalent of the Wisconsin authorization document or the Maryland lease term that makes the tenant arrange for the landlord to receive termination notices. So if you want warning, the lease is where you get it: ask the tenant to show evidence of payment on request and to tell you promptly of any notice that service will be discontinued, and keep your own eye on any account that stays in your name.

What Kansas does regulate sits on the municipal side, and it matters more than it looks. A municipality that provides utility service may not refuse to contract with a tenant for service to the property the tenant occupies, except where that person already owes the municipality unpaid utility charges — so a tenant who has an old balance with the city may be unable to get service in their own name, which is exactly when a landlord ends up holding the account. A municipality may require a single deposit covering all its utility services, capped at the expected average bills for a three-month period. And the collection powers are real: unpaid municipal utility charges can be refused service until paid, a city may discontinue water service for unpaid water or sewer charges, and a city may discontinue water to premises owned, managed or occupied by a consumer who is delinquent on sewer charges. None of those sections requires the city to notify the landlord first.

Two cautions. First, for the utilities the Kansas Corporation Commission regulates, the notice before disconnection comes from the commission's billing standards, adopted by commission order, not from a statute: 10 days' written notice to the customer at the account address and at the service address if different, an attempted phone call at least two days before, and from November 1 through March 31 the Cold Weather Rule's extra contacts and temperature limit. That notice goes to the customer, not to you. But the Cold Weather Rule requires each regulated utility to adopt and tell customers about a third-party notification plan, so a tenant who wants you warned can ask their utility to enrol you under it; each utility sets how its plan works. Second, none of this bears on you cutting a service off yourself. Kansas treats a landlord's interruption of electric, gas, water or other essential service as taking possession by self-help, and the tenant's remedy is immediate and expensive; see the separate guidance on that.

title: Submetering Gives You No Right to Cut the Service Off
bodyText:
Kansas has no submetered-utility interruption regime, and the general rule is absolute enough that it does not need one. A landlord may not recover or take possession of a dwelling unit by action or otherwise, including by willful diminution of services to the tenant by interrupting or causing the interruption of electric, gas, water or other essential service, except in case of abandonment, surrender or as the Act otherwise permits. There is no exception for a landlord who submeters, who bills the tenant directly, or whose tenant has not paid the utility portion of what they owe. Unlike Texas, Kansas gives you no right to interrupt submetered electricity after a set number of days; unlike Connecticut, it has no approval scheme for electric submeters at all.

If you cut a service off, the tenant may recover possession or terminate the lease, and in either case recover the greater of one and a half months' periodic rent or their actual damages, and on termination you must return the recoverable part of the security deposit. The tenant does not have to give you the thirty days' notice the habitability track requires first, so a deliberate interruption is actionable at once. The correct route for unpaid charges is the one the Act provides: written notice of nonpayment and of your intention to terminate if the rent is not paid within three days, then possession through the court.

The one Kansas submetering rule there is concerns water, and it is a set of limits on you rather than a set of powers. If a city or water district supplies the water and you furnish it to the tenant through a separate meter, you may bill the tenant for it without being treated as a public utility, but only at the same rate the city or district charges you, with no surcharge for installing or maintaining the meter or for anything else related to its use, and with a monthly statement showing the computation and both meter readings. Nothing in that section lets you shut the water off, and the rate cap and the surcharge ban mean you cannot recover the cost of a meter or a billing system through the tenant's water charge either.

One uncertainty to keep in mind. The statute protects electric, gas, water and other essential service, and Kansas nowhere defines what else is essential. Air conditioning is a plausible candidate, since the landlord must maintain air-conditioning appliances they supply in good and safe working order, and so, less obviously, is internet or cable where the lease includes it. Treat the list as open and do not interrupt any service the tenant is entitled to, essential or not.

title: When the Utility Account Is in Your Name
bodyText:
Kansas has nothing like the landlord-account schemes other states run. There is no statute requiring a utility to give you extended notice and your tenants separate notice before shutting off a building you are delinquent on, no right for a tenant to pay your utility bill and deduct it from rent, no tenant petition for a receiver to collect the rents and keep the service on, and no penalty for failing to identify your tenants to the utility. What Kansas gives instead is a duty on you, a narrow excuse from it, and a set of municipal collection powers that fall on the property rather than on the tenant.

The duty is to supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times and reasonable heat, unless the building is not required by law to be equipped for the purpose or the unit is built so that heat or hot water is generated by an installation inside the tenant's exclusive control and supplied by a direct public utility connection. Read the excuse carefully, because it is the whole of your protection: the duties are suspended only when prevented by an act of God, the failure of public utility services, or other conditions beyond your control. Service cut off because you did not pay the bill is not a condition beyond your control, so the duty stands and the tenant's remedies run. Those remedies are notice and termination rather than self-help: written notice specifying the breach, termination on a rent-paying date at least thirty days out, with a fourteen-day window for you to cure, plus damages and an injunction. The tenant may not withhold rent, pay the utility and deduct, or put rent in escrow — Kansas has none of those. And if the interruption looks willful rather than merely negligent, you are into much more expensive territory, where the tenant can recover possession or terminate and take the greater of one and a half months' rent or actual damages.

There is a lawful way to move the duty, in small buildings only. In a dwelling housing no more than four households with common areas, you and the tenants may agree in writing that the tenant takes on the water, hot water and heat duty, provided the arrangement is entered into in good faith and not to evade your obligations. In any larger building that duty cannot be shifted.

On the municipal side, the risk of keeping the account in your own name is concrete. Unpaid fees for service from a municipally owned utility become a lien on the property served — but not where the tenant, rather than the landlord or owner, contracted for the service. A city may refuse delivery until charges are paid, may discontinue water service for unpaid water or sewer charges, and a first-class city's board of public utilities may discontinue water to premises owned, managed or occupied by a consumer delinquent on sewer charges, none of it conditioned on notifying you first. One point runs the other way, and it is unusual: a Kansas city or county may not require you to hand over a list of your tenants' names, except after a citation for a health, safety or welfare ordinance violation on the property, no sooner than thirty days after the citation, and not at all if you comply with the ordinance. Kansas also protects tenant lists for offender-registration purposes. So the duty other states impose — identify your tenants to the authorities or the utility — is, in Kansas, something the city generally may not demand.

For utilities the Kansas Corporation Commission regulates, its billing standards, adopted by commission order, answer part of this. They do not bar disconnecting service for your unpaid bill, but you as the customer get 10 days' written notice, sent to the account address and, for a home, also to the address where service is provided, so a tenant in a single-unit rental will usually see it. Where the account serves more than one dwelling unit, the utility must also post a notice in a common area of the building at least five days before the disconnection date. The standards say nothing about letting a tenant take over or pay your account.

title: When the Utility Can Shut Service Off, and Where the Rule Actually Lives
bodyText:
Kansas has no utility-shutoff statute in the ordinary sense. There is no statutory winter moratorium, no statutory extension of the notice period in cold months, no bar on disconnection during a declared disaster or emergency, and no statutory notice period a utility must give a residential customer before cutting service off for nonpayment. Do not read that as meaning a Kansas utility may disconnect at will. For the utilities the Kansas Corporation Commission regulates, the disconnection rules are in the commission's billing standards, adopted by commission order rather than in the statute book. The utility must give the customer 10 days' written notice before disconnecting for nonpayment, sent separately from the bill to the account address and, for a home, to the service address too, and should try to phone the customer at least two days before. Where the account serves more than one dwelling unit, it must also post a notice in a common area of the building at least five days before the disconnection date. A customer who shows that disconnection would be especially dangerous to the health of someone living there, and that they cannot pay in full, gets either reasonable installments or at least 21 more days. From November 1 through March 31 the Cold Weather Rule adds more: the utility may not disconnect when the National Weather Service forecasts temperatures below 35 degrees, or in the mid-30s or colder, within the next 48 hours, and a customer who pays one-twelfth of the arrears, one-twelfth of the current bill, any disconnection and reconnection fees and any deposit can spread the rest over 11 months. A city's own utility within or near its limits is outside the commission's jurisdiction and these standards. Never tell a tenant there is no protection.

What the statutes do carry is the municipal side, and it is blunt. Where a municipally owned utility supplies the service, the governing body may refuse delivery until unpaid charges are paid in full, and unpaid charges become a lien on the property served unless the tenant, rather than the landlord or owner, contracted for the service. A city may discontinue water service for failure to pay either water or sewer charges, and in a first-class city the board of public utilities may discontinue water to premises owned, managed or occupied by a consumer delinquent on sewer charges. None of those sections requires the city to warn the landlord, and the procedural protections are in the ordinance rather than the statute, so they vary from city to city. A municipality may not refuse to contract with a tenant for service to the property the tenant occupies, unless that person already owes the municipality for utility service.

If you are the one who pays, understand what Kansas does not give your tenant and what it does. Kansas has no pay-and-deduct remedy, no rent withholding and no escrow, so a tenant whose service is threatened because you fell behind cannot lawfully pay the utility and take it off the rent, and there is no stay of your eviction cases of the kind New York imposes. But your duty to supply running water, reasonable hot water and reasonable heat is excused only for an act of God, the failure of public utility services, or other conditions beyond your control — and your own nonpayment is not one of those. The tenant's route is written notice and termination, with damages and an injunction available.

Finally, keep the two directions apart. This is about the utility cutting service off. A landlord cutting it off is a different and much more dangerous subject: Kansas treats interrupting electric, gas, water or other essential service as taking possession by self-help, with an immediate remedy for the tenant and no cure period.

title: Kansas Submetering: Water Only, and What You Must Show the Tenant
bodyText:
Kansas regulates exactly one kind of submetering, and it is water. If a city or water district supplies water to the building and you furnish it to the tenant through a separate meter measuring the tenant's use, you are not treated as a public utility and the arrangement is not a sale for resale within the state corporation commission's jurisdiction — so long as you charge the tenant the same rate the city or water district charges you. You may not charge any surcharge for installing or maintaining the meter, or for any other purpose related to its use. And each month you must give the tenant a water statement showing how the amount owed was computed, the tenant's meter reading for that statement period, and the tenant's meter reading for the prior period. Those three things are the whole of the Kansas regime, and the monthly statement is the only submetering disclosure Kansas requires.

Notice how much is missing by comparison with other states. There is no requirement to disclose the submetering or allocation arrangement at lease signing, no prescribed disclosure language and no type-size rule, no registration with a utility regulator, no building-size threshold, no water-efficiency fixture or leak-audit precondition, no approved allocation formula, no cap on a late fee for an unpaid submetered bill, and no mid-term opt-in procedure. There is also no permitted administrative or billing fee: where Colorado allows a small monthly fee and Texas allows limited fees under regulator rules, the Kansas rule is an outright ban on any surcharge related to the meter. The cost of metering and of billing is yours, recovered through rent if at all, not through the water charge.

Two further points. You may put the meters in: no city or public water supply system may prohibit installing a separate water meter for each dwelling unit in a multi-unit building in place of a master meter. But the protection covers water only. Kansas's public-utility definition reaches companies furnishing heat, light, water or power, and the landlord carve-out the legislature enacted in 2005 names only a landlord supplied water by a city or water district. Nothing in Kansas law tells you that submetering and reselling electricity or gas to tenants leaves you outside utility regulation, so do not assume the water rules transfer. Finally, if you charge more than the city's rate, you are outside the safe harbour altogether, and the question of whether you are an unregulated landlord or a regulated public utility reselling water is live rather than academic.

title: No Cutting Off Service a Tenant Failed to Transfer
bodyText:
Kansas has no transfer-or-cutoff rule. Nothing in Kansas law lets you terminate a utility still in your name because the tenant did not move the account into theirs within three days, or within any other period. Do not put a clause like that in a Kansas lease and do not act on one. Interrupting electric, gas, water or other essential service is how Kansas defines taking possession by self-help, and it is barred outright except on abandonment, surrender or as the Act otherwise allows. A tenant whose service you cut may recover possession or terminate the lease and, either way, take the greater of one and a half months' periodic rent or their actual damages, with the recoverable part of the deposit back on termination. Worse, a lease term purporting to give you that power is a waiver of the tenant's rights under the Act and unenforceable, and deliberately using a provision you know is prohibited exposes you to the tenant's actual damages on top.

So handle the transfer with the lease and with follow-up, not with a shutoff. Say which utilities the tenant must put in their own name, require it by a date, ask for proof, and check the account yourself rather than assuming. If the tenant does not transfer, the service stays yours: keep paying it, because your duty to supply running water, reasonable hot water and reasonable heat is excused only for an act of God, the failure of public utility services, or conditions beyond your control, and your own decision to stop paying is none of those. Non-transfer is a lease breach you address through the Act's notice and termination route, and through the deposit at the end of the tenancy.

One Kansas rule helps and one obstacle is worth knowing about. A municipality providing utility service may not refuse to contract with a tenant for service to the property the tenant occupies — but it is not required to contract with a person who already owes it for utility service. So a tenant with an old city balance may be genuinely unable to open an account, and a municipality may also require a deposit, capped at the expected average bills for a three-month period. Where service stays in your name, remember that unpaid municipal utility charges can become a lien on the property; that lien does not attach where the tenant, rather than the landlord or owner, contracted for the service. That is the strongest practical reason to get the account into the tenant's name early — and to find out at screening whether they can.

title: No Kansas Incentive for Renting to a Veteran
bodyText:
Kansas offers a landlord nothing for renting to a veteran. There is no vacancy-holding payment, no rent-arrears fund, no signing bonus, no deposit guarantee or deposit-waiver program, no damage-reimbursement fund and no tax credit for renting to a veteran or to a holder of a veterans housing voucher. Kansas's veterans preference statutes are about public employment, not housing, and the chapter devoted to the militia and veterans contains no landlord-tenant provision of any kind.

Two related points are worth knowing, because they are what a Kansas landlord will actually encounter. First, veteran or military status is not one of Kansas's protected classes in housing — the state list is race, religion, color, sex, disability, familial status, national origin or ancestry — so there is no state-law duty to rent to a veteran, and no state-law bar on preferring one either. Federal rules and any applicable program rules still apply, and a veteran with a service-connected disability is protected on the disability ground. Second, Kansas moved in the opposite direction from an incentive in 2026: a city or county may no longer adopt or enforce an ordinance prohibiting a landlord from refusing to lease privately owned residential property because the person's source of income to pay rent comes in whole or in part from the housing choice voucher program, any successor program, or any other housing assistance program in which a landlord's participation is voluntary, and any such ordinance adopted before 1 July 2026 is void. Veterans housing vouchers run through the housing choice voucher program, so the practical effect is that participation stays a landlord's choice statewide and no Kansas city can require it.

Where Kansas does give a servicemember something, it is a shortened notice rather than money: a tenant in the military service of the United States may end a periodic tenancy on fifteen days' written notice where military orders make termination necessary. That is covered separately. If you want to rent to veterans, the programs worth asking about are federal and local — the veterans housing voucher program administered by the local housing authority, and whatever a particular city, county or charity funds — not anything in Kansas statute.

title: No Kansas Water Heater Temperature Rule
bodyText:
Kansas sets no water heater temperature for a rental. There is no requirement to set the thermostat to a maximum before a new tenant moves in, as Wisconsin and Washington require, no manufacturer preset rule like Kentucky's, no minimum temperature, and no anti-scald or mixing-valve requirement. The phrase "water heater" does not appear in Kansas statute at all.

What Kansas requires is a standard without a number: you must supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times, unless the building is not required by law to be equipped for the purpose or the unit is built so that hot water is generated by an installation inside the tenant's exclusive control and supplied by a direct public utility connection. You must also maintain in good and safe working order all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning appliances you supply or are required to supply, and comply with applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety. So a water heater you provide has to work and has to deliver a reasonable amount of hot water; how hot is not specified.

There is one Kansas number attached to a water heater, and it is a regulatory threshold rather than a setting. A directly fired hot water supply boiler equipped with approved pressure and temperature safety relief valves sits outside the Kansas boiler and pressure vessel act only if it stays inside all three limits: heat input of 200,000 BTUH, water temperature of 210 degrees Fahrenheit, and nominal water capacity of 120 gallons. An ordinary residential water heater is comfortably inside those limits. A large central unit in an apartment building may not be, and if it is outside them it falls into the boiler act's inspection and certificate regime. That 210 degrees is a ceiling for staying out of a regulatory scheme, not a permitted or recommended setting.

Finally, where a numeric rule would normally live in other states, Kansas has put the decision in local hands: a city or county may adopt and enforce such plumbing codes, standards and regulations as it deems appropriate. There is no statewide plumbing code, so whether a maximum delivered water temperature or an anti-scald device applies to your property is a question about your city's or county's adopted code. Check it rather than assuming there is no rule. Practically, setting a unit-only heater at or below 120 degrees before a new tenancy, and recording the setting on the move-in inventory, is sensible even though Kansas does not require it.

title: No Kansas Waterbed Statute — but Three Limits on the Clause You Write
bodyText:
Kansas has no waterbed statute. There is no right to keep a waterbed or other liquid-filled bedding, no insurance requirement set by law, no extra deposit the law allows you to collect for one, and no certificate-of-occupancy cutoff of the kind California uses. Whether a waterbed, a water-filled sofa or a large aquarium is allowed is entirely a matter of your lease, so decide it and say so — a lease that is silent leaves you arguing about it later.

Three Kansas limits shape what you may write. First, you may not charge an extra deposit for it. The deposit cap is one month's rent for an unfurnished unit, one and a half months where the lease provides for the tenant to use furniture you own, and an additional half month where pets are permitted. That list is closed: a tenant's own waterbed is not furniture you own, so it buys no extra headroom, and any sum the lease requires before occupancy counts toward the cap however you label it. Second, you may not make the tenant indemnify you or limit your liability. No rental agreement may provide for the exculpation or limitation of either party's liability arising under law, or for indemnity against it, with one narrow exception — a tenant may agree to limit your liability for fire, theft or breakage with respect to common areas. A hold-harmless or indemnity clause aimed at waterbed damage falls outside that exception, is unenforceable, and if you use it knowing it is prohibited the tenant can recover actual damages. Requiring the tenant to carry their own renter's or liquid-filled-furniture insurance is a different thing and is not caught by that ban. Third, if you handle waterbeds by house rule rather than by lease clause, the rule binds the tenant only if its purpose is to promote the convenience, safety, peace or welfare of tenants, preserve your property from abusive use, or fairly distribute services; it is reasonably related to that purpose; it applies equally to all tenants in the premises; it is explicit enough to tell the tenant what to do; it is not for the purpose of evading your own obligations; and the tenant had notice of it when they entered the rental agreement.

Practically: permit or prohibit it in the lease, and if you permit it, require written permission before installation, require the tenant to carry insurance in their own name, specify where in the unit it may go, and record the floor's condition on the move-in inventory. Then deal with any actual damage through the deposit and a damages claim at the end of the tenancy, which is what Kansas law leaves you.

title: No Kansas Window Guard Requirement — but Your City's Code Becomes Your Duty
bodyText:
Kansas has no window guard law. No statute requires you to install window guards, window stops or any other window fall protection in a rental, none requires you to install them on a tenant's request where a young child lives in the unit, and none requires a window guard notice in the lease. There is no Kansas equivalent of the New Jersey boldface lease notice.

The point not to miss is how a local requirement reaches you anyway. Your statutory duties as a landlord begin with complying with the requirements of applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, and Kansas defines building and housing codes broadly — any law, ordinance or governmental regulation concerning fitness for habitation, or the construction, maintenance, operation, occupancy, use or appearance of any premises or dwelling unit. A city ordinance requiring window guards or fall protection is therefore not just a municipal matter: it becomes a duty under the landlord and tenant act, enforceable by the tenant through the act's notice and termination remedy. And where that code duty is greater than any of your other statutory duties, the code duty is the one that governs. So check your city's and county's adopted codes rather than relying on the absence of a state statute. Kansas leaves plumbing codes expressly to cities and counties and has no general statewide residential building code, so adopted codes genuinely vary.

The tenant has the matching obligation to comply with the parts of those codes primarily imposed on tenants, which is worth knowing if a tenant removes a guard or blocks a window.

What Kansas does regulate is narrow and elsewhere: the state fire marshal's rules cover exits and fire escapes from buildings including apartment houses, but not buildings used wholly as dwelling houses containing no more than two families, and those are regulations rather than statute. The state's accessibility standards for dwellings reach single-family, duplex and triplex units constructed with public financial assistance, not window safety. If a window guard matters for your property — a unit above the ground floor with young children in it — install one because it is sensible, say in the lease who may remove or alter it, and record its presence on the move-in inventory, rather than waiting for a rule that Kansas has not written.

title: The Kansas Notices That Must Be in Writing
bodyText:
Kansas says "written notice" notice by notice, and where it does, a lease cannot turn that notice into a phone call. A rental agreement may not provide that either party waives or foregoes rights or remedies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, so a clause allowing verbal notice in place of a statutory written one is unenforceable — and if you deliberately use a provision you know is prohibited, the tenant can recover actual damages. There is a certain irony in it: the lease itself may be oral in Kansas, because a rental agreement includes agreements written or oral, while the notices under it may not.

Your notices that Kansas requires in writing include: ending a week-to-week tenancy, by written notice given to the other at least seven days before the termination date; ending a month-to-month tenancy, by written notice stating that the tenancy terminates on a periodic rent-paying date not less than thirty days after receipt — fifteen days where the tenant is in the military service of the United States and military orders make termination necessary; a notice of the tenant's material noncompliance, specifying the acts and omissions constituting the breach and that the agreement terminates on a date not less than thirty days after receipt if the breach is not remedied in fourteen days, and the second written notice where the same or a similar breach recurs; the three-day nonpayment notice, which must state both the nonpayment and your intention to terminate if the rent is not paid; the itemized notice of anything you keep from the security deposit; the disclosure, at or before the start of the tenancy, of the name and address of the manager and of an owner or someone authorized to receive service and notices; notice of a conveyance to a bona fide purchaser, and notice that a manager's management has ended, each of which relieves you of liability only as to later events; and the pre-filing notice to leave the premises, which has to be a written copy. The pre-Act sections governing a tenancy at will and tenancies of three months or less use the same formula — thirty days' notice in writing, or ten days' written notice to vacate where premises are furnished or let by an employer to an employee, with ten days' notice in writing to quit for unpaid rent on a tenancy of three months or longer and three days' for a shorter one.

On the tenant's side the Act also requires writing: the notice specifying your breach and terminating on a rent-paying date at least thirty days out, the five-day notice terminating for failure to deliver possession, and, after vacating because of fire or casualty, written notice within five days of the intention to terminate.

Two practical cautions. First, writing is necessary but not sufficient — each notice also has a content requirement and a delivery method, and a notice that omits the statutory content does not do its work however it is delivered. Which service list governs a termination notice under the Act is itself an unsettled question, because the service section speaks of notice "as required in the preceding sections"; the safe course is to use a method that section recognises. Second, the lease may require writing where the statute does not — the Act lets the rental agreement require the tenant to notify you of an anticipated absence of more than seven days — but if you hand the tenant a notice-to-vacate document carrying terms that are not in the lease, it must carry the statutory boldface warning, or the tenant is not bound by those extra terms.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Kansas follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (K.S.A. 84-3-311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (K.S.A. 84-1-308(b)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Kansas's landlord-tenant statutes impose no general duty of good faith of the kind in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (the Kansas Residential Landlord and Tenant Act searched); good faith appears only in specific rules. Kansas's act defines 'good faith' as honesty in fact in the conduct of the transaction concerned (K.S.A. 58-2543(d)), the standard its specific good-faith rules use. Courts in many states read a covenant of good faith and fair dealing into every contract, a lease included; whether and how Kansas's courts do is case law, so act as if the duty applies. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.
